text_kjv: The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah opens his series of oracles against foreign nations with Babylon. The Hebrew word massa (rendered 'burden' in the KJV, 'oracle' in The Covenant Rendering) derives from nasa', meaning 'to lift' or 'to carry.' This is not mere poetic metaphor—a prophetic revelation is a burden the prophet bears. Isaiah 'saw' this oracle through chazah, a term for visionary perception distinct from ordinary sight. The same verb gives us chazon ('vision'), echoing Isaiah 1:1 where we are told Isaiah received 'the vision of Isaiah.' This opening verse establishes the prophetic authority and gravity of what follows: Isaiah has witnessed something in the spiritual realm that must now be declared.

The explicit naming of Babylon at the outset is remarkable. In Isaiah's day (8th century BCE), Babylon was not yet the dominant superpower—that role belonged to Assyria. Yet Isaiah's vision reaches forward to a future when Babylon will rise to prominence and eventually fall under God's judgment. This is prophecy in its fullest sense: not merely foretelling the near future, but discerning God's purposes across generations. The oracle is not sentimental or tentative; it is a weighty pronouncement that the prophet has seen and must now bear to the people.

word_study.meaning: An oracle or burden; derived from nasa' ('to lift, carry'). The term opens Isaiah's foreign-nation pronouncements (chapters 13–23) and carries a double meaning: both the prophetic utterance itself and the weight of bearing it. Some translations preserve 'burden' to capture this sense of obligation and gravity.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew thought, a prophet's word is not a light thing—it is something carried, something that weighs upon the one who speaks it. This term dignifies the prophet's role while also suggesting the seriousness of the judgment being pronounced.

word_study.meaning: To see, to perceive, especially in a visionary or prophetic sense. Distinct from the more common ra'ah (general seeing), chazah indicates direct spiritual perception. The noun form chazon means 'vision.'
word_study.significance: This verb grounds the oracle in genuine prophetic experience. Isaiah did not merely compose words about Babylon—he witnessed something in the prophetic vision that compelled him to speak. This reinforces the authority and reality of the proclamation.

cross_references.connection: Opens the entire book with the identical verb chazan, establishing that Isaiah's entire prophetic work flows from visions he has 'seen.'
Another oracle (massa) against a foreign nation (Dumah), using the same literary framework to introduce God's judgment on enemies of Israel.

John's Revelation similarly opens with 'the Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him...and he sent and signified it by his angel.' Both prophets ground their oracles in divinely-given visions.
Jeremiah's calling similarly involves seeing visions (chazah concept) as the foundation of his prophetic authority to proclaim judgment and restoration.
Alma describes his conversion in terms of 'seeing' spiritual realities, using language that parallels the prophetic chazah—direct spiritual perception beyond the natural eye.

commentary.historical_context: Babylon in the 8th century BCE was a relatively minor kingdom, overshadowed by Assyria. Yet Isaiah's oracle speaks of Babylon as if it were already the master of the world. This is prophetic telescoping—seeing into a future that lay roughly 150 years ahead, when Nebuchadnezzar II would indeed make Babylon the dominant power of the known world and would conquer Judah in 586 BCE. The oracle therefore carries a strange temporal tension: it addresses a threat not yet present, speaking to a future generation's actual exile and destruction. This demonstrates the nature of true prophecy—it sees what ordinary sight cannot perceive, and it speaks across the centuries.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently uses the language of 'burden' (alma) for the weight of prophecy. Alma the Younger, after his conversion, speaks of the burden of his sins and the burden of testifying of Christ. The same sense of weight-bearing appears in Lehi's vision and in Nephi's determination to keep the commandments—prophecy is not a privilege but a responsibility.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:76 speaks of the 'Lord of Hosts' (the title that appears in verse 4) organizing His armies to accomplish His purposes. Isaiah 13's vision of God marshaling armies for judgment aligns with the Restoration teaching that God directs the course of nations according to His covenant purposes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment teaches that the Lord has authority over all creation and all nations. Isaiah's vision of God commanding foreign armies to execute judgment on Babylon is a cosmic statement of divine governance that underlies temple theology—God is the ultimate sovereign whose purposes cannot be thwarted by human pride or power.

commentary.christological_typology: While this verse itself does not directly prefigure Christ, it establishes the pattern of divine judgment that Christ embodies. The 'day of the Lord' introduced in verse 6 ultimately refers to the Second Coming and final judgment, when Christ will execute the judgment of God upon all the earth. Isaiah's vision of judgment upon Babylon becomes, in Christian reading, a type of the final reckoning when Christ returns in glory.
commentary.application: For modern readers, this verse teaches that prophecy is not escape literature or entertainment—it is a serious burden. When we receive testimony of truth, we bear responsibility for it. The verse also invites us to trust that God sees across time, knows the future, and works according to purposes we may not immediately understand. Our role is to 'see' what God reveals and then to bear witness to it, even when the immediate world gives no sign that such revelation is real.

text_kjv: Lift ye up a banner upon the high mountain, exalt the voice unto them, shake the hand, that they may go into the gates of the nobles.

commentary.narrative: The prophet moves from the vision itself to its implementation—God's command (though imperatives addressed to the prophet or the reader) to summon the invading army. The rapid-fire imperatives ('lift,' 'exalt,' 'shake') create a breathless, urgent tone, as if a military commander is issuing orders to muster troops. The bare hilltop (har nishpeh, a 'swept hill' or exposed height) serves as the mustering point—high enough to be visible for miles, a place from which signals would be seen by approaching forces. Ancient armies used signal fires, flags, and smoke to coordinate movement across distance; the banner (nes) on the mountain is the visible proclamation that summons the enemy. This is inverted imagery: instead of Israel raising banners to rally its own defense, foreign armies are being called to assemble against Babylon. The 'gates of the nobles' (pitchei nedivim) may refer either to the grand gates through which Babylon's aristocracy passes or to the gates of noble cities—either way, the imagery moves from the mountain signal to the invasion of the enemy's strongholds.

word_study.meaning: A banner, flag, or signal; often used in military contexts for assembling troops or marking a gathering point. It can also mean a sign or miracle-working sign in contexts of divine intervention.
word_study.significance: The nes here is an instrument of God's command, visibly summoning the army. In other biblical contexts (Numbers 21:8–9, for instance), a nes marks divine presence and power. Here it is the tool by which God orchestrates the movements of nations.

word_study.meaning: A bare or swept hilltop, a treeless height that stands exposed and visible from afar. The word nishpeh derives from shaphah ('to sweep, to bare'). Contrast with mountains covered in forest or vegetation.
word_study.significance: The exposed hilltop is ideal for signaling—visible from great distances and unobstructed. It is where heaven and earth meet, the vantage point from which orders are given. Mountains in biblical thought are places of divine revelation and authority; this bare mountain is the platform from which God's purposes are announced.

word_study.meaning: Nobles, princes, or willing ones; those of high rank and authority. The root nadav means 'to volunteer' or 'to offer willingly,' lending a connotation of those who lead or offer themselves.
word_study.significance: The 'gates of the nobles' may refer to Babylon's palace gates or to the fortified cities of the great. The term underscores that the invasion breaches the seats of power—the locations where the highest authority is exercised. It is an affront to human pride and station.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah uses identical language of God lifting up a banner (nes) to signal to distant nations. This establishes a prophetic pattern: God summons armies through visible signs that command obedience across the earth.

Jeremiah also prophesies against Babylon, using military summoning language: 'Call together the kingdoms...prepare the nations...for the king of the Medes hath devised a device against Babylon.' The same pattern of orchestrated invasion appears.

Moses raises a nes (banner/sign) in the wilderness—the bronze serpent—which becomes a sign of deliverance. Here Isaiah's banner is a sign of judgment, demonstrating how the same instrument can serve opposite purposes depending on God's will.
The Lord promises to 'raise up a mighty nation' among the Lamanites. Like Isaiah's banner, it describes God gathering and directing peoples according to His purposes, not their own.

Nephi prophesies that the Gentiles will be gathered as 'a standard' (similar to a banner) to the house of Israel. The image of gathering peoples through visible signs of God's direction appears throughout scripture.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern military practice, armies coordinated movement through visible signals—flags, beacon fires, and smoke. A hilltop served as both a vantage point and a communication hub. The 'gates of the nobles' almost certainly refers to Babylon's famous walls and gates. Historical records indicate that Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians (combined forces under Cyrus) in 539 BCE—roughly 150 years after Isaiah's time. The actual siege involved surrounding the city and blocking supply routes, eventually forcing entry through the gates. Whether the conquest involved dramatic breaching of the noble gates or a negotiated entry, the symbolic point is the same: the invincible seemed invincible until the moment God's judgment fell. The imagery here—orderly assembly of distant forces, signal from on high, penetration of the city's strongholds—reflects actual siege warfare while also elevating it to the level of cosmic event orchestrated by divine command.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon uses the image of gathering under a standard or banner repeatedly. Alma 46:19–24 describes Moroni raising the title of liberty as a banner around which the covenant people gather. Here Isaiah's banner is raised not to gather God's people but to gather God's judgment against the wicked. Both uses underscore that banners represent gathering under divine authority.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 35:14 speaks of the Lord gathering 'all things into one' at the last day. Isaiah's summons of distant armies to Babylon prefigures the eschatological gathering of all nations before the judgment seat of Christ. The mechanism (a visible signal from on high) parallels Latter-day Saint teaching about the Second Coming—when all will see and hear.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that God has absolute dominion and authority over creation. The idea that God can summon armies to His purposes without their knowledge reflects the temple's emphasis on divine omniscience and sovereignty. The nobles entering gates under God's command illustrates what the temple dramatizes: all human power is ultimately subject to the Lord's will.

commentary.christological_typology: The banner on the high mountain points toward the eschatological banners and signs that will accompany Christ's return. Matthew 24:30 speaks of 'the sign of the Son of man' appearing in heaven, and all the earth seeing the Son of Man coming in clouds of glory. Isaiah's vision of summons-by-banner thus prefigures the final gathering of all peoples before Christ's judgment throne.
commentary.application: This verse reminds us that God's purposes are executed with order and visibility—not through deception or hidden manipulation. The banner is raised openly; the summons is clear. In our own lives, the 'banners' God raises—the restored gospel, the teachings of living prophets, the clear testimonies of the Spirit—are meant to be visible and unmistakable. We are invited to recognize them and respond. The urgency of the imperatives ('lift,' 'exalt,' 'shake') also suggests that the time of fulfillment is near and calls for immediate obedience, not delayed response.

text_kjv: I have commanded my sanctified ones, I have also called my mighty ones for mine anger, even them that rejoice in my highness.

commentary.narrative: God now speaks in the first person, revealing the divine agency behind the gathering described in verse 2. The shift is crucial: what seemed a merely military maneuver is revealed as God's direct command. The armies summoned to destroy Babylon are called God's 'sanctified ones' (mequddashim, from qadash—'to be holy' or 'to set apart'). This is startling language. These warriors are not priests or covenant people; they are foreign soldiers, likely Medes and Persians, whom God has designated for a sacred purpose. In sacred-war theology, a nation consecrated by God for holy war is set apart from ordinary war-making—their violence becomes an instrument of God's will, not mere conquest. The phrase 'my mighty ones' (gibborim) emphasizes their power, yet they are unmistakably 'mine'—owned by God, directed by His hand. The final clause presents an irony: these warriors 'rejoice in my highness' (allizei ga'avati), yet their rejoicing in their own pride and exultation is actually the working out of God's plan. They act from selfish ambition and pride, yet God uses their ambition to accomplish His justice. This is a profound theological statement about God's ability to work through human rebellion and self-interest without being implicated in the moral flaw.

word_study.meaning: Those who are holy or set apart; from qadash ('to be holy, to sanctify, to set apart'). In cultic contexts, things or people made holy are separated from the profane for sacred use.
word_study.significance: The use of this term for foreign, pagan warriors is unexpected and theologically significant. It teaches that God can consecrate any people for any purpose—they need not be God's covenant people to be 'set apart' for His work. This expanded understanding of 'sanctification' (being set apart for a specific, divinely-ordained task) deepens the theme of God's sovereignty over all nations.

word_study.meaning: Warriors, mighty ones, strong ones; those with great military prowess or physical power. Often paired with terms of courage (like 'lion-hearted').
word_study.significance: The term emphasizes military capability—these are not untrained conscripts but seasoned warriors. Yet they are identified as God's gibborim, His mighty ones, not autonomous actors. Their strength is in God's service, even if they do not recognize it.

word_study.meaning: Exulters/triumphers in my pride/highness. Aliz means 'to exult, to rejoice, to triumph,' and ga'avah means 'pride, haughtiness, exultation.' The phrase captures warriors who exult in their own dominance and power.
word_study.significance: This phrase is key to understanding Isaiah's theodicy: wicked, prideful warriors become unwitting instruments of God's justice precisely because of their pride. They are not righteous or humble; they are driven by ambition and self-glorification. Yet God uses these motives to accomplish His purposes. It is a sober teaching about how God can work through human wickedness without endorsing it.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah describes Assyria as the 'rod' of God's anger, sent to punish Israel, yet Assyria does not acknowledge this—the nation acts according to its own pride and evil intent. Like the Medes here, Assyria is sanctified for judgment while remaining morally culpable.

Paul teaches that civil authorities, even pagan ones, are 'ordained of God' to execute His justice. This echoes Isaiah's theology: God directs human power-structures, even those that do not worship Him, toward His purposes.

The Lord teaches Joseph Smith that He will 'cause the wicked to be constrained to acknowledge my hand...even those that do not believe in my name.' God uses the wicked's own desires and actions to accomplish His will.

Alma describes how the Lord 'compelleth all men...to bring about his eternal purposes in the end of man.' Like the Medes, all peoples are ultimately subject to God's purposes, whether or not they acknowledge it.
Amos asks, 'Shall there be evil in a city, and the Lord hath not done it?' emphasizing God's ultimate sovereignty over all events, including destruction and judgment.

commentary.historical_context: The Medes, based in what is now northern Iran, were powerful warriors and horsemen. By the 6th century BCE, Media was a major power in the ancient Near East, eventually combining with Persia (under Cyrus the Great) to form the dominant empire. Historically, the Medes and Persians did capture Babylon in 539 BCE, though later accounts suggest the conquest was negotiated or involved some deception (Herodotus records that Cyrus diverted the Euphrates river to lower the water level and allow troops to enter). Ancient siege warfare was brutal; armies were expected to be ruthless in achieving victory. From Isaiah's prophetic perspective, these pagan warriors—driven by ambition, conquest, and self-glory—are unconsciously fulfilling God's judgment against Babylon. They have no knowledge that they serve the God of Israel; they serve their own power and pride. Yet that very pride becomes the mechanism of God's justice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon teaches similar principles about God's use of wicked instruments. Nephi witnesses in vision that the Gentiles will both come to knowledge of the truth and will be used as a scourge upon the house of Israel (1 Nephi 13). Like the Medes, the Gentiles are 'set apart' for purposes they may not fully understand, serving God's will while following their own desires.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:36–37 teaches that the powers of heaven operate 'only upon the principles of persuasion' by the Holy Ghost, but also that others may be 'moved upon by the Holy Ghost to do good' without fully recognizing that agency. The wicked Medes are 'moved' by God's Spirit to accomplish His purpose, even as they act from pride.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment teaches that all power and dominion ultimately belong to God, even though many earthly powers do not acknowledge it. The teaching that God directs the wicked for His purposes illustrates a core temple principle: divine sovereignty is not limited by human understanding or moral worthiness.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse prefigures how Christ's crucifixion was accomplished through the agency of wicked people (Caiaphas, Pilate, the Roman soldiers) who acted from self-interest, pride, and desire for power, yet unwittingly fulfilled God's redemptive plan (see 1 Corinthians 2:7–8, where Paul notes that none of the rulers understood the 'wisdom of God' that was being accomplished through their actions). Just as the Medes are 'sanctified ones' for judgment, so too the wicked instruments of Christ's passion become, unknowingly, the means of salvation.
commentary.application: This verse teaches modern believers a sobering but liberating truth: God's purposes are not frustrated by human wickedness or pride. We need not fear that the plans of evil people will ultimately succeed—they may flourish for a season, but they ultimately serve God's justice. The verse also warns against pride: the Medes 'rejoice in their own highness,' yet that very exultation becomes their undoing. For us, the invitation is to align our will with God's purposes not from pride or self-interest, but from genuine faithfulness—so that we serve His will consciously and willingly, not unconsciously through the working out of our own ambition.

text_kjv: The noise of a multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people; a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together: the LORD of hosts mustereth the host of the battle.

commentary.narrative: The verse returns to sensory imagery—the sound of approaching armies. Isaiah describes the acoustic experience of a massive military assembly: the noise (qol) of a multitude (hamon) in the mountains, sounding like countless people. This is a multisensory prophecy: verse 2 was visual (the banner), verse 3 was theological (God's commandment), and now verse 4 emphasizes the auditory overwhelming of Babylon. The 'roar of kingdoms' (qol she'on mamlekhot) captures the discordance of many nations assembling—not one coordinated force but multiple contingents, yet all moving under a single purpose. The power of the verse lies in its accumulated sound-images: the effect on Babylon's inhabitants would be acoustic terror long before the armies breach the walls. The final clause contains a wordplay untranslatable in English: 'The LORD of Hosts is mustering the host of battle' (YHWH tseva'ot mephakked tseva milchamah). The title YHWH tseva'ot ('the LORD of Hosts'—the God whose name itself means 'the Lord of Armies') is now shown doing precisely what His title says He does: commanding armies (tseva) for war. This is not metaphorical; it is functional theology. God's name describes His role, and He is enacting that role.

word_study.meaning: Sound, voice, noise; the most basic auditory phenomenon. Often used for God's voice (the voice of the Lord), thunder, or any loud sound.
word_study.significance: The repeated use of qol in this verse (three times: 'noise of a multitude,' 'noise of kingdoms,' 'voice' in some renderings) creates an overwhelming acoustic image. Sound is the first indicator of approaching danger—Babylon hears the armies before seeing them.

word_study.meaning: A multitude, crowd, or throng; the noise or tumult of a crowd. Related to the verb hum ('to murmur, to make noise').
word_study.significance: The term emphasizes not individual soldiers but the overwhelming collective—an incomprehensibly large gathering of humanity, all moving in concert toward one objective.

word_study.meaning: The LORD of Armies/Hosts. Tseva'ot is the plural of tsava, meaning army, host, or gathering of warriors. The title emphasizes God's role as supreme commander of all celestial and earthly armies.
word_study.significance: This is one of Isaiah's favorite titles for God, appearing frequently in his prophecies. It is a title of cosmic authority—God commands not just earthly armies but the stars in their courses (see Isaiah 40:26). Here it is applied directly to the marshaling of historical forces against Babylon, teaching that earthly wars are directed by the one who commands the heavens.

word_study.meaning: To command, to appoint, to muster; from paqad ('to number, to visit, to appoint'). It carries connotations of precise organization and hierarchical command.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes divine organization and control. God is not merely aware of the armies—He is actively commanding, positioning, and directing them with military precision.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah later asks, 'Who hath created these things...and calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might...not one faileth?' The same God who commands the hosts of heaven commands the hosts of earth.

The psalmist asks, 'Who is this King of glory?' and answers: 'The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle...The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory.' Isaiah's vision of God mustering armies is the fulfillment of this title and description.

John's vision of Christ returning as the 'King of Kings and Lord of Lords,' with armies of heaven following Him, echoes Isaiah's vision of God as the supreme commander of all forces—though in Revelation it is Christ in His glory.
The Lord prophesies through Joseph Smith about wars and commotions—armies gathering, kingdoms warring. Like Isaiah, D&C teaches that earthly conflicts are subject to God's sovereignty and knowledge.
Nephi quotes Isaiah's prophecies about God's judgment and adds his own testimony that God directs the course of nations according to covenant purposes, tying Isaiah's vision to Restoration theology.

commentary.historical_context: The historical siege of Babylon by Median and Persian forces (539 BCE) would have involved the assembly of multiple contingents from various subject states and allied territories. Armies of this era operated under hierarchical command structures, with generals reporting to supreme commanders. The 'noise of kingdoms gathered together' reflects historical reality—ancient siege warfare was noisy and terrifying. The sound of approaching armies (war horns, marching feet, supply trains) would have preceded the sight of troops by hours or days, creating psychological terror before physical combat. For Isaiah's original audience, imagining multiple kingdoms united in one purpose would have been both awe-inspiring and terrifying—how could any city withstand such a gathering?

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Moroni 8:24 describes the 'awful situation' of those who have not the 'spirit of Christ' within them, using language that echoes the terror of approaching judgment. The Book of Mormon teaches that the gathering of armies and the flow of judgments are under divine direction, not human chance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:35–36 teaches that 'the day of the Lord is upon you, and you must stand up...For I the Lord have decreed in my heart, that I will...bring forth unto you all things...which have been kept hid from the foundation of the world.' God's orchestration of historical events serves His covenant purposes, as Isaiah's vision demonstrates.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that God has dominion over all creation and all powers. The image of the 'Lord of Hosts' mustering armies illustrates temple theology: the God of Israel is not a tribal deity confined to one land, but the universal sovereign. All kingdoms and all hosts—celestial and terrestrial—are subject to His command.

commentary.christological_typology: The 'LORD of Hosts' mustering armies for judgment prefigures the eschatological warfare described in Revelation, where Christ as the Commander of the celestial armies returns to execute final judgment. The title 'King of Kings and Lord of Lords' in Revelation 19:16 is a fuller revelation of the same theological principle Isaiah establishes here: God's authority transcends all earthly powers.
commentary.application: For modern believers, this verse teaches that human events are not random or beyond God's knowledge. The tumult of the world—wars, nations rising and falling, great conflicts—are all within the purview of the 'Lord of Hosts.' This is meant to be reassuring, not terrifying. We live in a universe governed by an intelligent, purposeful God. We are also invited to recognize the 'mustering' of spiritual forces in our own time—the gathering of the covenant people, the restoration of truth, the preparation for the Second Coming—as manifestations of the same divine command that directs all histories.

text_kjv: They come from a far country, from the end of heaven, even the LORD, and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land.

commentary.narrative: The armies are now described in their origin and purpose. They come from 'a far country' (me'eretz merchaq)—not simply distant geographically, but from 'the end of heaven' (miqtseh ha-shamayim), a phrase that expands the vision to cosmic proportions. The armies do not merely travel across land; they come from the horizon where earth meets heaven, suggesting that they emerge from the realm of divine reality. The phrasing 'the LORD and the weapons of his indignation' is grammatically ambiguous—it could mean that the LORD comes together with weapons, or that the weapons themselves are described as 'the LORD's' in the sense of belonging to Him, or that the soldiers themselves are God's weapons. This ambiguity is likely intentional: the entire military assembly—soldiers, commanders, and all implements—is God's apparatus. The phrase 'to destroy the whole land' (lachabbel kol-ha'aretz) uses the verb chabbel, which carries overtones of pain, travail, and birth pangs (related to chevel, 'birth pang' or 'rope'). This lexical choice is significant: the destruction is not merely military devastation but labor-like agony, anticipating verse 8 where Babylon's destruction is described as 'birth pangs' overtaking the city.

word_study.meaning: From the edge, end, or extremity (qatseh) of the heavens (shamayim). Shamayim can mean sky, heaven, or the realm of divine activity.
word_study.significance: This phrase transcends geographical distance and locates the armies' origin in the cosmic realm. They come not merely from a distant land but from the threshold where the visible world meets the invisible. This theophanic language (language of divine appearance) elevates military invasion to the level of divine visitation.

word_study.meaning: Implements, weapons, or instruments (kelim) of His anger/indignation (za'am). The noun za'am means wrath, fury, or indignation—the wrathful response to wickedness.
word_study.significance: The soldiers and their weapons are explicitly identified as God's instruments. They are not autonomous agents pursuing their own conquest but extensions of God's wrath. This is the most direct statement that Babylon's destruction is God's act of judgment, executed through human agency.

word_study.meaning: To devastate, to ruin, to destroy; from chabel (to break, to labor in pain). The root is related to chevel (cord, rope) and to the labor pains (chevlei leida) of childbirth.
word_study.significance: This verb carries an affective quality—it is not clean destruction but anguished, painful devastation. The choice of chabbel rather than a more neutral word for 'destroy' (like shamat or kalah) emphasizes the trauma and agony of Babylon's fall. The verb choice foreshadows verse 8, where birth pangs seize Babylon.

cross_references.connection: Moses warned Israel: 'The LORD shall bring a nation against thee from far, from the end of the earth...and shall besiege thee in all thy gates.' Isaiah applies this covenant curse formula to Babylon—the same language of distant judgment.
Jeremiah prophesies: 'The LORD hath raised up the spirit of the kings of the Medes...for his device is against Babylon, to destroy it.' The same divine agency and purpose appear in Jeremiah's oracle.

In John's Revelation, frog-like spirits gather 'the kings of the earth and of the whole world...to the battle of that great day of God Almighty.' Like Isaiah's vision, a divinely-orchestrated gathering of distant powers for judgment.

The Lord teaches Joseph Smith: 'I have made the earth rich, and behold it is my footstool...and I cause the heavens and the earth to be one.' God's dominion extends from heaven to earth; all armies and all powers serve His purposes.

Alma speaks of the last day when 'God shall cause that your clothes shall be made white like unto my clothes; and that ye shall be spotless before God...unless ye have faith.' Isaiah's vision of God's terrible judgment is balanced in Restoration scripture by the promise of cleansing and atonement.

commentary.historical_context: Media and Persia were indeed 'far countries' from Babylon's perspective—located to the east and north. The phrase 'from the end of heaven' reflects the ancient Near Eastern cosmology in which the horizon was conceived as the boundary between earthly and celestial realms. Babylonian texts and later Greek sources describe Cyrus the Great's armies as appearing almost miraculously—forces that suddenly materialized to transform the political landscape. From the Babylonian perspective, the invasion would have seemed to come from the distant horizon, unexpected and overwhelming. The historical fact that the conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE was relatively peaceful (no major battle is recorded, though Cyrus's forces did enter the city) does not contradict Isaiah's prophecy of 'destruction'—the destruction of Babylon's power and independence was complete, even if the physical city was not leveled.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon teaches similar principles about how God's judgments reach from the heavens to the earth. 2 Nephi 28:32 describes how 'the Lamb of God shall be made manifest unto them' at the last day. Like Isaiah's armies coming from the end of heaven, God's purposes come from the celestial realm to manifest in earthly history.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:11–12 teaches: 'Wherefore, I the Lord, knowing the calamity which should come upon the inhabitants of the earth, called upon my servant Joseph Smith, Jun., and spake unto him from heaven.' God's word comes from heaven to direct earthly affairs. Isaiah's vision of armies coming 'from the end of heaven' is thus a type of how God communicates and acts throughout history and covenant.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment teaches that celestial beings visit the terrestrial realm, and that heaven and earth are connected through covenant. Isaiah's description of forces coming 'from the end of heaven' illustrates this principle—the boundary between heaven and earth is permeable to God's purposes.

commentary.christological_typology: The armies coming 'from the end of heaven' to execute judgment prefigure Christ's Second Coming, when He will appear 'in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory' (Matthew 24:30, D&C 45:44). The weapons of God's indignation become, in ultimate fulfillment, the word of Christ proceeding from His mouth as a sharp sword (Revelation 19:15).
commentary.application: This verse teaches that God's judgment, though it may seem distant and unlikely, comes with absolute certainty and power. For modern believers, it is both a warning and a comfort. Wickedness may flourish for a season, but judgment comes 'from the end of heaven'—from the throne of God—and cannot be resisted. This is meant to encourage faithfulness: align yourself with God's purposes, and you need not fear the powers of this world. But it is also a warning: do not suppose that distance from judgment or the slowness of God's hand means His judgment will not fall.

text_kjv: Howl ye; for the day of the LORD is at hand; it shall come as a destruction from the Almighty.

commentary.narrative: The verse opens with an imperative cry: 'Wail!' (heililu), an onomatopoetic word that sounds like the very anguish it commands. The wailing is addressed to Babylon (understood by context)—a call to mourn the imminent judgment. The 'day of the LORD' (yom YHWH) is here introduced as a technical theological concept: this is not a calendar day but a moment of God's decisive intervention in history. Throughout the prophets, the 'day of the LORD' represents the moment when God moves in judgment, typically with overwhelming force and finality. The phrase 'is at hand' (qarov) suggests urgency—the day is near, not distant. The final clause presents an untranslatable wordplay in Hebrew: 'it comes as devastation (shod) from the Almighty (Shaddai),' in which the word for devastation echoes within the divine name Shaddai, creating a sonic link between the Almighty's identity and the destruction He brings. This wordplay, noted by The Covenant Rendering's translator, appears also in Joel 1:15. The effect is one of inevitable, inescapable doom—the Almighty (whose very name contains the word for devastation) brings what His name implies. Theologians debate whether this reversal of the expected 'day of the LORD' (which Amos 5:18–20 suggests Israel expected to bring blessing to them) represents irony or a straight application of the concept to Israel's enemies. Either way, the Babylonians are warned: the day draws near.

word_study.meaning: To wail, to cry out in anguish; an onomatopoetic word that mimics the sound of lamentation.
word_study.significance: The imperative form commands not mere announcement of bad news but an emotional, visceral response. The sound of the word itself—with its repeated 'i' vowels—mimics high-pitched wailing. This is not intellectual recognition of coming judgment but embodied anguish.

word_study.meaning: A fixed theological concept in biblical prophecy: the moment of God's decisive, inescapable intervention in history. It is always characterized by judgment, upheaval, and the vindication of God's will. It can be directed against Israel's enemies (as here) or against Israel itself (Amos 5:18–20).
word_study.significance: This is the first use of this terminus technicus in Isaiah 13. The concept structures all of Isaiah's foreign-nation oracles and his eschatological prophecies (chapters 24–27). For Babylon, the day of the LORD means the end of its power and pride; for believers, it becomes the day of Christ's coming and final judgment.

word_study.meaning: Near, at hand, close; expressing proximity in space or time. The root qrb means 'to approach, to draw near.'
word_study.significance: The use of 'at hand' heightens urgency. Qarov is not 'in the distant future' but imminent. This temporal pressure becomes a key theme in Isaiah's judgment oracles—the day is coming soon, closer than Babylon realizes.

word_study.meaning: The Almighty; traditionally understood as related to shad (breast) or shadday (abundance), though the etymology is debated. The name emphasizes God's power and sufficiency.
word_study.significance: Shaddai appears frequently in patriarchal narratives (Genesis 17:1, 28:3, 35:11) and in Job. In Isaiah, it appears less frequently than YHWH or 'Lord,' making its appearance here (and the wordplay with shod, 'devastation') more striking. The choice of this particular divine name underscores God's ultimate power over all circumstances.

cross_references.connection: Amos warns Israel against expecting the day of the LORD to bring them blessing: 'Woe unto you that desire the day of the LORD!...it is darkness, and not light.' Isaiah applies the concept to Babylon's judgment, reversing the expected outcome.

Joel uses nearly identical language: 'Alas for the day! for the day of the LORD is at hand, and as a destruction from the Almighty shall it come.' The same wordplay (shod/Shaddai) and warning appear in Joel.

Peter writes of the 'day of the Lord' in eschatological terms: 'The heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat.' The concept is applied to the final judgment.

The Lord teaches Joseph Smith about the signs of His coming and the day of judgment: 'And in that generation shall all the desolation come upon Zion...But my disciples shall stand in holy places.' Isaiah's warning to Babylon becomes a promise to the covenant people in Restoration scripture.

John writes: 'Behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him...and all kindreds of the earth shall wail because of him.' The wailing imperative in Isaiah's vision is echoed in Revelation's final vision of Christ's coming.

commentary.historical_context: The 'day of the LORD' in Isaiah's original context refers to the historical fall of Babylon in 539 BCE. For the prophet and his audience, this was a future event that would vindicate God's word and demonstrate His sovereignty. The theological weight given to this political/military event—calling it the 'day of the LORD' and comparing it to cosmic upheaval—reflects the ancient Israelite understanding that history itself is the arena of God's action. The wailing imperative reflects the actual experience of a besieged or conquered city: mourning, grief, and vocal lamentation were customary responses to military defeat and the loss of independence.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently employs similar language of wailing and lamentation for those who reject God's word. 2 Nephi 27:31 describes the 'day of the LORD' as a time when 'the book shall be sealed' and God's purposes will be made manifest. Like Isaiah's vision, the Book of Mormon ties historical events to God's sovereign purposes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 133:70–74 describes the 'day of the Lord' as a time of judgment: 'Wherefore be not troubled, for when they see all these things, they shall know that the hour is nigh.' The Restoration recaptures Isaiah's eschatological framework, applying it to the latter days.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that God's judgment is just and inevitable. The wailing in Isaiah's vision echoes the understanding that those who refuse to live covenant principles will ultimately face the consequences of their choices. The 'day of the LORD' in temple theology is a day of separation—the righteous are gathered on the Lord's right hand, while the wicked face His judgment.

commentary.christological_typology: The 'day of the LORD' described here and throughout Isaiah ultimately refers to the Second Coming of Christ and the final judgment. Jesus Himself applies day-of-the-Lord language to His return (Matthew 24:36–51, Luke 21:27–36). Isaiah's prophecy of Babylon's judgment becomes, in Christian typology, a type of the final reckoning when Christ appears 'in flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God' (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). The wailing imperative becomes a call to repentance before that day arrives.
commentary.application: For modern believers, this verse is both a warning and an incentive to repentance. The 'day of the LORD' is coming—not as an abstract theological concept but as a real day when God will act decisively in history and in individual lives. The wailing imperative is not meant to induce fear but to awaken us to reality: judgment is real, it is coming, and it cannot be prevented by wealth, power, or human ingenuity. But this is balanced by Restoration teaching: those who turn to God, make and keep covenants, and align their will with His purposes will find safety in the day of the LORD. The verse invites us to ask: Am I living in such a way that the day of the LORD would be a day of vindication for me, or a day of judgment?

text_kjv: Therefore shall all hands be faint, and every man's heart shall melt:

commentary.narrative: Isaiah transitions from the cosmic call to judgment (verses 2-6) to the human consequence: total collapse of will and strength. The word 'therefore' connects to the preceding summons of armies to the day of the LORD. When that day arrives, the very hands that would grasp weapons go limp, and hearts—the seat of courage and resolve in Hebrew thought—dissolve like wax. This is not a poetic exaggeration but a precise description of psychological and physical breakdown before overwhelming divine judgment. The parallelism of 'hands' and 'heart' covers both the capacity to act and the will to act; nothing remains intact.

word_study.meaning: to drop, to become slack or limp, to lose strength or grip. The root conveys the image of hands that can no longer hold a weapon, a tool, or any object of use. In Psalm 68:2, the same verb describes wax melting before fire.
word_study.significance: The choice of raphah emphasizes not mere weakness but the inability to grasp or act. This is the paralysis of complete despair—not injury, but the draining of the capacity to resist or function.

word_study.meaning: to melt, to dissolve, to liquefy. Used of wax melting before heat, of courage dissolving in fear, of solid things losing their form. The image is dissolution, not destruction—the transformation of something firm into something formless.
word_study.significance: The verb masas is central to the theology of judgment in Isaiah. When the heart melts, courage and faith undergo a fundamental transformation. This foreshadows the eschatological dissolution of all earthly powers before the presence of God.

cross_references.connection: Uses the same verb masas ('melt') to describe wax melting before fire and God's enemies fleeing before His presence. Isaiah 13:7 applies this image of dissolution to the hearts of humanity in the Day of the LORD.
Another day-of-judgment oracle describing hearts melting and knees trembling. Both passages use the standard vocabulary of eschatological terror to depict the human response to divine judgment.

Rahab's heart melts (masas) when she hears of the LORD's mighty works. The same verb describes both the courage-draining effect of God's judgment and the faith-draining effect of His power made manifest.

Joseph Smith's revelation describes the terrors of the last days when 'their hearts shall fail them.' The pattern of internal dissolution before divine judgment echoes Isaiah's imagery of melting hearts.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the collapse of hands and heart represented the total incapacity of a warrior or city to defend itself. The Babylonians, the implicit target of chapter 13, built their military supremacy on the reputation of their strength and the courage of their armies. Isaiah's prophecy inverts this: when the Day of the LORD comes, the very hands that wielded Babylon's power become useless, and the hearts that drove their ambition liquefy in terror. This would have been shocking language to an audience that measured a city's worth by its military might.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi quotes and expounds upon Isaiah 13 extensively in 1 Nephi 14:4, where he applies the judgment to the gentile nations in the latter days. The imagery of hands becoming faint connects to the broader Latter-day Saint understanding of the vulnerability of Babylon (materialism and worldly power) before the Restoration.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 133:38-40 references Isaiah's cosmic judgment language in the context of the coming of the Son of Man. The dissolution of courage described in Isaiah 13:7 is part of the larger schema of last-days judgment in the Restoration scriptures.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The melting of the heart and the dropping of hands reflect the spiritual preparation demanded in temple worship—the surrender of human will and strength before the presence of deity. The imagery of dissolution inverts the typical covenant language of strength and steadfastness, suggesting that only repentance and covenant-keeping provide the stability to withstand divine judgment.

commentary.christological_typology: While not explicitly Christological, the verse prefigures the universal judgment that Christ will execute at His second coming. The collapse of human power and courage anticipates the need for Christ's intervention to save the righteous and judge the wicked. The dissolution of hearts points to the penetrating knowledge of Christ as judge, before whom no human resolve or deception can stand (Hebrews 4:12-13).
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 13:7 challenges the illusion of security in earthly power—military, economic, or political. The verse asks: on what foundation do I build my security? If it rests on the arm of flesh, it will melt. The limp hands and dissolved heart represent the spiritual paralysis that comes from relying on anything but God. Conversely, those anchored in God's covenants and the Restoration experience the opposite: hands strengthened to serve, hearts firm in faith (see D&C 58:27).

text_kjv: And they shall be afraid: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them; they shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth: they shall be amazed one at another; their faces shall be as flames.

commentary.narrative: The prophet shifts from the physical collapse (verse 7) to the psychological and emotional terror that accompanies it. Fear seizes them; labor pangs bind them like a woman in childbirth. This is the classical prophetic metaphor for inescapable, involuntary suffering—the kind that cannot be controlled or escaped, only endured. The mutual staring in horror ('amazed one at another') captures the breakdown of social order; each person is isolated in terror, unable to find comfort or certainty in others. The final image—faces ablaze—may describe the flush of panic, the reflection of actual fire, or faces contorted by fear itself. The cumulative effect is a portrait of total social and psychological disintegration.

word_study.meaning: a pang, a constriction, a sudden sharp pain. Related to the imagery of siege and constraint. Tzir conveys the physical sensation of being squeezed or bound by pain.
word_study.significance: The word choice emphasizes not chronic suffering but acute, binding pain—the sudden contraction that seizes the body. This is the pain of acute crisis, not slow decline.

word_study.meaning: a cord, a rope, a bond; metaphorically, the cords or pangs of agony. The root suggests something that binds or constrains, like labor pains that bind a woman's body.
word_study.significance: Chavel adds the dimension of binding constraint. The sufferers are not merely in pain; they are bound by it, unable to move or escape. This reinforces the image of helplessness before judgment.

word_study.meaning: to writhe, to twist, to turn in agony. The root can also mean to form or to bring forth (as in childbirth). In Psalm 90:2, the same verb describes the earth brought forth in creation; here it describes creation's recoil in agony.
word_study.significance: The use of chul connects the judgment to a cosmic event—the same verb that brought the earth into being now describes its writhing in pain. This elevates the judgment from political event to cosmic occurrence.

word_study.meaning: to be astonished, to stare, to gaze in horror or bewilderment. The root conveys a fixed stare of incomprehension or shock, the inability to look away.
word_study.significance: Tamah suggests not momentary surprise but frozen terror—people staring at each other in mutual horror, unable to break the gaze or find reassurance. The social fabric dissolves into isolated pockets of fear.

word_study.meaning: flames, blazes. The root is lhv, suggesting something that flickers or blazes. The phrase penei lehavim peneihem literally means 'faces of flames [are] their faces,' creating an ambiguous image.
word_study.significance: The phrase can mean faces flushed red with terror, faces reflecting actual fire, or faces that flicker and contort like flames themselves. The ambiguity is intentional—the point is that faces become unrecognizable, transformed by terror or by the physical heat of judgment.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah uses the same birth-pangs metaphor (like a woman in travail) to describe the anguish of Jerusalem before judgment. Both prophets employ obstetric imagery to convey inescapable, involuntary suffering.
Micah prophesies that Zion will be like a woman in labor, writhing in pain. The metaphor is standard prophetic language for the inescapable suffering of cities or nations under judgment.

John's vision of a woman in travail combines obstetric imagery with cosmic judgment. The pattern of using childbirth metaphors for eschatological crisis spans Hebrew prophecy into New Testament Revelation.
Paul writes that judgment comes suddenly 'as travail upon a woman with child.' He adopts Isaiah's metaphor of birth pangs to describe the inescapable arrival of the Day of the LORD.

Joseph Smith's revelation describes the signs of the last days using similar imagery: hearts failing, terror overwhelming people. The pattern of psychological and emotional collapse before judgment echoes Isaiah 13:8.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern military contexts, the collapse of a city's morale before siege was a recognized phenomenon. The image of mutual staring in horror reflects the breakdown of military discipline and social hierarchy—when panic spreads, soldiers cannot support one another, and leadership dissolves. The faces ablaze may reference the actual fires of siege warfare, or they may be metaphorical (the flush of fear, the wildness of expression). Either way, the verse captures what happens when a military and social order disintegrates under overwhelming force.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 14:4-5 applies Isaiah 13 to the destruction visited upon the gentile nations (Babylon) in the latter days. Nephi emphasizes that those who remain righteous during these terrors will be preserved, contrasting them with those whose hearts melt in fear. The Book of Mormon adds the comforting counterpoint: the righteous are not subject to this anguish.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:31-35 describes the terrors of the last days, including plagues and bloodshed that cause the inhabitants of the earth to mourn. The pattern of social breakdown and fear described in Isaiah 13:8 is explicitly applied to the latter days in Joseph Smith's revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The writhing and anguish of verse 8 contrast sharply with the peace promised to those who enter into temple covenants. The covenant member is invited to escape the pangs and terrors of judgment through faith in Christ and participation in redemptive ordinances. The 'amazement one at another' reflects a world without the unity provided by shared covenantal vision.

commentary.christological_typology: The birth-pangs metaphor points typologically to the suffering of the righteous before Christ's second coming. In Matthew 24:8 and Mark 13:8, Christ uses the same language ('beginning of sorrows,' literally 'beginning of birth pangs') to describe the signs preceding His return. The connection is deliberate: just as judgment labor leads to new birth, the travail of the last days leads to the restoration of all things in Christ.
commentary.application: The verse teaches modern Latter-day Saints to expect turmoil in the last days and to prepare spiritually rather than psychologically relying on earthly securities. The image of people staring at one another in mutual confusion speaks to the isolation and alienation that come from severing oneself from God's covenant people and His truth. For those who have made covenants in the temple, however, Isaiah 13:8 should instill not fear but compassion for those still in darkness, and resolve to share the gospel message that alone can still the terror.

text_kjv: Behold, the day of the LORD cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate: and he shall destroy the sinners thereof out of it.
text_kjv_alt: Behold, the day of the LORD cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the earth desolate: and he shall destroy the sinners thereof out of it.

commentary.narrative: The prophet now makes explicit what has been building throughout verses 1-8: the 'day of the LORD' is arriving, and it brings divine judgment characterized by three escalating terms for wrath. This verse is the theological hinge of the chapter—it frames the preceding descriptions of human terror as the consequence of God's intervention, not as arbitrary catastrophe. Isaiah accumulates three words for divine anger to suggest that no single human term can capture the intensity of God's judgment. The shift from 'land' (ha-arets referring to Babylon specifically in context) to cosmic scope is characteristic of Day of the LORD oracles; the judgment on a particular nation becomes a template for universal judgment. The explicit mention of 'sinners' shows that judgment is discriminate—it targets the wicked, not the innocent.

word_study.meaning: The Day of the LORD is the climactic moment when God directly intervenes in history to execute judgment and restore His purposes. In prophetic literature, it is simultaneously a day of terror for the wicked and vindication for the righteous.
word_study.significance: This is the master term for eschatological judgment throughout the Hebrew prophets. Isaiah uses it to move the reader from the particular (Babylon's fall) to the universal (the ultimate reckoning of all things). The phrase signals that what follows is not merely political but cosmic in scope.

word_study.meaning: cruel, merciless, severe. The root suggests harshness without compassion. Akhzari emphasizes the absence of mercy or pity in judgment.
word_study.significance: The choice of akhzari foreshadows that God's judgment will not be tempered by mercy for those who have hardened themselves against Him. Mercy is available in repentance; those who refuse it meet judgment without mitigation.

word_study.meaning: fury, rage, an overflowing outpouring of anger. The root evrah suggests something that flows or overflows—anger that cannot be contained or controlled.
word_study.significance: Evrah adds the dimension of uncontrollable force. God's judgment is not a measured response but an overflow, a torrent. This captures the sense that divine judgment, once released, cannot be restrained by human effort or negotiation.

word_study.meaning: literally 'burning of the nose/face,' a Hebraism for intense anger. The image is of God's anger as heat that burns and consumes. Af (nose/face) is synecdoche for the person; God's anger is His direct presence turned toward judgment.
word_study.significance: The physical imagery of burning anger suggests not merely emotional upset but an incandescent intensity. God's af (His judgment) is the focal point of the threat. This connects to the later image of faces ablaze (verse 8)—human faces reflect the divine fire they cannot withstand.

word_study.meaning: desolation, waste, emptiness. To 'lay desolate' is to reduce a land to uninhabited wasteland. The root suggests the abandonment and emptying of a place.
word_study.significance: Shammah suggests not merely destruction but the removal of human presence and civilization. A desolate land is one where humans cannot remain—a negation of everything civilization has built.

word_study.meaning: to destroy, to exterminate, to wipe out. The root conveys totality—not partial damage but complete removal.
word_study.significance: The verb shamid is unambiguous: sinners will not be reformed or exiled but destroyed. This is terminal judgment. The verse offers no middle ground between repentance and annihilation.

cross_references.connection: Amos warns against longing for the Day of the LORD, describing it as darkness and judgment. Both prophets use the term to invoke universal, inescapable divine reckoning, not a selective blessing.

Joel's prophecy of the Day of the LORD combines plague imagery, darkness, and the call to repentance. Like Isaiah, Joel accumulates vivid descriptions of judgment to emphasize its severity and inescapability.
Zephaniah's Day of the LORD oracle uses similar language: wrath, anger, and the destruction of sinners. The pattern of divine judgment on the wicked is consistent across the prophetic corpus.

Jesus quotes Isaiah's cosmic judgment language and Day of the LORD tradition when describing His second coming. The connection shows that Jesus understands Himself as the executor of Isaiah's Day of the LORD prophecy.

Peter uses Day of the LORD language to describe the dissolution of creation in heat and fire. The pattern of cosmic judgment and the destruction of the wicked continues into New Testament eschatology.

commentary.historical_context: The 'Day of the LORD' is rooted in ancient Near Eastern thought about divine intervention—the idea that when a god acts decisively in history, it reshapes reality itself. For Israel's neighbors, specific military victories or defeats could be interpreted as a god's 'day.' Isaiah universalizes this concept: there will be one ultimate Day of the LORD that encompasses all of history and all nations. This was radical in its scope and transcendence of tribal or political interests. The accumulation of three terms for anger reflects the hyperbolic style of ancient judgment rhetoric, where piling up synonyms intensified the emotional impact and claimed to exhaust human language for the divine reality.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 14 applies Isaiah 13:9 to the destruction that will come upon the Gentile nations in the latter days, connected to the restoration of the gospel and the gathering of Israel. Nephi makes clear that the Day of the LORD in Isaiah is not merely past (Babylon's destruction) but is an ongoing reality in the latter days.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 133 is a revelation given to Joseph Smith on the Day of the LORD, using Isaiah's language to describe the Last Judgment and Christ's coming. D&C 88:87-91 similarly describes the dissolution of the wicked in heat and fire, directly echoing Isaiah's prophetic pattern.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, covenants provide protection from the judgment described in verse 9. Those who have made and kept sacred covenants are promised to be numbered among the righteous in the Day of the LORD, not among the sinners. The temple endowment includes explicit language about the separation of the righteous from the wicked in the last days.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 13:9 is explicitly Christological in New Testament interpretation. Jesus Christ is the executor of the Day of the LORD—He judges with righteousness and destroys sinners (those who reject Him). The accumulation of terms for wrath also foreshadows Christ's dual role: merciful to the repentant, merciless to the unrepentant. In Revelation 19:11-16, Christ comes as judge and warrior, wearing the robes of judgment—a direct connection to Isaiah's Day of the LORD prophecy.
commentary.application: For modern members, Isaiah 13:9 invites serious reflection on the reality of divine judgment. The verse does not teach that God is arbitrary or cruel (akhzari describes the judgment, not God's character—God is merciful to all who repent). Rather, it establishes that there is a reckoning, that wickedness will not finally prevail, and that covenant keeping is essential to surviving that day. The verse also challenges the notion that the gospel is merely about feeling good or personal fulfillment. It is about alignment with God's purposes and rejection of sin, knowing that the Day of the LORD will vindicate that choice.

text_kjv: For the stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine.

commentary.narrative: The cosmic judgment continues: if the Day of the LORD brings the dissolution of earthly powers and human courage, it also brings the failure of creation itself. Every source of celestial light—stars, constellations, sun, and moon—ceases to shine. This is not merely poetic; it is a statement that creation recoils from judgment. The darkening of the heavens becomes a sign and a statement: the order that has sustained human civilization is suspended. In ancient cosmology, the heavens were the seat of divine order; their darkening signals cosmic reversal. The passage is remarkable for its accumulation: not one light source but all of them, not merely diminished but entirely extinguished or darkened. This verse sets the template for cosmic-judgment imagery throughout the prophets and the New Testament.

word_study.meaning: stars, celestial bodies. In Hebrew thought, stars were tokens of order, divine permanence, and the unbreakable nature of God's covenant (Genesis 15:5, 22:17). To extinguish the stars is to unmake a fundamental symbol of divine promise.
word_study.significance: The choice of kokhabim emphasizes not random celestial objects but the very tokens of divine covenant and order. Their darkening signals not merely atmospheric change but cosmic undoing.

word_study.meaning: constellations, specifically Orion or major star groups. The root kesil (from Job 9:9 and 38:31) refers to Orion, but in plural, it means constellations generally—the major groupings of stars that ancient peoples used for navigation and timekeeping.
word_study.significance: The inclusion of constellations alongside stars suggests systematic failure of all celestial light, not just isolated points of illumination. The cumulative darkness is comprehensive. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve a plene spelling (כסיליהם) reflecting Qumran's fuller orthographic conventions, but the meaning is identical.

word_study.term_english: shall not give their light / will not flash their light
word_study.meaning: will not give, will not emit, will not flash forth their light. The verb hll (hil/yahl) suggests the flashing or emanation of light.
word_study.significance: The verb choice emphasizes not mere dimming but the cessation of emission—the light does not fade; it stops being produced. This is total failure, not partial eclipse.

word_study.meaning: to become dark, to be darkened. The root describes the transition from light to darkness, or the state of being shrouded in darkness.
word_study.significance: Chashakh is not merely the absence of light but the active process of darkening—as if darkness itself is a force. This suggests not natural eclipse but supernatural darkening.

word_study.meaning: at its going forth, at its rising. The preposition b' with tzet (to go forth) describes the sun's rising in the east.
word_study.significance: The specification 'in his going forth' emphasizes that the sun is darkened even at its moment of rising—the very moment when light should be strongest. This intensifies the abnormality and the totality of the darkening.

word_study.meaning: moon. From the root yarach (to give forth light), the moon is inherently defined by its light-giving function.
word_study.significance: In ancient cosmology, the moon was understood as the secondary light source, governing the night. Its failure to shine means not only physical darkness but the collapse of the temporal order (night and day) that depends on celestial light.

word_study.meaning: will not cause its light to shine, will not emit its glow. The verb ngah (to shine, to cause to shine) emphasizes active emission rather than passive reflection.
word_study.significance: The verb ngah suggests that the moon does not merely fail to reflect sunlight; it ceases its own luminous function. This adds to the sense of cosmic malfunction on a fundamental level.

cross_references.connection: Joel uses identical cosmic-darkening imagery: 'the sun and the moon shall be dark, and the stars shall withdraw their shining.' The pattern is standard Day of the LORD language across the prophets.
Joel repeats the cosmic darkening in the context of the Valley of Jehoshaphat. The recurrence of this imagery suggests it is a fixed token of eschatological judgment.
Amos prophesies that God will darken the sun at noon, turning day to darkness. The motif is consistent: the Day of the LORD reverses the basic order of creation (light to darkness).
Ezekiel, in a judgment oracle against Egypt, uses cosmic-darkening language: the sun will be covered, the moon will not give its light. The pattern extends across prophetic traditions.

Jesus quotes Isaiah 13:10 directly: 'Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light; and the stars shall fall from heaven.' Jesus appropriates Isaiah's cosmic-judgment language for His second coming.
Mark's parallel account includes Jesus quoting Isaiah: 'the stars of heaven shall fall, and the powers that are in heaven shall be shaken.' The connection to Isaiah 13:10 is explicit.

John's apocalypse uses cosmic-darkening language: 'the sun became black as sackcloth of hair, and the moon became as blood.' The pattern of cosmic dissolution continues into the New Testament revelation.
Peter describes the Day of the LORD with cosmic imagery: the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat. The pattern of cosmic failure is consistent.

Joseph Smith's revelation describes the sun being darkened and the moon ceasing to give light as signs of the coming of the Son of Man. The Latter-day Saint scriptures explicitly incorporate Isaiah's cosmic-judgment language.

Another revelation to Joseph Smith describes the complete dissolution of creation: 'the heavens shall be shaken, and the earth shall tremble and reel to and fro.' The same cosmic-reversal pattern appears in Doctrine and Covenants.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern cosmology, the heavens were not merely the sky but the seat of divine order, the realm of the gods, and the sustaining principle of creation. The sun was often identified with the god of justice; the stars with divine permanence; the moon with the regulation of time and seasons. To darken the heavens was, in that cosmological framework, to unmake the very structure of reality. Ancient peoples knew of solar and lunar eclipses, but Isaiah's language goes beyond natural astronomy to describe a cosmic catastrophe. The accumulation of darkened lights suggests not a single eclipse but a fundamental reversal of the created order. For a culture dependent on celestial navigation, agriculture timed to seasons, and night-watch traditions, the loss of all celestial light would mean the collapse of civilization's practical foundation as well as its theological center.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 12:4-5 describes cosmic signs preceding Christ's ministry in the New World: 'the sun and the moon shall be darkened.' The Book of Mormon appropriates Isaiah's language to describe the judgment that comes with Christ's advent. Similarly, 3 Nephi 8:3-7 describes the actual darkening of the heavens during the three days of Christ's resurrection.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:40-42 and D&C 88:87 use cosmic-darkening language in the context of the Last Judgment and the Second Coming. Joseph Smith's revelations make explicit what is implicit in Isaiah: the cosmic darkening is a sign of Christ's coming. D&C 29:14-15 also describes the heavens being rolled up as a scroll, directly referencing Revelation's appropriation of Isaiah.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the endowment, the creation sequence in the temple represents the ordering of chaos and the establishment of light. The reverse—the darkening and dissolution of that order—is what awaits those who reject covenant and Light. The temple teaches that those who remain covenant-faithful will be in the light when others are in darkness.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 13:10 points Christologically to Christ's second coming, where He executes the cosmic judgment described. The darkening of the heavens is a sign of His approach—the reversal of creation precedes its renewal. In one sense, Christ's first coming brought light into darkness (John 1:5, 8:12); His second coming will darken the heavens themselves, signaling the end of this dispensation and the ushering in of the next. The imagery also connects to Christ as judge—He who judges is described in Revelation 1:16 as having eyes 'as a flame of fire,' a focal point of light in darkness.
commentary.application: For modern members, Isaiah 13:10 challenges the assumption that current political, technological, and social orders are permanent or trustworthy. The verse teaches that all earthly signs of stability and progress—represented by the celestial lights that regulate society—can be reversed or withdrawn. This is not cause for despair but for focus: if the heavens themselves can be darkened, then security lies not in earthly systems but in covenants and faith in Christ. The verse also invites reflection on what provides true light in darkness: not the sun or moon, but the light of Christ (D&C 88:12) and the light that comes through temple ordinances and restored truth.

text_kjv: And I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the terrible.

commentary.narrative: The cosmic descriptions of verses 9-10 yield to the divine pronouncement in verse 11: God Himself speaks to explain the purpose of the judgment. It is not arbitrary catastrophe but righteous reckoning. The shift from third-person description (verses 1-8) to first-person divine speech ('I will punish') makes clear that God is the active agent of judgment, not merely an observer. God identifies two classes of targets: 'the world' and 'the wicked'—universal scope and moral discrimination. The focus then narrows to a specific sin: arrogance, pride, and the exaltation of the self above others and above God. The parallelism of 'pride of the arrogant' and 'haughtiness of tyrants' hammers at the reality that human self-exaltation is both the root sin and the specific charge against those who will be judged. The verb 'lay low' (ashpil) is the perfect antonym for the pride it opposes: those who exalted themselves will be brought down.

word_study.meaning: to visit, to muster, to count, to hold accountable. In judicial contexts, paqad means to call to account, to execute judgment. The root carries the sense of paying attention to someone—in judgment, to visit them with the consequence they deserve.
word_study.significance: Paqad is a 'visitation' of judgment—God turns His attention to an account that must be settled. This suggests that injustice does not go unnoticed by God; He is attentive, and He will settle accounts. This is both warning and comfort depending on one's standing.

word_study.meaning: the world, the inhabited earth, the ecumene. Tevel is specifically the human world, not the abstract cosmos.
word_study.significance: The use of tevel emphasizes that God's judgment is oriented toward human society and civilization. This is not cosmic indifference but a reckoning with how humans have ordered their world.

word_study.meaning: evil, harm, wickedness, that which damages or destroys. Ra is both moral and practical—it describes acts that violate God's order and damage community.
word_study.significance: The charge against the world is ra—undifferentiated evil. The world as a system (not merely individuals in it, though that too) has failed to order itself toward righteousness.

word_study.meaning: the wicked, the lawless, those who violate God's covenant and law. Resha'im are not merely unfortunate but actively opposed to God's order.
word_study.significance: The identification of resha'im as a distinct group from humanity in general suggests that not all are equally guilty. Some have actively chosen wickedness. They stand in contrast to those who have sought righteousness.

word_study.meaning: iniquity, guilt, the weight or burden of sin. The root avah (to bend, to twist) suggests that avon is a perversion or twisting of the right order.
word_study.significance: Avon emphasizes not merely wrongdoing but the distortion of proper order. This connects to the later mention of pride: avon is the iniquity of those who have twisted themselves away from God's order.

word_study.meaning: arrogance, pride, majesty. When applied to humans, ge'on is a negative quality—the arrogant claiming for themselves the status or prerogatives that belong to God alone. Applied to God, it is rightful majesty.
word_study.significance: The key insight is that ge'on is inherently presumptuous in humans because it claims for oneself the exaltation that belongs to God. The arrogant make themselves lords; the righteous acknowledge God as Lord.

word_study.meaning: the proud, the presumptuous, the insolent. From the root zud (to boil over, to be arrogant), zedim are those who overflow with self-confidence and contempt for others.
word_study.significance: Zedim suggests a kind of pride that is not merely personal but interpersonal—the arrogance that oppresses others, that makes them subordinate to one's own will.

word_study.meaning: to cease, to stop, to rest. As causative, it means to bring something to an end, to stop.
word_study.significance: God does not merely diminish pride; He causes it to cease entirely. This is complete cessation, not reformation. Pride ends not through persuasion but through divine intervention.

word_study.meaning: haughtiness, arrogance, proud bearing. A variant form of ge'on, emphasizing the outward display of pride.
word_study.significance: Ga'avat focuses on the manifestation of pride—the bearing, the display, the attitude. God will bring low the very posture of those who have exalted themselves.

word_study.meaning: tyrants, oppressors, fierce rulers. From the root artz (to be fierce, to treat harshly), aritsim are those who dominate through force and fear.
word_study.significance: The pairing of 'arrogant' and 'tyrants' shows that the charge is not merely against private conceit but against systemic oppression. Those who have used power to dominate others will themselves be brought down.

word_study.meaning: to bring low, to abase, to reduce. From the root shpal (low, beneath), ashpil is the active reduction of height or status.
word_study.significance: The verb ashpil is the perfect rhetorical counterpoint to ge'on and ga'avat: those who have elevated themselves will be brought to the lowest place. The linguistic parallelism embodies the poetic justice of the judgment.

cross_references.connection: Hannah's song declares that God 'maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up.' Isaiah 13:11 shows this principle applied at the cosmic scale: God brings low the proud and tyrants.

The psalmist declares, 'For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south. But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another.' Isaiah 13:11 is the ultimate expression of this principle—God will judge all pride at the End of Days.
'Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.' Proverbs states the principle; Isaiah 13:11 shows its cosmic execution.

Peter writes, 'God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.' The same principle of divine opposition to pride appears in the New Testament, grounded in the prophetic tradition Isaiah represents.

Mary's Magnificat declares that God 'hath shewed strength with his arm; he hath scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts. He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.' The language echoes Isaiah 13:11 and applies it to the coming of Christ.

Joseph Smith's revelation describes those who 'have set themselves up for gods, and have not kept my commandments.' Their judgment involves the bringing low of pride, consistent with Isaiah's pattern.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, kings and emperors built monuments to their own glory, inscribed records of their power, and demanded worship as divine beings. Babylon, in particular, was known for the grandiosity of its rulers and the scale of its building projects designed to glorify Babylonian power and wisdom.
