Isaiah's prophecy directly challenges this ideology: the very hands that built these monuments will go limp (verse 7), and the pride that motivated them will be brought down by a higher Power. The judgment on pride (ge'on) is not unique to Babylon but is universal—it applies to any nation or ruler that exalts itself above God. This would have been radical teaching in a world where self-exaltation was the defining strategy of imperial power.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 12:11-17 (quoting Isaiah 2:11-17) includes the theme: 'And the loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be made low: and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.' Nephi emphasizes that the destruction of pride is essential to the establishment of Zion.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 35:24 and D&C 64:2 address the pride of those who exalt themselves in the Church. The principle in Isaiah 13:11—that God will bring down the proud—is applied in the Restoration to members who resist God's word through the Prophet.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple theology teaches that the only legitimate exaltation is through covenants with God, not through self-assertion. The garment of the holy priesthood is a reminder that no degree of earthly pride or authority surpasses the bond between the individual and God. Isaiah 13:11 shows what becomes of those who seek exaltation through any other means.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 13:11 points to Christ as the executor of judgment against pride. In His ministry, Jesus repeatedly confronted the pride of religious leaders and the self-exaltation of the powerful. In Matthew 23, He pronounces woes on the Pharisees for their pride and hypocrisy. At His second coming, Christ will execute the final bringing-low of all human pride and arrogance. The principle that God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (1 Peter 5:5-6) is rooted in Christ's own humility and exaltation pattern: He humbled Himself to death, and the Father exalted Him (Philippians 2:8-9). Those who follow Christ must embrace the same pattern.
commentary.application: Isaiah 13:11 warns modern members against the subtle forms of pride that easily infect those with power, wealth, or influence. The verse challenges every presumption that human status, achievement, or dominance is durable. For Church members, it warns against spiritual pride—the sense that one's righteousness or calling places one above others or exempts one from continued repentance. The verse also teaches compassion for those who are currently exalted in the world's eyes, knowing that their exaltation is temporary. More positively, it calls members to the opposite of pride: humility, service, and the continual acknowledgment that all power and worth come from God through Christ. This is the foundation of covenant living.

text_kjv: I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir.

commentary.narrative: The final verse of Isaiah's opening judgment oracle is grimly ironic and must be read in context. God says He will make a man (enosh, emphasizing human frailty) rarer than fine gold (paz), and a human (adam, emphasizing creatureliness) rarer than the gold of Ophir (the legendary source of the finest gold in the ancient world). This is not a promise of dignity or honor; it is a prophecy of radical depopulation. When multitudes die in judgment, those who survive will be so few that a single human being will be more precious by scarcity than the rarest metal. The verse inverts the usual meaning of 'precious'—gold is precious because it is rare and desired; humans will be precious because judgment will have made them scarce. This is the culmination of verses 7-11: the collapse of hands, the melting of hearts, the writhing in anguish, the darkening of the heavens, the destruction of the proud—all lead to this final reality: survival itself becomes the measure of preciousness. The verse serves as the final emphasis that judgment is total and inescapable.

word_study.meaning: to make rare, to make precious, to make valuable by rarity. From the root qr (rare, hard to find), aqir suggests that something becomes precious through scarcity, not through intrinsic worth.
word_study.significance: The verb aqir is the key to understanding the irony: humans are not being exalted or honored but rendered rare through death. The preciousness is a function of scarcity caused by judgment, not by any honor conferred.

word_study.meaning: a man, a human being, specifically emphasizing the frailty, weakness, or creatureliness of humans. Enosh is used when the emphasis is on human dependence and vulnerability.
word_study.significance: The choice of enosh rather than ish (man, male) emphasizes the pathos of the judgment. It is not warriors or leaders who will be rare, but the fragile, mortal creatures themselves. This reinforces the universality of the judgment.

word_study.meaning: pure gold, refined gold, gold of the highest quality. From the root paz (to refine, to purify), paz is gold that has been refined to maximum purity.
word_study.significance: Paz is the standard of precious metals in the ancient world—the most valuable substance known to commerce and wealth. The comparison claims that humans will be rarer than this standard of value itself.

word_study.meaning: human being, mankind, humanity. Adam emphasizes not the individual but the human creature as a created being. It is the same word used for humanity in Genesis 1-3.
word_study.significance: The parallel use of both enosh (emphasizing frailty) and adam (emphasizing creatureliness) suggests that all dimensions of human being—the weak, the created, the mortal—will be scarce. There is no escape into a higher category of humanity.

word_study.meaning: gold of Ophir, the finest gold. Ophir was a legendary (and historically disputed) location renowned as the source of the most precious gold. 1 Kings 9:28 and 10:11 reference Ophir as the source of gold for Solomon's temple.
word_study.significance: Ophir represents the ultimate rarity in the ancient world—not merely gold, but the most perfect gold, imported from distant lands at great expense. The verse claims that humans will be rarer than this legendary commodity. The historical connection to Solomon's temple (the place of God's presence) adds a layer: humans, made in God's image, will become rarer than even the precious metals dedicated to God's house.

cross_references.connection: God forms adam (humanity) from the dust of the earth and breathes into him the breath of life. Isaiah 13:12 uses the same word (adam) to underscore that the creatures whose life comes from God will be reduced to scarcity through judgment.

The psalmist marvels: 'What is man, that thou art mindful of him? ...thou madest him a little lower than the angels.' Isaiah 13:12 inverts this: humans, whom God has honored, will become rare through their own rebellion and judgment.

Job describes the preciousness of wisdom, comparing it to gold and Ophir: 'It cannot be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for the price thereof.' Isaiah 13:12 uses the same comparison (Ophir) but with opposite meaning: humans will be more rare than even this ultimate standard of value.

Solomon's servants bring gold from Ophir for the temple. The connection suggests that the judgment on humanity is a reversal of Solomon's splendor—the gold remains, but the humans who made and valued it are gone.

The account of the Nephilim and the prelude to the Flood describes a period when the earth was filled with the sons of men. Isaiah 13:12 echoes a similar catastrophic reduction in human population through divine judgment.

Jesus describes the days of Noah—when humans multiplied and gave no heed to warning—preceding the Flood. The same pattern applies to the End Times: normal human activity continues until judgment suddenly arrives, drastically reducing the population.

commentary.historical_context: Ophir was understood in the ancient world as a real, though often inaccessible, location—the ultimate source of luxury and wealth. Solomon's reign was legendary for the abundance of gold from Ophir brought to Jerusalem (1 Kings 10:11, 2 Chronicles 8:18, 9:10). The historian is uncertain whether Ophir was in Africa, Arabia, or elsewhere, but the ancient and biblical writers treated it as a real place representing the extreme of human commercial and material achievement. Isaiah's comparison—that humans will be rarer than even gold of Ophir—would have struck ancient hearers as impossibly hyperbolic. Gold lasts; humans die and are born again. Yet Isaiah claims that judgment will so thoroughly depopulate the earth that the scarcity will reverse. This would have seemed either absurd or apocalyptically terrifying, depending on the hearer's distance from the sin Isaiah condemns.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 14:4-5 applies Isaiah 13 to the destruction that will come on the gentile nations, but with the covenantal understanding that the righteous remnant will be preserved. The irony of Isaiah 13:12—that humans become rare—is inverted in Book of Mormon thought: those who remain faithful will be gathered and preserved, precious in God's sight not by accident but by divine mercy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:40-42 describes the fate of those who reject light and truth: they will inherit a kingdom of glory proportionate to their choices, but those who reject God entirely will be few. The rarity of unrepentant sinners in the celestial kingdom parallels Isaiah's language of human scarcity through judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, the human being is understood as precious—made in God's image, eligible for exaltation through covenants. Isaiah 13:12 reminds temple-goers that this preciousness depends on remaining covenant-faithful. To reject the covenants available in the temple is to gamble with one's own preservation in the Day of the LORD.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 13:12 points to the principle of Christ as the only way of preservation. In the context of the Day of the LORD (which Christ executes), humans are made rare through judgment—except those who are in Christ. The verse anticipates Christ's teaching that 'strait is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it' (Matthew 7:14). Those who follow Christ are the remnant who survive judgment; they are indeed made precious, not by accident or scarcity, but by grace and redemption in Christ.
commentary.application: For modern members, Isaiah 13:12 should instill both humility and gratitude. The verse teaches that human life is fragile and that the continuation of civilization is not guaranteed. This counters the presumption of progress and endless stability that characterizes modern secular culture. More importantly, it teaches members to value covenant participation as the means of preservation: those who make and keep covenants with God, through Christ and His church, are numbered among the 'precious few' who will endure the judgments of the last days. The verse also challenges the cultural value of material wealth—gold of Ophir, the rarest treasure—as ultimate worth. When judgment comes, survival and righteousness are the true measures of preciousness. This should orient members toward spiritual preparation over material accumulation.

text_kjv: Therefore I will shake the heavens, and the earth shall remove out of her place, in the wrath of the LORD of hosts, and in the day of his fierce anger.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks the cosmic pivot of Isaiah 13. Up to this point, Isaiah has described the gathering of nations and the instruments of judgment. Now he shifts to what those instruments will accomplish: a complete unraveling of creation itself. The 'shaking' (argiz) of the heavens and 'removing' (tir'ash) of the earth are not metaphorical upheavals—they describe creation jolted off its foundation, a return toward pre-creation chaos (tohu va-vohu). The theological claim is staggering: the God who established the heavens and earth in Genesis 1 can unmake them through an act of wrath. This is not local destruction but cosmic dissolution.

The accumulation of divine titles intensifies the passage's gravity: 'LORD of hosts' (YHWH tseva'ot) presents God as commander of armies, both heavenly and earthly. The doubled language of wrath—'fury' (evrah) and 'the day of his burning anger' (yom charon appo)—escalates from general divine displeasure to the specific, terrible moment when judgment falls. The phrase 'day of the LORD' had become a technical term in prophetic literature for that moment when God directly intervenes in history to judge nations. Isaiah places Babylon's fall within that cosmic framework: what happens to one empire is part of a universal reckoning. The modern reader might expect a more measured tone; instead, Isaiah commits fully to the apocalyptic register.

word_study.meaning: Hiphil form of ragaz, meaning 'to cause to tremble, agitate, or shake.' The verb implies violent, continuous motion—not a single tremor but sustained convulsion. Used of God's agency in cosmic upheaval.
word_study.significance: The choice of argiz (rather than ra'ash, 'shake') emphasizes God's active causing of motion. Creation does not naturally shake; God makes it shake. This is divine *doing*, not divine permission of natural disaster. The Covenant Rendering captures this agent-focused meaning with 'make the heavens tremble.'

word_study.meaning: Niphal form of ra'ash, 'to quake, shake, or tremble.' Unlike argiz (active causation), tir'ash emphasizes the earth's *experience* of being shaken—its passive suffering of upheaval.
word_study.significance: The shift from hiphil (God's action) to niphal (earth's reaction) creates a grammatical mirror of cause and effect. God shakes the heavens (active); the earth shakes (passive). This mirrors the creation account where God actively makes and sustains; here God unmakes.

word_study.meaning: Divine wrath or fury, from a root suggesting 'overflowing' or 'surging.' It describes anger that cannot be contained or suppressed. Related to the concept of divine *passion* rather than cold judgment.
word_study.significance: Evrah appears throughout the prophets as the emotional component of divine judgment. It is not retribution computed rationally but wrath that surges and overflows. The pairing of 'fury' and 'burning anger' in verse 13 suggests an intensity that builds toward unbearable heat.

word_study.meaning: 'The burning of his nose/face'—a vivid idiom for wrathful emotion. In Hebrew anthropomorphic language, anger flares from the nostrils. Charon (from charah, 'to burn') emphasizes the heat of anger; appo ('his nose/face') is the site of that burning.
word_study.significance: This phrase appears frequently in descriptions of the Day of the LORD (e.g., Zephaniah 2:2–3). It conveys divine emotion as something that *burns*—intense, consuming, irrepressible. For an ancient reader, this phrase would have been shorthand for inevitable, overwhelming judgment.

cross_references.connection: The creation account establishes the heavens and earth as God's intentional work. Isaiah 13:13 envisions their undoing—a reversal of creation's order, suggesting that judgment can unmake what God has made.

John's vision of the end times echoes Isaiah's cosmic language: 'the stars of heaven fell unto the earth...and the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together.' This shows how Isaiah 13's apocalyptic imagery was interpreted in the New Testament as a template for eschatological upheaval.

Jeremiah describes judgment on Jerusalem using the same vocabulary of cosmic unmaking: the land returning to tohu va-vohu ('without form and void'), echoing Genesis 1:2. Both prophets frame divine judgment as an unwinding of creation.

In this revelation on the last days, Jesus describes the earth shaking and the heavens being shaken, followed by the sealing up of the heavens and earth—a complete reconstitution. Isaiah's Day of the LORD is reframed in LDS eschatology as part of the Father's and Son's preparations for the Millennium.

commentary.historical_context: The Medes and Persians who conquered Babylon in 539 BCE would have seemed, to exilic Jews, like instruments of cosmic upheaval. Babylon had been the superpower for nearly a century; its sudden fall at the hands of Cyrus II would have felt world-shaking. The imagery of cosmic dissolution reflects the *theological* magnitude of what seemed like an impossible historical event: the fall of the apparently invincible. Ancient Near Eastern mythology (Babylonian Enuma Elish, for example) often described cosmic chaos (apsu) being subdued by divine order. Isaiah inverts this: the Day of the LORD returns ordered creation to chaos, but *through* God's righteous judgment, not despite it.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mormon describes the Day of the LORD approaching in Mormon 8:2: 'Behold, I speak unto you as if ye were present.' The Book of Mormon does not directly quote Isaiah 13:13, but the theme of upheaval preceding the Millennium appears throughout (e.g., 3 Nephi 24, which quotes Malachi's apocalyptic language). Nephi's prophecies in 2 Nephi 25–30 similarly use cosmic imagery to describe the scattered state of Israel and the gatherings at the end times.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:14–21 is the primary connection: the Lord explicitly states that 'the heavens shall shake' and 'the earth shall tremble' as part of the last days. D&C 45:42–44 also describes the earth's convulsions before the Lord's coming. These D&C passages show that Joseph Smith understood Isaiah's apocalyptic language as literal, not merely poetic—an important distinction for members processing the full weight of Isaiah's judgment sayings.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment tradition speaks of creation, the Fall, and eventual restoration. Verse 13's inversion of creation (unmade heavens, displaced earth) would resonate with temple understand of the cosmos's malleability—that the earth is not eternal in its present form but subject to divine will and eventual re-making. The Day of the LORD is presented as a temple-like moment of cosmic transition.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 13 establishes Jesus Christ implicitly as the one through whom God's judgment operates. While Babylon is the immediate subject, the verse's cosmic language points to the eschatological moment when Christ will reign. Revelation 6:12–14 explicitly connects Isaiah's cosmic upheaval to Christ's return. In LDS understanding, Christ is the agent through whom the heavens and earth are shaken and remade at the end of days (D&C 29:15–16).
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 13 reframes temporal power structures as fragile. Babylon seemed eternal; God unmade it. The verse invites believers to recognize that no earthly kingdom—no empire, economy, or culture—is ultimately stable. Only God's kingdom endures. Practically, this means believers should invest faith and loyalty in God's work rather than in the world's apparent permanence. When facing seemingly overwhelming worldly pressures or injustices, this verse anchors believers in the knowledge that God will have the final word, and He is wholly capable of reshaping creation itself to do it.

text_kjv: And it shall be as the chased roe, and as a sheep that no man taketh up: they shall every man turn to his own people, and flee every one into his own land.

commentary.narrative:
The cosmic language of verse 13 descends suddenly into something intimate and human: the fate of individual people caught in Babylon's collapse. Isaiah uses two animal similes—the hunted gazelle and the shepherd-less sheep—to capture the panic of a cosmopolitan city emptying itself. Babylon was a gathering place of nations and peoples, a melting pot held together by imperial coercion. When judgment falls, that cohesion shatters instantly. The foreigners, soldiers, merchants, and slaves who served Babylon's interests will turn on a dime and flee to their home countries and peoples.

The irony is precise and bitter. Babylon built itself by gathering (qabats, in later verses) the wealth and peoples of other nations. Now, with no gathering force to hold them, those same peoples scatter like unsheltered sheep. Each person acts alone—turning to one's own people (am), fleeing to one's own land (eretz)—a dissolution of corporate identity into ethnic and tribal fragmentation. The passage moves from cosmic upheaval (v. 13) to human dissolution in a single breath, suggesting that the two are of a piece: shake creation, and human societies collapse. The Dead Sea Scrolls show no significant variant here, confirming the Masoretic reading.

word_study.meaning: Passive participle of nadach, 'to drive, thrust, or chase away.' A gazelle that is driven has no refuge, no stable ground. It is in perpetual flight.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests helplessness—the gazelle is not choosing flight but being forced into it. This is not strategic retreat but panic-stricken flight. For an ancient audience, the image of a chased gazelle would be immediately visceral: an animal separated from the herd, exposed, fleeing.

word_study.term_english: sheep / with no one to gather them
word_study.meaning: The second simile shifts from active pursuit (hunted gazelle) to passive abandonment (sheep without a shepherd or gatherer). A gatherer (meqabbets, from qabats, 'to gather') is the one who prevents dispersal. Without such a figure, the flock naturally scatters.
word_study.significance: The word meqabbets ('gatherer') echoes the imperial function of Babylon itself—it gathered nations. Now there is no meqabbets, so dispersal is inevitable. This wordplay deepens the irony: the force that held the empire together is removed, and centrifugal forces take over.

word_study.meaning: Hiphil of panah, 'to turn (toward), face, or look in a direction.' It suggests a reorientation—a turning from one allegiance or direction to another.
word_study.significance: The choice of yifnu (rather than, say, 'they will abandon') emphasizes the internal reorientation. People literally turn their faces and hearts toward their own people and land. This is not reluctant flight but an active reassertion of ethnic and tribal identity.

word_study.meaning: Qal of nus, 'to flee, run away.' The verb carries the sense of panic-stricken flight—not organized retreat but uncontrolled dispersal.
word_study.significance: Yanusu appears frequently in descriptions of military rout and panic. The pairing of yifnu (turn) and yanusu (flee) suggests both psychological reorientation and physical escape. First the heart turns; then the body follows.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah's oracle against Babylon similarly describes Babylon's warriors becoming helpless and her people scattering: 'A sword is upon the liars...a drought is upon her waters.' The same theme of imperial dissolution through the dispersion of dependent peoples.

Nahum's oracle against Nineveh uses nearly identical language to describe the fall of Assyria: 'Thy shepherds slumber...thy people is scattered upon the mountains, and no man gathereth them.' The 'no man gathereth them' echoes Isaiah 13:14's 'no one to gather them.'

Zechariah quotes Isaiah's language when describing the Messiah being struck and the sheep (disciples) being scattered: 'Smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.' Matthew 26:31 applies this to Jesus's arrest—showing how the shepherd/sheep imagery became christological in later Jewish interpretation.

The Lord's preface to the D&C describes the gathering of Israel as a primary work: 'Hear ye, O heavens, and give ear, O earth...I am speaking unto all people.' The opposite of this gathering—the scattering described in Isaiah 13:14—represents the breakdown of covenant community when judgment falls.

commentary.historical_context: Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar and his successors was indeed a cosmopolitan empire. It drew administrators, soldiers, priests, and merchants from across the Near East. When Cyrus II of Persia conquered the city in 539 BCE, the power structure that held these diverse peoples together suddenly reversed. Cyrus's policy was not to dismantle Babylon but to co-opt it; still, the shock of conquest would have sent many of Babylon's foreign residents fleeing toward home. The Dead Sea Scrolls show no variant affecting verse 14's meaning, preserving the MT reading intact.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently describes the scattering of Israel using similar language. 1 Nephi 22:3–4 discusses the 'scattering and gathering' as a covenant pattern. The image of sheep without a shepherd also appears in 3 Nephi 15:21–24, where Jesus speaks of his 'other sheep' in other lands—a scattering that will eventually be gathered through his voice. Isaiah's language of dispersal is reframed in the Book of Mormon as both judgment and the prelude to redemptive gathering.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:81–86 speaks of the Lord gathering his people in the last days, reversing the scattering that began with Babylon and continued through the ages. D&C 45:70–71 also describes the gathering as a sign of the times. Verse 14's image of people fleeing their common cause to return to their tribes and lands would resonate with LDS members as a description of what happens when the power structure holding a society together (even an ungodly one) collapses.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, members become part of a gathered people—a community centered on the Lord's work rather than on ethnic or tribal identity. Verse 14 shows the opposite: the dissolution of community and the reassertion of tribal and national identity. This would underscore for temple-endowed members the need for active commitment to the Lord's gathering work to prevent spiritual scattering.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 14's image of sheep without a shepherd points forward to Jesus as the Good Shepherd (John 10:11). When Jesus is arrested, his disciples scatter (Matthew 26:31, quoting Zechariah 13:7, which uses Isaiah-like language). The shepherd's removal causes the flock's dissolution. Conversely, Christ's mission is to gather sheep that have been scattered. Isaiah's judgment oracle, read christologically, describes what happens without the Shepherd, and implicitly points to the need for Christ's gathering work.
commentary.application: Verse 14 invites reflection on the fragility of human institutions and loyalties. Babylon's power was so absolute that its foreign residents and soldiers seemed permanently committed to its system. Yet the moment it fell, loyalty evaporated—people returned instantly to tribe and homeland. For modern members, this raises questions: Where does my ultimate allegiance lie? Am I so bound to worldly systems (career, status, cultural identity) that I would scatter if those systems fell? The covenant community of the Church offers an alternative: a gathering based not on coercion or imperial power but on shared faith and divine promise. The verse challenges members to assess whether their primary identity is tribal/national or covenant-based.

text_kjv: Every one that is found shall be thrust through; and every one that is joined unto them shall fall by the sword.

commentary.narrative: The panic and fleeing described in verse 14 will not save everyone. Isaiah narrows the focus to those who remain or are captured—the ones who cannot escape. The verse employs stark parallelism: those found will be pierced; those captured will fall by the sword. The Hebrew verbs are the standard language of battlefield slaughter, used in accounts of siege and military conquest throughout the Bible. The compression of the verse—two short, parallel lines, no elaboration—mirrors the swift, indiscriminate nature of the violence. A modern reader might expect more warning or hope; instead, Isaiah presents finality. The Dead Sea Scrolls show only minor scribal variations (the interchange of final aleph and he in passive participles), which do not affect meaning. The MT reading stands firm.

word_study.meaning: Niphal passive participle of matsa, 'to find or be found.' The passive voice emphasizes helplessness—the person is discovered, not voluntarily presenting themselves. In military contexts, nimtsa implies being caught unaware or having nowhere left to hide.
word_study.significance: The choice of nimtsa (found, discovered) rather than, say, 'taken' emphasizes the victim's lack of agency. They did not seek capture; they were simply located. The Dead Sea Scrolls read hinnmtzeh (with final he rather than aleph), a scribal variant that does not change the meaning.

word_study.meaning: Niphal of daqar, 'to pierce or stab.' The verb describes the action of a blade piercing the body. It is the vocabulary of hand-to-hand combat and execution.
word_study.significance: Yiddaqer is precise and brutal. It does not describe distant projectile fire but intimate violence—a sword blade entering flesh. This is not accidental death but intentional killing.

word_study.meaning: Niphal of safah, 'to sweep, gather, or carry away.' The passive participle suggests being caught up in a wave of violence—swept along with others, unable to escape the tide.
word_study.significance: Nispeh conveys mass casualty—not individual capture but being swept away as part of a group. The irony is that verse 14 described people scattering individually; verse 15 shows that many will be swept up collectively and slain regardless.

word_study.meaning: Qal of naphal, 'to fall.' In military contexts, naphal means to be slain or defeated. It is the standard term for soldiers killed in battle.
word_study.significance: Yippol is deliberately understated—it simply says 'fall,' but in the context of sword violence, the meaning is death. The word appears frequently in battle narratives (e.g., 1 Samuel 4:10, describing Israelites falling before Philistines).

cross_references.connection: Moses's song describes God's vengeance on his enemies: 'I will make mine arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh.' Isaiah 13:15 echoes this language of divine retribution through the sword—an ancient formula for judgment.

The psalmist, remembering Babylon's destruction, describes the fate of Babylon's children: 'O daughter of Babylon...happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones.' This parallels Isaiah 13:16's brutal imagery, showing that later psalmists understood Isaiah's judgment oracle as prophetic of actual Babylonian fall.

Jeremiah's oracle against Babylon uses similar language: 'The slain of Israel shall fall in Babylon, and they that be slain in all the earth.' The theme of indiscriminate slaughter as judgment appears across multiple prophetic books.

Section 87 prophecies of the last days describe warfare where 'blood shall cover the earth in consequence thereof.' Isaiah's ancient prophecy against Babylon is echoed in D&C's eschatological language, suggesting a continuity of divine judgment across ages.

commentary.historical_context: When Cyrus II conquered Babylon in 539 BCE, the siege and aftermath likely involved military casualties, though Cyrus's approach was generally less destructive than Nebuchadnezzar's had been. However, Isaiah wrote *before* that event, in the exilic period, so his language reflects the standard pattern of ancient siege warfare: those caught in a city during conquest would face slaughter. The prophetic form of verse 15—with its sharp, parallel lines and stark vocabulary—mimics the way ancient prophets pronounced judgment: not as prediction of probability but as divine pronouncement of inevitability.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains similar language describing warfare and judgment. Alma 2:29–31 describes the Zoramite conflict with graphic realism: 'They were met by the Lamanites...and they began to slay them.' The Book of Mormon does not soften the reality of violence, though it also emphasizes the moral causes of such judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 97:25–26 describes the Lord's judgment on those who reject his work: 'The Lord's scourge shall pass over by night and by day, and the report thereof shall vex all people.' While not explicitly invoking Isaiah 13:15, it uses similar language of divine judgment and slaughter.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony includes language of judgment and consequences for covenant violation (e.g., the penalties). Verse 15's description of indiscriminate judgment—those found, those captured—would resonate with the temple's emphasis on the need for faithful covenant-keeping to avoid judgment.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 15 describes the consequence of rejecting God's judgment—death by the sword. Christologically, Christ is both the judge whose sentence falls on the wicked and the one who died by the sword (though figuratively, in crucifixion). Revelation 19:15 describes Christ at the end of days coming 'out of his mouth [goeth] a sharp sword, that with it he should smite the nations.' Isaiah's sword of judgment is ultimately wielded by Christ, the final judge.
commentary.application: Verse 15 is difficult to apply without sounding callous. Its primary application for modern members is eschatological: to recognize that God's judgment is real and inescapable for those who refuse his word. However, a secondary, more pastoral application exists. The verse emphasizes the importance of *fleeing*—verse 14's flight motif. Those who cannot escape are those who stayed. For believers, this suggests the importance of responding to God's warnings and leaving systems of unrighteousness before judgment falls. In practical terms, staying entangled in sin, unrepentance, or covenant-breaking is like remaining in a doomed city. The only way to escape is to heed the warning and flee.

text_kjv: Their children also shall be dashed to pieces before their eyes; their houses shall be spoiled, and their wives ravished.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 16 escalates the horror to its peak. Having described the fate of those who cannot flee (v. 15), Isaiah now catalogs the devastation that befalls those who remain: infanticide, property destruction, and sexual violence. This verse contains some of the most brutal imagery in the Bible—not because Isaiah celebrates violence but because he refuses to sanitize judgment. The prophet does not flinch from describing what siege warfare and conquest actually entail. The piling up of atrocities—children first, then property, then wives—creates a comprehensive picture of complete devastation. Every generation, every possession, every intimate relationship is destroyed.

The Masoretic tradition here contains an interesting variant in the Qere/Ketiv tradition (not affecting the DSS reading here). The final verb appears in the MT as tishkavnah ('will be lain with'), a euphemism replacing what scholars believe was originally tishagalnah (a coarser term for sexual violation). The Covenant Rendering renders this as 'violated,' capturing the force without the crude original. The theological point remains unaltered: the violence is total and encompasses all dimensions of human life. This is not a celebration of violence but a statement of what the Day of the LORD looks like when it actually manifests on the ground, in human terms. Modern readers sometimes assume that biblical judgment language is metaphorical; Isaiah insists it is devastatingly literal.

word_study.meaning: Hiphil of ratash, 'to dash, smash, or break in pieces.' The verb is used of infants' skulls being smashed against stone or walls during siege warfare. Psalm 137:9 uses identical language: 'Happy shall he be, that taketh...thy little ones and dasheth them against the stones.'
word_study.significance: The verb yerutashu is deliberately visceral and specific. It does not describe death in abstract terms but the physical shattering of small bodies. For an ancient audience, this would have been the unspeakable horror of siege warfare—the killing of children who posed no military threat. The verb appears in accounts of ancient siege and conquest.

word_study.meaning: Prepositional phrase meaning 'before, in front of, or in the sight of their eyes.' The phrase emphasizes not just that children will die but that parents will be *forced to witness* the killing.
word_study.significance: This detail transforms the verse from describing mass death into describing psychological trauma. The parents are not quickly slain in ignorance; they are made to see their children's deaths. This is a deliberate intensification of cruelty.

word_study.meaning: Hiphil of shasah, 'to plunder, rob, or despoil.' The verb describes the systematic taking of possessions—not casual looting but organized destruction of property.
word_study.significance: Yissasu appears frequently in accounts of siege and conquest. It suggests not just theft but the *stripping* of a people of their material basis for survival—their homes, furnishings, stored food, tools. Complete despoliation.

word_study.meaning: Niphal of shakav, 'to lie down.' In the context of military conquest, this is a euphemism for sexual assault. The Masoretes substituted tishkavnah for what scholars believe was originally tishgalnah (from a less formal root), replacing a crude term with a euphemistic one.
word_study.significance: The use of euphemism here reveals something important about how ancient scribes handled violent content: they did not remove the reference but softened its language. The Covenant Rendering's 'violated' captures the force. The point remains that sexual assault on women and girls is presented as part of the comprehensive devastation of conquest.

cross_references.connection: This psalm, composed by exiles remembering Babylon, prays for Babylon's downfall using near-identical language: 'O daughter of Babylon...happy shall he be, that taketh...thy little ones and dasheth them against the stones.' The psalmist confirms that Isaiah's prophecy was understood as predictive of actual Babylonian siege.

Hosea's oracle against Israel uses nearly the same vocabulary to describe judgment: 'Their infants shall be dashed in pieces, and their women with child shall be ripped up.' This suggests that Isaiah's language of escalating violence was a standard prophetic formula for describing the total devastation of defeat.

Elisha, responding to Hazael's question about why he weeps, describes the devastations Hazael will cause in Israel: 'Their strong holds wilt thou set on fire, and their young men wilt thou slay with the sword, and wilt dash their children, and rip up their women with child.' Again, the identical sequence of violence.

Jeremiah's lament over Jerusalem's destruction asks whether God would 'slay in the temple thy Lord?' and describes infants and youths falling in streets. The theme of innocent children suffering in siege and conquest runs through these texts, reflecting the historical reality of ancient warfare.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient siege warfare—whether Babylonian, Assyrian, or other Near Eastern powers—involved exactly the devastations Isaiah describes. Archaeological evidence from destroyed cities (e.g., Lachish under Assyria, or Jerusalem under Babylon) confirms that civilians, including children, were killed or enslaved. Sexual violence was an instrument of conquest and terror. Isaiah does not invent these horrors but reports them as the actual consequences of defeat. His role as a prophet is to warn that these consequences await Babylon if it does not repent—or in this case, to assure the exiled Judahites that God will bring judgment on their oppressor, even if that judgment includes the brutal realities of ancient warfare. The Masoretic variant (tishkavnah for tishgalnah) suggests that later scribes found the crude language difficult to preserve, preferring a euphemism. But the meaning remains unchanged.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains similar descriptions of the devastations of war, particularly in Alma's account of battles between Nephites and Lamanites. Alma 2:29–30 describes soldiers being slain; the Book of Mormon does not dwell on atrocities against children or women, but it does not hide the brutal reality that warfare harms entire populations.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 97:25–26 describes the Lord's judgment as something that will not spare any: 'But, behold, if they receive not my words, and this testimony which I have caused to be sent forth unto them, they shall be rejected from my presence.' While the D&C uses less graphic language, the principle of comprehensive judgment remains.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony includes a covenant that binds entire families—husbands and wives, parents and children. Verse 16's description of the destruction of family units would stand in stark contrast to the temple's emphasis on binding families together eternally. The verse might prompt reflection on the importance of protecting and preserving family covenants rather than allowing them to be violated or destroyed.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 16's description of infanticide and violence against the innocent echoes the pattern of Herod's massacre of innocent children (Matthew 2:16–18), which Matthew explicitly links to Jeremiah's prophecy but which resonates with all biblical prophecies about violence and the shedding of innocent blood. The suffering of children in judgment oracles points forward to Christ's own suffering of the innocent—the God who takes upon himself the very judgment he pronounces. Christ's crucifixion, in a sense, reverses Isaiah's judgment oracle by absorbing judgment in his own body rather than inflicting it on others.
commentary.application: Verse 16 is perhaps the most difficult verse in the passage to apply to modern members without causing harm. Its immediate application is eschatological and cautionary: those who reject God's word and covenant will face severe consequences. However, a more measured application emerges from recognizing that Isaiah describes these atrocities not to celebrate violence but to emphasize the *seriousness* of judgment. The verse warns that covenant unfaithfulness is not a minor matter—it carries real consequences for families and communities. For members, this might prompt reflection: Am I taking my covenants seriously? Am I protecting my family's spiritual well-being? Am I awake to the reality that compromising my covenant commitments places my family at spiritual risk? The verse invites sober assessment rather than fear.

text_kjv: Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it.

commentary.narrative:
After five verses of describing the horrors that will befall Babylon, Isaiah now names the instrument of judgment: the Medes. The Medo-Persian empire under Cyrus II conquered Babylon in 539 BCE, roughly 150 years after Isaiah's time. Isaiah's use of the divine hineni ('behold, I am about to') signals a shift from description of devastation to direct divine agency. God does not passively allow Babylon to fall; God *stirs up* (me'ir) the Medes. This is crucial theologically: the prophet claims that history's apparently natural events (conquest, dynastic succession, military strategy) are actually directed by the God of Israel. Cyrus may have thought he was conquering Babylon for Persian imperial reasons; Isaiah insists he is an instrument of YHWH's purpose.

The detail that the Medes 'will not regard silver' and 'will not delight in gold' serves a specific rhetorical purpose. Babylon built itself on wealth and the accumulation of tribute. A conquering army that could be bought off, corrupted, or bribed might be negotiated with. But the Medes cannot be corrupted because they seek no plunder. Their motivation is destruction itself, not enrichment. This makes them unstoppable—no amount of Babylonian wealth can purchase mercy. From a literary standpoint, this detail intensifies the hopelessness: Babylon's greatest asset, its wealth, is rendered useless. The logic of power and wealth collapses.

word_study.meaning: Interjection and first-person pronoun form meaning 'behold, I am, or look—I am about to.' Often introduces an imminent divine action or pronouncement. The form combines the attention-demanding interjection hen ('behold') with ani ('I').
word_study.significance: Hinni establishes the speaker as the active agent in what follows. God is not predicting what might happen but announcing what *will* happen because God is directly causing it. This is the language of divine power and intention.

word_study.meaning: Hiphil participle of ur, 'to wake, rouse, or stir up.' Applied to God, it means to rouse a nation or people to action—in this case, the Medes.
word_study.significance: The verb me'ir emphasizes that the Medes are not acting on their own initiative. They are roused, awakened, stirred into motion by God. They may not know they serve God's purposes, but they do. This reflects a broader prophetic claim: that even pagan kings execute God's will (see also Isaiah 45 regarding Cyrus).

word_study.meaning: Qal of chashav, 'to think, reckon, account, or value.' The verb describes a mental calculation of worth or importance.
word_study.significance: Yachshobu means the Medes do not *value* silver—they do not reckon it as significant or worthwhile. This is not ignorance but indifference. The prophet implies that the Medes' value system is fundamentally different from Babylon's wealth-based order.

word_study.meaning: Qal of chafets, 'to delight in, desire, or take pleasure in.' It describes an emotional or aesthetic preference, not just a rational calculation.
word_study.significance: Yachpetzu goes deeper than yachshobu. It is not just that the Medes see no value in gold; they actively *dislike* it, find no pleasure in it. Their motivation lies elsewhere—in conquest, power, or ideology, but not in wealth.

cross_references.connection: Later in Isaiah, the Lord calls Cyrus the Mede by name as his 'anointed' (messiah), saying 'thou hast not known me,' yet God uses him to execute divine purposes. Verse 17 introduces the Medes as God's instruments; verse 45 expands this, showing that even gentile rulers serve God's agenda.

Jeremiah also prophesies the Medes' role in Babylon's fall: 'Make bright the arrows; gather the shields: the LORD hath raised up the spirit of the kings of the Medes.' Like Isaiah, Jeremiah attributes the Medes' actions directly to God stirring them up.

Daniel's account of Babylon's conquest describes 'Darius the Median' taking the kingdom. Daniel presents the fall of Babylon as an act of God through the Medes, confirming that later Jewish tradition understood the Medes as God's instruments.

The Lord's instructions to the migrating Saints speak of how God 'stirreth up the hearts' of people to accomplish divine purposes. This language echoes Isaiah's claim that God stirs up nations. D&C emphasizes that even when people think they are acting on their own, God may be directing their actions toward his purposes.

commentary.historical_context: Cyrus II of Persia (c. 600–530 BCE) conquered Babylon around 539 BCE. Historical accounts (Xenophon, the Nabonidus Chronicle, and other ancient sources) describe the conquest as relatively bloodless. Cyrus's approach was pragmatic: absorb Babylon into his empire rather than destroy it. However, for exiled Judahites, the result was the same—the overthrow of their oppressor and the opportunity to return home. Isaiah's language of the Medes as not valuing silver or gold may reflect historical reality: the Persians pursued territorial expansion and administrative control more than plunder. Unlike Nebuchadnezzar's Babylonians, who stripped nations of treasures as tribute, the Persians incorporated subject peoples into a larger bureaucratic system. Isaiah's perception was astute.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains a similar principle in Alma 37:6–7, where Alma tells Helaman: 'By small and simple things are great things brought to pass...therefore Alma desired that he should remember these things.' While the context differs, the principle that God works through seemingly small or unexpected means (like the Medes in Isaiah's prophecy) parallels the Book of Mormon's emphasis on faith and divine direction of apparently mundane events.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:33 states: 'That the rights of the priesthood are inseparably connected with the powers of heaven, and that the powers of heaven cannot be controlled nor handled only upon the principles of righteousness.' This principle underlies Isaiah 17: the Medes are instruments because they serve God's justice. Their incorruptibility—their refusal to be bought off by Babylon's wealth—is what makes them effective tools of divine judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple emphasizes covenant and divine order. Verse 17 shows God directing history according to divine will. In the temple, members covenant to align their will with God's; verse 17 illustrates God's own alignment of history toward purposes of justice and mercy (for the exiled Judahites, liberation).

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 17 presents God stirring up instruments to accomplish divine purposes. Christologically, Christ becomes the ultimate instrument through whom God accomplishes judgment and redemption. Just as God 'stirs up' the Medes to execute judgment on Babylon, God ultimately sends Christ to execute judgment on sin and to offer redemption. The pattern of God using agents to fulfill divine will reaches its apex in Christ.
commentary.application: For modern members, verse 17 teaches a powerful principle about divine providence: God directs history and can use seemingly unlikely instruments (even those who 'do not know him') to accomplish divine purposes. This should inspire confidence that God's work cannot be frustrated by the opposition of wealth, power, or worldly systems. Practically, it means believers should not be anxious about whether the world's powerful will listen to or support the gospel—God's purposes do not depend on worldly sanction. Additionally, the detail about the Medes not valuing silver or gold suggests that those who serve God most effectively are those not motivated by worldly gain. For members, the application is: Am I serving God from desire for wealth, status, or other worldly rewards? Or am I serving from conviction that God's purposes are right, regardless of personal advantage? The Medes' indifference to Babylon's wealth is a model of single-minded purpose.

text_kjv: Their bows also shall dash the young men to pieces; and they shall have no pity on the fruit of the womb; their eyes shall not spare children.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 18 returns to the concrete devastations of conquest, now specifying the Medes as the agents. The structure mirrors verse 16 but escalates the imagery by focusing on the Medes' *mercilessness*. The verse moves from young men (ne'arim) to the unborn ('fruit of the womb') to children (banim)—an escalation downward through human categories toward the most vulnerable. The Medes' bows will 'cut down' young men—military-age men who might offer resistance. But the Medes' indifference extends beyond military necessity to the complete absence of mercy even toward those who pose no threat: the unborn and the young. The prophet reinforces this with a wordplay: the Medes will have no rechem (mercy) even toward peri-veten (fruit of the womb), and rachem means 'womb.' Those who came from the womb will find no 'womb-compassion' from their destroyers.

The final phrase—'their eyes shall not spare children'—emphasizes that this is not absentminded cruelty but deliberate mercilessness. The Medes' eyes see children and *choose* not to spare them. This is the culmination of verses 13–18: Babylon's cosmos will shake, its people will scatter, those who remain will be slaughtered with increasing brutality, and the Medes, as God's instruments, will execute this judgment without hesitation or pity. Yet—and this is crucial—all of this is presented as *just*. Isaiah does not distance himself from the violence or apologize for its description. The Day of the LORD *is* violent because Babylon's sins warrant it. The Dead Sea Scrolls show no significant variant here, confirming the Masoretic reading.

word_study.meaning: Hiphil third-person feminine plural of ratash, 'to dash, break, or shatter.' The feminine form is used because 'bows' (qeshatot) is feminine in Hebrew. The verb describes violent breaking.
word_study.significance: Teratashna echoes verse 16's yerutashu (dashed to pieces), but applied to young men by Median bows. The parallel structure emphasizes that the violence is comprehensive: children are dashed (v. 16), and so are young men (v. 18). No age group escapes.

word_study.meaning: Plural of na'ar, 'youth, young man, or boy.' In military contexts, typically refers to men of fighting age who might offer resistance.
word_study.significance: Ne'arim represents the category most able to defend themselves. By mentioning them first, Isaiah establishes that even the strongest will fall; the subsequent mention of the unborn and children then deepens the horror.

word_study.meaning: Qal of racham, 'to have mercy, pity, or compassion.' Rechem can mean 'womb' or 'mercy/compassion' (metaphorically, a womb-like tenderness). The semantic range creates a wordplay: those from the womb will find no 'womb-mercy.'
word_study.significance: The wordplay yerachemu...peri-veten (no compassion for the fruit of the womb) is devastating in the original Hebrew because racham and rechem are related. The Medes will feel no maternal/womb-like tenderness even toward the unborn. This is a linguistic reinforcement of pitilessness.

word_study.meaning: Compound phrase: 'fruit of the womb,' referring to the unborn or very young. The metaphor of 'fruit' emphasizes pregnancy as bearing a crop that can be harvested or destroyed.
word_study.significance: Peri-veten is more vulnerable than ne'arim (young men); these are the unborn and newly born. The escalation from men to the unborn to children is a movement toward absolute vulnerability and innocence.

word_study.meaning: Negative particle + qal of chass, 'to spare, pity, or have compassion.' Tachuss emphasizes an active choice *not* to spare, not merely an absence of pity.
word_study.significance: Lo-tachuss is a deliberate withholding of mercy. The phrase 'their eyes shall not spare' (lo-tachuss einam) suggests that the Medes will *see* children and, *seeing*, will choose not to spare them. This is mercilessness as a choice.

cross_references.connection: The preceding verses of chapter 13 describe the cosmic upheaval and darkness accompanying the Day of the LORD, establishing that Babylon's fall is not merely a military defeat but a cosmic event. Verse 18 shows the human dimension of that cosmic event.

Jeremiah's lament over Jerusalem's destruction uses the same vocabulary of being trodden down. Lamentations 4:10 also describes the suffering of children in siege: 'The hands of the pitiful women have sodden their own children.' The parallel language suggests that Isaiah 13 was understood as a prophecy of the kind of siege devastation described in Lamentations.

Nahum's oracle against Nineveh similarly describes the complete scattering and vulnerability of the city's inhabitants. The theme of merciless conquest causing devastation across all age groups appears in multiple prophetic oracles.

The Lord's description of the last days in Section 29 includes language of upheaval and judgment. While less graphic than Isaiah, the principle that divine judgment is real and affects all people is maintained. The D&C frames such judgment as necessary for the cleansing and renewal of creation.

commentary.historical_context: The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve no significant variant for verse 18. The consonantal text of 1QIsaᵃ reads identically to the MT, though with standard Qumran spelling variations. The historical backdrop remains the Medo-Persian conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE. While Cyrus's approach was generally pragmatic and even generous to conquered peoples (as evidenced by his preservation of Babylonian institutions), the ideological reality for Judahites in exile was that their oppressor had fallen—swiftly and decisively. Isaiah's prophetic language reflects the totality of that reversal from Babylon's perspective: what had seemed permanent and unassailable crumbled in what must have appeared like a cosmic blink.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains accounts of military conquest and its effects on vulnerable populations (e.g., Alma 2:24–30). However, the Book of Mormon generally does not linger over atrocities in the way Isaiah does. The book emphasizes moral causes of defeat (wickedness, covenant-breaking) more than graphic descriptions of violence. Still, the principle that judgment includes vulnerability and hardship runs through both texts.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:4–6 speaks of the Lord's willingness to withdraw his hand of protection: 'Nevertheless, when the wicked rule the people mourn. Wherefore, honest men and wise men should be sought for diligently...and the voice of the people shall have a tendency to choose good, and wise officers, for the punishment of transgressors.' Verse 18's description of the Medes as God's instrument of judgment parallels the D&C principle that God may remove protective forces when people become wicked. The Medes, being indifferent to mercy, are the opposite of 'wise officers' who would act according to divine principles.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony emphasizes the protection afforded by covenant and the consequences of covenant-breaking. Verse 18's description of children and the unborn facing destruction due to Babylon's rebellion would underscore the temple's message about the importance of maintaining righteous covenants not just for oneself but for one's posterity. The Medes' mercilessness toward children parallels the spiritual consequences that can affect family lines when covenant is violated.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 18's description of the Medes' mercilessness stands in stark contrast to Christ's meekness and mercy. Where the Medes spare no one—not even children—Christ's first act in his earthly ministry was to bless children (Matthew 19:13–15). The contrast between the merciless instruments of judgment in Isaiah 13 and the merciful judge in the New Testament points to a fundamental shift in how God's judgment is ultimately administered: through Christ's sacrifice rather than through military conquest. Christ embodies the mercy the Medes lacked.
commentary.application: Verse 18 concludes Isaiah's portrait of Babylon's judgment with an emphasis on mercilessness. For modern believers, the application might first seem dark: this is what happens to those who reject God's way. But a more constructive application emerges: the verse challenges members to examine their own capacity for mercy and their commitment to protecting the vulnerable. The Medes' deliberate choice not to spare children—seeing them but choosing not to spare—is presented as *evil*. For believers, the inverse is the call: to actively *choose* to show mercy, especially to those who are vulnerable. Additionally, verse 18 in context reminds members that God's judgment, while certain, is never arbitrary or merciful to the unrepentant. The application is practical: take seriously the reality that compromise with evil systems leads to judgment. But also: cultivate mercy and compassion as virtues that stand in opposition to the Median mercilessness described here.

text_kjv: For the LORD will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and set them in their own land: and the strangers shall be joined with them, and they shall cleave to the house of Jacob.

commentary.narrative:
This verse opens the restoration oracle that follows the doom-oracle against Babylon in chapter 13. Isaiah pivots from judgment on the oppressor to mercy on the oppressed. The word 'yet' (od) signals continuity—God's election of Israel was not revoked by exile, merely interrupted. The covenant remained intact beneath the surface of punishment. The restoration will be physical ('set them in their own land'), relational ('strangers joined with them'), and familial ('cleave to the house of Jacob'). Notice the progression: first Israel returns; then foreigners voluntarily attach themselves. This is not conquest but attraction—the nations drawn to Israel's restoration because they recognize God's hand in it.

The phrase 'have mercy on Jacob' uses the root r-ch-m (from 'rechem,' womb), evoking God's maternal, visceral compassion. This is not grudging forgiveness but tender renewal. Isaiah grounds restoration not in Israel's merit but in God's womb-love for His people. The dual mention of 'Jacob' and 'Israel' emphasizes that both the patriarch's name and the nation's name belong to them—they retain their identity even after exile. The inclusion of 'strangers' (gerim) who join the restoration community is remarkable in an oracle of national restoration. It signals that God's purposes extend beyond Israel's redemption alone; the nations themselves will participate in the restoration.

word_study.meaning: will have compassion, will show womb-love. From the root r-ch-m (rechem, womb). The verb expresses visceral, maternal compassion—not abstract forgiveness but embodied tenderness.
word_study.significance: This root appears in God's self-description in Exodus 34:6 ('merciful') and underlies the Hebrew concept of God's hesed (covenant mercy). The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'compassion' captures the active, relational quality that 'mercy' can miss.

word_study.meaning: and will again choose. The verb bachar means to select or elect; od means 'again, still, yet.' The phrase restates election rather than announcing it anew.
word_study.significance: This signals that exile did not void Israel's election. God's choice of Israel (Deuteronomy 7:7) remains in force. The 'yet' emphasizes that God's purpose persists through judgment.

word_study.meaning: foreigner, resident alien. In biblical law, the ger occupied a unique status—not a full citizen but protected by covenant law (Exodus 12:49, Leviticus 19:34).
word_study.significance: Isaiah anticipates a universal ingathering, developed fully in chapters 56 and 60. Even the restoration of Jacob includes the stranger, foreshadowing the break-down of ethnic exclusivity in the messianic age.

word_study.meaning: will attach themselves, will join, will adhere. From the root s-p-ch, meaning to join or bind together. Used of organic union.
word_study.significance: The foreigners do not remain separate but integrate into the household of Jacob. The intimacy of the bond is emphasized by the language of adhesion—they become part of the family structure.

cross_references.connection: God's original election of Israel is unconditional and grounded in His love, not Israel's merit. Isaiah 14:1's restatement of election echoes this foundational covenant promise.
God describes Himself as 'merciful' (rachum)—using the same root r-ch-m as Isaiah 14:1. God's compassion toward Israel is a core attribute of His character.
Isaiah later develops the theme of foreigners joining Israel's restoration community, explicitly welcoming eunuchs and foreigners into the covenant household without discrimination.
Jeremiah's letter to the Babylonian exiles promises return after seventy years. Isaiah 14:1 complements this promise, grounding return in God's renewed choice rather than temporal calculation alone.
Nephi applies Isaiah's restoration language to the latter-day gathering of Israel, affirming that God's covenant with Jacob persists beyond the scattering.

commentary.historical_context: By the time Isaiah composed or compiled this oracle (whether 8th century or exilic period), the theological question was acute: Has God abandoned Israel? The exile to Babylon seemed to confirm that covenant had been broken. Yet Isaiah insists restoration will happen—not as a reward for virtue but as an expression of God's renewed choice. The mention of 'strangers' reflects the multicultural reality of the Babylonian Empire and anticipates the cosmopolitan character of the restoration community. Ancient Near Eastern conquest narratives frequently mention subjugated peoples serving the victors, but Isaiah's version is transformed by covenant theology: the servant relationship is real but voluntarily embraced by the nations who recognize God's hand in Israel's elevation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 25:10-11, Nephi applies Isaiah's words to the latter-day scattering and gathering of Israel, affirming that the elect of Jacob will be gathered in the 'last days' through the Savior's power. Lehi's prophecy in 2 Nephi 3:20 also parallels Isaiah's vision of restoration through God's covenant mercy. The Book of Mormon presents Isaiah's restoration oracle as referring to both the return from Babylon and the ultimate gathering of all Israel in the latter days.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:7-8 and 35:24-25 speak of the Lord's power to gather Israel from all nations and places. D&C 110:11 references the restoration of all things, which is the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah's vision. The temple ceremony itself teaches of Israel's gathering and covenant renewal—the restoration of 'all things' that Isaiah proclaims.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The theme of cleaving to the house of Jacob and foreigners joining the covenant community resonates with temple covenants, where all who enter become part of God's household regardless of ethnic origin. The washing and anointing, the robes of the priesthood, and the sealing ordinances all represent the integration of the faithful into Israel regardless of their ancestral lineage.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah's restoration of Israel points to Christ as the agent of gathering. Though verse 1 does not explicitly name Christ, the restoration itself is His work—He is the 'ensign to the nations' (Isaiah 11:10-12) who draws all peoples to Himself. The inclusion of strangers in the restoration community prefigures Christ's breaking down of the middle wall of partition (Ephesians 2:14) and His formation of a single body in which Jew and Gentile are united.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse teaches that belonging to the people of God is not determined by ethnicity, birth, or current status. Just as Isaiah promises that 'strangers' may cleave to the house of Jacob, the Restoration teaches that all who make covenants with God become part of His family. The phrase 'cleave to the house of Jacob' challenges us: Are we, whatever our background, truly attached to the covenant household of faith? How do we, like the strangers in Isaiah's vision, voluntarily embrace God's people and their restored religion?

text_kjv: And the people shall take them, and bring them to their place: and the house of Israel shall possess them in the land of the LORD for servants and handmaids: and they shall take them captives, whose captives they were; and they shall rule over their oppressors.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 2 completes the reversal begun in verse 1. The restoration is not passive—Israel will be actively restored by the nations ('peoples will take them and bring them to their place'), and the house of Israel will gain dominion over those who enslaved them. The verse describes a complete inversion of power: the enslaved become masters, the oppressed become oppressors of their former oppressors. This is poetic justice rendered in covenant terms. The phrase 'in the land of the LORD' grounds this reversal in theological geography—the promised land, the place of covenant blessing, is where the inversion occurs.

The translator's note on verse 2 is crucial: the reversal is total and unsettling to modern sensibilities. Israel's captors become servants. Yet Isaiah presents this not as moral instruction about slavery but as poetic symmetry—a mirror of what was done to them. The language is brutal and concrete: they will rule over 'those who oppressed them' (nogsheihem). The word nogesh (oppressor, taskmaster) appears in descriptions of Egyptian bondage (Exodus 1:11, 3:7) and Babylonian rule. Isaiah casts the return from exile as a second Exodus, but with a twist: this time, the deliverer is God acting through the nations themselves.

word_study.meaning: will take them as inheritance, will possess them. From the root n-ch-l (nahal), meaning to inherit, to possess as a portion. The hitpael form indicates they take possession for themselves.
word_study.significance: The word nahalah (inheritance) is central to Israel's theology—the promised land is Israel's nahalah from the Lord. Now Isaiah extends this language to mean Israel will inherit the nations themselves, a radical inversion. The Dead Sea Scrolls read identically, confirming the meaning.

word_study.meaning: will take captive those who took them captive. The root sh-b-h means to capture, take captive. The double use creates a verbal mirror: subject and object use the same root but in inverted positions.
word_study.significance: This is a brilliant rhetorical technique—the same verb used in both directions creates a perfect reversal. The translator's note emphasizes that the echo of the root in both directions is intentional, making the symmetry unmistakable.

word_study.meaning: will trample, will rule over their oppressors. From the root r-d, meaning to rule, to tread down, to dominate. Nogesh is the oppressor or taskmaster.
word_study.significance: The verb radu (will rule) carries the sense of trampling or dominating harshly. Isaiah does not soften the reversal—Israel's rule over oppressors will match the brutality of their former oppression. This unflinching depiction of power-reversal is part of Isaiah's realism about human nature under the old covenant.

word_study.meaning: male servants and female servants. Avad (servant, slave) and shfachah (handmaid, female servant) denote servile status. The pairing is common in covenant law.
word_study.significance: The translator's note rightly observes that this language is uncomfortable to modern readers, yet it reflects ancient Near Eastern realities. Isaiah uses the vocabulary of servitude to emphasize the total reversal: those who were masters become servants, those who were servants become masters.

cross_references.connection: The language of Egyptian oppression (taskmaster, hard labor, groaning) parallels Isaiah's description. Isaiah casts the return from Babylon as a new Exodus, with the same vocabulary of bondage and release.
At the Exodus, Israel leaves Egypt with spoils. Isaiah 14:2's language of the nations bringing Israel back parallels this motif of the oppressed receiving recompense from their oppressors.
Obadiah's vision of Israel's possession of their enemies' territory echoes Isaiah 14:2's theme of reversal and dominion. Both prophets see the oppressed elevated over the oppressor.

The righteous are described as inheriting 'all things,' a spiritual version of Isaiah's promise that Israel will inherit/possess the nations. The logic of covenant blessing remains: God exalts the faithful.
Christ's promise that the overcomers will sit with Him on His throne parallels Isaiah's vision of reversal—the oppressed will rule. Both passages promise power to the faithful.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern monarchs routinely boasted of conquering nations and enslaving peoples. Isaiah subverts this genre by announcing that Israel—the small, defeated nation—will not conquer through military might but will be elevated by the cosmic will of God. The mention of the nations bringing Israel back reflects the real phenomenon of diaspora communities and the Persian policy under Cyrus II, which did permit Judean exiles to return. However, Isaiah's language exceeds historical realism: he speaks of total reversal, not mere return. The nations become servants, not merely hosts. This is theological poetry, not historical chronicle.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 37:30-34, Alma speaks of the scattered remnants of the house of Israel being 'brought together' and dwelling in the promised land. The Book of Mormon applies Isaiah's restoration language to Lehi's posterity, affirming that God will regather His people. In 1 Nephi 10:12-14, Nephi explicitly interprets Isaiah as referring to the scattering and gathering of Israel in the latter days.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 35:24-25 promises that the Lord will gather Israel 'from all nations,' echoing Isaiah's vision of worldwide restoration. D&C 45:24-25 speaks of the gathering of the faithful before the Lord comes to reign, a fulfillment of Isaiah's restoration oracle. D&C 133 is largely devoted to the gathering of Israel and the role of the Church in facilitating it.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The principle of inheriting all things, central to temple theology, reflects Isaiah's promise. In the temple, the endowed member takes upon themselves the name of God and becomes part of His household, inheriting the promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The reversal of status—from fallen humanity to sealed and exalted status—mirrors Isaiah's theme.

commentary.christological_typology: While verse 2 does not explicitly mention Christ, the ultimate reversal—where the persecuted become the exalted—points to Christ's own reversal. He was cast down, executed as a criminal, yet is now seated at the right hand of God. His exaltation is the archetype for all reversals within the covenant community. The nations serving Israel prefigures all creation being subject to Christ the King.
commentary.application: For covenant members, verse 2 teaches that God sees injustice and will ultimately right it. But the application is not simplistic. The promise is not that we will brutally dominate those who opposed us, but that God will restore us to our proper place and dignity in His household. The verse challenges us to trust in God's justice rather than our own vindication. It also raises the hard question: Once restored to power, how will we treat former oppressors? Isaiah's vision suggests a complete reversal, but later passages (like chapter 56) suggest that even former enemies can become part of the covenant community. The tension between justice and mercy remains.

text_kjv: And it shall come to pass in the day that the LORD shall give thee rest from thy sorrow, and from thy fear, and from the hard bondage wherein thou wast made to serve,

commentary.narrative:
Verse 3 serves as a hinge between the restoration promise (verses 1-2) and the taunt-song against the Babylonian king (verses 4-11). It announces the emotional and physical relief that will accompany Israel's restoration: rest from sorrow, fear, and hard labor. The phrase 'in that day' (be-yom ha-niyach) signals a future moment when God will grant rest—the same language used throughout Isaiah to describe the messianic age. The three burdens removed—otsev (pain, sorrow), rogez (turmoil, agitation), and avodah qashah (hard labor)—are not merely physical but existential. Exile was not only economic oppression but spiritual anxiety: the fear that God had abandoned His covenant.

The translator's note is crucial: these three terms echo Exodus vocabulary, specifically describing Egyptian bondage. Isaiah deliberately casts the Babylonian exile as a new bondage and its relief as a new Exodus. This is not accidental repetition but theological strategy. The verse transitions from promise to taunt by establishing why the taunt is appropriate: when Israel is relieved of its burdens, it will look back at its oppressor and sing a mocking funeral dirge. The oppressor's fate—broken staff, lost dominion—stands in stark contrast to Israel's relief. The logic is clear: if God relieves Israel of bondage, God's judgment on the oppressor is certain.

word_study.meaning: will cause to rest, will give rest. From the root n-w-ch (nuach), meaning rest, quietness, to settle. Related to the word menuchat (rest) and the Sabbath concept.
word_study.significance: This root appears in the Sabbath command (Exodus 20:11) and in promises of rest from enemies (Deuteronomy 12:9-10). Isaiah uses covenant language to describe the restoration—it is a Sabbath rest, a settling into the promised land.

word_study.meaning: your pain, your sorrow, your affliction. From the root ts-b (tsab), meaning to labor painfully, to be pained.
word_study.significance: The same root appears in Genesis 3:16-17 ('in pain/otsev you shall bring forth children'; 'in pain/otsev you shall eat'). Isaiah links Israel's bondage to the primordial human condition of toil and suffering, suggesting that relief from exile is restoration to a pre-Fall condition.

word_study.meaning: your turmoil, your agitation, your trembling. From the root r-g-z (ragaz), meaning to shake, to tremble, to be agitated.
word_study.significance: This term describes not merely fear but the emotional turmoil of living under oppression—the constant shaking of anxiety. The cessation of fear is freedom not just from external threat but from internal agitation.

word_study.meaning: the hard labor, the severe servile work. Avodah means labor or slavery; qashah means harsh, severe, difficult.
word_study.significance: This phrase appears verbatim in Exodus 1:14 and 6:9, describing Egyptian slavery. Isaiah deliberately echoes the Exodus narrative to assert that Israel's restoration from Babylon is a second Exodus. The use of past tense ('wherein thou wast made to serve') suggests the bondage is already ending from God's perspective.

cross_references.connection: The phrase 'hard bondage' (avodah qashah) appears identically in Exodus, describing Egyptian slavery. Isaiah casts the Babylonian exile as a new Egypt and the restoration as a new Exodus.
The Exodus passage mentions that Israel did not listen to Moses because of their 'hard bondage.' Isaiah's language of relief from sorrow, fear, and hard labor mirrors the Exodus experience.
Isaiah later promises that the Lord will set His hand a second time to recover the remnant of Israel from all the earth. Verse 3 anticipates this second redemptive act.
The New Testament interprets Isaiah's promise of Sabbath rest as pointing to Christ and the rest of faith. The eschatological rest that Isaiah promises is ultimately found in Jesus.
The Doctrine and Covenants speaks of being led out of bondage by the hand of the Lord. Isaiah's promise of relief from servitude is paralleled in modern revelation.

commentary.historical_context: The Babylonian exile (586-538 BCE) was traumatic for Judean consciousness. Not only were people deported and communities destroyed, but the Temple was razed and the land lay desolate for decades. The psychological burden—the fear that God had permanently abandoned Israel—may have been worse than the physical labor. Isaiah's promise of rest addresses both dimensions. The mention of 'hard labor' reflects the reality of exile as servitude; many exiles did become slaves or indentured servants in Babylon.
