commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern treaty language, curses and blessings were standard features. The Hittite vassal treaties (14th-13th centuries BCE) included elaborate curse formulas invoking divine wrath upon those who violated terms. The Aramaic Sefire inscriptions include similar covenant blessings and curses. In Israel's covenantal tradition, Deuteronomy 27–28 is the systematic presentation of covenant blessings and curses. However, Isaiah 24:6 represents an escalation: the curses are not invoked for a single nation's covenant violation but for universal human transgression. The curse consumes not a vassal state but the entire earth.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon teaches that the curse follows transgression inevitably. In Alma 41:11–15, Alma explains: 'Do not suppose, because I said ye are not guilty, that ye shall escape the bands of justice; for I say unto you, that ye shall have a perfect knowledge of all things which you have done, save it were the things which were wiped out by the mercies of God. But behold, the Spirit hath said, this may not be; saying: The Lord cannot look upon sin with the least degree of allowance.' The curse of covenant violation cannot be escaped except through Christ's mercy. The Book of Mormon offers hope that the remnant can repent and be saved (Alma 46:24).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:31–32 warns of the curse: 'For I the Lord cannot look upon sin with the least degree of allowance; Nevertheless, he that repents and does the commandments of the Lord shall be forgiven.' The curse is real and inevitable unless repented of. D&C 87–88 describes the judgments to come in the latter days—wars, famines, earthquakes—as the activated curse of covenant violation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that sin separates us from God's presence (symbolized by the veil). The curse of judgment is represented in the temple by expulsion from the celestial room. However, the temple also teaches that repentance and obedience to covenants restore us. The blood of Christ (represented in the covenant ceremony) is the means by which the curse is lifted.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the one who bears the curse. Galatians 3:13 states: 'Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.' Christ's crucifixion—the ultimate curse under Jewish law—becomes the means of redemption. When Isaiah describes the curse 'devouring the earth,' and when Christ suffers as the curse-bearer, his suffering becomes the means by which the curse is satisfied and removed for those who believe. In this sense, the remnant that survives verse 6's judgment is preserved through Christ's future redemptive work. Romans 5:9 teaches: 'Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him.' Christ is the one who transforms the curse into blessing through his Atonement.
commentary.application: This verse is difficult to apply because it is not primarily exhortatory but descriptive—it announces what *is* happening, not what *ought* to happen. Yet it contains two crucial truths for the modern covenant member. First, it affirms the reality of judgment: 'I live in a moral universe where covenant violation has consequences. These consequences are not arbitrary but built into the structure of creation itself. I cannot break my covenants without experiencing the curse.' This is both sobering and empowering: sobering because it teaches that our choices have cosmic weight, empowering because it means we are not victims of random fate but agents in a universe that responds to our faithfulness. Second, it offers the promise of the remnant: 'Even in judgment, a remnant survives. I may be numbered among the few because God's mercy preserves the faithful.' For the modern member, this means: 'Do I take my covenant seriously enough to keep it even when others break theirs? Am I willing to be part of the remnant—the small, faithful group—rather than being consumed with the masses who abandon their covenants?' The verse also challenges us to discern the difference between natural consequences (the curse flowing from transgression) and redemptive suffering (the suffering that purifies and refines the faithful). In our own trials, are we experiencing the curse of our own transgression, or are we experiencing the refinement that comes through faithfulness?

text_kjv: The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth, all the merryhearted do sigh.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah's apocalyptic vision shifts from cosmic judgment to its most intimate consequence: the collapse of human celebration. The new wine and vine—symbols of fertility, abundance, and covenant blessing throughout Hebrew scripture—now mourn and languish. This is not merely agricultural failure; it is the silencing of joy itself. In ancient Near Eastern culture, wine represented the fruits of God's covenant blessing (Deuteronomy 7:13), and its failure signals a fundamental rupture in the relationship between heaven and earth. The verb 'mourneth' (אָבַל, evel) uses the language of funeral lament, suggesting that wine itself grieves the end of creation's order.

The poetic parallelism moves from the personified wine and vine to 'all the merryhearted'—those whose entire existence revolved around simchah (joy, gladness). The Covenant Rendering captures this precisely: 'all who were glad at heart now sigh.' These are not frivolous people; they are those whose hearts were naturally disposed toward rejoicing, whose baseline disposition was one of celebration. The sigh (נֶאֶנְח֖וּ, ne'enchu) is the sound of profound disappointment—a breath expelled when hope dies. In the Day of the Lord, even the capacity for joy is taken from humanity.

word_study.meaning: To mourn, grieve, lament; used especially of funeral mourning and deep sorrow
word_study.significance: This verb appears in contexts of intense grief (Genesis 37:34, where Jacob mourns Joseph). Applying it to wine personalizes the catastrophe—nature itself grieves the end of the old world.

word_study.meaning: To wither, droop, languish; to lose vitality and vigor
word_study.significance: The vine loses its fundamental character. The word suggests not just damage but a loss of essence—the vine can no longer be what it was created to be.

word_study.meaning: Those glad of heart; literally, 'gladness-of-heart people'—those whose hearts are characterized by joy
word_study.significance: This is not a description of a momentary emotion but of a fundamental character disposition. These are the optimists, the celebrants, the ones who have built their entire lives around the assumption that creation is fundamentally good and that joy is humanity's proper condition. Their sigh marks a spiritual catastrophe.

word_study.meaning: To sigh, groan, breathe heavily—an involuntary expression of grief or weariness
word_study.significance: The sigh is not articulate prayer or lament; it is the wordless sound of someone whose spirit has been broken. It appears also in Ezekiel 21:7, describing the sighing of the despairing.

cross_references.connection: Wine is listed as part of God's covenantal blessing: 'He will...give thee wine and oil.' Its mourning in Isaiah 24:7 represents the reversal of all covenant promises.
Wine 'maketh glad the heart of man,' establishing wine as a divinely appointed means of human joy and thanksgiving—making its languishing in Isaiah 24 a rupture of divine order.
A parallel apocalyptic vision where vine and fig tree wither and agricultural produce fails, collapsing human celebration into mourning.
Warnings about vineyard plantations becoming desolate as judgment for social injustice; Isaiah 24:7 fulfills this prophetic threat on a cosmic scale.
New Testament apocalyptic echo: cosmic disorder following divine judgment, including the failure of natural order and human systems built upon it.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, wine festivals were central to religious and civic life. The autumn vintage (grape harvest) was associated with the Feast of Ingathering and represented successful completion of the agricultural cycle. Vineyards required years of cultivation and were metaphors for corporate peace and stability (Micah 4:4). The collapse of vineyards—whether through war, blight, or divine judgment—was understood as a civilizational catastrophe, not merely an economic setback. Archaeological evidence from Iron Age Levantine sites shows that wine production and distribution were critical to elite status and interstate relationships. When Isaiah speaks of wine mourning, he invokes the deepest anxieties of an agrarian society dependent on seasonal cycles and divine favor.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains echoes of this pattern in 3 Nephi 8:6-10, where Nephite civilization collapses and the natural world is thrown into chaos by divine judgment following rejection of Jesus Christ. Like Isaiah's mourning wine, Nephite agriculture fails and celebrations cease.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:29-30 warns that those who receive not the gospel 'shall have pestilence, and plague, and earthquake, and the thunder of heaven' and 'shall hear of wars and rumors of wars'—precisely the collapse of natural order and human celebration that Isaiah 24:7 describes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The wine of the sacrament, associated with covenant renewal in the temple, stands in direct contrast to Isaiah's mourning wine. The sacrament wine represents the restoration of joy through Christ; Isaiah's wine mourns the absence of the redemptive ordinance.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 24:7 prefigures the darkness that falls at Christ's crucifixion (Matthew 27:45), when even natural light is extinguished. More profoundly, it points to the necessary judgment that precedes redemption: the old world order must collapse so that Christ can establish His eternal kingdom. The mourning of the vine anticipates the vine imagery of John 15:1-5, where Christ becomes 'the true vine' and restoration of fruitfulness depends on abiding in Him.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse asks a searching question: Upon what are you building your joy? If your gladness is rooted in the wine of worldly prosperity, entertainment, and natural abundance—things that will fail in the last days—your foundation is unstable. True Christian joy, by contrast, is built on Christ and covenant, which cannot be shaken. This verse calls us to examine whether we are 'simchei-lev,' truly glad of heart in the deeper sense: glad because of the Restoration, glad because of covenants made, glad because of Christ's atoning promise. When trials come and earthly joys languish, the joy of the covenant remains.

text_kjv: The mirth of tabrets ceaseth, the noise of them that rejoice endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth.

commentary.narrative:
If verse 7 moved from agricultural symbol to human emotion, verse 8 eliminates the instruments of celebration themselves. Three musical instruments represent the full range of celebratory sound in ancient Israel: the tambourine (tupim) for percussion, the unnamed tumult of the revelers (alizzim) suggesting spontaneous vocal celebration, and the lyre (kinnor) for melodic accompaniment. Each instrument is associated with specific contexts: tambourines with women's dances and victory celebrations (Exodus 15:20, Judges 11:34), the lyre with professional musicians and court entertainment (1 Samuel 16:23), and spontaneous rejoicing with harvest festivals and religious processions. The triple cessation is not accidental; it is comprehensive—every mode of human musical expression, every channel through which joy was expressed, falls silent.

The verb 'ceaseth' (שָׁבַת, shavat) carries ironic weight. Ordinarily, shavat means to cease work and observe the Sabbath—a day of rest and cessation from labor. But here, shavat describes the cessation of joy, music, and celebration. The Day of the Lord inverts the Sabbath itself: instead of resting from work, humanity is silenced into a horrifying quiet. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes this silence: 'The joyful tambourines have ceased... the noise of the revelers has stopped... the joyful lyre has ceased.' The triple repetition of 'ceased' or 'stopped' creates a cascading finality, like dominoes falling: one instrument falls silent, then another, then another, until all sound has been extinguished.

word_study.meaning: Joy, merriment, gladness—the pleasurable feeling and its outward expression
word_study.significance: Mesosim is joy expressed and celebrated, not merely felt. It is the joy of community and festival. Its cessation means not only inner sorrow but the collapse of shared celebration and communal identity.

word_study.meaning: Tambourines, hand-drums, percussion instruments; associated particularly with women and with celebratory occasions
word_study.significance: Tuppim appear throughout scripture in contexts of joy: miriam's dance at the Red Sea crossing (Exodus 15:20), celebrations at David's coronation (2 Samuel 6:5). Their silencing represents the end of women's voices and the cessation of family and community celebration.

word_study.meaning: The exultant ones, the revelers, those lifted up (from alaz, to be jubilant); may also suggest those who are arrogant or proud in their celebration
word_study.significance: Alizzim describes not quiet contentment but boisterous, ecstatic rejoicing. The root alaz sometimes carries connotations of pride or presumption in jubilation. Their ending may suggest judgment not only on joy itself but on the arrogant confidence that presumed endless security.

word_study.meaning: Lyre, harp; a stringed instrument of the Levantine musical tradition, associated with skilled musicians and court entertainment
word_study.significance: The kinnor represents artistic beauty and refined expression. Its silence marks the end not only of crude celebration but of refined culture, music, and art. David's playing of the kinnor (1 Samuel 16:23) soothed troubled spirits; its cessation represents the loss of music's healing and spiritual power.

word_study.meaning: To cease, stop, rest; used in Exodus 20:11 for God's rest on the seventh day (Sabbath); can also mean to desist or give up
word_study.significance: The ironic reversal of Sabbath language is crucial. Ordinary shavat brings peace and restoration; this shavat brings desolation. It is a false Sabbath, a cessation that brings no healing.

cross_references.connection: Miriam and the women celebrate the Red Sea deliverance with tambourines and dance—the opposite of Isaiah 24:8, where all such celebration is silenced by judgment.
David's harp brings comfort and healing to Saul's troubled spirit; in Isaiah 24:8, the harp's healing power is removed and silence reigns.
Exiled Jews cannot play their harps in a foreign land; similarly, in Isaiah 24, the instruments of joy are forcibly stilled by judgment.
Babylon's judgment includes the silence of harpists and musicians—a direct echo of Isaiah 24:8 applied to end-times judgment of a worldly city.
Amos condemns those who 'invent to yourselves instruments of music' and indulge in luxury while ignoring injustice; Isaiah 24:8 fulfills this warning as judgment falls.

commentary.historical_context: Music in the ancient Near East served multiple functions: religious procession and temple worship, military morale, court entertainment, and community celebration. Archaeological evidence from Levantine sites shows musical instruments (lyres, harps, tambourines, lutes) were prestige items, often featured in royal tomb paintings and palace reliefs. The Assyrian siege reliefs depict conquered peoples as characterized by silence and captivity—the end of music marked the end of freedom and identity. In Israel's covenantal theology, music and celebration were expected responses to divine blessing (Leviticus 23:40, where instruments and song are part of the Feast of Booths). The silencing of instruments thus represented not merely cultural loss but theological catastrophe: the signs of God's favor had been withdrawn.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 3 Nephi 8:10-14, the destruction visited upon the Nephites includes overwhelming darkness where 'there could be no light, because of the smoke which did arise up unto heaven.' Like Isaiah's silenced instruments, there is a profound absence of the normal signs of life and joy. The restoration comes through Christ's voice (3 Nephi 9:1-2), suggesting that true joy is restored only through hearing the word of Christ, not through human musical instruments alone.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 25:12 (given to Emma Smith) speaks of the value of 'music and the sound thereof...a pleasant thing before me.' This directly reverses Isaiah 24:8; in the Restoration, music is restored as a covenant gift. The hymnody of the Restoration—both in Smith's era and in modern LDS practice—represents the recovery of joy and music as sacred and central to covenant life.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple worship includes music and singing (particularly in the endowment); this represents the fulfillment of what Isaiah 24:8 foresees as lost. The temple is the place where the silence of judgment is reversed and the instruments of praise are heard again in the presence of God.

commentary.christological_typology: The silencing of musical celebration anticipates the darkness and silence that fell at Christ's crucifixion—'from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land' (Matthew 27:45). Yet this typologically points to the greater restoration: Christ's resurrection restores the song of triumph and the music of redemption. Revelation 5:8-9 envisions the eternal counterpart to Isaiah 24:8: 'And when he had taken the book, the four beasts and four and twenty elders fell down before the Lamb, having every one of them harps...and they sung a new song.' Where Isaiah's instruments fall silent, Revelation's are eternally restored through Christ.
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, this verse invites us to consider: What is the source of your joy and celebration? Are your happiness and security rooted in worldly entertainment, music, and cultural celebration—things that will fail? Or are they rooted in Christ and His covenants, which cannot be shaken? For Latter-day Saints, music and the arts are important (D&C 25:12), but they are subordinate to the covenants themselves. When trials come and earthly celebrations cease—whether through personal loss, economic collapse, or the final judgment—will your foundation remain? The verse calls us to ensure that our deepest joy comes not from the harp and tambourine but from hearing the voice of Christ and keeping His covenants.

text_kjv: They shall not drink wine with a song; strong drink shall be bitter to them that drink it.

commentary.narrative:
The vision has now moved from the failure of agricultural production (verse 7) and the silencing of instruments (verse 8) to the complete inversion of the sensory and emotional experience of wine itself. In ordinary times, wine is drunk 'with a song'—the act of drinking is inseparable from celebration, from the raising of a cup in joy accompanied by music and vocal praise. This pairing of wine and song represents the full social and spiritual integration of celebration: the taste, the sound, the community, and the sacred occasion all reinforce one another. But in the Day of the Lord, this integration collapses. Wine can still be consumed, but it no longer tastes like joy; instead, it becomes bitter.

The verb 'yemar' (יֵמַ֥ר, is bitter) carries profound theological weight. Bitterness in Hebrew scripture is associated with grief, hardship, and the reversal of blessing (Ruth 1:20, where Naomi calls herself Mara, 'bitter,' after losing her husband and sons). The Covenant Rendering notes this connection precisely. But more than that, bitter wine was explicitly forbidden in the temple's libation offerings—bitterness was incompatible with covenant worship. Here, the wine itself has become ritually corrupted, unable to serve its function as a symbol of joy and blessing. The parallelism between verses 9a ('They shall not drink wine with a song') and 9b ('strong drink shall be bitter') suggests a causal relationship: wine becomes bitter precisely because it can no longer be drunk in the context of celebration. The joy is gone, and without joy, even the wine tastes like sorrow.

word_study.meaning: In/with singing they shall not drink wine; the preposition ba- (in/with) connects drinking inseparably to song
word_study.significance: The pairing of wine and song is not accidental but constitutive; to drink wine was always to drink it accompanied by singing. The severance of this pairing represents a fundamental rupture in human social and spiritual experience. Wine divorced from song is wine divested of its meaning.

word_study.meaning: To be or become bitter; from the root m-r-r, which denotes both the taste of bitterness and the emotional state of grief and hardship
word_study.significance: The same root appears in Ruth 1:20 ('call me not Naomi [pleasant], but call me Mara [bitter]') and in Exodus 12:8 (bitter herbs at Passover, eaten in remembrance of slavery). Here, the bitterness is involuntary—the wine itself has become bitter, not by choice but by the judgment of God. Taste and emotion merge: the wine tastes bitter because the heart is broken.

word_study.meaning: Strong drink, intoxicating beverage—not specifically wine but any fermented or distilled drink with higher alcohol content
word_study.significance: The Hebrew distinguishes between yayin (wine, from grapes) and shekar (strong drink, from other sources—barley, dates, etc.). The parallelism suggests that no fermented beverage, whether wine or shekar, retains its sweetness and celebration value in the Day of the Lord. Even the strongest drink becomes bitter.

cross_references.connection: Naomi renames herself Mara (bitter) after losing her husband and sons, using the same root m-r-r as Isaiah 24:9; both verses connect bitterness to the reversal of blessing.
Bitter herbs eaten at Passover commemorate slavery and suffering; in Isaiah 24:9, the bitterness of wine represents not remembrance but the actual presence of judgment.
Those who plant vineyards shall not drink wine from them (because judgment will take the harvest); Isaiah 24:9 extends this—even the wine that remains becomes bitter.
God holds a cup of wine 'full of mixture,' and the wicked must drink it and wring out its dregs; Isaiah 24:9 describes the universal drinking of this bitter cup in the Day of the Lord.
At Christ's crucifixion, He is offered sour wine (vinegar)—a foreshadowing of the inversion of joy and blessing that Isaiah 24:9 describes as characteristic of divine judgment.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, wine was fundamentally connected to celebration, covenant-making, and religious observance. Drinking wine was an act embedded in social ritual: the host offered wine to guests as a sign of welcome and honor, covenants were sealed with shared wine, and religious festivals included prescribed wine libations. Egyptian tomb paintings show wine-drinking scenes; Mesopotamian texts describe royal banquets with wine as the centerpiece of hospitality. In Israel specifically, wine was integral to the three pilgrimage festivals (Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles) and was forbidden in certain contexts (Nazarite vows, priestly service) to mark separation or consecration. The bitterness of wine would have been experienced not merely as a taste sensation but as a complete inversion of social order: the sign of blessing becomes the sign of curse; the emblem of hospitality becomes a symbol of alienation; the drink of covenant becomes the drink of judgment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 3 Nephi 8:6-10, the Nephites experience a similar reversal of the natural world following their rejection of Christ and their wickedness. The catastrophic darkness and destruction represent the inversion of blessing. Notably, the Book of Mormon Restoration (post-crucifixion Christ appearances) restores joy and celebration; the resurrected Lord's presence is accompanied not by bitter drink but by the restored promise of eternal covenant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 27:2-3 reveals that in the celestial kingdom, the sacramental wine will be 'pure wine of the grape' and will be taken 'as symbolical of my blood.' This directly reverses Isaiah 24:9: in the Restoration, wine is restored to its proper function as a symbol of covenant and redemption, no longer bitter but sweetened by the atonement of Christ. The sacrament represents the ultimate reversal of Isaiah's prophecy of bitterness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The sacrament of the Lord's Supper, central to LDS covenant practice, uses wine (or water as substitute) to commemorate Christ's blood shed for the remission of sins. This ordinance is performed in a context of joy and thanksgiving—the opposite of Isaiah 24:9. The temple, as the place where covenants are made and renewed, is where the bitterness of judgment is transformed into the sweetness of redemption.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 24:9 prefigures Christ's drinking of the bitter cup in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39-42, Mark 14:36), where He prays, 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.' Christ willingly drinks the bitter cup of judgment—the cup of divine wrath against sin—so that humanity need not. Yet through His atonement, the bitterness is transformed: the wine of the new covenant becomes 'the blood of Christ shed for the remission of sins' (D&C 27:2), which is celebrated with joy rather than mourning. The verse points to the necessity of Christ's vicarious suffering; only through His willingness to taste bitterness can the eternal sweetness of redemption be restored.
commentary.application: For modern members of the Church, this verse teaches a vital lesson about the sources of true satisfaction. Wine and strong drink are used in Isaiah 24 as symbols of worldly pleasure and the satisfaction sought through material indulgence. In the Day of the Lord, these sources of joy fail and become bitter. The verse calls us to examine: Are we seeking satisfaction in alcohol, entertainment, or material luxury? If so, we are building on sand. True satisfaction comes through Christ and covenant. The sacrament, taken in place of wine in the LDS tradition, represents the substitution of eternal covenant for temporary indulgence. When we partake of bread and water in remembrance of Christ, we are choosing the joy that cannot be taken away—the joy of forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal life. This verse warns that all other joys will ultimately fail; only covenant joy endures.

text_kjv: The city of confusion is broken down: every house is shut up, that no man may come in.

commentary.narrative:
With verse 10, Isaiah's apocalyptic vision shifts from the sensory and emotional devastation of nature and celebration to the complete structural collapse of human civilization itself. The mysterious 'city of confusion' (qiryat-tohu) stands at the center of this verse, and its identity has puzzled interpreters for centuries. Scholars have proposed Babylon, Jerusalem, or even a generic, archetypal city representing all human civilization built without God. The deliberate vagueness may be intentional: in the final judgment, every city becomes the city of chaos. Yet the name itself is theologically charged. The word 'tohu' (תֹּהוּ) appears in Genesis 1:2, describing the primordial chaos before God's creative word brought order: 'And the earth was without form [tohu] and void.' Isaiah suggests that human cities, no matter their grandeur or perceived permanence, are fundamentally unstable—they are built upon sand and will revert to the formlessness from which all creation emerged.

The practical consequence is total social collapse: 'every house is shut up, that no man may come in.' Houses represent not merely shelter but the fundamental unit of social organization, family continuity, and community. In ancient Mediterranean societies, the house was the economic center, the repository of family identity across generations, and the basic unit of social participation. The sealing of houses means the end of hospitality, the cessation of economic activity, the breakdown of family and community life. The verb 'shut up' (סֻגַּר, sugar) suggests forced closure—not willing retreat but compulsory abandonment. No one enters because there is nothing left to enter for; no one is there to welcome; the structure that gave meaning to human habitation has been unmade. The Covenant Rendering's simpler phrasing—'The city of chaos is broken; every house is shut, none may enter'—emphasizes the absolute finality: there is no recovery, no eventual reopening, no possibility of return.

word_study.meaning: City of chaos, city of formlessness, city of emptiness; tohu is the state of primordial disorder before creation's ordering
word_study.significance: The Hebrew tohu is theological language borrowed from creation theology (Genesis 1:2). To call a city 'qiryat-tohu' is to say it has been unmade, returned to pre-creation disorder. Whether specific or archetypal, the city represents all human efforts to build lasting civilization independent of God's creative and sustaining word. The identification with tohu suggests that without covenant relationship to God, all human cities are fundamentally unstable.

word_study.meaning: Is broken, shattered, fractured; suggests not demolition but the shattering of something that was thought to be solid
word_study.significance: The verb suggests the violent, sudden fracturing of what had seemed permanent and stable. The city's collapse is not gradual decay but catastrophic failure—the breaking of what was presumed unbreakable.

word_study.meaning: House, dwelling, household, family; the fundamental unit of social and economic organization
word_study.significance: In Hebrew thinking, bayit is not merely a structure but a social and economic institution. To shut every bayit is to destroy the basic social fabric. The household is where family identity persists across generations; its sealing represents the end of continuity and hope.

word_study.meaning: Shut, closed, sealed; suggests being locked or barred from entry
word_study.significance: The passive voice suggests enforced closure—not chosen but imposed. No one can enter because entry is impossible, the structure is unusable, or the purpose for which houses exist has been eliminated.

cross_references.connection: The earth was 'without form' (tohu) before God's creative word; Isaiah 24:10 suggests that without God's covenant, human cities revert to this primordial tohu—unmade by judgment.
Another apocalyptic vision using tohu language: the prophet sees the earth 'without form and void' (tohu) as if uncreation had reversed God's work, paralleling Isaiah's vision of the unmade city.
After Jerusalem's destruction: 'Our inheritance is turned to strangers, our houses to aliens'—the loss of homes and the shutting of houses as judgment.
Christ prophesies: 'There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down'—the city and its buildings will be utterly broken, echoing Isaiah 24:10.
The destruction of Babylon in Revelation uses imagery of a broken, desolate city with no inhabitants entering or dwelling—a direct fulfillment of Isaiah 24:10's prophecy.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, cities were the centers of civilization, commerce, and political power. Mesopotamian and Egyptian cities like Babylon, Memphis, and Thebes were understood as permanent achievements—monumental, wealthy, and enduring. City walls represented security and identity; breaking the walls meant the end of a city's independence and power. The concept of a city reduced to desolation was deeply threatening to ancient thinking because it represented the reversal of civilization itself. Archaeological evidence shows that conquered cities were often systematically dismantled: walls broken, buildings burned, houses left empty. Assyrian and Babylonian siege accounts (like the Annals of Sargon II) describe the total destruction of cities as a demonstration of the conquering nation's absolute power. For Isaiah's original audience, the prophecy would have resonated with this historical experience: they had seen Assyrian destruction and knew the reality of broken cities and sealed houses. The addition of tohu language, however, elevates this beyond historical destruction to cosmic reversal.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon describes the destruction visited upon Nephite cities in 3 Nephi 8:8-14: 'And thus the face of the whole earth became deformed, because of the tempests, and the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the quaking of the earth.' The cities are broken, and 'there were no lights seen, nor fires kindled by the children of men' (3 Nephi 8:22). Like Isaiah's sealed houses, the Nephite cities are emptied of life and light. The Restoration message, however, is that Christ's appearance ends this desolation (3 Nephi 9:1-2), suggesting that judgment is not final but preparatory for redemption.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:8-9 describes the Lord's judgment: 'And I have sent forth the fullness of my gospel by the hand of my servant Joseph; and in weakness have I blessed him...that the residue of my people might be converted from all unrighteousness, that they may be numbered with the righteous, that I may preserve them.' The sealing of houses in Isaiah represents judgment on those who refuse the gospel; the Restoration offers the alternative: accept the gospel and escape the desolation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple stands in contrast to the sealed houses of Isaiah 24:10. In the temple, houses of covenant are opened; families are sealed together; the destruction of natural family bonds through death is reversed by eternal covenants. The temple family sealing (D&C 132) represents the opening of the sealed houses and the preservation of family continuity—the opposite of Isaiah's vision of sealed, desolate houses.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 24:10 foreshadows the destruction of the Jerusalem temple and the city itself under Roman siege in 70 CE, events that became a type of the final judgment and the end of the old covenant order. Yet Christ's resurrection inaugurates a new covenant and a new city—the New Jerusalem of Revelation 21:2-4, where God dwells with men and every tear is wiped away. The sealed houses of Isaiah become the open dwelling of God with humanity in Christ; the broken city becomes the eternal city with foundations and builder is God (Hebrews 11:10). Christ is the one who, through His death and resurrection, transforms the judgment represented by sealed and broken cities into the promise of an eternal, unbreakable covenant.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, this verse asks: What are you building your life upon? If your security is rooted in material wealth, property ownership, career status, or civic prestige—things that can be broken and sealed away—then you are building upon tohu, the formlessness that will ultimately undo all human civilization. The verse calls us to build our houses (both literal and spiritual families) upon the rock of Christ and covenant, not upon the shifting sand of worldly achievement. In a time of uncertainty, when economic collapse, war, or natural disaster can reduce cities to desolation, the only secure foundation is the eternal covenant of marriage and family sealed in the temple. Those who have made and kept temple covenants possess a 'house' that cannot be broken or sealed away—an eternal family union that transcends mortal destruction. The sealing ordinances of the temple represent the answer to Isaiah's vision of sealed, desolate houses.

text_kjv: There is a crying for wine in the streets; all joy is darkened, the mirth of the land is gone.

commentary.narrative:
Having moved from personal grief (verse 7), to the silencing of instruments (verse 8), to the bitterness of wine (verse 9), to the breaking of civilization (verse 10), Isaiah now captures the human response to total desolation: a desperate, anguished cry for the very thing that can no longer be found. The 'crying for wine in the streets' (צְוָחָ֥ה עַל־הַיַּ֖יִן בַּחוּצ֑וֹת, tzva'acha al-hayayin ba-chutzot) is not a mere request but an anguished outcry—the shout of those who desperately seek restoration of what has been lost. Wine, which throughout these verses has represented blessing, celebration, and covenant joy, is now the object of desperate longing precisely because it is absent. The verb 'tzva'acha' (צְוָחָה) denotes a sharp, piercing cry—not a quiet whimper but an anguished shout that pierces the silence of the desolate streets.

The remaining parallel phrases deepen the desolation: 'all joy is darkened, the mirth of the land is gone.' The Covenant Rendering captures these precisely with 'all joy has grown dark; the gladness of the earth is banished.' The verb 'arvah' (עָֽרְבָה, has grown dark) is exceptionally vivid—it literally means to grow dark or set (as the sun sets), using sunset imagery to describe the disappearance of joy. Joy has not been destroyed but has sunk below the horizon, as though light itself has left the world. Meanwhile, the verb 'galah' (גָּלָ֖ה, has been banished, exiled) uses the language of exile—the same word used for the Babylonian captivity of Judah's people. Here, joy itself has been exiled from the earth, deported like a captive people, never to return. The escalation is stark: first wine mourns and tastes bitter, then joy is darkened, then gladness itself is banished—there is no joy left, not even in memory or hope.

word_study.meaning: Outcry over the wine, anguished shouting for wine; the preposition 'al' (over/for) suggests both lamentation and urgent seeking
word_study.significance: The people cry out, but their cry is futile—there is no wine, no restoration. The cry itself becomes a sign of the absolute deprivation. The word tzva'acha appears elsewhere in contexts of extreme distress (Exodus 12:30, the cry at the firstborn's death; Judges 15:14, Samson's shout in battle). Here it is the cry of those confronting utter loss.

word_study.meaning: Joy, gladness, happiness—both the feeling and its celebration
word_study.significance: Simcha is more comprehensive than momentary happiness; it represents the fundamental orientation of life toward the good and the blessed. Its darkening means not a temporary sadness but the permanent eclipse of human hope and well-being.

word_study.meaning: Has become dark, grown dark, set (as a sun setting); from the root 'arav, suggesting obscurity or sunset
word_study.significance: The sunset metaphor is precise: joy does not cease violently but gradually disappears over the horizon, the way the sun disappears at dusk. There is no explosion, no drama—only a slow, inexorable dimming until darkness is complete. The word appears elsewhere in contexts of approaching night or concealment.

word_study.meaning: Joy, merriment, celebration—the outward expression and communal sharing of gladness (see verse 8)
word_study.significance: Mesosim, like simcha, represents not individual emotion but communal celebration. The banishing of mesosim means not only the end of private happiness but the collapse of all shared celebration and community identity.

word_study.meaning: To depart, go into exile, be removed, banished; the word used for the Babylonian exile of Judah
word_study.significance: The use of exile language suggests that joy does not merely fade but is forcibly removed, deported, expelled—an active judgment rather than passive loss. Joy is treated as a captive people torn from its homeland and scattered, never to return. The Israelites' historical experience of exile is here universalized as the exile of joy itself in the end times.

cross_references.connection: A great cry (tzva'acha) goes through Egypt when the firstborn die; similarly, Isaiah 24:11 describes a despairing cry in the streets, but this time over the absence of wine and joy.
Jerusalem after destruction: 'How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow!'—the desolate city where joy has vanished, mirroring Isaiah 24:11.

God's judgment on Babylon: 'And I will take from them the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride'—a direct parallel to Isaiah's vision of silenced mirth.
Agricultural collapse results in lamentation: 'The fields are wasted...the joy of the sons of men is withered'—the same progression from harvest failure to joy's disappearance.

The merchants weep and mourn when Babylon falls: 'The fruit that thy soul lusted after is departed from thee...and the light of a candle shall shine no more at all in thee'—eschatological desolation parallel to Isaiah 24:11.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the public streets were centers of economic, social, and religious life. They were where merchants conducted business, where news was proclaimed, where celebrations occurred, and where the vulnerable gathered seeking help. The silencing of the streets—their reduction to places of desperation and futility—represented the total collapse of civilization. Archaeological excavations of destroyed cities show that streets remain, but emptied of their functions and meaning. The image of people crying out in deserted streets would have been viscerally real to Isaiah's audience: they had witnessed this in cities conquered by Assyria. The crying for wine specifically would have resonated as a symbol of the end of all normalcy and blessing—wine being the most universally valued commodity in the ancient Mediterranean economy and the central symbol of festivity and covenant.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 60:21, Moroni describes the temporal consequences of rejecting God's covenant: 'Ye also know that Nephi was a righteous man, notwithstanding the many afflictions which he endured...And behold, his name hath not perished.' The contrast is that even in desolation, the righteous preserve their name and covenant. In 3 Nephi 8:20-22, the darkness covers the land when Christ dies, but Christ's appearance (3 Nephi 9:1-2) restores light and joy—suggesting that Isaiah's vision of darkened joy is temporary and preparatory for restoration through Christ.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:87 speaks of the time when 'every corruptible thing, both of man and of the beasts of the field, and of the fowls of the heavens, and of the fish of the sea, shall be consumed'—the end state foreseen in Isaiah 24:11. Yet D&C 76 and 88 promise that the righteous will be preserved, their joy not banished but eternal. The Restoration teaching is that while the world's joy fails, the joy of the covenant people continues and is exalted.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where joy is consciously preserved and celebrated—not the frivolous joy of worldly celebration but the deep joy of covenant union with God and family. Temple work, including ordinances for the dead, represents the refusal to allow joy and connection to be banished; instead, these bonds are sealed eternally and made accessible beyond mortality.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 24:11 foreshadows Christ's experience on the cross, where He takes upon Himself the weight of human sin and alienation, crying out 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' (Matthew 27:46, quoting Psalm 22:1). Yet Christ's resurrection reverses this: the darkness gives way to light, the banishment of joy gives way to eternal celebration. The post-resurrection appearances of Christ in the Book of Mormon include joyful celebration and feasting (3 Nephi 20:8-9), suggesting that Christ's work restores what Isaiah 24:11 shows as lost. The 'marriage supper of the Lamb' (Revelation 19:7-9) represents the ultimate reversal: not crying for wine in empty streets, but celebration in the presence of God's redemptive work.
commentary.application: For modern members of the Church, this verse teaches a sobering but liberating truth: worldly joy is temporary and fragile, subject to being stripped away. Economic collapse, personal loss, or global catastrophe can silence the celebrations on which people have built their identity and hope. But covenant joy—the joy that comes from keeping sacred covenants, from family bonds sealed eternally, from the knowledge of Christ's atonement—cannot be banished. The verse calls us to ensure that our deepest source of joy is not the wine of worldly success but the water of eternal life, not the mirth of temporal celebrations but the gladness of covenant community. When trials come and the streets of the world fall silent, will your joy remain? It will, if it is rooted in Christ and covenant rather than in material circumstance. This verse is an invitation to choose the joy that cannot be darkened or banished.

text_kjv: In the city is left desolation, and the gate is smitten with destruction.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah's apocalyptic vision concludes this opening section with a final image of total civic collapse. Having described the crying for wine in the streets (verse 11), the prophet now zooms in on two specific features of ancient city life: the desolate city itself and the broken gate. The Covenant Rendering renders this concisely: 'Desolation remains in the city; the gate is battered to ruins.' The shift from crying in the streets to absolute desolation suggests a progression: first there are still people present, desperately seeking what has been lost, but ultimately even their presence ceases and only emptiness remains. The verb 'nish'ar' (נִשְׁאַ֥ר, is left, remains) suggests not activity but what persists when all else has been stripped away—desolation is what remains when desolation is complete.

The gate, in particular, deserves attention. In ancient Near Eastern cities, the gate was far more than a physical structure; it was the center of civic, commercial, and judicial life. The city gate was where merchants negotiated contracts, where judges rendered decisions, where elders sat in counsel, where news was announced, and where the city's identity was maintained and defended. The destruction of the gate was therefore not merely architectural but the destruction of the city's fundamental function and identity. The verb 'yuka' (יֻכַּת, is smitten, struck) uses the language of military assault—the gate has been beaten down as if by an invading army or by the hand of a warrior. The Hebrew word for destruction here (שָֽׁעַר, sha'ar) echoes the gate itself (also sha'ar), creating a pun: the gate (sha'ar) is beaten to ruins (sha'ar)—the gate's very name becomes associated with its destruction. What once stood as a symbol of the city's security and identity is reduced to ruins.

word_study.meaning: Desolation, devastation, ruin, waste; the state of being emptied and abandoned
word_study.significance: Shammah appears frequently in Deuteronomy and the Prophets as the consequence of covenant violation and judgment (Deuteronomy 29:23, Isaiah 61:4). It describes not mere damage but the reduction of a place to emptiness and non-functionality. The persistence of shammah ('is left') suggests a permanent state, not temporary damage.

word_study.meaning: Is left, remains, is preserved, survives; often used of a remnant or what persists after destruction
word_study.significance: The verb suggests that while other things have been stripped away (people, joy, celebration, function), desolation persists. It is the only thing left standing. The same root appears in Isaiah 24:6 and other passages describing the remnant of Israel (she'ar), creating a thematic connection: what remains (nish'ar) is desolation, unless grace preserves a remnant (she'ar).

word_study.meaning: Gate, city gate; the entrance structure of a city; metaphorically, the place of authority, law, and community decision-making
word_study.significance: In Hebrew thinking, the gate is not merely defensive but civic. The elders sat at the gate (Ruth 4:1-12), judges rendered verdicts at the gate (Amos 5:12-15), and the health of the gate reflected the health of the city (Proverbs 31:31). Its destruction represents the end of civic order and authority.

word_study.meaning: Is smitten, is struck, is beaten; past participle suggesting a completed action of violent striking
word_study.significance: The word appears in military contexts (warriors striking enemies) and in contexts of divine judgment (God striking down the wicked). It suggests not decay or gradual wear but violent, sudden destruction—the gate has been actively destroyed by force.

word_study.meaning: Both terms mean desolation, ruin, waste—the first more general, the second suggesting utter emptiness and complete abandonment
word_study.significance: The pairing of shammah and she'iyyah creates a poetic emphasis through synonym parallelism, as the Covenant Rendering notes. The gate is not partially damaged but utterly ruined; the city is not wounded but completely desolate. The repetition of the concept through different words underscores absolute, total destruction.

cross_references.connection: The gate is the place where Boaz conducts legal business and establishes covenants; Isaiah 24:12 describes the gate reduced to ruins, ending all such civic and covenantal activity.
Amos condemns those who 'afflict the just, take a bribe...and turn aside the poor in the gate'; Isaiah 24:12 fulfills the threat that the corrupt gate will be destroyed and justice eliminated.
Jerusalem's destruction: 'Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars'—the same image of the shattered gate as sign of total civic collapse.
The collapse of Nineveh: 'The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved'—the gate's destruction as the final sign of a city's end.
Christ promises that 'the gates of hell shall not prevail against' His church—a reversal of Isaiah's vision; Christ's covenant community will stand when all worldly gates crumble.

commentary.historical_context: Archaeologists excavating destroyed ancient cities find that gates are often the most heavily damaged structures, as they were primary points of assault in siege warfare. Excavations at sites like Lachish, Megiddo, and Hazor show gates reduced to rubble by Assyrian and Babylonian siege forces. The gate was architecturally one of the most complex structures in an ancient city, with multiple chambers and defensive features. Its destruction was both symbolic (the end of the city's identity and authority) and practical (the end of the city's ability to control access and commerce). In cuneiform sources, the destruction of a city's gate was often specifically mentioned in annals as proof of conquest. For Isaiah's audience, the image would have been historically vivid: they had witnessed or heard of gates being battered down. But Isaiah's use of the language suggests not merely historical conquest but eschatological judgment—the gate is not just broken by invading armies but by the hand of God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 3 Nephi 8:8-10, the destruction of Nephite cities includes the breaking of structures and the desolation of the land. Yet in 4 Nephi 1:7-9, after Christ's appearance, the cities are rebuilt and 'there were no contentions and disputations' in the reconstructed cities. The restoration of the city (and its gates, by implication) follows Christ's appearance, suggesting that only Christ's redemptive work can repair what Isaiah 24:12 describes as broken beyond human power to fix.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:17-19 describes the final judgment: 'And the moment that the Gentiles repent, and the gospel is preached to them, then cometh the time of the Gentiles...and then cometh the judgment of the nations.' The destruction of the city gate in Isaiah represents the end of the old civic and political order that rejects the gospel; the Restoration promises that those who accept the gospel will be preserved in a city whose builder is God (Hebrews 11:10, referenced in LDS theology).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the spiritual counterpart to the destroyed city gate. Where the city gate was the center of earthly authority and law, the temple is the center of covenant authority and eternal law. The ordinances performed in the temple (particularly sealing ordinances) establish eternal bonds that transcend the destruction of mortal cities and gates. Those sealed in the temple possess citizenship not in mortal cities but in the 'city of Zion' (D&C 45:66-67), whose gates will never be broken.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 24:12 foreshadows the destruction of the Jerusalem temple and its gates during the Roman siege of 70 CE, events that marked the end of the old temple-based system and prepared for Christ's establishment of a new, spiritual temple. Christ Himself becomes the new gate: 'I am the door [gate]: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved' (John 10:9). Where the city gate is destroyed, Christ becomes the eternal gate through which access to the Father is secured. Revelation 21:12-14 describes the eternal city with twelve gates, each made of pearl—an inversion of Isaiah's broken gates, suggesting that in the redeemed creation, the gates are not destroyed but perfected and eternalized through Christ's redemptive work.
commentary.application: For modern members of the Church, Isaiah 24:12 teaches that mortal cities and their systems of authority—whether civic, commercial, or political—are temporary and subject to destruction. No amount of human engineering, law-making, or institutional strength can prevent the final judgment. But there is an alternative: to seek not citizenship in earthly cities but in 'Zion,' the spiritual city of covenant people. D&C 45:66-67 promises that those who gather in Zion will be preserved: 'Zion shall escape if she observe to do all things whatsoever I have commanded her...for I will protect her against all the nations of the earth.' The verse calls us to ask: Am I seeking security and identity in mortal institutions and cities, or in the covenant of the gospel? Am I trusting in human gates (human authority and systems), or in Christ as the eternal gate? Those who make covenants in the temple and seek to build Zion possess an identity and citizenship that cannot be shattered by the destruction of mortal gates—they are citizens of an eternal city whose foundation is Christ.

text_kjv: When thus it shall be in the midst of the land among the people, there shall be as the shaking of an olive tree, and as the gleaning grapes when the vintage is done.

commentary.narrative:
After twelve verses depicting total desolation—the earth laid waste, its inhabitants scattered, cities broken—Isaiah suddenly shifts from destruction to survival. Verse 13 uses two agricultural metaphors to signal that judgment, though overwhelming, is not annihilation. The olive tree that is beaten (a harvest technique where branches are struck to dislodge ripe fruit) leaves some olives clinging to the highest branches, difficult to reach and thus overlooked. Similarly, grape gleaning (the careful second pass through vineyards to gather missed clusters) always leaves something behind. These are images of remnant, not totality.

The 'midst of the land' and 'among the people' emphasize that this survival happens right where the judgment occurred—no escape to safety, no distant refuge. The survivors are those left behind, the few clusters, the remnant. This is the theological pivot Isaiah announces: even in catastrophic judgment, the Lord preserves a seed. The phrase 'when the vintage is done' (literally 'when the vintage is finished') marks the end of harvesting, yet something remains. The translator notes to The Covenant Rendering observe that this same olive-beating and gleaning imagery appears in Isaiah 17:6, where it explicitly describes a surviving remnant after Assyrian invasion.

word_study.meaning: to beat, strike, shake; specifically the action of striking olive branches to harvest fruit. The root conveys forceful action but with a purpose—this is not random destruction but deliberate harvesting.
word_study.significance: The word reframes judgment as a harvest: violent, yes, but directed and partial. God is not destroying indiscriminately; He is collecting what remains as a farmer collects olives. This dignifies the remnant—they are the harvest, the preserved fruit.

word_study.meaning: gleanings, grape clusters left after the main harvest. The root 'ulla means to glean or gather what remains. These are the forgotten or intentionally left-behind grapes.
word_study.significance: In Torah law (Leviticus 19:10, Deuteronomy 24:21), gleaning was explicitly left for the poor and the foreigner—a covenant mercy. By using this term, Isaiah associates the remnant with those protected by God's law. What is left is not rejected; it is preserved under divine care.

word_study.meaning: grape harvest, the act of vintage or picking grapes. Literally, the word refers to the harvested grapes themselves, but here it names the entire season of harvest.
word_study.significance: The harvest is 'done'—kalah, finished, complete. Yet gleaning continues after. This temporal language suggests that even after judgment is complete, survival persists. A new phase begins after the main destruction.

cross_references.connection: Uses the identical olive-beating and gleaning metaphor to describe the remnant surviving Assyrian judgment. Isaiah returns to this image because it carries consistent theological weight: judgment leaves survivors.

'But yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil tree, and as an oak, whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves: so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof.' The remnant concept is central to Isaiah's entire message.
Mandates leaving gleanings for the poor and stranger, establishing gleaning as an act of covenantal mercy. Isaiah's use of gleaning language evokes this protective law.
Paul cites Isaiah's remnant theology ('though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved'), applying it to the eschatological preservation of Israel.

The parable of the wheat and tares: some are gathered as fruit to the Lord's storehouse, others are bound as bundles for burning. The Lord always separates and preserves the righteous within judgment.

commentary.historical_context: The olive harvest in the ancient Near East occurred in fall; workers would strike branches with rods or poles to dislodge ripe fruit. This was standard agrarian practice. The grape harvest (vintage) was similarly a labor-intensive seasonal event. Isaiah's original audience, whether facing Assyrian or Babylonian threat, would have immediately grasped the agricultural metaphor: just as some fruit always remains after harvest (either on high branches too difficult to reach, or as deliberate gleaning left for the poor), some people would survive the judgment. The imagery would have offered both realism and hope—not 'no judgment' but 'judgment with survival.'

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi quotes and interprets Isaiah's remnant theology extensively (2 Nephi 25–30). The Book of Mormon community understood itself as a literal remnant preserved by the Lord to carry the true faith. Jacob's use of the Isaiah prophecies (2 Nephi 6–10) emphasizes God's mercy to a surviving people. The 'gleaning' metaphor resonates with the theme of God gathering His covenant people from all nations.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 86 (parable of wheat and tares) and D&C 33:6 ('the ends of the earth are full of my glory') reflect similar language of divine preservation within judgment. The concept of the remnant is foundational to Restoration theology—God always preserves a people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ordinances include the concept of gathering and sealing—the sacred work of preserving and binding families to God, much as gleaning preserves and gathers the remaining fruit. The temple is where the remnant is sealed to God.

commentary.christological_typology: The remnant that survives judgment prefigures Christ as the ultimate remnant—'a root out of dry ground' (Isaiah 53:2), the single preserved seed from whom salvation grows. Christ embodies the principle that judgment does not erase mercy; a faithful remnant survives to inherit the covenant.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern readers to understand judgment theologically as precise, not random, and always paired with mercy. When personal crisis, church challenge, or national upheaval feels like total destruction, Isaiah 24:13 teaches that the Lord always preserves a remnant. For the modern covenant community, this means: even in seasons of deep trial, God has a people who remain, who continue the work, who are gathered like precious fruit. The question for each member is: Am I among the remnant that clings to the highest branches—the most faithful—or am I gathered by the Lord as gleaning? Either way, survival in God's hands is not accidental; it is harvested.

text_kjv: They shall lift up their voice, they shall sing for the majesty of the LORD, they shall cry aloud from the sea.

commentary.narrative:
The abruptness of verse 14 is one of the most startling pivots in Isaiah. After thirteen verses of unrelenting judgment—earth laid waste, inhabitants dead or scattered, cities ruined, covenant broken—suddenly the remnant (those who survived the gleaning of v. 13) lift their voices in praise. This is not muted relief or quiet thanksgiving; it is robust, public worship: they 'sing' (literally 'cry out in jubilation'), they 'lift up their voice' (qol, the word for utterance, proclamation, authority), they 'cry aloud.' The emotional and theological shift is disorienting by design—it announces that judgment has an endpoint, and beyond it lies restoration and praise.

The phrase 'from the sea' (or, in The Covenant Rendering, 'from the west') is geographically significant. Ancient Hebrew thought-patterns often used directional references: east = rising, origin; west = setting, horizon. The 'sea' in Hebrew cosmology refers to the Mediterranean, the western boundary. To say the remnant cries aloud 'from the sea' is to suggest that even those in the farthest reaches—the diaspora, the scattered, those pushed to the margins—join in unified praise. Or it may indicate that judgment reaches globally, and the response to it is universal. The phrase 'majesty of the LORD' (ge'on YHWH) uses a word that elsewhere describes human arrogance or pride (ge'on can mean the pride of Moab, the haughtiness of Jacob) but here is applied rightly and exclusively to God. Only God's majesty is legitimate; all human pride is exposed as futility by judgment.

word_study.meaning: pride, splendor, majesty, arrogance. The root carries the sense of rising up, exaltation. It can describe the proud boasting of human kingdoms or the rightful glory of God.
word_study.significance: Throughout Isaiah, ge'on describes human pride that will be brought low (Isaiah 5:15, 10:33). Here, after all human pride has been demolished by judgment, ge'on belongs only to the Lord. The remnant's praise implicitly confesses that all earthly arrogance has been judged away, leaving only the true majesty of God standing.

word_study.meaning: they will raise their voice; qol is utterance, proclamation, authority. To 'lift up' a voice is to make proclamation, to testify, to declare aloud.
word_study.significance: This is not private devotion but public testimony. The remnant declares the majesty of God before witnesses. The act of lifting the voice is an assertion of authority—the survivors become proclaimers of God's righteousness.

word_study.meaning: they shall sing, shout for joy, cry aloud in jubilation. The root raon suggests loud, exuberant vocalization—not restrained hymn-singing but joyful outcry.
word_study.significance: The joy is not tentative or conditional; it is the full-throated response of those who have survived catastrophe and now perceive God's faithfulness. This verb appears in contexts of deliverance and victory (Psalm 20:5, Psalm 65:13).

cross_references.connection: Continues the remnant's praise: 'Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us.' The theme of the remnant rejoicing after judgment is sustained throughout the Isaiah Apocalypse.
The redeemed sing 'the song of Moses' and worship God's majesty after eschatological judgment. John's Apocalypse mirrors Isaiah's pattern: judgment, then universal praise.
The vision of the celestial kingdom describes the righteous raising their voices in praise and exaltation to God. The remnant's rejoicing in Isaiah prefigures the eternal jubilation of the saved.

Universal praise with lifted voice and loud jubilation: 'Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all the earth: make a loud noise, and rejoice, and sing praise.' The psalm echoes Isaiah's pattern of eschatological praise.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions and psalms, praise of the gods (or the king) often followed military victory or deliverance from danger. The pattern is consistent: threat, judgment, then restoration and praise. Isaiah invokes this familiar structure but gives it cosmic weight—the judgment is not merely political (defeat of a neighboring nation) but eschatological (transformation of the earth itself). The 'singing' and 'crying aloud' reflect ancient practices of public celebration and testimony. In the context of Judaean identity in the 8th–6th centuries BCE, facing Assyrian and Babylonian empires, such words would have sounded almost impossible—how can a devastated people sing?—yet they offer the counterintuitive promise that faithful remnants do emerge and do praise.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's own 'Praise the Lord' song (1 Nephi 4:26–27, expanded in 2 Nephi 4:15–35) echoes this remnant praise. The Nephite remnant continually praises the Lord despite trials. Alma's people at the Waters of Mormon (Mosiah 18) similarly lift their voices in praise after covenanting to bear witness—a small remnant making bold proclamation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 97:16 ('And inasmuch as my people build a house unto me in the name of the Lord, and do not suffer any unclean thing to come into it, that it be not defiled, my glory shall rest upon it') speaks of God's presence dwelling with the faithful remnant. The Doctrine and Covenants repeatedly emphasizes that God's people, despite trials, are called to 'lift up your voices and rejoice' (D&C 19:29).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where the remnant gathers to lift their voices in worship, to testify of God's majesty, to participate in sacred ordinances. The Hosanna Shout in temple dedications embodies this principle—the gathered saints voicing their praise and allegiance to God aloud and together.

commentary.christological_typology: The remnant's praise of God's majesty after judgment prefigures the scene in Revelation 5, where the Lamb (Christ) is praised by all creation after His redemptive work. Christ's resurrection transforms despair into joy; His majesty is revealed after apparent destruction. The remnant's voice foreshadows the eternal chorus that will sing the Savior's praises.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 14 teaches that authentic faith includes both realism about judgment and certainty about praise. We live between verses 13 (the remnant survives) and 14 (the remnant sings). The application is not to pretend trials are absent but to recognize that they are temporary, that God's majesty endures, and that those who remain faithful will ultimately lift their voices together in praise. In personal trials, in church challenges, in national upheaval, this verse invites the question: Will I be among those who, having survived judgment, lift my voice to testify of God's majesty? The remnant's praise is not naive or forced; it is the mature recognition that God's rule outlasts all earthly power and that His name is worthy of exultation.

text_kjv: Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the fires, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 15 shifts from the remnant's spontaneous praise (v. 14) to an exhortation—a direct command to glorify the Lord. The word 'wherefore' (al-ken, 'therefore, for this reason') connects the imperative to what precedes: because the remnant has survived, because God's majesty has been revealed, therefore glorify the Lord. But where and to whom is this command addressed? The text says 'in the fires' (or 'in the east,' if reading ba'urim as 'in the east' rather than 'in the fires') and 'in the isles of the sea' (the western coastlands). The Covenant Rendering interprets this as a merism—a figure of speech using opposite extremes to denote totality. From east to west, from sunrise to sunset, all regions are called to glorify God. This is universal geography: there is no place on earth exempt from the duty to praise the Lord.

The phrase 'the name of the LORD God of Israel' is theologically significant. It uses the full covenantal title: YHWH (the eternal, revealed name) is identified as the God of Israel—not a generic deity, but the God bound by covenant to a specific people. Yet the command spans the entire earth. This announces that Israel's covenant God is claiming universal lordship. The paradox runs through Isaiah: the Lord is Israel's God, yet He judges and redeems all nations. The call to glorify resonates with the covenant renewal language of Deuteronomy and with the eschatological vision that all nations will eventually acknowledge Israel's God. The 'fires' (if that reading stands) may allude to the fires of judgment mentioned throughout chapter 24, or they may refer metaphorically to the dawn (light/fire of the east). Either way, verse 15 moves from the remnant's praise to an imperative demanding that all peoples, everywhere, turn to glorify the Lord.

word_study.meaning: honor, glorify, give weight to; from kabed, meaning heavy, weighty, honorable. To glorify is to ascribe weight, substance, honor, and authority to someone.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew thought, kabod (glory) and kabed (honor) are closely related. To glorify the Lord is to acknowledge His true weight and substance—He is the only one worthy of honor. In a world where judgment has exposed all earthly power as insignificant, only the Lord's honor remains.

word_study.meaning: fires, lights; the word ur/or refers to fire or light (as in the dawn). The Covenant Rendering interprets this as 'in the east' (the region of light/sunrise) based on the parallel with 'isles of the sea' (west), but the text literally reads 'in the fires.'
word_study.significance: Whether 'fires' or 'east,' the term suggests illumination or revelation. Glorifying the Lord 'in the fires' may mean glorifying Him in the very midst of judgment, recognizing His righteousness even in the fire of His wrath. Or, reading as 'east,' it suggests the direction of light and new beginnings—praising the Lord at the dawn of a new age.

word_study.meaning: coastlands, islands of the sea; literally the islands or distant coastlands accessible by sea. In Isaiah, this often refers to remote gentile lands (Isaiah 41:1, 42:10).
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes distance and foreignness—yet even the remotest coastlands are called to glorify the God of Israel. This reinforces the universal scope of the command.

cross_references.connection: A similar command to distant coastlands and islands: 'Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth.' The theme of universal praise reaching the earth's extremities runs throughout Isaiah's eschatology.

'For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering.' Malachi echoes Isaiah's merism of east and west—universal recognition of the Lord's name.

'That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow...and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.' Paul applies the theme of universal glorification to Christ, grounding it in Isaiah's eschatological vision.

The Lord speaks of calling 'all men' in the last days and bringing all things into account. The command to glorify the Lord universally resonates with Restoration eschatology of the gathering and universal judgment.

commentary.historical_context: The phrase 'isles of the sea' (iyei hayam) is used in Isaiah to refer to the Mediterranean coastlands and distant maritime peoples. In the 8th–6th centuries BCE, these areas were known to Judaeans through trade and Assyrian/Babylonian expansion. When Isaiah commands the 'isles of the sea' to glorify the Lord, he is calling for the allegiance of peoples on the imperial periphery—those whom earthly powers had tried to dominate. The merism of east and west reflects an ancient worldview in which east and west marked the extremities of known space. The command is not merely poetic; it reflects a real eschatological belief that in the future age, all nations would acknowledge Israel's God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently speaks of gathering from the four corners of the earth (3 Nephi 20:30–31, 2 Nephi 10:8–9). The image of east and west joining in covenant is echoed in Latter-day Saint thought about the gathering of Israel in the last days—from all corners, from all nations, to glorify the Lord together.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:26-28 ('And all things shall be in commotion...all shall be gathered unto their own place, then shall the righteous be separated from the wicked, and fire shall be given unto their faces') speaks of a final gathering and judgment. D&C 101:23 ('I, the Lord, have decreed to grace you...with one more offering') suggests the Lord's call reaches all peoples. The universality of verse 15 aligns with the Restoration's vision of a worldwide work.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where the covenant name of the Lord is glorified and all nations are invited to participate (through baptism for the dead, sealing, covenant-making). The temple work reaches across all geography and all time—the spiritual equivalent of glorifying the Lord 'from the east to the west.'

commentary.christological_typology: The command to glorify the Lord's name universally, from every corner of the earth, finds its ultimate fulfillment in the testimony of Jesus Christ, the name above all names. Christ is the 'name of the LORD God' revealed to all nations. The universal glorification Isaiah foresees is the recognition of Christ's authority by all peoples.
commentary.application: Verse 15 calls modern covenant members to expand their understanding of discipleship beyond personal piety to universal witness. 'Glorifying the Lord' is not a private practice but a proclamation that spans geography, culture, and nationality. The exhortation to glorify God 'from the east' and 'among the isles of the sea' invites the question: Am I a witness to the Lord's name in my sphere—whether that is my workplace, my community, my nation, or through the Church's worldwide work? The Restoration teaches that the same gospel restored through Joseph Smith is intended for all kindreds and tongues. To glorify the Lord is to recognize His eternal authority and to extend that recognition—through testimony, service, and covenant—to all people.

text_kjv: From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, even glory to the righteous. But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me! the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 16 is perhaps the most psychologically complex verse in Isaiah 24—a collision between universal jubilation and the prophet's personal anguish. The verse begins as a continuation of the remnant's rejoicing: from the earth's uttermost parts (literally 'from the wings of the earth,' using the image of the earth having edges or extremities), songs are heard. The refrain is 'glory to the Righteous One'—a confession that the tsaddiq (the Just One, the Righteous Judge) is worthy of honor. This is the eschatological vision realized: the ends of the earth join in acclamation.

But then the speaker abruptly turns inward: 'But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me!' The sudden rupture is jarring. While the earth sings, the prophet declares his own dissolution. The word razi—variously interpreted as 'my leanness,' 'my secret,' or 'woe to me'—is notoriously difficult. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve the identical text (razi li, razi li), confirming that the ambiguity is original, not scribal corruption. The Covenant Rendering interprets it as 'I waste away! I waste away!'—a cry of physical and emotional deterioration. This makes coherent sense: the prophet, witnessing global praise, also witnesses global treachery. The final half of the verse hammers this home with relentless wordplay: 'the treacherous betray, the treacherous utterly betray' (bogdim bagadu, beged bogdim bagadu). The repetition of the root b-g-d (to betray, act treacherously) creates an incantatory effect—treachery is endemic, pervasive, inescapable. The prophet's wasting away is not physical illness but the soul-sickness of witnessing betrayal while the world sings. This is the cost of prophecy: to see both the eschatological victory of God and the present reality of human faithlessness.

word_study.meaning: my leanness, my wasting; from razah, to waste away, grow lean, diminish. The word can also mean 'my secret' or 'my mystery' (from raz, secret), but the more natural reading in context is 'my wasting.' The word carries the sense of physical and spiritual emaciation.
word_study.significance: To waste away is to lose substance, weight, presence. The prophet, confronted by the contrast between cosmic praise and earthly treachery, feels spiritually hollowed out. This is the prophet's empathetic suffering—he bears the weight of witnessing both God's triumph and human failure.

word_study.meaning: righteous, just, innocent; from the root tsedek (righteousness, justice). The righteous one is the one who stands in right relationship with God and covenant.
word_study.significance: The earth sings glory to 'the Righteous One'—whether this refers to God, to the Messiah, or to the faithful remnant (collectively) remains interpretively open. But the meaning is clear: righteousness is the only standard, the only ground for glory. Yet the prophet immediately confesses that treachery abounds. The two realities—God's righteousness and human betrayal—create the tension.

word_study.meaning: treacherous ones, those who betray; from bagad, to act treacherously, deal faithlessly, transgress. The root implies breaking covenant, shattering trust.
