word_study.significance: The repetition of this root three times in rapid succession (bagdu, beged, bogdim, bagadu) is untranslatable sound-design—the Hebrew language itself is being forced to echo the relentless fact of betrayal. In covenant theology, bogdim (the treacherous) are those who abandon the covenant. The prophet's lament is that treachery persists even as heaven rejoices.

cross_references.connection: The Righteous Servant is numbered with transgressors; the one who makes intercession stands among the faithless. The prophet's personal anguish in 24:16 prefigures the Servant's suffering, bearing the weight of human treachery.

'O LORD, thou hast deceived me...then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire.' Jeremiah articulates the same prophet's burden: seeing divine truth while drowning in human faithlessness.
'Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me?' The psalmist wrestles with the same tension between faith in God's righteous rule and present despair.

Nephi's lament: 'O wretched man that I am!...Notwithstanding the great goodness of the Lord, in showing me his great and marvelous works, yet I have allowed the weakness of the flesh to blind me, that I have not discerned all his goodness.' Nephi echoes the prophet's self-accusation in the face of God's righteousness.
Joseph Smith's vision shows those who 'received not the love of the truth'—a direct reference to 2 Thessalonians 2:10 but echoing Isaiah's concern with treachery and refusal of covenant.

commentary.historical_context: The prophet's anguish in verse 16 may reflect the specific historical moment of Isaiah's ministry—whether 8th-century Judah facing Assyrian invasion or exilic community (6th century) facing Babylonian captivity. In either case, the prophecy of cosmic restoration (vv. 14-15) would have felt like bitter irony to those living amid betrayal, injustice, and covenant-breaking. The 'uttermost parts of the earth' singing while prophets weep is the classic tension of eschatological faith: the future victory is certain, yet the present reality is broken. The word choice—'treacherous dealers'—likely refers not just to political enemies but to unfaithful Judaeans themselves, those who have broken covenant, aligned with foreign powers, or abandoned Torah. The prophet's personal wasting away reflects his identification with God's own anguish at His people's infidelity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob's lament in Jacob 5—the allegory of the olive tree—depicts the same prophetic sorrow: laborers in the vineyard work amid widespread decay and apostasy, even as the Master plans restoration. Jacob's empathetic identification with God's grief over His people's betrayal parallels the prophet's wasting in Isaiah 24:16. 2 Nephi 26–27 (Nephi's prophecy of apostasy) similarly balances eschatological hope with lament over present faithlessness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:87-88 reflects Isaiah's tension: 'Prepare ye for that which is to come, for the Lord is nigh...even those who shall be apostate and betray the holy covenant' (emphasis added). The Doctrine and Covenants acknowledges that even in the latter days, betrayal and apostasy persist. D&C 112:24-26 speaks of Joseph Smith's suffering as he bears witness of God's truth amid human treachery.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes the promise of faithfulness and a renunciation of treachery. Those who enter the temple commit to remain loyal to covenant; the temple becomes the place where, amid a world of betrayal, the faithful gather to reaffirm their fidelity. The temple ritual acknowledges the reality of human weakness and treachery while affirming the possibility of covenantal faithfulness.

commentary.christological_typology: The 'Righteous One' (tsaddiq) to whom the earth sings glory ultimately refers to Christ, the only fully righteous being. The prophet's wasting away and anguish over human treachery foreshadows Christ's Gethsemane sorrow—the moment when, on the eve of universal redemption, Christ bears the weight of all human betrayal and faithlessness (Matthew 26:38, Luke 22:44). Christ is both the ground of the earth's jubilation (vv. 14-15) and the bearer of the prophet's anguish (v. 16).
commentary.application: Verse 16 grants permission for honest prophetic grief—the recognition that faith in God's righteousness does not require denial of present betrayal and failure. For modern covenant members, this is deeply relevant: to be a person of deep faith is not to be naive about human treachery, including treachery within the covenant community itself. The verse teaches that authentic discipleship can include both certainty that God will ultimately triumph and sorrow that many betray His covenant now. This is not pessimism but realism grounded in faith. The application is to ask: Do I bear the prophet's burden of witnessing both God's truth and human failure? Am I willing to waste away (metaphorically, to sacrifice and mourn) rather than pretend that all is well when it is not? The verse invites covenant members to hold both truths: God's victory is sure, and faithlessness is real and costly.

text_kjv: Fear, and the pit, and the snare, are upon thee, O inhabitant of the earth.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 17 strips away the personal lament of verse 16 and returns to address the inhabitants of the earth directly. But now the tone is accusatory and warning. The verse is constructed as a series of three nouns, each naming a stage of entrapment: fear, pit, snare. These are not metaphorical dangers but existential realities pressing upon 'thee, O inhabitant of the earth.' The person addressed is not a specific individual but humanity itself—the generic 'inhabitant of the earth.' This universalizes the threat. The three terms work together to describe an inescapable trap. Fear is the emotional/psychological response to danger; the pit is the physical fall or capture; the snare is the mechanical entrapment that prevents escape. Read sequentially, they describe the progression of judgment: first awareness of danger (fear), then collapse into the depths (pit), then immobilization (snare).

The verse's power lies in its sound design. The Hebrew triple alliteration—pachad, pachat, pach—creates a hammering effect. Each word begins with the same consonant cluster (p-ch), and each one is a step closer to the preceding one phonetically and conceptually. This is Isaiah's most striking onomatopoeia—the language itself enacts entrapment. The 'O inhabitant of the earth' (yushev ha'aretz) is an archaic phrase recalling covenant language, as if to say: those who dwell on God's earth, who should be stewards of covenant, now find themselves trapped by judgment. The verse stands as a stark warning: there is no escape from the coming judgment. This is not comfort but stark prophecy.

word_study.meaning: terror, dread, panic; from the root pachad, to tremble, be afraid. The word carries the sense of overwhelming terror that shakes the whole being.
word_study.significance: Fear is the first stage of judgment's descent. It is not merely concern but existential panic—the recognition of danger that cannot be evaded. Pachad appears in contexts of divine judgment (Job 3:25, Proverbs 3:25).

word_study.meaning: pit, snare pit, trap; a cavity dug into the ground to capture animals or as a prison. In biblical imagery, the pit represents death, Sheol, destruction.
word_study.significance: The pit is the physical manifestation of the threat—the actual trap. Once one falls into the pit, ascent is difficult. In covenant contexts, the pit often represents exile or separation from God's presence (Isaiah 14:15, Proverbs 28:10).

word_study.meaning: snare, trap, noose; a mechanical device designed to capture prey. The word implies entrapment from which escape is nearly impossible.
word_study.significance: The snare is the final, immobilizing trap. Once caught in a pach, there is no self-release. In covenant theology, the snare often represents spiritual bondage or divine judgment (Psalm 91:3, 2 Timothy 2:26).

cross_references.connection: The very next verse elaborates on verse 17's trap, describing the inescapable progression: flee the terror, fall in the pit; climb out, be caught in the snare. Verse 18 is the lived-out reality of verse 17's warning.

'A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.' Verse 17's warning is exactly this: those who recognize the judgment coming can prepare; those who ignore it are trapped.

Jesus warns: 'Take ye heed, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares...Watch ye therefore, and pray always.' Jesus echoes Isaiah's warning of inescapable judgment from which only watchfulness and prayer offer protection.

'Woe unto you that desire the day of the Lord!...Shall not the day of the Lord be darkness, and not light?' Amos uses similar terminology of judgment as an inescapable reality bearing down on all inhabitants of the earth.

'And all things shall be in commotion; and surely, men's hearts shall fail them.' Joseph Smith's modern revelation echoes the vocabulary of cosmic fear and entrapment, warning that the day of judgment will come upon all the earth.

commentary.historical_context: The alliterative device (pachad, pachat, pach) is characteristic of Isaiah's style—creating mnemonic power through sound. In oral cultures, such poetic techniques aid memory and endow the prophecy with prophetic weight. The 'inhabitant of the earth' (yushev ha'aretz) language echoes treaty and covenant language, as if to emphasize that those bound by covenant to God face the gravest consequences for breach. The imagery of fear, pit, and snare would have been vivid to ancient audiences: pit-traps for animals (and enemies) were common; the progression from panic to physical capture to immobilization was a known horror. The verse uses familiar danger to underscore the inevitability of divine judgment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma the Younger's experience of being trapped in sin (Alma 36) uses similar language: he is caught, unable to escape, in the grip of fear and torment. His deliverance comes only through Christ. 2 Nephi 27:23 (the sealed book) and 2 Nephi 28 (warnings against pride and deception) similarly warn of inescapable traps set for the unfaithful.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:21 ('I will cause that the earth shall shake in mine anger') and D&C 38:12 ('all things in commotion') use the language of inevitable, inescapable judgment. D&C 56:8 warns of the dangers that come to those who harden their hearts against the Lord's warnings.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes protective ordinances—the endowment is understood by the faithful as a refuge and preparation for the judgment to come. The temple teaches that only through covenant relationship with God can one escape the 'fear, pit, and snare' of worldly judgment. The covenants become a kind of spiritual protection against the traps that await the unfaithful.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the only one who escapes the threefold entrapment of fear, pit, and snare. His resurrection opens the pit; His power breaks the snare; His love casts out fear (1 John 4:18). For those who come to Christ, the judgment that falls on 'the inhabitant of the earth' is transformed into the hope of resurrection and eternal life.
commentary.application: Verse 17's stark warning invites modern readers to consider: What traps am I walking toward? The verse teaches that judgment is not arbitrary or distant but comes inevitably upon those who reject God's covenant. The application is not to live in fear but to be 'prudent' (as Proverbs 22:3 says)—to heed the warning, to examine one's life and covenant commitments, to ask whether one is moving toward or away from God's protection. For covenant members, verse 17 is a call to serious discipleship: the world is full of traps that lead to fear, descent, and bondage, but the covenant community has been warned. To be a disciple of Christ is to learn to recognize the traps and to choose the path of faithful covenant-keeping that leads away from them.

text_kjv: And it shall come to pass, that he who fleeth from the noise of the fear shall fall into the pit; and he that cometh up out of the midst of the pit shall be taken in the snare: for the windows from on high are open, and the foundations of the earth do shake.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 18 is the nightmare made manifest. Verse 17 warned of fear, pit, and snare; verse 18 shows that these are not three separate dangers but a single inescapable trap. The verse describes the futility of escape: flee the terror of the pachad, and you fall into the pachat. Climb out of the pit, and you are caught in the pach. There is no escape. The logic is relentless—every avenue of escape leads to a worse entrapment. This is the ancient Near Eastern formula for describing judgment from which there is no refuge. The person addressed ('he who') is no longer the collective 'inhabitant of the earth' but an individual experiencing the trap, making the prophecy intensely personal even as it remains universally applicable.

The verse then explains why escape is impossible: 'For the windows from on high are open, and the foundations of the earth do shake.' This language echoes Genesis 7:11 (the flood narrative): 'In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month, the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened.' The 'windows' (arubbot) are apertures in the cosmic structure through which divine judgment pours down. When God opens them, human resistance is futile. The 'foundations of the earth' (mosdei eretz) trembling evokes the cosmic instability of judgment day—not merely political upheaval but the unraveling of creation itself. In biblical theology, the earth's foundations represent the stability of God's order; when they shake, it indicates the reversal of creation, the return to chaos, the unmaking of the world. Together, the opened windows and trembling foundations describe a reality in which normal physical laws no longer apply. Escape routes that seemed viable cease to exist. The judgment is not localized but cosmic. This is Isaiah's most terrifying vision: the cosmos itself becomes the instrument of judgment.

word_study.meaning: windows from on high, apertures in the sky; arubbot are windows, doors, or openings; marom means height, the upper regions. The phrase denotes the cosmic openings through which heaven communicates with earth.
word_study.significance: This is the language of cosmic architecture—the idea that the sky has structure and openings through which divine power flows. When arubbot mimarom open, it is God's deliberate action to send judgment. The phrase echoes the flood (Genesis 7:11) and suggests that divine judgment is a reversal or remaking of creation itself.

word_study.meaning: foundations of the earth; mosad means foundation, base, establishment; the plural suggests the earth has multiple foundational supports, like a building resting on pillars.
word_study.significance: In biblical cosmology, the earth rests on foundations; when they shake (ra'ash, quake, tremble), it indicates the unraveling of cosmic order. The foundations of the earth represent stability, creation's endurance. Their shaking means the unmmaking of the world. This is not mere earthquake but eschatological upheaval.

word_study.meaning: they shall shake, quake, tremble; from raash, to shake, shudder, rattle. The word implies violent, involuntary movement.
word_study.significance: The shaking of the earth's foundations is not gradual but violent and total. This verb is used of fear (trembling) and of earthquakes (earth shaking). Here both senses merge: the earth experiences cosmic terror as its own foundations give way.

cross_references.connection: 'In the six hundredth year of Noah's life...the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened.' Isaiah directly invokes the flood language to underscore the cosmic scale of judgment.

'And lo, there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black as sackcloth of hair, and the moon became as blood...and the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and every mountain and island were moved out of their places.' John's Apocalypse mirrors Isaiah's cosmic upheaval—the opening of heaven's structures and the shaking of earth's foundations.

'The heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up.' Peter echoes Isaiah's theme of cosmic dissolution as judgment.

The Lord's description of the last days: 'the heavens shall shake, and the earth shall tremble, and the skies shall fall...and all things shall be in commotion; and surely, men's hearts shall fail them; for fear shall come upon all people.' Joseph Smith's revelation directly draws on Isaiah's language of cosmic trembling and universal fear.

An exegesis of Haggai 2:6: 'Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven...that those things which cannot be shaken may remain.' The author uses the image of cosmic shaking to teach spiritual endurance—only the unshakeable (God's kingdom) will remain.

commentary.historical_context: The image of the 'windows of heaven' opening is ancient Near Eastern cosmological language. The flat earth was believed to rest on foundations; above it, the sky (firmament) was a solid structure with apertures (windows, gates) through which rain (or divine judgment) fell. The Babylonians, Egyptians, and Hebrews all shared this basic cosmological model. Isaiah's invocation of Genesis 7:11 (the flood) to describe his eschatological vision grounds his prophecy in Israel's foundational narrative—the last days will be like the flood, a remaking of the world through cosmic catastrophe. The triple trap progression (flee terror, fall in pit, climb out, caught in snare) is common in ancient warfare literature—describing how military defeat is inescapable. Isaiah universalizes this military imagery to cosmic judgment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains multiple scenes of cosmic upheaval—3 Nephi 8-9 (Christ's death in the Americas) describes earthquakes, the shaking of the earth, darkness, and the trembling of foundations. This is understood as a sign confirming Christ's death and redemption. The Nephite experience of cosmic judgment and salvation parallels Isaiah's vision. Samuel the Lamanite's prophecy (Helaman 14) similarly warns of cosmic signs preceding Christ's coming.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29, 45, and 88 contain modern revelations about the last days using similar language: windows opening (revelation), foundations shaking (upheaval), universal fear (all flesh becomes trembling). D&C 88:88-89 exhorts: 'Therefore, let your hearts be comforted concerning Zion' because 'the glory of the Lord shall be upon thy people'—contrasting cosmic judgment with the refuge of Zion (covenant community).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that the celestial order (covenant, sealing, eternal families) is the only 'unshakeable' foundation. D&C 127-128 emphasizes that temple work (sealing) reaches beyond the temporal disruptions of mortality and judgment—the sealing power is not subject to the earth's trembling. The temple becomes a refuge (figuratively and symbolically) during times of judgment.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's resurrection conquers the forces of cosmic judgment—He ascends through the opened windows (heavens) and stands firm even as the foundations tremble. For those who are sealed to Christ through covenant, the cosmic upheaval that brings terror to the unfaithful becomes the context of their exaltation. Christ's triumph over cosmic forces (Colossians 1:16-20) means that believers need not fear the trembling of the earth—their foundation is the rock of Christ.
commentary.application: Verse 18 presents a radical choice: In a world where no escape route is safe and the very foundations are unreliable, what foundation do I choose? The verse teaches that human planning, earthly possessions, political alignments, and physical safety are all contingent—subject to the shaking of judgment. The application is to ask: Have I built my life on the shaking foundations of the world, or on the unshakeable covenant with God? The Restoration teaches that temple covenants and sealing ordinances are precisely the answer Isaiah poses—when all else shakes, the sealed covenant endures. Modern disciples are invited to recognize that preparation for judgment is not primarily physical but spiritual: entering covenant, keeping the commandments, building one's house on the rock of Christ (3 Nephi 14:24-27). Verse 18 is not meant to paralyze with fear but to clarify priorities: only the covenantal relationship with God and Christ offers true refuge.

text_kjv: The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah now moves from the specific consequences of judgment (verses 16-18) to the cosmic reality of it. Verse 19 presents the physical world itself in complete collapse — not merely political upheaval or economic ruin, but the literal structure of creation undone. The threefold repetition of 'the earth' (erets, erets, erets) is relentless, each clause driving home that this is not partial or localized destruction but total annihilation. The three infinitive absolutes — ro'ah hitro'a'ah (shattering it is shattered), por hitporrah (splitting it is split apart), mot hitmottatah (shaking it is shaken) — create a crescendo of violent action. In Hebrew, the infinitive absolute with the conjugated verb intensifies and emphasizes the verbal action itself; here, the earth does not merely shake but is violently, completely, undeniably shaken.

This verse establishes the apocalyptic register that Isaiah Apocalypse (chapters 24-27) will maintain throughout. The world is not being corrected or reformed — it is being unmade. For an ancient Near Eastern reader familiar with creation accounts, this language would recall the reversal of creation itself, as if the LORD is returning the cosmos to its pre-creation state of chaos. The Covenant Rendering captures this with 'utterly shattered,' 'split apart,' and 'violently shaken' — more forceful than the KJV's 'broken down,' 'dissolved,' and 'moved exceedingly,' which can sound almost bureaucratic by comparison.

word_study.meaning: The infinitive absolute (ro'ah) joined with the passive niphal verb (hitro'a'ah) creates the sense 'shattering it is utterly shattered' — an emphatic, intensive form that cannot be weakened or diminished. The root ra'a conveys violent breaking, shattering, or crashing.
word_study.significance: This construction appears in Isaiah's most severe judgment language. The doubling emphasizes totality and inevitability — the shattering is not conditional or partial but absolute.

word_study.meaning: Another doubled infinitive absolute construction. Por relates to the idea of splitting, tearing, or scattering. The earth does not merely crack — it splits apart violently, its coherence undone.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests not just breaking but separation, the coming-apart of what was unified. This captures the loss of structural integrity at the most fundamental level.

word_study.meaning: Mot means to shake, stagger, or totter. The niphal form with the infinitive absolute creates the sense 'shaking it is shaken.' The KJV's 'moved exceedingly' understates the Hebrew; the Covenant Rendering's 'violently shaken' captures the convulsive, destabilizing action.
word_study.significance: This is the same root used for the trembling that accompanies theophany in the Old Testament. Here the earth staggers as if in response to God's cosmic judgment.

cross_references.connection: Peter describes the end of this world in similar apocalyptic language: 'the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat.' Both passages depict cosmic dissolution as the prelude to God's reign.

The Revelation account of seals echoes Isaiah's cosmic upheaval: 'the stars of heaven fell unto the earth... and the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together.' The apocalyptic tradition draws directly from Isaiah's language.

The Doctrine and Covenants affirms that 'the earth shall tremble and reel to and fro as a drunken man,' directly borrowing Isaiah's language for the Last Days. This shows the Restoration's continuity with Isaiah's eschatology.

Earlier in Isaiah, people 'shall go into the holes of the rocks... for fear of the LORD' when He arises 'to shake terribly the earth.' Here the fear is realized as the earth itself is shaken to its foundation.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern worldview held the earth as a stable, ordered creation — the domain of humans and the seat of human civilization. To speak of the earth 'shattering' and 'splitting apart' was to invoke the ultimate horror: the unmade world, a return to primordial chaos. Mesopotamian creation myths like the Enuma Elish portrayed cosmic order (ma'at, in Egyptian thought) as a constant achievement, always threatened by chaos. Isaiah's vision of the earth's complete dissolution would have struck an ancient listener as the dissolution of all meaning, all order, all possibility. The threefold emphatic repetition follows a pattern common in Hebrew poetry and prophetic speech, where the most important truths are hammered home through relentless reiteration.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 19:10-12, Nephi quotes Isaiah 2 (a passage about the Lord's judgment on the proud and lofty) and extends it to the destruction that will come upon the wicked. The Nephite understanding of Isaiah's apocalyptic language treats it as literal and certain, not merely symbolic.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:86-92 provides a Restoration expansion on Isaiah's apocalypse, describing the earth's transformation and the time when 'the earth shall be changed and receive its paradisiacal glory.' The Latter-day Saint understanding frames Isaiah's destruction not as annihilation but as renovation — the earth's return to its prelapsarian glory.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The undoing of the created world in Isaiah 24 stands in sharp contrast to the temple as the place where creation is ritually enacted and renewed. The cosmic dissolution of verse 19 sets up the eschatological reversal in verse 23, where the LORD will reign in Zion — the temple mountain.

commentary.christological_typology: The unmade world of Isaiah 24:19 anticipates the judgment that comes through Christ. In Revelation 20-21, John describes the old heavens and earth passing away and a new creation emerging — the fulfillment of Isaiah's apocalyptic vision through Christ's return and the establishment of His kingdom. Christ is the means by which creation itself will be transformed.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern readers with a reality that comfort and material progress can obscure: the physical world as we know it is not permanent. This is not meant to generate despair but clarity. If earthly structures are temporary, where should our deepest trust lie? What are we building our lives upon? For covenant members, this verses asks: Are we building on the rock of Christ, or on sand that will be shaken away?

text_kjv: The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again.

commentary.narrative:
If verse 19 announces the earth's shattering in cosmic terms, verse 20 makes it vivid and personal through two memorable similes. The earth 'reels to and fro like a drunkard' — the noun nu'a combined with the infinitive absolute tanu'a (stagger-staggers) captures not steady falling but lurching, unpredictable movement. A drunkard has no control, no balance, no dignity. The comparison is startling: the solid, dependable earth, humanity's foundation, is now as unstable and unreliable as an intoxicated person. The second image is even more cutting: the earth 'shall be removed like a cottage' — not a palace, not a permanent dwelling, but a melunah, a flimsy field-shelter, a temporary booth made of branches or cloth. Such structures sway in the wind and can be dismantled in moments. The secure foundation has become a fragile, movable hut.

The theological center of the verse, however, lies in the phrase 'and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it.' The verb kavad (to be heavy) is the root of kavod (glory, honor) — the same word that closes this entire chapter. Here, transgression is weighty, crushing, a burden the earth cannot bear. The earth 'falls, and not rise again' — once fallen, it remains fallen. No recovery is possible. This is final. The world as constituted by human sin has reached its breaking point. The double negative in the Hebrew ('and not it-will-add to-rise') emphasizes the permanence: this falling is not temporary setback but terminal collapse.

word_study.meaning: The infinitive absolute nu'a (stagger, reel, totter) paired with the conjugated verb tanu'a creates the sense 'stagger-it staggers.' The root suggests uncontrolled, repetitive movement — swaying back and forth without stability.
word_study.significance: This verb appears in descriptions of theophanic earthquakes and cosmic disturbance. Here, the earth itself becomes like a person in a state of helplessness.

word_study.meaning: A simile comparing the earth's movement to that of a drunkard (shikor). The image is humorous in form but devastating in implication — what should be solid is reeling with lack of control.
word_study.significance: Drunkards appear elsewhere in Isaiah (5:11, 29:9) as examples of those who reject God's word. Here, the earth itself becomes drunk on judgment, its movements as chaotic as theirs.

word_study.meaning: A melunah is a temporary lodge or hut — the kind of flimsy shelter used during harvest or by shepherds. It is made to be taken down and moved. The image of the solid earth being 'removed' like such a structure is profoundly ironic.
word_study.significance: The melunah appears in Isaiah 1:8 as an image of Jerusalem left alone like a lodge in a vineyard. Here, all creation becomes as impermanent as that lodge.

word_study.meaning: To be heavy, weighty, burdensome. The verb root connects to kavod (glory, honor) — that which has weight and substance. Here, transgression (pisha'ah) weighs so heavily on the earth that it cannot stand.
word_study.significance: This is a double irony: kavod (glory) is mentioned at the verse's end of the chapter as God's revealed presence, while here kavad (heaviness) describes the weight of human sin. The two forms of 'weight' — one destructive, one redemptive — frame the chapter's movement.

cross_references.connection: Joseph Smith taught that creation groans under the weight of human transgression and will be cleansed through Christ's power. The doctrine of the earth's suffering and renewal directly expands Isaiah's vision of the earth bearing transgression.
Paul writes that 'the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now,' echoing Isaiah's understanding that creation itself suffers from human sin and awaits redemption.

Nephi quotes Isaiah on the judgment that will come and describes how 'all things shall be revealed... and all lies and deceits.' The earth's judgment is connected to the revelation of hidden transgressions.

Alma teaches that God 'knoweth all the thoughts and intents of the heart,' and the Book of Mormon applies Isaiah's vision of judgment to the personal reckoning that awaits the wicked. Sin that seems hidden is known, and judgment is certain.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient world, a 'cottage' or temporary shelter represented the absolute opposite of a fortified city, a palace, or a temple. These structures were built to last, to endure, to represent permanence and authority. The melunah, by contrast, was dismantled after the harvest or the grazing season. To compare the earth itself to such a structure was to invert all expectations of permanence. Ancient Near Eastern cosmology held the earth as the stable base of reality — the stage on which human kingdoms rose and fell, but the stage itself remained. Isaiah's vision shatters that assumption. The earth is not the stable ground; it is the unstable, transgression-bearing platform that will collapse.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Jacob 5-6, the allegory of the olive tree describes how the vineyard (the world) has become corrupted by transgression and must be pruned and eventually burned. Like Isaiah's earth that 'shall fall, and not rise again,' the vineyard must be cleansed completely before new growth can occur. The Nephite understanding frames this not as annihilation but as necessary preparation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:86 states that 'the earth shall be cleansed from all uncleanness.' The cleansing requires the falling described in Isaiah 24:20. The earth must be emptied of its transgression before it can receive its paradisiacal glory.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where transgression is forgiven and souls are renewed. Isaiah's vision of the earth's fall under the weight of transgression stands in contrast to the temple as the place of redemption. The endpoint of Isaiah's apocalypse (verse 23, the LORD reigning in Zion) is the inverse: redemption, not condemnation, centered on the temple mountain.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ bears the weight of human transgression (the 'heaviness' of verse 20) in His atoning sacrifice. In Isaiah 53:6, 'the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.' The earth cannot bear the weight of sin and falls, but Christ bore that weight and rose — overcoming what the earth cannot overcome. His resurrection is the antidote to the earth's permanent fall.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that sin is never victimless — it affects not just the sinner but the whole creation. The modern tendency to compartmentalize morality ('What I do in private doesn't affect anyone else') is directly contradicted by Isaiah's vision. Transgression weighs on the entire earth. For covenant members, this suggests that personal integrity has cosmic significance. Our faithfulness or unfaithfulness is not a small personal matter but part of the larger weight that either crushes or sustains the world.

text_kjv: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the LORD shall punish the host of the high ones that are on high, and the kings of the earth upon the earth.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 21 reveals the full scope of the LORD's judgment: it is not limited to earthly rulers and human corruption, but extends to the heavenly realm itself. The phrase 'in that day' signals the eschatological moment when the apocalypse reaches its culmination. Two domains are mentioned: 'the host of the high ones that are on high' (tseva hamarom bamarom) and 'the kings of the earth upon the earth.' The doubling of each location — 'high ones' in 'the heights,' 'kings' on 'the earth' — emphasizes that nowhere is exempt from judgment. Some interpreters understand 'the host of the high ones' to refer to celestial bodies (sun, moon, stars), others to angelic beings, and still others to the deified powers and astral deities worshipped by the pagan nations. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse identically to the Masoretic Text, showing that this dual judgment — celestial and terrestrial — was consistent in the tradition.

The verb 'punish' (yipqod) carries the sense of 'visit' or 'take account of.' It is the same root that appears in verse 22 ('they will be visited'). God will visit judgment upon all powers, human and supernatural alike. This vision anticipates the apocalyptic theology of Daniel (chapters 10-12), where spiritual forces behind earthly kingdoms are revealed and judged, and later Revelation (12:7-12), where war breaks out in heaven and Satan is cast down. For Isaiah's original audience, this was radical: the gods and powers they feared or worshipped were subject to the same judgment as human rulers. The true God's authority extends over all realms.

word_study.meaning: Tseva means 'army, host, multitude.' Marom means 'the heights, the high place.' Together, 'the host of the heights' refers to celestial powers — whether stars, angels, or divine beings. The term is ambiguous by design, suggesting multiple layers of meaning.
word_study.significance: This term appears in Daniel 8:10 ('cast down some of the host of heaven') and is picked up in later Jewish and Christian apocalyptic tradition to refer to spiritual forces arrayed against God's purposes.

word_study.meaning: The verb paqad means 'to visit, to muster, to take account, to judge.' It can mean to visit for blessing or for judgment, depending on context. Here, in the context of apocalyptic judgment, it means to hold accountable.
word_study.significance: This same verb is used in 1 Peter 2:12 (where God will 'visit' the Gentiles) and throughout Isaiah to describe God's coming to reckon with sin. It is not a casual or tentative action but a decisive visitation.

word_study.meaning: Malkim ('kings') combined with adamah ('earth, ground'). This phrase emphasizes human rulers in their earthly dominion, contrasted with the celestial powers mentioned in the first clause.
word_study.significance: The 'kings of the earth' are condemned throughout the prophets and Revelation as those who have failed to acknowledge the true King. Here they are brought into judgment.

cross_references.connection: John describes the final judgment where the Beast and the kings of the earth gather against the LORD, only to be defeated. Isaiah 24:21 provides the prophetic foundation for this New Testament apocalypse.

Daniel is told that 'the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me,' revealing that earthly kingdoms are sustained by celestial powers. Isaiah 24:21 announces the judgment of these hidden spiritual forces.
Paul writes that Christ 'spoiled principalities and powers, making a shew of them openly,' triumphing over both earthly and heavenly powers. This is the fulfillment of Isaiah's vision through Christ.

Joseph Smith's vision of the degrees of glory describes how Satan and his hosts will be defeated and confined. The Doctrine and Covenants applies Isaiah's eschatological vision to the event of the Last Judgment.

The war in heaven where Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels directly parallels Isaiah's vision of judgment on 'the host of the high ones.' Celestial and earthly rebellion are simultaneously defeated.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern worldview, earthly kings were often understood to have celestial counterparts or divine patrons. The Babylonians, for instance, saw their kings as representatives of the gods on earth. Isaiah's pronouncement that judgment would fall on both 'the high ones' and 'the kings of the earth' was therefore an assertion that no power — human or divine, earthly or heavenly — could resist the God of Israel. This was a radical claim to monotheistic supremacy. The pagan empires that dominated the Near East in Isaiah's time believed in a multiplicity of divine powers that maintained cosmic order. Isaiah systematically denies this: all powers, of whatever rank or realm, are subject to the one true God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 10:3, Nephi teaches that 'there is none other nation on earth that would serve our God.' The Book of Mormon consistently teaches that earthly kingdoms rise and fall, but the kingdom of God is eternal. Alma 37:35 affirms that 'by small and simple things are great things brought to pass,' contrasting the lasting power of God with the temporary authority of earthly rulers.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:4-5 presents the doctrine of priesthood power: 'Behold, all those who have this law prepared unto them shall be ordained and prepared, and those who refuse to take upon them the obligations of my law and covenants shall have taken away from them the powers and the glories of the same.' The judgment of verse 21 extends to all who reject God's authority, whether earthly or celestial.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is where the priesthood — God's delegated authority — is administered. Isaiah 24:21's judgment on all false authorities points to the temple as the source of legitimate power and order in the cosmos.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the one through whom this judgment is executed. In John 12:31, Jesus says, 'Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of this world be cast out.' Christ's death and resurrection accomplish what Isaiah foresaw — the defeat of all opposing powers, celestial and earthly. Hebrews 1:3 describes Christ as 'the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power' — the one who sustains all existence and judges all powers.
commentary.application: This verse offers perspective for believers facing earthly powers that seem overwhelming. Political rulers, corporate powers, social pressures — all of these operate under the authority of the one true God and are subject to His judgment. For covenant members, this should liberate them from fear of earthly authorities and anchor their trust in God alone. It also calls for discernment: which 'hosts of the high ones' — which spiritual forces, philosophies, or ideologies — are we serving? Are we aligned with the coming kingdom of God or with powers that will be judged and cast down?

text_kjv: And they shall be gathered together, as prisoners are gathered in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison, and after many days shall they be visited.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 22 describes the fate of the judged powers — both celestial and earthly. They will be 'gathered together' (yiusffu asefah), the doubled form emphasizing the comprehensive collection of all who opposed God. The simile 'as prisoners are gathered in the pit' is vivid: they are rounded up like captives and confined in a dungeon. The verb ussfru ('shall be shut up') suggests being imprisoned, sealed away from action and influence. What follows is the most theologically ambiguous statement in the passage: 'and after many days shall they be visited.' The verb yippaqedu (from paqad, 'to visit') can mean to visit for judgment or to visit for mercy — the text deliberately preserves this ambiguity. The 'many days' suggests a prolonged period of confinement before God's return or final disposition of these prisoners.

The verse's ambiguity is theologically productive. Are these powers imprisoned pending final destruction, or imprisoned pending some surprising outcome? The Covenant Rendering preserves this tension: 'after many days they will be visited.' The verse does not tell us what happens at the visitation. This leaves open the profound question: Does even rebellion against God ultimately meet with some form of restoration or redemption? Or is the visitation merely the final judgment? The text does not answer. What is clear is the progression: judgment, imprisonment, isolation from power, and then — after ages pass — a reckoning with God. This structure appears in later Jewish and Christian apocalyptic (e.g., Revelation 20:1-3, where Satan is bound for a thousand years before his final judgment) and suggests a staged apocalypse rather than a single moment of final judgment.

word_study.meaning: The verb asaf means 'to gather, to collect.' The doubled form (infinitive absolute + conjugated verb) creates emphasis: 'gathered-they-are-gathered.' The sense is thoroughness — every rebel is rounded up, none escape.
word_study.significance: This verb is used in Isaiah 13:5 for the gathering of God's army for judgment. Here, it reverses: the judged are gathered up like prisoners.

word_study.meaning: A pit, cistern, or dungeon. In the ancient Near East, prisoners were often confined in underground pits or chambers. The term evokes confinement, darkness, and isolation.
word_study.significance: This is the place of imprisonment before judgment, possibly echoing the 'pit' where Jeremiah is thrown (Jeremiah 38:6) and anticipating the abyss of Revelation 20:1-3.

word_study.meaning: The verb sagar means 'to shut, to close, to enclose.' The passive form suggests being locked in, with masger ('prison, enclosure') referring to the place of confinement. The preposition 'upon' (al) suggests that the prison itself is imposed upon them.
word_study.significance: This is not a voluntary confinement but an imposed limitation. The rebels are shut away from the creation and from power.

word_study.meaning: The niphal form of paqad. As discussed earlier, paqad can mean 'to visit,' 'to muster,' 'to count,' or 'to hold accountable.' The context here — judgment, imprisonment, passage of time — suggests accountability, but the nature of that accountability is unspecified.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering preserves the ambiguity intentionally. The text leaves open what happens 'after many days.' This is more faithful to the Hebrew than interpreting it as necessarily destruction or necessarily restoration.

cross_references.connection: John describes Satan being 'bound a thousand years,' imprisoned in an abyss so he cannot deceive the nations. This directly parallels Isaiah 24:22's vision of prolonged imprisonment before visitation, suggesting apocalyptic continuity across Scripture.

Peter writes that 'God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment.' This applies Isaiah's vision to the imprisonment of fallen angels.

Jude similarly describes angels 'which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation' as being 'reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.' This confirms the apocalyptic pattern of Isaiah 24:22.

Joseph Smith describes the imprisonment of Satan and his hosts in outer darkness 'where there is weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth.' The Doctrine and Covenants applies Isaiah's vision to the final state of rebellion.

commentary.historical_context: The image of a dungeon or pit was familiar to ancient Near Eastern listeners. Kings and military leaders routinely imprisoned captives and rebels in underground chambers to neutralize their threat. The practice of prolonged confinement before execution or final judgment was also known. Isaiah uses this familiar imagery to make the abstract concept of cosmic judgment comprehensible. The 'many days' suggests both the patience of God (allowing time for repentance) and the protracted nature of the apocalyptic process — not a single instant of judgment but a series of acts unfolding over ages.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 40:11-14, Alma describes the state of spirits after death: the righteous enter 'a state of happiness' while the wicked enter 'a state of darkness and awful fear.' The confined state described in Isaiah 24:22 is analogous to this intermediate state — a confinement pending final judgment or disposition.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:27-28 describes how 'an angel of God' will 'thrust [Satan] down, that he shall not have power over the saints.' Isaiah 24:22's imprisonment of the powers of rebellion is part of the same cosmic drama. D&C 76:103-109 expands on this with more detail about outer darkness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place of covenant renewal and deliverance from sin. Isaiah 24:22's imprisonment of rebels points, by contrast, to the temple as the refuge from judgment. Those who enter the temple covenants are not imprisoned but are instead prepared to stand in God's presence.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's descent into Hades (1 Peter 3:18-20) and His resurrection involve a passage through the place of the dead and confinement. But unlike the rebels of Isaiah 24:22, Christ's confinement is temporary and redemptive — He breaks its bonds and rises. In Matthew 12:40, Jesus is 'in the heart of the earth three days and three nights,' a prophetic echo of the 'many days' of confinement. But Christ's confinement ends in resurrection and triumph, not in final judgment.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse teaches that rebellion against God, whether personal or cosmic, ultimately leads to confinement, isolation, and a reckoning. The 'many days' before visitation suggests that God's judgment may be delayed but is not avoided. The ambiguity about what happens at the visitation itself — is it mercy or destruction? — invites humility. We do not fully know God's final intentions toward all creation. What we know is that God's justice will ultimately be executed, and all powers will be held accountable. This should inspire both reverence and hope: reverence because judgment is real, and hope because God's visitation, whatever form it takes, is ultimately God's presence and sovereignty.

text_kjv: Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 24 culminates in verse 23, which pivots from judgment to glory. The chapter opened with cosmic dissolution and imprisonment of rebel powers; it closes with the LORD reigning in Zion. The opening movements of the Apocalypse have been destructive — the earth shattered, the powers judged and imprisoned. Now comes the revelation of why: to make room for God's reign. The sun and moon, which have commanded awe since creation, are now 'confounded' (haprah, 'ashamed, humiliated') and 'ashamed' (hosah, 'filled with shame'). These are the most dependable lights in the cosmos, worshipped by pagan nations as deities. Yet when the LORD reigns, their light is eclipsed and irrelevant. They are not destroyed but are outshone, embarrassed by comparison with God's glory.

The center of God's reign is Mount Zion in Jerusalem — the temple mountain, the place where the earth meets heaven, where God's presence dwells among His covenant people. The phrase 'before his ancients gloriously' echoes Exodus 24:9-11, where the seventy elders of Israel 'saw God, and did eat and drink' — they beheld God's presence directly. Here, the same 'ancients' (ziqenim, 'elders') will witness God's full revelation of glory (kavod). The final word of the chapter — and of the Apocalypse's opening movement — is 'glory' (kavod), the visible, weighty manifestation of God's presence. This is the answer to all the catastrophe and chaos: God's glory, long hidden and obscured, will finally be revealed in full. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse identically to the Masoretic Text, showing this vision of eschatological vindication was consistent in the Jewish tradition.

The Covenant Rendering translates the final phrase more literally: 'and before His elders — glory.' Rather than 'gloriously' as an adverb, the Hebrew simply places 'glory' as the noun at the verse's end, making it stand alone with full weight. This is more powerful — not a description of how the LORD reigns, but the declaration of what will be revealed: glory itself, the presence and power of God made visible.

word_study.meaning: The verb parah means 'to be ashamed, to be abashed, to blush.' In the niphal form hafrah, it becomes passive: 'is humiliated.' The emotional content is intense — not merely dimmed but embarrassed, put to shame.
word_study.significance: This verb is used in Isaiah's condemnations of idolatry (45:16-17) and the futility of human wisdom (29:14). The sun and moon, long objects of worship, will be shamed by God's greater glory.

word_study.meaning: The verb yosh means 'to be ashamed, to be abashed.' The Hebrew uses both hafrah and boshah in succession, creating a heightened, intensified expression of the sun's shame. The doubling emphasizes totality.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah 50:7, the Servant (Christ) says 'I will not be ashamed' — contrasting with the cosmic powers that will be shamed. Christ's dignity is opposed to their humiliation.

word_study.meaning: The verb malakh means 'to be king, to rule, to reign.' Here in the simple qal form (past tense used prophetically): the LORD 'reigned' — asserting that what Isaiah announces is certain, already accomplished in God's purposes.
word_study.significance: This verb is fundamental to Isaiah's eschatology. From 6:1 ('I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up') to this verse, Isaiah has been announcing God's ultimate kingship. The verb frames the entire book.

word_study.meaning: Neged means 'before, in the presence of.' Zeqenim ('elders') are the covenant witnesses and leaders of Israel. This is the same group who ate and drank before God at Sinai (Exodus 24:9-11).
word_study.significance: The elders represent the covenant community. God's final glory is revealed not to all creation but to those bound in covenant — they are the witnesses and recipients of the promise.

word_study.meaning: The substantive noun kavod ('glory, honor, weight, substance') describes the visible manifestation of God's presence — the radiance and reality of the divine. This is the same root as the verb kavad ('to be heavy') in verse 20, where transgression weighs heavily. Here, God's glory — the ultimate weight, reality, and substance — outshines all else.
word_study.significance: Kavod appears in Exodus 40:34 (filling the tabernacle), 1 Kings 8:11 (filling the temple), and throughout Isaiah as the ultimate revelation. It is the climax of the divine plan: not judgment alone, but God's revealed presence.

cross_references.connection: John's vision of the New Jerusalem declares 'the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it.' This directly fulfills Isaiah 24:23's vision: God's glory outshines all other light sources.

The elders of Israel 'saw God' and 'did eat and drink' at Sinai. Isaiah 24:23 hearkens to this moment and announces its eschatological fulfillment — the covenant community will again directly witness God's presence.

Joseph Smith taught that 'all spirit is matter, but more fine or pure' and that glory is the light and power of God. The Doctrine and Covenants explains the metaphysics of the 'glory' that will be revealed: it is God's actual power made manifest.

The psalm asks 'Who is this King of glory?' and answers 'The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory.' Isaiah 24:23 answers the psalm's question: the LORD of Hosts will reign in Zion, and His glory will be made known.
Earlier in Isaiah, the temple mountain is exalted 'above the hills' and people 'shall flow unto it.' Isaiah 24:23 completes this vision: Zion becomes the center of God's revealed reign.

Zechariah prophesies 'And the LORD shall be king over all the earth' — a parallel eschatological vision that develops from Isaiah's Apocalypse. Both prophets announce God's universal kingship centered on Jerusalem.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient world, the sun and moon were among the most universally worshipped deities. In Egypt, Ra or Aten; in Mesopotamia, Shamash and Sin; in Greece, Helios and Selene. Isaiah's declaration that these cosmic powers will be 'ashamed' before the God of Israel was a remarkable assertion of exclusive monotheism and the supremacy of the God who created both sun and moon. For an ancient reader familiar with star worship and planetary deities, the image would have been scandalous and liberating in equal measure: no power in heaven or earth rivals Israel's God. The reference to Mount Zion and Jerusalem — the historical capital of the Judean kingdom — grounds the cosmic vision in a concrete, recognizable place. God's reign is not abstract or distant but will be visibly, concretely established on earth, in the holy city.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 10:15-18, Nephi promises that 'the Lord will be merciful unto all them that believe in his name.' The 'ancients' of Isaiah 24:23 are those who have kept covenant and believed. In 1 Nephi 22:23-24, Nephi teaches that the righteous will 'rejoice' and 'be made white, even as white as snow' when God's covenant is fulfilled.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:50-70 describes the Celestial Kingdom, where the righteous will 'see the face of God' and 'dwell in his presence.' This is the Restoration's expansion of Isaiah 24:23 — the covenanted people will witness God's glory directly. D&C 84:20-22 speaks of 'all that [the Father] hath' being given to those who receive the ordinances and keep covenant, directly echoing the promise to the 'ancients' in Zion.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is where this promise is enacted symbolically in our day. In temple worship, we approach the presence of God (represented by the veil and higher ordinances) and are brought into proximity with the divine glory. Isaiah 24:23's vision of the elders standing before God in Zion is the eschatological fulfillment of what temple worship shadows forth.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the source and revealer of this glory. In John 1:14, 'the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.' Christ is the kavod (glory) incarnate. He appears in the temple (Malachi 3:1), and His return to Zion signals the establishment of God's kingdom. In Revelation 5, Christ is revealed as the worthy one to open the seals and execute the judgment that Isaiah 24 describes. The apocalyptic judgment of verses 19-22 leads to the triumphant reign of verse 23 — the movement from Christ's judgment to His eternal kingship.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 23 offers profound hope. In a world that often feels chaotic, unjust, and spiritually dark, Isaiah announces that God's reign is coming, His glory will be revealed, and the covenant people will witness it. The 'ancients' standing before God's glory represents the privilege and responsibility of covenant holders to maintain faithfulness until that day arrives. The sun and moon — once symbols of cosmic permanence — will pale before God's presence. What are the 'suns and moons' in our lives that we have been treating as ultimate authorities? What earthly powers or values have we worshipped or feared? Isaiah calls us to reorient: the glory of God, revealed through Christ and in the temple, is the only light that ultimately matters. Our covenant membership is an invitation to be among the 'ancients' who stand before that glory.

text_kjv: O LORD, thou art my God; I will exalt thee, I will praise thy name; for thou hast done wonderful things; thy counsels of old are faithfulness and truth.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah opens chapter 25 with a doxology of praise that shifts the emotional register dramatically from the devastation of chapter 24. The prophet has witnessed cosmic judgment — the earth laid waste, its inhabitants scattered — and now responds not with despair but with radical trust in God's character. The phrase 'thy counsels of old' (etsot merachoq in Hebrew) is theologically crucial: it affirms that the judgment Isaiah has just described was not improvised or reactive, but planned from ages past. God did not wake up in chapter 24 and decide to punish the earth. His intentions have been consistent, steadfast, loyal (emunah — 'faithfulness') from the beginning of time.

This opening verse establishes the hermeneutical key for all that follows: the devastation is not chaos or tragedy, but the execution of God's ancient purpose. The poet calls on others to join him in exalting and praising God precisely because of these 'wonderful things' — which includes the judgments that others might find fearful. The repetition of 'I will exalt thee, I will praise thy name' (with 'exalt' preceding 'praise') suggests a movement from elevation of God's rank to acknowledgment of His character. The prophet is inviting the reader into a posture of trust despite, or rather through, the devastation.

word_study.meaning: Plans formed long ago, literally 'counsels from afar.' The phrase combines etsot ('plans, counsels, purposes') with merachoq ('from afar, from a distance'). This suggests purposes conceived in the distant past, or viewed from divine distance/perspective.
word_study.significance: Emphasizes God's eternality and prescience. The judgments of chapter 24 were not improvised but ancient in their origin. This term appears only here in Isaiah and anchors the eschatological vision in God's timeless purposes. The Covenant Rendering's 'plans formed long ago' captures the sense of temporal depth.

word_study.meaning: Emunah derives from the root amn ('to be firm, stable, reliable') and describes unwavering consistency, loyalty, and trustworthiness — foundational to covenant relationship. Omen ('sureness, truth, stability') reinforces the idea of dependability. These are paired terms describing God's character as both loyal and reliable.
word_study.significance: In the context of covenant theology, emunah is the bedrock virtue — it is what makes God's word trustworthy and His promises binding. The pairing of emunah with omen stresses that God's plans are not merely true intellectually but emotionally and relationally trustworthy. Modern readers might miss that 'faithfulness' here is not sentiment but covenantal obligation.

word_study.meaning: A wonder, marvel, or remarkable deed. The root pele' suggests something beyond ordinary expectation or explanation — it carries connotations of the miraculous and the transcendent.
word_study.significance: The prophet calls the devastations and judgments of chapter 24 'wonderful things' (pele'ot). This reframes catastrophe as manifestation of divine power. In biblical usage, pele' often describes miracles (Exodus 3:20, Psalm 77:14), making it theologically provocative to apply it to judgment.

cross_references.connection: The immediate context: the earth is laid waste, its inhabitants scattered, judgment falling universally. Verse 1 praises God for executing these very judgments described in chapter 24.

The LORD established the earth through understanding and knowledge; His depths break forth as fountains. Isaiah's affirmation of God's ancient counsels parallels wisdom literature's portrayal of God's foundational planning.

The vision of the Three Degrees of Glory opens with praise for God's councils (organized 'in the days of old') and affirmation that His purposes are 'faithful and sure' — directly echoing Isaiah's language.

The Lord has taken upon Himself 'the pains and the sicknesses of his people' to know how to minister unto them — reflecting God's ancient counsel to redeem humanity, which Isaiah celebrates as 'wonderful things.'

The heavenly doxology echoes Isaiah's praise structure: 'Worthy art thou, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things.' Both passages join the prophet in exalting God's character and purposes.

commentary.historical_context: The historical background of Isaiah 25 is debated among scholars, but the chapter clearly responds to a moment of divine judgment on the nations. Some scholars place it after the destruction of an Assyrian army or in the context of Babylonian exile; others read it as purely eschatological. Regardless of historical occasion, the cultural context is crucial: ancient Near Eastern conquest narratives typically celebrated the conqueror's power. Isaiah's innovation is to celebrate God's judgment as expression of His eternally consistent character, not as reactive violence. The 'counsels of old' language reflects the Israelite conviction that God's purposes transcend human history — He does not change course based on circumstances. The poet is using the language of stability and permanence (emunah, omen) that would have resonated deeply in covenant renewal contexts, where Israel would reaffirm its trust in God's unbroken loyalty despite historical turmoil.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi quotes and expounds Isaiah 25:1-9 in 2 Nephi 8:24-9:2, applying Isaiah's eschatological vision to the restoration of the house of Israel and the promised land. Nephi emphasizes that God's plans are 'from the beginning' and that His judgments serve His eternal purpose of gathering His people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76 presents Joseph Smith's vision of the degrees of glory as fulfillment of God's 'councils organized in the days of old.' The parallel to Isaiah's 'counsels of old' suggests that the restoration is the unveiling of purposes formed before the foundation of the world. D&C 88:6-13 similarly portrays light (the spirit of truth) as the mechanism through which God's eternal purposes are revealed to humanity.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The movement from judgment (chapter 24) to feasting on the holy mountain (chapter 25:6) mirrors the temple experience: ascending to God's house involves ascending through trials and testing, then receiving abundance and covenant. Isaiah's praise of God's 'wonderful things' anticipates the temple covenant, where the individual recognizes God's hand in both refinement and blessing.

commentary.christological_typology: The 'wonderful things' Isaiah praises include the judgment that Christ will execute as judge. More subtly, Christ embodies the 'faithfulness and truth' (emunah and omen) that characterize God's ancient counsels — He is the fulfillment of purposes formed before the foundation of the world. In John 1:14, the Word becomes flesh 'full of grace and truth' (echoing the covenantal language of emunah). The doxology that opens Isaiah 25 anticipates the eschatological praise of the Lamb in Revelation 5:12-13, where Christ is exalted for His redemptive work.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members face a world that often appears chaotic and ungoverned — a 'laid waste' earth in some respects (ecological crisis, social fragmentation, war). Isaiah 25:1 invites us into a counterintuitive posture: to praise God not despite judgment and devastation, but because we trust that His purposes are being executed according to an ancient, faithful plan. This is not passive fatalism but active faith — recognizing that when we cannot see the whole tapestry, we can trust the Weaver's character. The challenge to the modern reader is whether we will join Isaiah in exalting God for His 'counsels of old' even when we cannot yet see how they redeem the present moment. This requires moving from sentiment ('God loves me') to conviction ('God's plans are faithful and true').

text_kjv: For thou hast made of a city an heap; of a defenced city a ruin: a palace of strangers to be no city; it shall never be built.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 2 provides concrete historical instantiation of the abstract 'wonderful things' praised in verse 1. The prophet now describes the execution of God's ancient counsel in specific, devastating terms: a city has been reduced to rubble. The threefold progression — city to heap, fortified city to ruin, palace to non-city — traces the complete annihilation of human achievement and pride. The definite article suggests a specific city well-known to Isaiah's audience, though the text does not name it. Historically, scholars have proposed various candidates (Moab's capital, an Assyrian stronghold, Jerusalem's enemies), but the textual anonymity is theologically intentional: the city becomes an archetype of human rebellion and divine judgment.

The phrase 'it shall never be built' (le'olam lo yibbaneh) echoes the language of cherem in ancient Near Eastern treaties — a city placed under eternal curse, rendered permanently uninhabitable. This is not mere destruction but obliteration, removal from the realm of possibility. Yet this verse is not gratuitous violence; it is the fulfillment of God's 'counsels of old' — justice executing according to design. The repetition of destruction language (heap, ruin, no city) hammers home the totality of the reversal. What was fortified is now defenseless; what was built is now undone. The prophet is inviting the reader to see in this historical moment the hand of God's ancient purpose.

word_study.meaning: A heap or pile of stones. Gal literally denotes a mound or cairn — in this context, the rubble of a destroyed city.
word_study.significance: In ancient Near Eastern conquest rhetoric, reducing a city to a 'heap' was a formula of total victory (cf. Joshua 8:28, 11:13). The term evokes both the physical reality (broken walls, scattered stones) and the symbolic meaning (the obliteration of ordered civilization).

word_study.meaning: A fortified city; literally 'a city + fortified/strong.' Bezurah derives from tzur ('rock, strength, fortress') and describes cities built with defensive architecture and walls.
word_study.significance: The parallelism emphasizes that no human fortification can withstand God's judgment. The besieged city, however strong its walls, becomes 'no city' — its infrastructure negated.

word_study.meaning: Armon ('palace, fortress') refers to royal or noble residence; zarim ('strangers, foreigners, aliens') designates those outside the covenant community. The palace of foreigners is the seat of alien rule.
word_study.significance: This phrase suggests the city belongs to an occupying power or hostile nation. Its destruction removes foreign rule from God's land. The term zarim resonates throughout Isaiah 25-26 as a recurring motif — the alienation of those outside God's covenant.

word_study.meaning: Forever will it not be built; le'olam ('forever, eternity') + lo ('not') + yibbaneh ('will be built, shall rise'). This is absolute negation across all time.
word_study.significance: The permanence of this curse is theologically significant. This is not temporary judgment but eternal removal — the city cannot recover or be restored. It echoes the language of cherem (devoted to destruction) in ancient Israelite law, where certain cities or peoples were placed beyond redemption.

cross_references.connection: The preceding chapter describes the entire earth laid waste; verse 2 provides a specific instance — the city that embodies human civilization reduced to ruin.
Jericho is utterly destroyed under the cherem (devoted/cursed thing), and Joshua pronounces that whoever rebuilds it will incur a curse — paralleling Isaiah's 'shall never be built.'
Jeremiah uses identical language — 'it shall be a desolate heap' — echoing the formula of divine judgment on cities and nations that oppose God's people.

The Lord speaks of His judgment: 'I will come... with all the power of my might, and will make a veil of darkness cover the earth.' Isaiah's vision of universal judgment is echoed in latter-day revelation.

Alma recognizes that God's judgments are 'just and true' and come upon those who rebel. The destruction of the city in Isaiah 25:2 exemplifies the principle that divine judgment follows rebellion against God's purposes.

commentary.historical_context: The reduction of a fortified city to 'a heap of stones' was a common outcome of ancient Near Eastern sieges, particularly in the Assyrian period. Archaeological excavation at sites like Lachish, Samaria, and others shows evidence of destruction layers corresponding to Assyrian campaigns. The cultural significance of 'heap' language cannot be overstated: in the ancient mind, a city that had been destroyed was not merely temporarily disabled but fundamentally delegitimized. The prophet's prediction that it 'shall never be built' would have resonated powerfully in a context where ruined cities sometimes were rebuilt (as Samaria was). For a city to be placed under eternal curse meant no future generation would reclaim it — it passed from human history into memory of divine judgment. The 'palace of strangers' language suggests a city occupied by a foreign power (possibly Assyrian, Babylonian, or even Arab tribes), making its destruction a act of liberation and restoration of God's sovereignty over His land.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi applies Isaiah's prophecies of destroyed cities to the future destruction of those who reject the gospel (2 Nephi 15:24-30, quoting Isaiah 5:24-30). The pattern of judgment against cities and nations that oppose God's purposes is central to Book of Mormon theology — Nephite and Lamanite cities are destroyed when they turn from covenant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:36-37 warns: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful... those who receive my commandments keep them shall grow up in me, and unto them will I reveal all things. But those who receive not my commandments... the heavens withdraw themselves, the Spirit of the Lord is withdrawn.' The destruction of the city echoes this principle of conditional blessing — the city that does not acknowledge God's sovereignty is removed from possibility.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The destruction and non-rebuilding of the city contrasts with the building of God's house (the temple, Zion) which will be exalted above all mountains (Isaiah 2:2-3). The removal of human cities that rebel against God makes room for the establishment of God's holy dwelling.

commentary.christological_typology: In Revelation 18:2-19, the fall of Babylon ('a great city') is described in language directly dependent on Isaiah 25:2 — reduced to ruin, smoke ascending forever, never to be rebuilt. This eschatological judgment on the city that opposes God's kingdom finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ's final judgment. More subtly, Christ is the stone that becomes 'a great mountain' (Daniel 2:35), replacing the ruined cities of human rebellion with God's eternal kingdom.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse presents a challenging question: What 'cities' (symbols of human achievement, institutional power, worldly success) are we building that may not survive God's judgment? The verse does not call for fatalism but for discernment — recognizing which pursuits are aligned with God's eternal purposes and which are destined for ruin. The promise that the city 'shall never be built' is simultaneously a warning: investments in rebellion against God's purposes yield no lasting return. This invites believers to redirect their building efforts toward God's Zion, which will endure forever.

text_kjv: Therefore shall the strong people glorify thee, the city of the terrible nations shall fear thee.

commentary.narrative:
Having witnessed the destruction of the city (verse 2), Isaiah now pivots to an unexpected reversal: the very 'strong people' and 'terrible nations' who were instruments of judgment — or who might have regarded themselves as invulnerable — now glorify and fear God. This verse articulates a central theme of Isaiah's apocalyptic vision: the judgment of chapter 24 has a converting power. Those who experience God's power in judgment are brought to recognition of His sovereignty.

The parallelism is precise: 'strong people will glorify thee' parallels 'terrible nations will fear thee.' Glorification and fear are complementary responses to divine power — the former is affirmation of God's worth and rank, the latter is acknowledgment of His awesome majesty and the consequences of opposing Him. The word 'therefore' (ken) links this response causally to the destruction just described: because God has executed judgment, even the strong and terrible bow. There is no resistance left; the cosmic order has been reestablished. The shift is from God's power manifested in destruction (verse 2) to the nations' response of submission and reverence (verse 3). This is the eschatological goal — all peoples acknowledging God's kingship.

word_study.meaning: Az ('strength, might, power') describes the fierce, powerful, strong. Am oz literally means 'mighty people' or 'fierce people.' The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'fierce' captures the aggressive, overwhelming nature implied.
word_study.significance: This is the same word used to describe the ruthless, tyrannical oppressors in verse 4 (goyim aritsim, 'ruthless nations'). The powerful who inflict suffering are now brought low and made to glorify God — there is no exception to God's sovereignty.

word_study.meaning: To honor, glorify, make heavy/weighty. Kabad derives from the sense of 'weight' or 'heaviness' and means to ascribe weight, importance, rank to someone. To glorify God is to acknowledge His supreme worth.
word_study.significance: The same verb appears in the Kaddish ('Yitkaddal v'Yitkaddash shemkha' — 'Magnified and sanctified be His name'). To glorify is both a public acknowledgment and an internal transformation — the recognition that God deserves the highest rank.

word_study.meaning: Qiryah ('city') + goyim ('nations, peoples') + aritsim ('terrible, ruthless, tyrannical'). Aritsim derives from arats ('to tremble, shake') and suggests those who inspire fear through violence and oppression.
word_study.significance: The 'terrible nations' are the oppressive powers; their 'city' is the seat of their authority. Yet even this stronghold of tyranny bows to God. The plural 'nations' suggests not one power but the collective opposition of the world against God's purposes.

word_study.meaning: To fear, reverence, stand in awe of. Fear of God (yirat Elohim) is a central virtue in Hebrew wisdom and covenant theology — it means to regard God with appropriate weight and reverence.
word_study.significance: The 'fear of the Lord' is not primarily emotional terror but covenantal recognition — the acknowledgment that God deserves absolute loyalty because of His power and justice. The terrible nations, who have inspired fear in others, now experience the only fear that endures: reverence before God.

cross_references.connection: Paul quotes Isaiah: 'Every knee shall bow... and every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.' This is the fulfillment of Isaiah's vision — all peoples, strong and weak, acknowledging God's sovereignty.
The saints sing: 'Who shall not fear thee, O Lord, and glorify thy name? for thou only art holy.' This echoes Isaiah's eschatological vision — all creation brought to glorify God.
'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.' Isaiah's vision of the nations fearing God expresses the hope that all peoples will attain true wisdom through acknowledgment of divine sovereignty.

In the Vision of the Three Degrees of Glory, all beings ultimately acknowledge God's sovereignty: 'And then shall the faithful Saints go to Heaven, and the earth shall be renewed in its paradisiacal glory.' The universal glorification of God is the eschatological goal.

King Benjamin's people fall to the earth and cry out: 'O have mercy, and apply the atoning blood of Christ that we may receive forgiveness of our sins.' The fear and glorification of God arising from recognition of His power is the catalyst for repentance.
