The verse concludes the prayer with a profound affirmation of divine sovereignty that transforms the entire arc of verses 7-12. The speaker moves from petition to confidence, declaring that God 'will ordain peace for us' (*tishpot shalom lanu*). The verb *shapat* (ordain, judge, establish) is the same root as 'judge' and 'judgment' throughout this chapter, suggesting that the ultimate vindication of judgment is peace. God's judgments, which seem harsh in the moment, are establishing peace for the righteous. This is not mere hope but confident declaration: the speaker trusts that God will bring justice to completion.

But the final clause is even more radical: 'for thou also hast wrought all our works in us' (*kol ma'aseinu pa'alta lanu*). The speaker attributes all human achievement and accomplishment to God. This is not fatalism or denial of human effort but a recognition that whatever good has been accomplished—the community's faithfulness through exile, their return, their rebuilding—is ultimately God's work. The righteous do not earn peace through their own works but receive it as a gift rooted in God's sovereignty. The verse thus resolves the tension between human obedience (verses 7-8, 9) and divine action (verses 7, 12): the righteous walk the level path, seek God in darkness, wait in judgment—and all of this is empowered by God working in and through them. There is no contradiction between human responsibility and divine sovereignty; they are two sides of the same reality.

word_study.meaning: to ordain, to establish, to judge, to determine; shapat is the verb for divine judgment and the basis of shalom (peace). God judges in order to establish justice and peace.
word_study.significance: The same root (shapat) appears throughout the chapter in reference to God's 'judgments' (mishpatim). The final resolution is that judgment establishes peace. This reframes all the preceding talk of judgment as purposive and redemptive.

word_study.meaning: peace, wholeness, completeness, well-being, reconciliation; shalom is not merely the absence of conflict but the presence of right order, justice, and relationship.
word_study.significance: Shalom is the goal and fruit of God's judgments. The righteous do not seek escape from judgment but understand that judgment leads to peace—the restoration of right relationship with God and each other.

word_study.meaning: to work, to accomplish, to do, to make; pa'al emphasizes the actual doing and accomplishing of something significant.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests that God is the active agent—He works, He accomplishes, He brings things to pass. Human works are real, but they are empowered by God's work.

word_study.meaning: works, deeds, accomplishments, actions; ma'aseh refers to concrete actions and their results. The plural form suggests the totality of human effort and achievement.
word_study.significance: The affirmation covers 'all our works'—not just some spiritual achievements but every accomplishment, every step, every work of rebuilding and faithfulness. All is attributed to God.

word_study.meaning: for us, to us; lanu suggests the divine action is not abstract but directed toward the community's benefit.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes that God's work is not impersonal but for the sake of His people. God works 'for us'—this is personal, covenantal action.

cross_references.connection: Paul writes, 'Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure'—the paradox of human effort empowered by divine action mirrors Isaiah 26:12.

'Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass. And he shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday'—peace and vindication are God's work, not human.

Jesus teaches, 'Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me...for without me ye can do nothing'—human work depends entirely on divine empowerment.

'Verily I say unto you, the Lord thy God hath spoken it; the messenger whom I have sent hath said it...Wherefore, he that preach the gospel of peace, and not of contention, is called to the work of my Father.'

The Lamanites declare, 'Yea, I do thank my God for the exceeding goodness...which I have received in giving me an awakening unto the knowledge of his word'—acknowledging that awakening and all good works come from God.

commentary.historical_context: This verse reflects post-exilic theology where the community, having experienced exile and judgment, returned to Jerusalem to rebuild. The affirmation that 'all our works' are God's work would have spoken directly to the question: How can we—a weak remnant facing opposition—possibly rebuild the temple and restore our nation? The answer: all the work is God's. This is not to diminish human effort but to locate its source and power. The Deuteronomic worldview that dominated post-exilic thought held that national survival and restoration depended entirely on covenant faithfulness and God's power. Isaiah 26:12 articulates this with profound clarity: whatever the remnant accomplishes is God's accomplishment through them.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 31:19 teaches, 'Wherefore, my beloved brethren, I know that if ye shall follow the Son, with full purpose of heart, acting no hypocrisy and no deception before God, but with real intent, repenting of your sins, witnessing unto the Father that ye are willing to take upon you the name of Christ by baptism...Ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men.' Human 'pressing forward' is real, but it is empowered by God working through the covenant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:33 reveals, 'Behold, thou hast a gift, and blessed art thou because of thy gift. Remember it is sacred and cometh from above.' All gifts and accomplishments are attributed to God. Furthermore, D&C 84:48-49 teaches that when the righteous take upon them the name of Christ and keep His covenants, 'their works shall be white as snow; and their garments shall be white, and I will not suffer that they shall be defiled.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, the initiate learns that all power comes from God—the righteous work through ordinances and covenants, but the power by which transformation occurs is God's. Isaiah 26:12 provides scriptural foundation for this understanding: 'thou...hast wrought all our works in us.'

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah 26:12. His entire earthly ministry was accomplished 'not I, but the Father that dwelleth in me' (John 14:10). His works—the healings, the teachings, the atonement itself—are God's works. Yet Christ is fully human and fully divine; He works and the Father works through Him. In the Resurrection, the ultimate peace is established: death is conquered, division between God and humanity is healed, and the Father's work is complete. The righteous, grafted into Christ, participate in His pattern: they work, yet God works through them.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members often struggle with the balance between personal responsibility and divine grace. Isaiah 26:12 resolves this tension: you are responsible to keep commandments, make covenants, and serve faithfully. But the ultimate source of all progress—spiritual and temporal—is God's work in and through you. When you accomplish something significant in righteousness, do not take pride in your effort alone but attribute it to God working in you. When you repent and change, recognize that the Holy Ghost is doing the deeper work. When your family grows in faith or your callings bear fruit, see God's hand. This is not to excuse yourself from effort but to locate your effort within a larger divine framework. The peace that God 'ordains' for you is not merely an external state but an internal recognition that you are part of God's redemptive work—your ordinary labors, done in covenant, participate in His purposes. This reorients your sense of accomplishment from pride to gratitude, and transforms your works from burdens into participation in God's work.

text_kjv: O LORD our God, other lords beside thee have had dominion over us: but by thee only will we make mention of thy name.

commentary.narrative: This verse opens a powerful confession of Israel's unfaithfulness and renewed commitment. The people acknowledge a stark historical reality: foreign powers and false gods have held dominion over them. The Hebrew word ba'al (from be'alunu, 'have mastered us') carries a double meaning—it refers both to 'mastery' and to the Canaanite fertility deity Baal, the chief rival to Israel's covenant loyalty. The translator notes from The Covenant Rendering highlight this wordplay: 'other ba'als have been our ba'al'—a devastating admission that Israel has served both foreign political masters and the idolatrous practices those powers brought with them. This is not a boast about past sins but a turning point: having named the problem, the people now turn decisively away from all rival allegiances.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second half of the verse marks the pivot: 'but by thee only will we make mention of thy name.' The Hebrew phrase levad-bekha nazkir shemekha ('by You alone we invoke Your name') is an exclusive covenant renewal. To 'invoke the name' in ancient Israelite practice was to place oneself under the protection and authority of that deity—it was a solemn act of allegiance. The people are not merely praying; they are publicly renouncing all other masters and declaring themselves once more the exclusive servants of YHWH. In the context of Isaiah's prophecy, this confession comes after deep suffering under Assyrian and Babylonian domination. The renunciation is therefore costly—it is made in the face of actual military defeat and captivity. The message is that submission to foreign powers, however real, cannot compare to the call of covenant fidelity. Modern readers might hear this as an invitation to examine what 'lords' (distractions, false securities, rival loyalties) have gained dominion in their own lives.

word_study.meaning: Other lords/masters besides You. Adonim is the plural of adon (lord, master, owner). Zulatekha means 'other than You.' The term adon carries authority and ownership language.
word_study.significance: The people confess that they have been ruled by other powers—both literal foreign rulers and the spiritual masters (false gods) those rulers served. This is a direct acknowledgment of covenantal breach.

word_study.meaning: Have mastered/owned us. From the root ba'al, meaning 'to master, to own, to rule.' The word also names the Canaanite deity Baal.
word_study.significance: The wordplay is intentional and theologically loaded: other ba'als (both the deity and the concept of mastery) have made themselves ba'al (master) over Israel. This verbal connection makes explicit the link between political subjugation and spiritual idolatry. The Covenant Rendering preserves this richness by recognizing ba'al as a proper name in this context.

word_study.meaning: We will make mention of, invoke, or call upon Your name. From zakar, 'to remember, to mention.' Shem means 'name' but also 'reputation, character, being.'
word_study.significance: To invoke God's name in covenant context is to place oneself under His authority and protection. It is an act of exclusive allegiance and relational dependence. The plural 'we' indicates this is a communal, corporate renewal of covenant.

cross_references.connection: The Shema—'Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD'—is the foundational statement of exclusive monotheistic allegiance that this verse echoes and renews.

Israel's confession of unfaithfulness and turning from 'other lords' mirrors the repentance language Jeremiah calls God's people to make: 'Only acknowledge thine iniquity, that thou hast transgressed against the LORD thy God.'
Paul's discussion of idols and the exclusive lordship of Christ ('one Lord Jesus Christ') reflects the same exclusive monotheistic stance Isaiah's people are renewing here.
Joshua's challenge—'choose you this day whom ye will serve'—frames the same moment of exclusive covenant choice that Isaiah 26:13 represents in a later, post-exile context.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah 26 is part of the 'Isaiah Apocalypse' (chapters 24–27), likely composed during the late Babylonian exile or early Persian period when Jerusalem had been destroyed and Judah's population displaced. The 'other lords' who had 'dominion' are the Babylonian and Assyrian empires that had successively conquered Israel and Judah. The confession is remarkably honest about the political reality: Israel had fallen under foreign rule. However, the deeper concern is spiritual—the military defeat had also exposed the people's prior turning to the gods of their conquerors, a common survival strategy in the ancient world. By the time of this passage, the people are reclaiming an exclusive monotheistic identity. The mention of invoking God's name exclusively suggests a post-exilic context where religious identity became the primary marker of Judean survival, since political independence was not yet restored. The cultural practice of 'invoking a name' in the ancient Near East was a formal acknowledgment of vassalage or protection—by invoking YHWH's name alone, Israel is choosing theological fealty over political pragmatism.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 5:41-42 records a similar moment of covenant renewal when the people of Ammon 'did covenant with their God, that rather than shed the blood of their brethren they would give up their own lives.' Like Isaiah's people, they are renouncing rival allegiances (in their case, to weapons and violence) and reinvesting exclusive loyalty in God's covenant. The language of exclusive devotion recurs throughout Book of Mormon narratives of spiritual recovery.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:34-35 records Jesus teaching that when people serve 'other lords,' the consequences are bondage and darkness, but those who serve Him exclusively receive light and understanding. This echoes Isaiah's diagnosis that other masters bring no lasting good—only the LORD offers true deliverance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The invocation of God's name connects to temple covenant language, where individuals explicitly place themselves under divine authority and renounce all other masters. The renewal aspect parallels the periodic renewal of covenants in temple worship and in Latter-day Saint practice generally.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah's people are renouncing rival lords and invoking God's name exclusively—a posture that points forward to Christ's supremacy over all other powers and authorities. In the New Testament, Jesus embodies this exclusivity: 'No one cometh unto the Father, but by me' (John 14:6). The covenant renewal in verse 13 foreshadows the exclusive claim Christ makes on human allegiance.
commentary.application: Modern disciples face subtle versions of the same choice Isaiah's people faced. While few of us literally serve foreign gods, we can ask: What 'lords' have dominion over my attention, my resources, my time, my sense of security? Consumer culture, career advancement, social approval, or personal comfort can become functional 'ba'als'—masters that rule our decisions. This verse invites us to name those rival allegiances honestly and then, like Isaiah's people, to make an explicit covenant renewal: to invoke God's name—His character, His authority, His will—as the singular master of our choices. The text suggests this is not a passive internal attitude but an active, spoken, communal declaration. What would change if you explicitly, regularly, and publicly renewed the claim that God alone is your Lord?

text_kjv: They are dead, they shall not live; they are deceased, they shall not rise: therefore hast thou visited and destroyed them, and made all their memory to perish.

commentary.narrative: Verse 14 completes the thought begun in verse 13 by declaring the ultimate fate of those 'other lords' who had ruled over Israel. The verse shifts focus from human political masters to the false gods and spiritual powers those masters embodied. The people make a stark declaration: the dead do not live, the shades (refa'im) do not rise. This is a categorical assertion of divine finality—unlike living nations or human beings, the false gods and the powers they represent are consigned to permanent powerlessness in Sheol, the realm of the dead. The theological force is stunning: whatever temporary dominion these false lords exercised over Israel is now finished, nullified, consigned to oblivion.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second half of the verse attributes this finality to God's action: 'therefore hast thou visited and destroyed them.' God has 'visited' (punished, judged) the false lords and 'made all their memory to perish.' The word zeikher (memory) is crucial—to erase someone's memory in ancient Near Eastern thought was to erase their name, their influence, their very existence in the collective consciousness. This verse anticipates the resurrection promise of verse 19 by contrast: if the false lords are dead and shall not rise, then when God's own people rise from the dead, it will be an incomparable vindication. The refa'im (shades) are the powerless dead—not demons or malevolent spirits in the modern sense, but simply the empty shadows of the departed who cannot act, cannot speak, cannot rise. By associating the false gods with the refa'im, Isaiah declares them utterly impotent.

word_study.meaning: Dead ones, the dead. From the root mot, 'to die.' Used of both literal death and metaphorically of spiritual powerlessness or inactivity.
word_study.significance: The dead in ancient Hebrew thought were those cut off from the land of the living, from community, from covenant relationship. To call the false gods metim is to declare them utterly severed from active power in the human realm.

word_study.meaning: Shades, departed spirits, the powerless dead in Sheol. From rapha, 'to heal' or 'to be weak.' The refa'im are the weakened, empty shadows of those who have died.
word_study.significance: The term refa'im in Isaiah often carries a pejorative sense—these are not honored ancestors but faded, powerless remnants. To call false gods refa'im is to strip them of all grandeur and declare them utterly weak. Elsewhere in Isaiah, refa'im can also refer to the pre-Israelite giant inhabitants of Canaan, all consigned to weakness before Israel's God.

word_study.meaning: You have visited, punished, judged, or attended to. From paqad, which has a wide semantic range: to visit, to muster, to count, to judge, to punish.
word_study.significance: Paqad in judicial contexts often means 'to hold accountable' or 'to bring judgment upon.' God's 'visitation' of the false lords is His definitive judgment upon them. The same root appears in verse 16 when the people 'visit' (seek) God in distress—God's visitation is inescapable judgment, while human visitation of God is desperate prayer.

word_study.meaning: Memory, remembrance, record, name. From zakar, 'to remember.' In ancient thought, to have your zeikher erased was to be utterly annihilated—not just dead, but forgotten.
word_study.significance: In covenant language, God remembers His people and His promises (He performs 'zeikherim'—acts that cause His people to be remembered). Here, God erases the zeikher of the false gods—the ultimate annihilation. This sets up the dramatic reversal in verse 19, where God will remember (cause to live and rise) His own dead.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist condemns Israel for joining themselves to 'Baalpeor' and 'eating the sacrifices of the dead'—the same false gods Isaiah here consigns to permanent powerlessness and oblivion.

Earlier in Isaiah, Sheol itself is called forth to witness the arrival of the king of Babylon, and even the refa'im (shades) rise to mock him—illustrating the powerlessness and mockery that awaits the false lords consigned to death.

Paul's assertion that 'Death is swallowed up in victory' directly inverts the permanence Isaiah attributes to the false gods' death—Christ's resurrection negates death's finality for God's people, though not for the powers of darkness.

The immediate following verse provides the stunning reversal: 'Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise'—the people of God will do what the false lords never can: rise from the dead.

Joseph Smith's vision of the degrees of glory describes those who will not rise with the celestial or terrestrial bodies—consigned to outer darkness—paralleling Isaiah's description of the permanent powerlessness of those separated from God.

commentary.historical_context: The refa'im in the ancient Near Eastern context were understood not as demons but as the enfeebled dead in Sheol (the underworld). Greek parallel texts (like Homer's Odyssey) describe the dead as mere shadows, unable to act or speak without ritual invocation. Israel's conception was similar, though theirs was more theologically focused: the dead were those cut off from the covenant community and from active relationship with the living God. By consigning the false gods to this state, Isaiah is asserting that they have no more power than a shade in Sheol—they cannot speak, act, or claim allegiance. The context of post-exilic Judah adds weight: the people had seen the great empires (Babylon, Assyria) that once seemed invincible now weakened or fallen. Isaiah declares that the gods those empires served are equally powerless. The doctrine of resurrection—which is the opposite of what verse 14 says about the false gods—was developing in late Second Temple Judaism, and Isaiah 26:19 is one of the clearest early statements of bodily resurrection in Hebrew scripture.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently contrasts the power of God with the powerlessness of false gods and idols. In 1 Nephi 13:37, the Lord teaches that those who follow false ways 'shall be brought down into captivity, and shall be carried about as captives by their enemies.' Like Isaiah's false lords consigned to Sheol, false doctrines and idols ultimately deliver those who serve them into bondage and darkness, not power or deliverance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 123:7-8 teaches that those who serve false principles and oppressive systems will eventually be brought to naught: 'And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God... and are called according to his purpose.' The inverse is true for those who serve false masters—their dominion is temporary and will ultimately be destroyed, as Isaiah declares.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, the righteous are sealed and raised to eternal life, while those who reject the covenant are not raised to celestial glory—mirroring Isaiah's distinction between God's dead (who will rise) and the false lords (who will not). The temple ceremony itself is an act of covenant renewal that renounces all other masters and invokes God's name exclusively.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is implicitly the one who will raise the dead in verse 19—a prerogative that belongs only to God. By declaring that false gods cannot raise the dead, Isaiah points forward to Christ's resurrection power and His unique authority over death and Sheol. In the New Testament, Paul explicitly teaches that Christ alone has conquered death and holds the keys to Hades (Revelation 1:18). The false lords' permanent death contrasts with Christ's triumphant resurrection and His power to grant resurrection to His followers.
commentary.application: This verse invites disciples to ask: What 'false lords' still have subtle power over me, even though they are ultimately powerless? Anxiety about an uncertain future, shame about past failures, addiction to approval, fear of enemies—these are contemporary versions of the refa'im, the powerless shades that can only haunt us if we allow them to. The verse asserts that their apparent power is an illusion; their fate is already sealed in God's judgment. The application is psychological and spiritual: to recognize that false masters (whether internal or external) are already consigned to powerlessness by God's decree. The only real power lies with the God who raises the dead. In what areas of your life are you still submitting to lords who are, in fact, already powerless?

text_kjv: Thou hast increased the nation, O LORD, thou hast increased the nation: thou art glorified: thou hadst removed it far unto all the ends of the earth.

commentary.narrative: Verse 15 shifts from judgment on false gods to celebration of God's faithfulness in blessing and expanding Israel. The doubling of the phrase 'Thou hast increased the nation'—yasafta laggoy repeated twice—is a rhetorical device that emphasizes the magnitude of God's blessing and Israel's growth. This is not a historical statement about current political size (the post-exilic community was relatively small), but rather an eschatological or covenantal affirmation: God has promised and will fulfill the multiplication of Abraham's descendants. The doubled phrase conveys both affirmation and wonder—it is almost a repeated exclamation of gratitude. The following line, 'thou art glorified,' makes clear that Israel's enlargement is not about national pride but about God's reputation: through increasing His people, God's own name is glorified among the nations.
commentary.narrative_continued: The final line, 'thou hadst removed it far unto all the ends of the earth,' is the most debated phrase in this verse. The Covenant Rendering renders it 'You have extended all the borders of the land,' suggesting expansion of Israel's territory. However, the phrase may also mean that God has extended His people 'unto all the ends of the earth'—that is, scattered or dispersed them for blessing. In the post-exilic context, this could refer to the diaspora of Jewish communities throughout the Persian Empire and beyond. Rather than seeing dispersal as punishment, the verse frames it as God's work of extending His name and people across the known world. This reading makes theological sense: even in exile and dispersion, God's covenant purposes are being fulfilled through the scattering of His people. The verse thus moves from acknowledgment of past faithlessness (verse 13) and the judgment on false gods (verse 14) to confident assertion that God's covenantal promises to multiply Abraham's seed have not been revoked.

word_study.meaning: You have added to the nation, increased the nation, multiplied the nation. From yasaf, 'to add, to increase, to multiply.'
word_study.significance: The verb yasaf in covenantal contexts often refers to God's fulfillment of the promise to multiply Abraham's seed ('I will multiply your descendants'). The doubling of the phrase is emphatic—it expresses both the certainty and the wonder of God's covenantal faithfulness.

word_study.meaning: You are glorified, honored, made heavy with honor. From kavad, meaning 'to be heavy, to be weighty, to be honored.' The qal perfect here emphasizes the completed reality of God's glorification.
word_study.significance: God's glory (kavod) is His weightiness, His substance, His honor. When Israel is multiplied and spread throughout the earth, the weight of God's name is increased—His reputation and power become manifest to the nations. This connects to themes throughout Isaiah about God's glory being revealed to all peoples.

word_study.meaning: You have made distant, removed, extended. From rachaq, 'to be distant, to separate, to extend.' Can mean either 'removed' (physically separated) or 'extended' (spread out).
word_study.significance: The ambiguity in richaqta is theologically productive. It can mean God has scattered/dispersed the people (a reversal of exile as punishment) or extended/expanded the territory and influence of Israel. Either reading affirms that God's hand is behind Israel's dispersion or expansion—what appears to be loss or separation is actually the instrument of God's covenantal purposes.

cross_references.connection: God's promise to Abraham: 'I will make of thee a great nation...and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.' Verse 15 affirms that this ancient promise is being fulfilled through Israel's multiplication and extension to the ends of the earth.

A parallel passage in which God promises the barren Jerusalem, 'Enlarge the place of thy tent...for thou shalt break forth on the right hand and on the left; and thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles.' The same theme of multiplication and expansion appears in Isaianic promise.
The righteous king's dominion will 'extend from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth'—a parallel vision of God's kingdom spreading to all peoples and places.

In Joseph Smith's vision of the redemption of the dead, the gospel is taken to all nations and kindreds—fulfilling the Abrahamic promise that Isaiah here celebrates, now in its eschatological fullness through Christ.

commentary.historical_context: Post-exilic Judah was a small community, numerically and politically marginal within the Persian Empire. Yet Isaiah 26:15 asserts God's covenantal faithfulness in terms of multiplication and expansion. This is characteristic of post-exilic eschatological hope: the present community may be small, but God's promises stand firm, and the future multiplication and expansion are assured. The 'ends of the earth' language reflects the cosmological scope typical of Isaiah—God's dominion extends beyond mere political boundaries to cosmic significance. The doubling of 'thou hast increased the nation' may also reflect liturgical or poetic intensity: this is not a calm statement of fact but an emotional, celebratory affirmation despite present diminishment. The verse is thus an act of faith in God's promises even when current circumstances seem to contradict them.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms the fulfillment of the Abrahamic covenant—that the seed of Israel would be multiplied and scattered, and that the gospel would reach all nations. 1 Nephi 13:34-37 describes the gathering of Israel in the latter days and the extension of the Lord's work unto all nations. The language of multiplication and expansion in verse 15 is echoed throughout Book of Mormon prophecy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:7-8 teaches that 'the arm of the Lord shall be revealed in the latter days,' with the work extending to all the earth. Section 133 describes the gathering of the elect from all nations—a fulfillment of the promise in Isaiah 26:15 that God's people would be increased and extended to the ends of the earth.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant is part of God's covenantal structure for blessing and multiplying His people. The endowment includes promises of eternal increase and exaltation—connected to the Abrahamic promise of seed and multiplication that Isaiah here celebrates.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is the ultimate 'seed of Abraham' (Galatians 3:16), through whom the covenantal promise of multiplication and blessing to all nations is fulfilled. His kingdom extends to all peoples and all ages, fulfilling the vision of expansion 'unto all the ends of the earth' that Isaiah celebrates. The doubling of the promise may also foreshadow the principle of redemption made available to all humanity through Christ's atonement.
commentary.application: In a smaller, more personal sense, this verse speaks to the truth that God's covenantal promises to us—growth in faith, multiplication of spiritual fruit, and extension of our influence for good—are fulfilled even when circumstances seem to deny them. Modern disciples can ask: How is God multiplying my capacity for righteousness, even in difficult seasons? How is my witness being extended beyond my immediate circle? The verse invites trust in God's covenantal faithfulness despite apparent limitations. Where do you see God increasing your spiritual influence, even if the visible kingdom seems small? The verse calls us to a wider, more cosmic perspective on God's purposes—He is working across generations and nations, not just in our personal moment.

text_kjv: LORD, in trouble have they visited thee, they poured out a prayer when thy chastening was upon them.

commentary.narrative: Verse 16 returns to the people's acknowledgment of their own experience—how they have sought God in distress. The construction creates an intimate, personal note after the grand affirmations of verses 13-15. The people confess that 'in trouble' (batsar, literally 'in straits, in confinement') they have 'visited thee'—sought God, called upon Him. The verb paqadukha (from the same root paqad we saw in verse 14) here means to visit or seek out, creating a striking contrast: in verse 14, God 'visited' (judged) the false gods in judgment; here, the people 'visit' (seek) God in desperation. This reversal of agency is theologically profound: false gods judge their servants and consign them to death; the true God is sought out by His people in their need and responds with salvation.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second half of the verse provides further texture: 'they poured out a prayer when thy chastening was upon them.' The phrase 'poured out' (tsaqun, a word suggesting an intense pouring forth) describes the desperate intensity of prayer. The specific mention of 'a whispered prayer' (lachash, 'whisper') in The Covenant Rendering captures an important nuance: this is not loud, public prayer but intimate, urgent petition—a prayer so intense it is almost inaudible, spoken in the depths of suffering. The acknowledgment that God's 'chastening' (musar, discipline, instruction) was upon them contextualizes the prayer: suffering was the occasion for seeking God. This verse teaches a profound truth about the nature of God's correction: it is not merely punitive but pedagogical—it is designed to draw the covenant people back to covenantal relationship. The people's desperate prayer in the midst of chastening is precisely what God intends: the breaking down of false securities so that the soul cries out for the only true source of help.

word_study.meaning: In straits, in confinement, in trouble. From tsar, meaning 'narrow, tight, constricted, in distress.' Batsar can mean literal military siege or metaphorical psychological/spiritual constriction.
word_study.significance: The root tsar is used throughout Isaiah to describe the confinement and distress that precedes salvation (cf. Isaiah 30:6, 43:2). Trouble here is not random suffering but covenantal chastisement—the tightening of God's grip on His people to turn them back to Him.

word_study.meaning: They sought You, visited You, turned to You. From paqad, which can mean 'to visit, to seek out, to attend to, to hold accountable.' In context here, it means to seek out or turn toward.
word_study.significance: The people's 'visitation' of God in prayer mirrors God's 'visitation' of the false gods in judgment (verse 14). The verb creates a parallel: just as God visits (judges) false gods, His people visit (seek) Him. This is the correct relationship restored—the people orienting their desperation toward the true God rather than false alternatives.

word_study.meaning: Poured out a whispered prayer; uttered a whispering/quiet prayer. Tsaq means 'to pour, to pour out'; lachash means 'to whisper, to hiss, to murmur.'
word_study.significance: The combination suggests an intense but quiet utterance—not public proclamation but private, desperate petition. The 'whisper' may also carry the sense of magical incantation or summoning, but here it is transformed into urgent prayer. The KJV's 'poured out a prayer' captures the sense of emotional intensity and the emptying out of self that characterization requires.

word_study.meaning: Your discipline, instruction, correction. From yasar, 'to discipline, to instruct, to chasten.' Musar is the noun form referring to formative discipline rather than mere punishment.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew wisdom tradition (cf. Proverbs), musar is formative discipline—it is meant to teach, to correct course, to restore proper relationship. God's musar is not vindictive but redemptive. When the people pray in response to musar, they are receiving the very correction intended to bring them back to covenant fidelity.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist cries, 'My eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net...Turn thee unto me, and have mercy upon me; for I am desolate and afflicted.' Like Isaiah 26:16, the psalmist seeks God in distress and expects God to respond with deliverance.

The prophet laments, 'Arise, cry out in the night...pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord.' The same 'pouring out' language and the context of distress as occasion for seeking God appear in both passages.

The epistle describes Jesus offering 'up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death...and being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation.' The intimate, anguished prayer in distress—seeking God's deliverance through chastisement—is exemplified in Christ.

Joseph Smith's prayer in Liberty Jail—'O God, where art thou?'—is an anguished seeking of God in the midst of severe chastisement. Like Isaiah's people, the prophet pours out his soul to God in distress, expecting that God's purposes are being accomplished through the trial.

commentary.historical_context: The post-exilic community had experienced the ultimate covenantal 'chastening': the destruction of Jerusalem, the temple's desecration, and the exile into Babylon. By the time Isaiah 26 was composed or compiled, the people had been returned by Persia but faced ongoing hardship, loss of autonomy, and uncertain hope. Verse 16 reflects the mature spiritual understanding that had come through this suffering: they had learned to 'visit' (seek) God in their distress rather than turn to false gods or false securities. The 'whispered prayer' is characteristic of this later period—prayer became more interiorized and personal when public religious practice was limited or constrained. The acknowledgment that God's 'chastening was upon them' represents a theology of history that makes sense of catastrophic suffering not as divine abandonment but as covenantal discipline meant to restore fidelity. This theology is extremely important for understanding how post-exilic Jewish thought reframed national catastrophe as spiritual opportunity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly teaches that God's people are chastened through trials so that they will turn back to Him. Helaman 12:3 states: 'And thus we see that except the Lord doth chasten his people with many afflictions, yea, except he doth visit them with death and with terror, and with famine and all manner of pestilence, they will not remember him.' Like Isaiah's people, Nephite nations learn to seek God through the experience of chastisement.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 95:1-2 records the Lord's chastisement of the Saints: 'Verily, thus saith the Lord unto you whom I love...I have forgiven you your sins.' God's chastening and forgiveness go together; the purpose is restoration, not punishment. This echoes Isaiah's understanding that musar (discipline) leads to repentance and renewed covenant.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple experience itself can be understood as a form of spiritual 'visitation' of God—a seeking out of divine presence and truth in the sanctuary. The covenants made in the temple are partly a response to God's chastisement and a renewed commitment to seek His face and keep His commandments.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ in Gethsemane represents the ultimate example of pouring out one's soul to God in the midst of chastisement and trial. Luke 22:44 describes Jesus 'being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground.' Like Isaiah's people, Christ turns to God in intense distress, seeking deliverance through covenant obedience. Christ's willingness to be disciplined and chastened—to accept the cup of suffering—becomes the pattern for all who follow Him.
commentary.application: This verse speaks directly to the experience of trial and suffering in a disciple's life. It teaches that difficulty and loss—what feels like God's 'chastening'—are occasions to deepen our seeking of Him, not occasions to turn away. The verse invites honesty: In what troubles have you sought God most intimately? Has suffering ever driven you to a depth of prayer you would not otherwise have reached? The application is not to seek out suffering but to recognize that when chastisement comes, it is an invitation to visit God—to pour out your soul to Him in honest, intense prayer. The whispered prayer—the quiet, desperate turning of the heart toward God—is precisely what God intends. Do you resist God's chastening, or have you learned to use it as an opportunity to seek Him more earnestly?

text_kjv: Like as a woman with child, that draweth near the time of her delivery, is in pain, and crieth out in her pangs; so have we been in thy sight, O LORD.

commentary.narrative: Verse 17 introduces one of the most powerful metaphors in Isaiah: the community's experience of distress and waiting is like a woman in labor. The comparison begins with 'like as a woman with child' (kemo harah) and develops through vivid sensory details: she 'draweth near the time of her delivery' (taqriv laledet), she is 'in pain and crieth out' (tachil tiz'aq), she writhes 'in her pangs' (bachavaleiha, literally 'in her labor cords'). The metaphor is not abstract but intensely physical and emotional—the reader is meant to feel the woman's anguish. The final phrase, 'so have we been in thy sight, O LORD,' makes the comparison direct and communal: Israel as a whole has experienced the community equivalent of this labor—a prolonged, agonizing, costly experience of pain in the presence of God.
commentary.narrative_continued: The genius of the labor metaphor is that it carries both agony and hope. Labor is the most painful physical experience a human can undergo, yet it is not purposeless suffering—it points toward birth, new life, the fulfillment of pregnancy's long months of waiting. By comparing their distress to labor, Israel is implicitly affirming that their suffering is not random or meaningless but is meant to issue in something new, some divine purpose. The phrase 'in thy sight' (mippanekha) is crucial: their suffering is not hidden from God, nor is it a sign of His indifference. Rather, it occurs 'before His face,' in His presence and under His attention. The people are not alone in their travail; God witnesses and, by implication, will bring it to fulfillment. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse identically to the Masoretic Text, confirming the stability of the metaphor across centuries. In verse 18, the metaphor reaches its devastating twist: after all this labor, what is delivered?

word_study.meaning: Pregnant woman, woman with child. From the root harah, 'to become pregnant, to conceive.' Harah is both a state (pregnancy) and an active process (conception).
word_study.significance: The term harah emphasizes the reality and the visibility of pregnancy—not a hidden condition but a manifest one. Israel's distress, like the pregnant woman's condition, is evident and undeniable. There is no hiding from or denying the reality of either.

word_study.term_english: draweth near the time of her delivery
word_study.meaning: Draws near to giving birth, approaches the time of delivery. From qarav, 'to draw near, to approach,' and yalad, 'to give birth, to bear.'
word_study.significance: The verb taqriv (he/she draws near) emphasizes the inevitable approach of birth—the moment cannot be postponed or avoided. Israel's moment of testing and deliverance is similarly drawing inexorably near. The phrasing conveys both dread and anticipation.

word_study.term_english: is in pain, and crieth out
word_study.meaning: Writhes, is in agony / cries out, shrieks. From chul, 'to writhe, to twist, to be in agony,' and za'aq, 'to cry out, to scream, to call for help.'
word_study.significance: The two verbs together express the full spectrum of the birthing woman's experience: the involuntary physical agony (tachil) and the conscious vocalization of that agony (tiz'aq). Israel's distress involves both dimensions—bodily suffering and the cry of the soul.

word_study.meaning: In her labor pains, in her contractions. From chabli, 'labor pain, birthpang, contraction.' The term also can mean 'rope' or 'cord,' evoking the image of being bound or held by the contractions.
word_study.significance: The metaphor of being held by labor cords captures the sense that the agony is not random but rhythmic, purposeful, and productive. Each contraction brings the birth closer. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this term identically (1QIsaᵃ col. XXII, line 2), confirming the metaphor's antiquity and stability.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah himself experiences a similar bodily agony: 'Therefore are my loins filled with pain: pangs have taken hold upon me...I was bowed down at the hearing of it; I was dismayed at the seeing of it.' The prophet embodies the metaphor of verse 17—suffering anticipates divine revelation or judgment.

Jeremiah uses similar labor metaphor language: 'O inhabitant of Lebanon, that makest thy nest in the cedars, how gracious shall thou be when pangs come upon thee, the pain as of a woman in travail!' The comparison of political and spiritual distress to labor is Jeremianic as well as Isaianic.

Jesus uses the labor metaphor to describe the disciples' coming sorrow and joy: 'A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come: but as soon as she is delivered of the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world.' The metaphor points to the paschal mystery and the disciples' suffering before resurrection joy.

The woman clothed with the sun is 'with child; and she cried out, travailing in birth, and pained to be delivered.' The imagery of the pregnant woman in Revelation echoes and amplifies Isaiah's labor metaphor in an eschatological context.

commentary.historical_context: The labor metaphor would have been immediately recognizable to ancient Jewish readers—every listener had witnessed or knew of the agony of childbirth. It was the most common metaphor for intense but purposeful suffering in ancient Near Eastern literature. In the context of post-exilic Judah, the metaphor carried particular force: the people had endured the 'pains' of exile, destruction, and loss, and were now being told that these were not meaningless but were like the labor that precedes new birth. The metaphor also carries social significance: it identifies the community with a woman's body and experience—an unusual identification in patriarchal ancient literature, suggesting vulnerability, interdependence, and the natural rhythms of human existence rather than heroic or military power. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve identical spelling and form (1QIsaᵃ col. XXII, line 2), confirming that this powerful image has been passed down unchanged for over 2,000 years.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon uses similar birth imagery to describe spiritual renewal and deliverance. Mosiah 27:24-26 describes the Sons of Mosiah as 'born of God' through their conversion experience, suggesting that spiritual transformation involves a kind of labor and rebirth. The metaphor connects physical and spiritual procreation—both involve agony and new creation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 42:5-8 teaches that the Saints are 'born again' through covenant and receive new life in Christ. The labor metaphor of Isaiah 26:17 parallels the process of becoming 'born of the water and the spirit' described in latter-day revelation. The pain of transformation and the joy of new creation are linked.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment includes rebirth and covenant renewal imagery. The journey through the temple involves a kind of spiritual labor—a process of stripping away, reform, and emerging into new identity and understanding. The labor metaphor of verse 17 applies to the initiatory and endowment experiences as well.

commentary.christological_typology: The labor metaphor points directly to Christ's passion and resurrection. Christ Himself is the promised 'child' or 'son' who will be 'born' through the agony of the cross and the labor of redemption. Hebrews 5:8 states that Christ 'learned obedience by the things which he suffered,' suggesting that His own redemptive work involved a kind of divine labor. The metaphor also anticipates that Christ will 'see the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied' (Isaiah 53:11)—the labor will issue in the birth of a redeemed people.
commentary.application: This verse speaks to any season of prolonged difficulty in a disciple's life. It asks: Are you willing to trust that your current distress is like labor—painful but purposeful, pointing toward new birth or transformation? The metaphor suggests that suffering that seems only destructive may in fact be formative. It invites the question: What is God birthing in me through this trial? What new capacity, compassion, or understanding is being labored forth? The verse also normalizes spiritual pain: just as physical labor is intense and natural, spiritual labor is intense and natural. Rather than fighting the pain or seeing it as a sign of divine abandonment, the metaphor invites acceptance of difficulty as the precondition for something genuinely new. In what area of your life are you in 'labor'—in pain but moving toward birth? Can you surrender to the process rather than trying to escape it?

text_kjv: We have been with child, we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind; we have not wrought any deliverance in the earth; neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen.

commentary.narrative: Verse 18 delivers a devastating reversal of the labor metaphor from verse 17. After all the agony, after the intense crying out and writhing in pain—what has been delivered? Not a living child, but 'wind' (ruach). The Hebrew word ruach has multiple meanings: wind, breath, spirit, the intangible and powerless. By giving birth to wind, the people have produced nothing of substance—no deliverance (yeshu'ot), no transformation of reality. The verse expands the confession: 'we have not wrought any deliverance in the earth' (yeshu'ot bal-na'aseh erets). This is Israel's admission that despite their suffering, their prayer, their effort, they have not been able to accomplish salvation by their own power. The false gods have not delivered them; their own striving has not delivered them.
commentary.narrative_continued: The final clause completes the portrait of futility: 'neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen' (bal-yippelu yosehvei tevvel). The 'inhabitants of the world' likely refers to the pagan nations or, more broadly, to all those who oppose God's purposes. Despite Israel's agony, the wicked have not been overthrown. This verse expresses a profound crisis of faith or, perhaps more accurately, a moment of brutal honesty within faith. It is almost a lament: We have endured all this suffering, we have sought God, we have prayed desperately—yet we see no results. The wicked flourish, the world has not changed, deliverance remains distant. This is precisely the posture of the lament psalms, where the psalmist pours out frustration and seeming divine inactivity. However, verse 18 is not the end of the song. It is followed immediately by verse 19, one of the most powerful affirmations in all of scripture: 'Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise.' The despair of verse 18 sets up the hope of verse 19 in the most dramatic way possible. Until God acts—not through human effort but through divine resurrection—there is no deliverance. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse identically to the Masoretic Text, confirming the stability of this challenging confession across time.

word_study.meaning: We gave birth to / brought forth wind / spirit / breath. From yalad, 'to give birth, to bear,' and ruach, which means 'wind, breath, spirit, the intangible.'
word_study.significance: The phrase 'gave birth to wind' is deliberately anticlimactic and deflating. Wind is intangible, powerless, and vanishes—the opposite of a living child. To give birth to ruach is to produce nothing of lasting substance. The term ruach contrasts sharply with 'flesh,' 'bone,' 'body'—all that is substantial and real. This is the opposite of the hoped-for outcome of labor.

word_study.meaning: Deliverances, salvations, saves. From yasha, 'to save, to deliver, to make safe.' The plural form emphasizes the multiple dimensions of salvation—physical, spiritual, political.
word_study.significance: Yeshu'ot is one of Isaiah's key terms for God's saving work. The people's confession 'we have not wrought any yeshu'ot in the earth' is an admission that salvation is not achieved through human effort but is God's gift. This sets up the divine action of verse 19, where God Himself provides the deliverance humans cannot.

word_study.meaning: The inhabitants of the world / earth. From yashav, 'to dwell, to sit,' and tevvel, which means 'world, earth, the habitable world.'
word_study.significance: Tevvel in Isaiah often refers to the nations and powers that oppose God's reign. The phrase 'inhabitants of the world' encompasses all those not aligned with God's purposes. The people's confession that these inhabitants 'have not fallen' (bal-yippelu) despite Israel's agony suggests that the overthrow of the wicked, the victory of God's kingdom, remains incomplete—a work only God can accomplish through divine action.

word_study.meaning: Have not fallen, have not been overthrown. From naphal, 'to fall, to be overthrown, to be defeated.' The negative construction (bal) + future tense creates a statement of what has not occurred despite the people's expectation.
word_study.significance: The verb naphal in prophetic contexts often refers to the fall of pagan nations and the overthrow of idolatry when God acts. That the wicked 'have not fallen' is presented as a painful reality—the expected divine action has not yet occurred. This sustains the tension until verse 19.

cross_references.connection: The Teacher declares, 'What profit hath he that hath laboured for the wind?'—echoing verse 18's image of all human effort producing only wind, insubstantial and fleeting.

The psalmist affirms, 'Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it'—expressing the same truth as verse 18, that human labor without God's initiative produces nothing of lasting value.

Paul writes, 'Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.' Paul implicitly responds to the despair of verse 18 by anchoring work in Christ, where it is no longer 'vain labor' but fruit-bearing.

The immediate following verse provides the divine answer to verse 18's despair: 'Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise.' God's action, not human effort, accomplishes what verse 18 said humans cannot.

The Lord teaches that human efforts alone cannot accomplish salvation: 'Therefore, I the Lord, knowing the calamity which should come upon the inhabitants of the earth, called upon my servant Joseph Smith, Jun., and spake unto him from heaven, and gave him commandments'—human effort must be joined with divine initiative.

commentary.historical_context: Verse 18 reflects the spiritual crisis of post-exilic Judah: despite decades of exile, prayer, repentance, and the return to Jerusalem, the kingdom had not been restored, the Gentile nations had not been overthrown, and the messianic age had not dawned. The people had endured 'labor'—the pain of displacement, loss, and longing—yet the expected deliverance had not materialized. The verse is theologically honest about this delay and frustration. This is not a heretical doubt but a faithful confession: we have done all we can (sought God, prayed, repented), yet our efforts have not produced the salvation we hoped for. Only God can accomplish what humans cannot. The philosophical worldview here—that human effort, however sincere, cannot produce ultimate salvation—is characteristic of apocalyptic thought, which awaited God's direct intervention rather than trusting in historical progress or human achievement. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this verse unchanged (1QIsaᵃ col. XXII, line 3), confirming that this challenging theological statement has been transmitted faithfully across centuries.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon expresses a similar truth in Helaman 10:4-5, where the Lord teaches that no human power can endure against the power of God. The people's confession that they 'have not wrought any deliverance' parallels the Book of Mormon's repeated teaching that salvation comes through God's power, not human strength. Moroni 10:32 teaches, 'Yea, come unto Christ, and be perfected in him, and deny yourselves of all ungodliness; and if ye shall deny yourselves of all ungodliness, and love God with all your might, mind and strength, then is his grace sufficient for you.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 18:36 teaches that no human can save themselves: 'Wherefore, be faithful, stand in the office which I have appointed unto you; succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees.' Human effort must be coordinated with divine grace. Section 29:34 teaches that 'all the inhabitants of the earth shall mourn; and they shall fall before me, and shall be consumed by the glory of my coming' (verse 18's hoped-for event is fulfilled only through Christ's coming, not through human action).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that while humans can make covenants and strive, their ultimate exaltation and salvation depend on God's grace and power, not on their effort alone. The ordinances of the temple are gifts from God, not achievements of human will. This mirrors verse 18's confession that humans cannot 'bring forth deliverance.'

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 18's despair of human effort points directly to Christ as the only source of deliverance. Jesus explicitly teaches, 'Without me ye can do nothing' (John 15:5), and 'I am the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6). Christ is the embodiment of divine power that accomplishes what human effort cannot. His resurrection is the ultimate answer to verse 18's despair—the 'dead' who shall live and arise, as verse 19 declares. The labor of verse 17 and the despair of verse 18 together point to Christ's redemptive labor and triumphant resurrection as the ultimate deliverance.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern disciples with a difficult but liberating truth: you cannot save yourself, nor can you save the world. Human effort, however sincere and sustained, cannot produce ultimate deliverance. This is simultaneously humbling and freeing. It invites the question: In what areas of your life are you still trying to 'bring forth deliverance' through effort alone? Where are you exhausted because you are trying to accomplish what only God can accomplish? The verse calls for a surrender: to release your grip on the illusion that you can accomplish salvation by your own power, and instead to open yourself to receive God's grace. This does not mean ceasing effort—but it means ceasing to expect that effort alone will save you. The application is spiritual realism: acknowledge your limits, your dependence on God, and your need for divine intervention. Where have you been trying to birth something of substance, only to find yourself birthing wind? What would change if you surrendered that effort and waited for God's action instead?

text_kjv: Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise. Awake and sing, ye that dwell in dust: for thy dew is as the dew of herbs, and the earth shall cast out the dead.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 26:19 stands as one of the Hebrew Bible's most explicit affirmations of bodily resurrection, and it arrives not as abstract doctrine but as the climactic answer to the preceding lament. In verses 16-18, Isaiah has confessed that despite God's discipline, human effort is futile — 'we have as it were brought forth wind; we have not wrought any deliverance in the earth.' The people have labored, prayed, and endured, yet remained powerless. Now, at the narrative's turning point, Isaiah pivots: God Himself will accomplish what humans cannot. The dead will live again. This is not metaphorical language about spiritual awakening; the phrase 'thy dead men shall live...together with my dead body shall they arise' uses concrete terminology (nevalati, bodies; yequmun, shall rise) that demands physical resurrection.

The address 'Awake and sing, ye that dwell in dust' directly echoes Genesis 3:19 — 'dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.' Those who have returned to dust, who have paid the wages of sin, are now summoned to wakefulness and song. This reversal of death is inseparable from covenant identity: the dead who rise belong to God ('thy dead'), and Isaiah claims personal participation in this resurrection ('my dead body'). The 1QIsaᵃ variant preserves this first-person claim, suggesting Isaiah sees himself not as a disembodied prophet but as one whose flesh will participate in God's ultimate vindication.

The phrase 'thy dew is as the dew of lights' (tal orot) appears nowhere else in Scripture. In the ancient Near East, dew was the symbol of divine blessing and life-giving moisture (Hosea 14:5; Psalm 133:3). But here, this dew is luminous—made of 'lights' (orot), carrying the radiance of heaven itself. This is not ordinary moisture but a supernatural life-force that penetrates the grave. The earth, described as 'giving birth to the shades' (refa'im tappil), becomes a womb that expels the dead—a deliberate reversal of verse 18, where human effort produced only wind. God's creative power succeeds where covenant community has failed. The 'shades' (refa'im) of verse 14, the false lords and dead powers that could not be revived, remain dead; but God's dead—His people—rise.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'your dead shall live' — the verb chayah (to live) is in the imperfect, indicating future, certain action. The dead belong to God ('your dead'), establishing covenantal relationship even in death.
word_study.significance: This is resurrection language of the most direct kind. The dead are not reincarnated or spiritually elevated; they 'live' — they return to embodied, conscious existence. The possessive 'your' (kha) frames resurrection as covenantal fulfillment, not universal event.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'my corpse' or 'my body' — from navél, the decaying flesh. Isaiah uses first-person singular here, claiming personal stake in resurrection hope.
word_study.significance: The first-person claim is crucial: Isaiah does not speak as detached prophet but as one whose own flesh will rise. The DSS variant preserves this emphasis. This moves resurrection from theological assertion to personal testimony.

word_study.meaning: Third-person plural imperfect of qum (to stand, to rise). The verb carries both physical rising and standing firm — those who rise remain standing, stable, alive.
word_study.significance: The plural form encompasses both Isaiah's body and the collective dead of God's people. Resurrection is not a one-time event but a sustained condition: they rise and remain risen.

word_study.meaning: A unique biblical phrase. Tal (dew) symbolizes life-giving moisture and divine blessing. Orot (lights) suggests luminescence, dawn-light, or divine radiance. Together: a supernatural, light-bearing moisture from heaven that penetrates earth and grave.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes this phrase appears nowhere else in Scripture. It envisions resurrection not as natural process but as heavenly intervention—light itself descending to awaken the dead. In Jewish tradition, resurrection is often associated with divine light breaking into the realm of death. This phrase captures that mystery.

word_study.meaning: Third-person feminine singular imperfect of naphál (to fall, to give birth, to cast out). Here it means 'to give birth' or 'to expel'—the earth becomes a mother who releases what it held.
word_study.significance: This verb creates a powerful image: the earth, which consumed the dead in burial, now actively gives birth to them. It echoes the labor and delivery language of verse 18, where human effort proved fruitless. The earth's labor succeeds; the people's does not. Resurrection is God's work, not human achievement.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'healers' or 'shades'—the Hebrew term for the dead departed, those in Sheol. In Isaiah 14:9, the refa'im are the former rulers now powerless in death.
word_study.significance: The same refa'im mentioned in verse 14 ('the dead [refa'im] will not live') are now 'cast out' by the earth. This is selective resurrection: the dead who belonged to God rise, while false powers and dead lords remain dead. Resurrection is covenantal, not universal.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah's 'ye that dwell in dust' directly invokes the Genesis curse: 'dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.' Resurrection reverses this sentence by calling the dust-dwellers to awake and sing.
Hosea uses dew as symbol of God's blessing and life-giving grace. Isaiah's 'dew of lights' extends this: the dew that revived Israel becomes the dew that resurrects the dead.

Earlier in Isaiah, the refa'im (shades) of former rulers are summoned from Sheol but remain powerless. Here, by contrast, the refa'im of God's people are expelled from the earth—true resurrection, not mere haunting.

Daniel 12:2 is often cited as the clearest Old Testament resurrection text ('many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake'), but Isaiah 26:19 precedes it and is equally explicit in affirming bodily resurrection of the righteous.
Psalm 133 uses dew as symbol of divine blessing and unity. Isaiah 26:19's dew carries that blessing into the grave itself, sanctifying the dust and summoning life from death.

commentary.historical_context: Bodily resurrection was not a widespread concept in ancient Near Eastern religion during the monarchy period (Isaiah's own time, 8th century BCE). Mesopotamian literature depicts the afterlife as a dim, powerless existence; Egyptian afterlife theology involved preservation of the body but not resurrection into new life. Isaiah's vision stands singularly bold: the earth itself will reverse death's dominion. The command to 'hide yourselves' (verse 20) and the subsequent coming judgment (verse 21) suggest a historical crisis—likely the Assyrian siege or another moment of national catastrophe—which frames the resurrection promise. In such extremity, when political power fails and the nation faces annihilation, Isaiah stakes hope not on military might or diplomatic skill but on God's unilateral act of resurrection. The dew imagery may also reflect the agricultural reality of a land dependent on dew in the dry season; thus 'dew of lights' becomes a metaphor for life-giving grace that appears when human resources are exhausted. The 1QIsaᵃ manuscript (125 BCE) confirms that this passage was preserved as central to Jewish hope centuries before Christianity, and pre-dating by decades the clearest parallel in Daniel 12:2.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Book of Mormon prophets echo Isaiah's resurrection language. Alma 11:41-45 explicitly teaches bodily resurrection, with language recalling Isaiah's 'bodies shall rise': 'the spirit and the body shall be reunited again in its perfect form, both limb and joint shall be restored to its proper frame.' Alma's formulation of resurrection—inseparable from judgment and divine justice—mirrors Isaiah's framework: resurrection happens not in abstract eternity but at a specific moment when God 'comes forth' (Isaiah 26:21) to settle accounts.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:14-16 draws on Isaiah's vision: 'Wherefore, as God by his Spirit hath created and made man, so the same Spirit is in man to make a new creature, a perfect body...therefore the spirit and the body are the soul of man; and the resurrection from the dead is the redemption of the soul.' Isaiah's 'dew of lights' becomes in Doctrine and Covenants language the Spirit's power to restore spirit and body in perfect unity. The selective nature of resurrection (God's dead rise; false lords remain dead) aligns with D&C teaching on degrees of glory and resurrection according to faithfulness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The resurrection passage in Isaiah 26:19 is fundamentally a temple text. The progression from verse 18 (human inability) through verse 19 (God's resurrection power) to verse 20 (sheltering within divine chambers) to verse 21 (God's coming forth to judge) mirrors the temple progression of covenant making, divine protection, and ultimate vindication. The chambers of verse 20 may echo the holy chambers of God's house, where His people are hidden until judgment passes. Resurrection, in temple theology, is the ultimate covenant fulfillment: the body sealed in mortality becomes the eternal form in the celestial kingdom.
restoration_lens.restoration_blessing: The Restoration reaffirms Isaiah's vision as literal, not metaphorical. Joseph Smith's teachings on resurrection in the Doctrine and Covenants (76:64-70; 131:1-4) confirm bodily resurrection as central to salvation. The 'dew of lights' becomes the influence of the Holy Ghost—the celestial power that penetrates the grave and resurrects the body. In Latter-day Saint theology, resurrection is not escape from the body but its redemption and glorification.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 26:19 is fundamentally Christological. Jesus Christ is the first-fruits of resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20-23), and His resurrection is the guarantee and template of all covenant resurrection. The 'dew of lights' that resurrects the dead foreshadows the glory that radiates from the risen Christ. When the dead who belong to God rise, they rise through covenant relationship with Jesus, the Mediator. The selective nature of resurrection (God's dead rise; others remain dead) finds its resolution in Christ: all who are sealed to Him through covenant receive resurrection; those who reject covenant remain in death. Isaiah's vision of the earth 'giving birth' to the dead anticipates the empty tomb—earth itself forced to release its hold on the body of the Messiah, the Son of God. In John 11:25-26, Jesus claims, 'I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live'—a direct echo of Isaiah 26:19, 'Thy dead men shall live.'
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 26:19 teaches that resurrection is not distant abstraction but bodily, covenantal reality. The struggle depicted in verses 16-18—prayer without visible answer, effort without apparent success—is every believer's experience of faith in a fallen world. Isaiah's response is not false comfort but radical hope: what humans cannot accomplish, God will. This does not excuse us from the labor of discipleship, but it reframes our labor within God's ultimate resurrection economy. The 'dew of lights' is the Holy Ghost's influence in our lives now, beginning the process of sanctification that culminates in resurrection. To 'awake and sing' is the covenant member's posture: singing not because circumstances are favorable, but because we have seen into eternity and know that death—whether literal death or the daily deaths of disappointment, loss, and opposition—is not final. The earth will give birth to what it seemed to have swallowed. God will resurrect what seemed irretrievably lost.

text_kjv: Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 20 shifts from proclamation to command, from cosmic vision to intimate protection. Immediately after announcing resurrection, Isaiah's God turns to His people with tender urgency: 'Go, my people, enter your rooms and shut your doors behind you.' The transition is stark and deliberate. The dead will rise; but before that vindication comes, there is danger. The indignation—the wrath of God descending upon the earth—will sweep through creation. The people of God are not exempt from this time of trial, but they are protected within it. They do not escape judgment; they are sheltered through it.

The language echoes the Exodus narrative with unmistakable precision. On the night of Passover (Exodus 12:22-23), Israel was commanded to enter their homes, mark their doorposts with blood, and remain inside while the destroyer passed through Egypt. 'The LORD will pass through to smite the Egyptians; and when he sees the blood upon the lintel, and on the two side posts, the LORD will pass over the door, and will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses to smite you.' Isaiah invokes this memory not accidentally but as the template for God's protection during the end-time indignation. Just as the Passover was protection through judgment—not exemption from it—so this sheltering in chambers is refuge during, not removal from, God's wrath.

The parenthetical 'for a little moment' (kim'at rega) is theologically crucial. However terrible the indignation may be, it is limited, temporary, passing. A 'moment' (rega) in biblical language often denotes a brief, fleeting span (Psalm 30:5: 'weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning'). The covenant people are called to an act of faith: trust that the indignation is not eternal, that God's wrath is not His final word, that the sheltering is real and sufficient. This is not passive waiting but covenantal obedience—entering chambers, shutting doors, hiding themselves—acts of trust performed in darkness, with no visible guarantee that the next moment will bring safety.

word_study.meaning: Imperative of halak (to go, to walk) with direct address. 'My people' (ammi) establishes intimate covenant relationship—not subjects or servants, but the speaker's own people.
word_study.significance: This is not a command given from distance but from heart-relationship. The God who has just proclaimed resurrection now shelters His people with personal care. The covenant bond is evident in both the command and the implied promise of protection.

word_study.meaning: Verb bo (to come, to enter) with plural noun chadarim (rooms, chambers). These are the innermost chambers of a house—places of privacy, security, and isolation from outside danger.
word_study.significance: The chambers represent both literal refuge and spiritual shelter. In temple imagery, divine chambers are the holy of holies, the place of God's presence. The people are instructed to enter their own chambers as places of covenant safety.

word_study.meaning: Imperative of sagar (to shut, to close, to lock). Doors (delatim) are the boundary between inside safety and outside danger.
word_study.significance: This is concrete, practical obedience. Shutting doors is an act of faith—declaring that this boundary will protect from the surrounding indignation. The imagery recalls both Passover (Exodus 12:22) and the flood account (Genesis 7:16, where God Himself shuts Noah into the ark).

word_study.meaning: Imperative of chavah (to hide, to conceal). The verb suggests both concealment and safety—to hide is to remove oneself from exposure to danger.
word_study.significance: Hiding is not cowardice but covenant obedience. During the indignation, the people hide not in shame but in trust, shielded by God's protective intent.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'like a little moment'—kim'at means 'a little, barely' and rega means 'moment, instant.' Together: a brief, fleeting span of time.
word_study.significance: This phrase relativizes suffering. No matter how intense or prolonged the indignation feels, it is from eternity's perspective a mere moment. Paul echoes this in 2 Corinthians 4:17: 'our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.'

word_study.meaning: Noun meaning indignation, anger, wrath—specifically God's wrath directed at injustice and rebellion. It is the active, passionate response of God to covenant violation.
word_study.significance: Za'am is not cold judgment but hot, righteous anger. It will 'pass'—suggesting that it has a trajectory, an appointed duration, and a conclusion. God's wrath, though terrible, is not infinite or everlasting toward His people.

cross_references.connection: The Passover template: 'And ye shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood that is in the bason...and the LORD will pass over the door, and will not suffer the destroyer to come in.' Isaiah's people are told to hide in chambers just as Israel hid behind marked doors during the plague of the firstborn.

David sings, 'For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me.' Isaiah's call to hide in chambers echoes this image of divine shelter in extremity.
Weeping endures for a night, but joy comes in the morning'—this psalm captures the same 'brief moment' theology. Suffering is real but temporary; God's favor is eternal.
During the flood, 'the LORD shut him [Noah] in'—God Himself seals the ark. Isaiah's closed doors echo this divine sealing, protective of those within.

Paul writes, 'our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.' This directly echoes Isaiah's 'kim'at rega'—the indignation is brief when measured against eternity.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah 26:20 likely addresses a historical crisis—either the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem (701 BCE, when Sennacherib surrounded the city) or another catastrophic threat to Judah's survival. The command to hide in chambers reflects the reality of siege warfare: the population would indeed shelter indoors during bombardment or assault. But Isaiah elevates this physical reality to theological significance. The 'indignation' (za'am) is not primarily military but divine—God's judgment against both the persecutors of His people and the sins of His own people. The Exodus Passover, which would have been celebrated annually as Israel's founding deliverance, provides the narrative framework: just as God protected His people through the tenth plague, so He will shelter them through the final judgment.
