The 'little moment' language also reflects ancient Near Eastern understandings of time. To ancient minds, the span of human suffering within God's vast, eternal purposes would indeed seem brief. The astronomical and cosmic imagery of chapter 26 (the fortified city, the walls) places this local crisis within a cosmic framework: God's purposes are not limited to Judah's political fate but encompass all creation's renewal.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly uses Isaiah's language of refuge and protection. 1 Nephi 22:17 applies Isaiah's words to the gathering and protection of the covenant people in the last days: 'Wherefore, as it is written, they shall be scattered and smitten...But behold, thus saith the Lord God: when the day cometh that they shall believe in me...then shall the power of the Lord work with them, to bring about their salvation.' The pattern is Isaiah's: temporary scattering and trial, followed by divine protection and ultimate vindication. Nephi's application shows that Isaiah's 'chambers' and 'brief moment' language resonates throughout Book of Mormon eschatology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections:
Doctrine and Covenants 86:1-7 speaks of the 'field' and the 'wheat' and the 'tares,' and the gathering of the righteous prior to judgment—an application of Isaiah's protective shelter theme. D&C 109:24 includes temple dedication language invoking God's protection: 'And we ask thee, Holy Father, to establish the people that shall dwell in this house...that we may rise up and praise thee.'

More broadly, D&C 63:33-34 addresses the wicked: 'Therefore, let the wicked take heed, and the unbelieving fear and tremble; and let the faithful labors of my people be remembered by me...Verily I say unto you, if you desire the blessing of Father Abraham...ye must do the works of Abraham; if ye desire to be the sons of Moses, ye shall do the works of Moses.' This echoes Isaiah's structure: the faithful hide and are protected; the wicked remain exposed to indignation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Isaiah 26:20 is profoundly temple language. The command to 'enter your chambers' evokes the holy of holies, the innermost sanctum of the temple where God's presence dwells. In temple theology, the faithful are covenanted into God's sanctuary—a place of protection from the world's chaos. The sealing ordinances of the temple create this covenant relationship: the people are 'sealed' (analogous to shutting doors) into the protection of God's house. The 'brief moment' of indignation corresponds to the mortal probation; the 'chambers' of God correspond to eternal life sealed by temple covenant.
restoration_lens.restoration_blessing: For Latter-day Saints, verse 20 takes on particular significance in light of latter-day prophecies about the gathering and protection of the faithful. The closing of the tent flaps, the gathering to Zion, the building of temples as refuges—all these carry Isaiah's language forward. The promise that the indignation will 'pass' is comfort during times of societal upheaval, religious opposition, or personal trial. The 'brief moment' extends our perspective: what seems like enduring persecution or hardship is, from eternity's view, momentary. God's people are sheltered through judgment, not exempted from it—a teaching that resonates throughout modern revelation.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 26:20 points to Jesus Christ as the ultimate chamber of refuge. In John 14:2, Jesus says to His disciples, 'In my Father's house are many mansions...I go to prepare a place for you.' This is Isaiah's 'chambers' language applied christologically: Jesus prepares rooms in His Father's house where the faithful will be protected forever. The Passover (invoked in verse 20's language) finds its fulfillment in Christ, the Passover Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), whose blood marks the doorposts of believers' hearts, protecting them from death and judgment. The 'brief moment' of indignation is the final tribulation and judgment, from which the elect are sealed and protected—a protection purchased by Christ's atonement. The resurrection of verse 19 and the protection of verse 20 are inseparable: Christ's resurrection guarantees the resurrection of all who are sealed to Him; His triumph over death assures their shelter through judgment.
commentary.application: Verse 20 addresses the faithful during times of external threat or internal darkness. The command is not to escape the world but to enter covenant chambers—the temple, prayer, the intimate relationship with God—and remain there, trusting that the indignation will pass. For modern disciples, this teaches that trials and opposition are real, not imaginary, but they are also temporary and within God's oversight. The 'doors shut behind you' is not isolation but covenant protection: entering the temple, keeping covenants, maintaining relationship with God through ordinances and prayer. The phrase 'hide thyself...for a little moment' is radical reframing of suffering. The moment we identify with God's people and seal ourselves to His covenant, we are no longer waiting helplessly for judgment; we are sheltered within it, protected by blood—the atoning blood of Christ that marks our doorposts. When opposition or trial comes, the response is not to flee the church but to deepen covenant relationship, to 'enter chambers' more fully. The promise is not that indignation will be light, but that it is brief and does not ultimately separate us from God's protective care.

text_kjv: For, behold, the LORD cometh out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity: the earth also shall disclose her blood, and shall no more cover her slain.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 26:21 provides the reason for the sheltering of verse 20: the LORD is coming out of His place to judge. This is the moment when judgment breaks into history. The verb 'cometh out' (yotse) suggests that God has been, until now, in His place—heaven, the holy of holies, the realm of transcendence—but now moves into the world of time and matter to execute judgment. This is not abstract, distant condemnation but God's active, personal intervention in human affairs. The 'inhabitants of the earth' (yosh'vei ha'arets) refers to all who dwell outside covenant relationship, all who have built their lives on unjust foundations.

The phrase 'to punish the iniquity' (lifqod avon) uses a verb (paqad) that means both to visit and to reckon—God inspects what humanity has done and holds it accountable. The iniquity is not merely individual transgression but systemic violence, the accumulation of injustice that has soaked into the earth itself. This connects directly to the next clause: 'the earth also shall disclose her blood.' The earth, conceived as alive and conscious, has absorbed the blood of the innocent, the murdered, the oppressed. All the violence committed in secret—hidden from human justice, covered by darkness or political power—will be exposed. The earth will give up its testimony.

This echoes Genesis 4:10, where Abel's blood cries out to God from the ground after Cain murders him. 'The voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground.' The earth is not neutral repository but active witness and accuser. Isaiah's vision extends this: not just one cry from one murdered victim, but all the blood ever shed unjustly will be disclosed at once. The final clause, 'and shall no more cover her slain,' means that the earth itself will refuse to conceal the evidence of injustice any longer. The ground that once hid bodies in darkness will expel them into light. This is not vindication of the perpetrators but exposure of their crimes. The righteous dead—already resurrected in verse 19—will stand beside the disclosed blood as witnesses to the iniquity it represents.

The sequence is now clear: the righteous (verse 19) are resurrected; the faithful (verse 20) are sheltered through judgment; and the wicked (verse 21) are exposed and condemned. God's coming forth completes the covenantal cycle: the dead who belonged to Him are raised; His people are protected; and injustice is finally, eternally, remedied.

word_study.meaning: The verb yatsa (to come forth, to go out) with 'from his place' (mimmeqomo). God moves from His dwelling place—heaven, the holy of holies—into creation to execute judgment.
word_study.significance: This is incarnational language before incarnation: God does not judge from distance but comes forth into the world. It emphasizes God's active, personal commitment to justice. The Messiah, as God's ultimate coming forth into the world, fulfills this pattern.

word_study.meaning: The verb paqad (to visit, to number, to reckon, to punish) with avon (iniquity, perversity). God 'visits' or 'reckons' the iniquity—He counts it, inspects it, holds it accountable.
word_study.significance: Paqad is not merely punitive but investigative: God examines the record of injustice and renders judgment. This is forensic divine justice, where nothing is overlooked or forgotten. In Job 7:18, Job asks, 'What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him?' — using the same verb paqad in reversed sense, asking why God 'visits' or pays such attention to mortal humans. Here, that divine attention becomes judgment.

word_study.meaning: Those who dwell on the earth, those rooted in the material world and disconnected from covenant relationship. In prophetic literature, this often refers to the wicked who oppose God's purposes.
word_study.significance: The contrast is with 'my people' (ammi) of verse 20. The inhabitants of the earth are not God's people; they have not entered covenant relationship and thus have no shelter. They dwell in the material realm only, without transcendent connection to the divine.

word_study.term_original: תַּפִּיל עֲוֺן יֹשְׁבֵי־הָאָרֶץ עָלָיו וְגִלְּתָה הָאָרֶץ אֶת־דָּמֶיהָ (vegiltah ha'arets et-dameiha)
word_study.meaning: The verb galah (to uncover, to reveal, to expose) with blood (dam) as object. The earth reveals the blood it has held—making visible what was hidden.
word_study.significance: This verb is used for exposing shame (Lamentations 2:14) and revealing divine glory (Psalm 98:2). Here it means the blood—evidence of injustice—will be made visible. The passive voice emphasizes that the earth itself is agent: the earth will expose the blood; nothing can keep it hidden longer.

word_study.meaning: The verb kasah (to cover, to hide, to conceal) in negative form: 'will not cover.' The slain (harugim, those killed in violence) will no longer be covered by the earth.
word_study.significance: This is direct contradiction of Cain's hope in Genesis 4: 'Now am I cursed from the earth, which hath opened her mouth to receive thy brother's blood from thy hand...a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.' But the earth—which received Abel's blood—cannot finally hide it. All murdered innocents will be exposed, their injustice witnessed by the earth itself.

word_study.meaning: Plural form of harugim (the slain, those killed in violence). Refers to victims of injustice, murder, oppression.
word_study.significance: The slain are not abstract victims but real persons whose deaths matter to God. Their bodies, their blood, their lives—all will be vindicated when the earth exposes what has been hidden. In Revelation 6:9-11, martyrs under the altar cry out for vindication, and Isaiah's vision of exposed blood answers that cry.

cross_references.connection: Abel's blood cries out to God from the ground; the earth opens its mouth to receive his blood. Isaiah 26:21 extends this: not just one cry but all blood will be exposed at the final judgment. The earth that received Abel's blood will ultimately discharge it as witness.

Martyrs under the altar cry out, 'How long, O Lord, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood?' Isaiah's promise that the earth will disclose blood is answered in John's vision: the slain will be vindicated and their blood avenged.

Isaiah 14 depicts the refa'im (shades of the dead) as helpless and powerless. Chapter 26:21 contrasts this: the righteous dead are raised (v. 19) and the injustice against them is exposed (v. 21). Justice reverses the powerlessness of Sheol.

Job speaks of Sheol where 'the weary are at rest' and 'the prisoners rest together; they hear not the voice of the oppressor.' Isaiah 26:21 suggests that Sheol's hiddenness ends: the oppressors' crimes, hidden there, will be exposed at the final judgment.

Daniel 12:2 speaks of resurrection of 'many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth...some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.' Isaiah 26:19-21 provides the basis: the righteous rise to life, the wicked rise to exposure and condemnation.

commentary.historical_context:
Isaiah 26:21 envisions a day when divine justice will overturn the historical pattern where the powerful hide their crimes and the innocent go unavenged. In Isaiah's own time (8th century BCE), Judah faced Assyrian military dominance: Assyrian armies were known for brutality, mass deportation, and erasure of peoples. Yet there seemed to be no reckoning. Isaiah's prophecy answers the ancient question of theodicy: Why do the wicked prosper? Why are the oppressed left unavenged? The answer is eschatological: God will come forth, and on that day, all hidden injustice will be exposed.

The language of the earth 'disclosing blood' reflects ancient understanding of the earth as a living entity that could testify to crimes. In Ancient Near Eastern law codes and literature, the earth itself is sometimes invoked as witness. The biblical prohibition against shedding innocent blood (Genesis 9:6) emphasizes that murder is not merely a human crime but cosmic violation that demands response. The earth, soaked with blood, becomes both victim and witness—unable to rest until justice is served.

The promise of exposure also reflects a belief that nothing hidden remains hidden forever. Ancient Israel had no concept of eternal hiddenness or permanent concealment in a cosmic sense. What is buried will be unearthed; what is covered will be uncovered. This belief, applied to the final judgment, means that the very earth that has been forced to hide injustice will participate in its exposure and judgment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels:
The Book of Mormon repeatedly teaches that all things are known to God and will be revealed. Alma 40:23 states: 'And then shall it come to pass, that the spirits of the wicked...shall be brought before the bar of God; and they shall be judged according to their works.' Alma 5:15-18 speaks of the day when all are 'brought to stand before God' to be judged 'according to [their] works.' This is Isaiah's 'coming forth' to judge transformed into Book of Mormon eschatology: nothing is hidden from the Lord's knowledge, and all will be exposed at judgment.

Moreover, 2 Nephi 27:10-11 applies Isaiah's language: 'And they shall cry unto the LORD because of their enemies: and a king shall be raised up among them, and he shall cry unto them...And it shall come to pass that the Lord God shall send forth his power to break the chains which are bound about my people.' The exposure of hidden iniquity (Isaiah 26:21) becomes the means by which God's people are freed from oppression.
restoration_lens.dc_connections:
Doctrine and Covenants 88:44-45 speaks of the coming judgment: 'And again, verily I say unto you, my friends, I leave these sayings with you to ponder in your hearts, with this commandment which I give unto you, that ye shall call upon me while I am near—Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you.' The counterpoint to verse 21 is that God comes forth to judge, but those who have drawn near to Him will not be exposed in shame. D&C 76:3-10 describes the vision of kingdoms of glory, which assumes the prior judgment where all deeds are known and all blood is counted.

D&C 88:34-35 is especially relevant: 'Thou art the light and the life of the world; thou art more intelligent than they all. The place where God resides is holy, undignified space. And all things are before him, and all things are round about him; and he is above all things, and in all things, and is through all things, and is round about all things; and all things are by him, and of him, consist the things which are seen and the things which are not seen, as well the things which are spiritual as the things which are temporal; it being one body, one spirit, one element, and all being comprehended within one power.' This divine omniscience means that nothing—no hidden blood, no concealed crime—escapes God's awareness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Isaiah 26:21 is a temple judgment text. The temple is the place where God dwells; from the temple (God's place) judgment will proceed. In temple theology, judgment is not primarily negative but covenantal: those sealed to God are vindicated; those outside covenant are exposed. The sealing ordinances of the temple create the protection spoken of in verse 20; those not sealed are left exposed to judgment. The disclosure of blood can be understood as the forensic examination that takes place before God in the temple: all deeds are exposed before the Lord. The temple president (or ultimately the Messiah as judge) examines the record and renders judgment according to works.
restoration_lens.restoration_blessing: For latter-day covenant members, verse 21 is both warning and comfort. Warning: all deeds will be exposed, nothing is hidden from God's sight (Doctrine and Covenants 88:41: 'Verily, I say unto you, that all things are known unto God, our God'). Comfort: injustice will not endure forever. The oppressed who have had no earthly redress will find vindication when God comes forth to judge. Moreover, those who are sealed to Christ through temple covenant will stand protected while judgment falls on the wicked. The resurrection of the righteous (v. 19) and the shelter of the faithful (v. 20) together affirm that covenant relationship with God offers both resurrection and protection, both vindication and safety. The 'coming forth' of God from His place is the ultimate theophany—the revealed glory of God—and in latter-day revelation, this is understood as the coming of Jesus Christ to judge all nations.

commentary.christological_typology:
Isaiah 26:21 points prophetically to Jesus Christ as the judge who comes forth to expose all hidden things. In Matthew 12:36, Jesus teaches, 'Every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment'—a direct echo of Isaiah's vision that nothing remains hidden. John 3:20-21 speaks of judgment: 'Every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved. But he that doeth truth cometh to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest, that they are wrought in God.' This is Isaiah's disclosure of blood made personal: Christ's judgment brings all deeds into light.

More profoundly, Christ is the one who 'comes forth from His place'—He comes from heaven to earth, from the Father's side to the world of human judgment. Revelation 19:11-15 describes the rider on the white horse (Christ), 'coming forth to judge and make war,' and verse 13 states, 'his name is called The Word of God'—the one by whom all things are exposed and evaluated. Isaiah 26:21 is the Old Testament prophecy of the one who, in His coming, will separate light from darkness, the righteous from the wicked, and vindicate the blood of all the innocent slain from the foundation of the world.
commentary.application: Isaiah 26:21 teaches modern disciples several profound truths. First, divine justice is real and inevitable. Whatever injustice we witness or experience—whatever crimes go unpunished in earthly courts, whatever oppression seems to succeed—will ultimately be exposed and judged. This does not excuse us from pursuing justice in the here and now; rather, it places our efforts within a larger, divine purpose. Second, nothing is hidden from God. This has practical implications: we cannot hide behind appearances, cannot cloak sin in respectability, cannot assume that what we do in secret has no cosmic significance. As the temple teaches, all deeds are before the Lord. Third, the exposure of hidden blood is vindication of the innocent. For those who have been wronged, oppressed, or murdered unjustly, Isaiah's promise that 'the earth shall disclose her blood' is the answer to the cry, 'How long, O Lord?' When we learn of injustice in the world—whether ancient injustice in scripture or contemporary injustice in our own time—we can rest in the knowledge that God knows, has not forgotten, and will judge. Fourth, for the righteous, the coming forth of the Lord is not threat but promise. Because they are resurrected (v. 19) and sheltered (v. 20), they need not fear verse 21; rather, they anticipate vindication. The implication for covenant members is that faithfulness to covenants is the shelter from judgment; living in violation of covenants is exposure. Finally, Christ's ultimate coming—His Second Coming—will accomplish what Isaiah envisions: the raising of the dead, the shelter of the faithful, and the exposure of all hidden things. Our preparation for that day is fidelity to covenant, trust in God's justice, and alignment with His purposes of righteousness.

text_kjv: In that day the LORD with his sore and great and strong sword shall punish leviathan the piercing serpent, even leviathan that crooked serpent; and he shall slay the dragon that is in the sea.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 27:1 opens the final movement of the Isaiah Apocalypse with a cosmic act of judgment: the defeat of Leviathan. The phrase "in that day" (bayyom hahu) ties this eschatological moment to the Day of the Lord sequence established in chapters 24–26, where God judges the earth and its nations. But now Isaiah transcends human and political enemies to confront the primordial chaos-power itself. Leviathan is not merely a sea-creature; it is a symbol of cosmic disorder, the ancient waters of chaos that existed before creation. By depicting the LORD wielding a sword against Leviathan, Isaiah declares that God's final victory extends beyond earthly kingdoms to the ultimate spiritual reality behind all rebellion against His throne.

The threefold description of Leviathan—the fleeing serpent (nachash bariach), the twisting serpent (nachash aqallaton), and the dragon in the sea (tannin bayyam)—parallels the threefold description of the sword itself: cruel (qashah), great (gedolah), and mighty (chazaqah). This poetic symmetry emphasizes that the weapon matches the enemy in every dimension. The Ugaritic texts from Ras Shamra (c. 1400–1200 BCE) describe Baal's combat with Litanu using nearly identical epithets: the "fleeing serpent" (btn brch) and "twisting serpent" (btn 'qltn). Isaiah has taken a mythic pattern familiar to his Near Eastern audience and resituated it in eschatological time—not as something that happened in the mythic past, but as the final act of the Day of the Lord yet to come.

For the modern reader, this verse encodes a profound theological claim: the chaos that opposes God's kingdom is not ultimately powerful, not ultimately victorious, and not ultimately permanent. It will be conquered. The specificity of the sword's attributes—its harshness, magnitude, and power—assures that no enemy, however ancient or formidable, can stand against the LORD's will. This is not weakness or hesitation but decisive, absolute judgment.

word_study.meaning: From a Semitic root meaning 'to twist' or 'to coil.' A primordial sea-serpent or chaos-dragon known from both biblical and Ugaritic literature. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes the etymological connection to coiling motion, capturing the serpent's sinuous, evasive nature.
word_study.significance: In Psalm 74:14 and Job 41, Leviathan appears as a fearsome creature beyond human control. Isaiah eschatologically projects its defeat onto the Day of the Lord, declaring that what humans cannot subdue, God will destroy. This transforms Leviathan from an untameable reality into a symbol of chaos destined for judgment.

word_study.meaning: A blade weapon; metaphorically, an instrument of judgment, divine will, or separation. The sword appears throughout Isaiah as both a literal weapon and an emblem of the word of the LORD.
word_study.significance: Here, the LORD's sword is not merely physical but cosmically efficacious. Three adjectives equip it for eschatological battle: qashah ('harsh, cruel, keen'), gedolah ('great, mighty in scope'), and chazaqah ('strong, firm, immovable'). The Covenant Rendering preserves this triple emphasis, underscoring that God's judgment instrument is comprehensive and unstoppable.

word_study.meaning: To kill, to slay, to bring to death. A verb of finality; no resurrection or restoration follows.
word_study.significance: The dragon in the sea (tannin) will be harag—utterly destroyed. Unlike the serpent's cunning evasion, the dragon experiences absolute termination. This is God's final word on chaos.

word_study.meaning: A formulaic phrase marking eschatological or judgment time; 'in that day' refers to the Day of the Lord when God executes final justice.
word_study.significance: This phrase anchors Isaiah 27:1–6 within the apocalyptic timeline. The same formula opens verses 2 and 12, creating a triad of eschatological acts: judgment on chaos (v. 1), restoration of the vineyard (vv. 2–6), and ingathering of Israel (vv. 12–13). It signals that all three—destruction of Leviathan, redemption of Jacob, blessing of the nations—occur simultaneously in God's plan.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist recalls God breaking Leviathan's heads in the wilderness (the ancient past), and Isaiah 27:1 projects the final crushing of this chaos-power onto the eschatological future, completing the victory.
Job's description of Leviathan as untameable, fearless, and beyond human power underscores why only the LORD can subdue it; Isaiah 27:1 declares that this impossible creature will indeed be slain.
The New Testament identifies the serpent (dragon) as Satan; Isaiah's slaying of Leviathan foreshadows the eschatological defeat of evil itself in John's Apocalypse.
Isaiah later appeals to God's ancient victory over Rahab (the sea-chaos), asking Him to awake and repeat that triumph; 27:1 confirms God's will to slay chaos once and for all.
The Doctrine and Covenants affirms that Christ will come and 'tread upon the enemy' and 'overcome him'; this echoes the eschatological combat pattern of Isaiah 27:1.

commentary.historical_context: Leviathan imagery belongs to the ancient Near Eastern cosmology shared by Israel and Canaan. The Ugaritic texts (particularly KTU 1.5.I) describe the storm god Baal's victory over Litanu (Leviathan), the seven-headed serpent of the sea. This myth encoded the triumph of order (represented by Baal and the cosmos) over chaos (represented by the sea and its monsters). When Isaiah uses identical epithets—bariach (fleeing) and aqallaton (twisting)—he demonstrates intimate knowledge of this mythic tradition, yet he radically reframes it. Rather than a past mythic event or cyclical cosmological process, Isaiah places Leviathan's defeat in Israel's future, under YHWH's sovereignty, on the Day of the Lord. This is part of Isaiah's larger strategy: he takes the cultural and mythological vocabulary his audience understands and reorients it toward monotheistic faith in Israel's God. The sword wielded by YHWH is not the thunderbolt of Baal but the instrument of Israel's covenant God—far more ultimate and unstoppable.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon preserves Isaiah's eschatological vision and applies it to Nephite history and latter-day restoration. In 2 Nephi 8 (Isaiah 51–52), Nephi emphasizes God's power over chaos and evil; the slaying of Leviathan in Isaiah 27:1 complements this theme of ultimate divine triumph over spiritual enemies.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:22 states that Christ will 'tread upon [the enemy] and overcome him.' This directly parallels the LORD's victory over Leviathan in Isaiah 27:1, tying the Isaiah Apocalypse to Latter-day Saint eschatology. Additionally, D&C 88:94–98 describes the final dissolution of the wicked and the triumph of the righteous, which occurs 'in that day'—the same temporal frame as Isaiah 27:1.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple cosmos in Latter-day Saint understanding involves the eternal struggle between order (God's kingdom) and chaos (the adversary and his dominions). Isaiah 27:1 describes the final resolution of this conflict, with chaos utterly destroyed. This mirrors the temple's representation of God's victory over disorder and the establishment of His perfect kingdom.

commentary.christological_typology: Leviathan, as primordial chaos and a symbol of rebellion against God's order, represents the ultimate adversary—Satan himself. Christ's victory in the Atonement and His final judgment at His coming constitute the definitive slaying of this spiritual Leviathan. The sword of the LORD becomes, in later revelation, the word of Christ (Revelation 1:16; 19:21), which defeats evil and establishes His eternal kingdom. Isaiah 27:1 is thus a type of Christ's ultimate triumph over all powers opposed to God.
commentary.application: This verse assures modern covenant members that the evil and chaos opposing God's kingdom—both personal and cosmic—are not permanent fixtures. The forces that seem most ancient, most entrenched, most powerful will be judged and destroyed by God's will. When facing spiritual opposition, fear, or the apparent permanence of evil in the world, Isaiah 27:1 declares that the LORD holds an instrument of judgment more terrible and sure than any chaos-power. The application is double: first, it invites confidence that God's plan will be completed and evil will not triumph; second, it calls the righteous to align themselves with the winning side—with the LORD whose sword will prevail.

text_kjv: In that day sing ye unto her, A vineyard of red wine.

commentary.narrative:
The shift from cosmic warfare to horticultural blessing is deliberate and stunning. In the same day that Leviathan falls, a new vineyard song erupts. This is not a return to Isaiah 5's famous vineyard parable—where the LORD planted a vineyard expecting good fruit but it yielded only wild grapes. That vineyard became a symbol of Israel's failure and the LORD's judgment: He removed its hedge, broke down its wall, and left it to be trampled (5:5–6). Now, in Isaiah 27:2–6, a vineyard of delight (kerem chemed) replaces the bitter harvest. The command to sing—annu-lah ('sing of it, respond to it')—invites rejoicing, celebration, and proclamation. This is a public song, not a lament.

The phrase "vineyard of red wine" (kerem chemer or kerem chemed, depending on manuscript tradition—the Dead Sea Scrolls read chemer, 'wine') draws from ancient viticulture. Red wine was prized, costly, and symbolic of abundance and joy. In Old Testament usage, wine often represents blessing (Genesis 27:28; Deuteronomy 33:28) but also divine wrath when it represents the judgment cup (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Here it is unambiguously blessing: wine produced by a vineyard that YHWH Himself tends. The same rhetorical strategy employed in Isaiah 5:1–7 is inverted: instead of a judicial pronouncement against a failed vineyard, we have a celebratory command to sing about a restored and fruitful one.

The structural parallel is crucial for understanding Isaiah 27 as reversal and redemption. Chapter 5 presented a court case against Israel (rib, 'lawsuit'). Chapter 27 presents Israel's vindication and restoration. The vineyard that was destroyed is now replanted, tended, and productive. This speaks to a fundamental promise about Israel's future: judgment is not final; restoration follows; the LORD does not abandon His vine.

word_study.meaning: A cultivated field of grapevines; metaphorically, Israel itself (Isaiah 5:7: 'For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel').
word_study.significance: By using the identical word (kerem) from Isaiah 5's parable, the prophet establishes a direct dialogue between judgment (ch. 5) and restoration (ch. 27). The same vineyard that was judged is now redeemed.

word_study.meaning: Chemed: 'delight, desire, that which is pleasant and desirable.' Chemer: 'wine, fermented grape juice.' Both readings are attested: the Masoretic Text tradition favors chemed ('vineyard of delight'), while the Dead Sea Scrolls read chemer ('vineyard of wine').
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering opts for chemed, which emphasizes the qualitative transformation: this is not just a productive vineyard but a delightful one—a vineyard of desire. The Dead Sea Scrolls' chemer, by contrast, emphasizes the tangible product (wine) that results. Both convey blessing, but chemed is more affective and poetic, while chemer is more concrete and material.

word_study.meaning: Anah can mean 'to answer, respond, sing in response'; shir means 'to sing, to make music.' The imperative form invites Israel and the nations to voice joy about this vineyard.
word_study.significance: The command to sing is a summons to communal celebration and testimony. It mirrors the 'song of the vineyard' in Isaiah 5:1, but with opposite effect: not lament but jubilation.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah 5 presents the LORD's lawsuit against the vineyard of Israel; Isaiah 27:2 reverses this verdict by commanding a song to a new, delightful vineyard—the same metaphor transformed from judgment to redemption.
The Song also mentions vineyards as images of love and desirability; Isaiah 27:2's 'vineyard of delight' shares this erotic-relational significance, depicting the LORD's renewed love for Israel.
The psalmist describes God planting Israel as a vine in Egypt and causing it to flourish; Isaiah 27:2–6 completes this image with the restoration of a vine that was uprooted in judgment.
Jeremiah promises that the LORD will 'plant them in this land with all my heart and soul'; Isaiah 27:2 presents the song of that replanting.

The Doctrine and Covenants applies the parable of the vineyard to the Church in latter days; Isaiah 27:2 informs understanding of how God restores and tends His vineyard in the dispensation of the fullness of times.

commentary.historical_context: Vineyards were central to ancient Levantine agriculture and economy. The terraced hillsides of Judah and northern Israel were planted with grapes, which were processed into wine for local consumption, cultic offering, and trade. An ancient Israelite would have understood the vineyard as both literal agricultural reality and metaphorical representation of communal identity and covenant. The shift from the ruined vineyard of Isaiah 5 to the restored vineyard of Isaiah 27 would have resonated powerfully: if your vineyard is destroyed, you lose livelihood, heritage, and blessing all at once. Restoration of the vineyard means restoration of everything. This is not mere agricultural imagery but existential restoration.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, Jacob teaches about the olive tree and wild branches (Jacob 5), a parable that parallels Isaiah's vineyard imagery. The theme of replanting, tending, and bringing forth good fruit is central to both. Jacob 5:75 describes the Lord's joy when His vineyard yields fruit again, echoing the celebratory tone of Isaiah 27:2.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 86 explicitly applies the vineyard parable to the Church. D&C 86:1–7 describes the tares and the wheat growing together, and the ultimate separation and harvest. Isaiah 27:2's song of the delightful vineyard points toward the final gathering of Israel and the triumph of God's kingdom in the latter days, which D&C imagery also emphasizes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the restored vineyard—a place where God's presence dwells, where fruit is produced, and where the covenant is renewed. Isaiah 27:2's command to sing of the vineyard finds its fulfillment in temple worship, where Israel sings praises to God in the house of the LORD.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the true vine (John 15:1–8), and the restored vineyard of Isaiah 27:2 points to His redemptive work. Through His Atonement, the vine that was cut off (Israel in judgment) is replanted and made productive again. The song commanded in Isaiah 27:2 is ultimately a song of Christ's redemptive power—the vineyard sings because Christ has made it whole.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 27:2 offers profound encouragement. When personal or corporate covenant relationships have been damaged—when the 'vineyard' of your life or family or faith community has been trampled—this verse promises that restoration is possible. God is not content to leave the vineyard in ruins. He commands a song of delight over restoration. The application calls us to participate in that song: to testify of God's power to restore what was broken, to rejoice in redemption, and to help others recognize the vineyard being replanted in their own lives and in the gathering of Israel in the latter days.

text_kjv: I the LORD do keep it; I will water it every moment: lest any hurt it, I will keep it night and day.

commentary.narrative:
God now speaks in the first person, entering the vineyard song with absolute authority and tenderness. The pronouncement "I the LORD do keep it" (ani YHWH notsrah) is emphatic: the subject is not Israel's effort or worthiness, but God's active guardianship. This stands in radical contrast to Isaiah 5:4–5, where God laments: "What more could have been done to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? Wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes?... I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down." In that passage, God removes protection and allows destruction. Here, the inverse occurs: God stations Himself as the vineyard's perpetual guardian.

The phrase "every moment" (lirga'im) conveys unceasing care. The Hebrew ragah means 'moment, instant,' and the plural with the preposition 'l' (to/for) suggests momentary intervals throughout day and night. Watering in the ancient Levant was labor-intensive and critical; insufficient irrigation meant crop failure. By promising to water "every moment," God commits to constant, meticulous attention—nothing is overlooked, no interval is left unwatered. This is not a once-and-done blessing but an ongoing, vigilant providence.

The structure of verse 3 presents a cause and effect relationship. The reason for God's constant care is explicit: "lest any hurt it" (pen yifqod aleha). The verb paqad in this context means 'to visit with judgment, to harm.' God guards against any harm coming to the vineyard. The phrase "night and day" (laylah veyomam) emphasizes totality—there is no hour when the vineyard is unguarded. This contrasts sharply with human vulnerability: humans sleep, grow weary, forget. But God never sleeps. He is the keeper (natsar) who watches without ceasing. The verb natsar (to keep, guard, watch) appears twice in this verse, framing the promise: the LORD keeps it, and therefore no one will keep harm from it.

word_study.meaning: To keep, to guard, to watch over, to preserve. The root conveys both protection and careful oversight, as a shepherd keeps sheep or a watchman keeps a city.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah 27:3, natsar appears twice—at the beginning ('I keep it') and at the end ('I will keep it night and day'). This repetition frames the entire promise. Natsar is the opposite of abandonment; it is the covenant posture God assumes toward His vineyard. This same verb appears in Psalm 121:4–5, where the psalmist affirms that God 'sleeps not' but 'keeps' Israel.

word_study.meaning: To water, to irrigate, to cause to drink. In ancient agricultural practice, shaqah refers to the intentional, life-giving act of supplying water to crops.
word_study.significance: The promise 'I will water it every moment' (lirga'im ashqenah) is extraordinary in its frequency. God does not water the vineyard once and leave it; He provides constant irrigation. This parallels the promise in Psalm 65:9–10, where God visits the earth and 'waterest it; thou greatly enrichest it,' ensuring fertility.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'to moments' or 'moment by moment.' The Hebrew rega can mean an instant or a very brief time, and the plural form emphasizes the succession of moments—each one cared for.
word_study.significance: This phrase emphasizes constancy without interruption. In modern theological language, it suggests God's omnipresence and His ability to attend to His vineyard in every moment without exhaustion or distraction.

word_study.meaning: To visit, to appoint, to punish, to harm. In this context, 'lest any hurt it' (pen yifqod aleha) means 'lest anyone come to visit judgment or damage upon it.'
word_study.significance: The verb paqad carries a note of judgment or visitation. God will not permit any paqad (judgment or harm) to fall upon the vineyard. He stands between it and all threats.

word_study.meaning: A merism—a figure of speech that expresses totality by pairing opposites. 'Night and day' together mean 'at all times, constantly, without interruption.'
word_study.significance: This phrase emphasizes that God's guardianship is ceaseless. Unlike human watchmen who work in shifts, God requires no rest. The vineyard is guarded continuously.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist declares that God neither slumbers nor sleeps, and He keeps Israel from evil; Isaiah 27:3 echoes this same promise of constant divine watchfulness over God's covenant people.

The psalmist appeals to God: 'Return, we beseech thee, O God of hosts... Look down from heaven, and behold, and visit this vine.' Isaiah 27:3 is the answer: God will indeed look down, and He will protect it constantly.

The contrast is essential: in Isaiah 5, God removes the hedge and allows the vineyard to be trampled; in Isaiah 27:3, God Himself becomes the keeper, watering it every moment and guarding it night and day.

Jesus states that He is the vine and the Father is the vinedresser who tends and prunes the branches; Isaiah 27:3's vision of constant tending foreshadows Christ's promise of intimate, ongoing care for His church.

In a revelation to the Church in the latter days, the Lord says 'I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Wherefore, I am the same yesterday, to-day, and forever.' Isaiah 27:3's promise of constant keeping reflects the eternal, unchanging nature of God's covenant commitment.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Mediterranean world, irrigation was a labor-intensive, specialized skill. A vineyard owner or manager would need to direct water from a well or spring to each plant, often during drought seasons. The promise of constant watering ('every moment') would have conveyed to an ancient audience that no expense, effort, or concern is spared. The vineyard is valued above all other uses of the water. This reflects the priority God assigns to His relationship with Israel: He lavishes care on the vineyard as a farmer lavishes care on his most precious crop. The 'night and day' guardianship also reflects ancient practice: vineyards required night watches against thieves and animals. God promises to provide this vigilance continuously.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Helaman 7:16, Nephi laments that Israel has turned away, but the overarching Book of Mormon message affirms that God remains the keeper of His covenant people despite their failings. Isaiah 27:3's promise of God's constant care and protection resonates with the Book of Mormon's repeated affirmation that God guides and protects those who keep His covenants.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 84:77–80 promises that those who keep covenants will be guided and kept by the Lord: 'And the Lord shall guard and protect his people, notwithstanding their iniquities.' Isaiah 27:3's promise of God's constant, moment-by-moment care informs this latter-day covenant language.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where God's protective care is most explicitly felt and renewed. Isaiah 27:3's promise of constant keeping and watering relates to the temple covenant, where members receive the assurance that they are sealed and kept in God's kingdom despite opposition.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ, as the vine and the expression of God's care, embodies the promise of Isaiah 27:3. In His atoning sacrifice, Christ waters the vineyard with His own blood (John 6:53–56). His role as Savior is to keep His covenant people constantly, moment by moment, in His redemptive work. The promise of protection 'night and day' finds ultimate fulfillment in Christ's eternal intercession for the saints (Hebrews 7:25).
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 27:3 provides unprecedented comfort and confidence. The constant care promised here is not earned by perfectionism or constant performance; it is given freely by a God who commits to guard the vineyard every moment. When personal circumstances feel chaotic, when opposition seems relentless, when self-doubt whispers that God might have abandoned you, Isaiah 27:3 declares the opposite: God waters you every moment, watches you night and day, and permits no harm to come to those who are His. The application calls for radical trust: to accept that your spiritual life is not dependent on your vigilance alone but on God's covenant commitment to keep you. This invites relief from the burden of self-salvation and alignment with God's protective purpose.

text_kjv: Fury is not in me: who would set the briers and thorns against me in battle? I would go through them, I would burn them together.

commentary.narrative:
This verse completes the contrast between God's posture in Isaiah 5 and Isaiah 27. In Isaiah 5:6, God announced judgment: "I will lay it waste; it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns." The briers and thorns are instruments of judgment, symbols of desolation. In Isaiah 27:4, the same briers and thorns reappear, but God's relationship to them has transformed. His opening declaration—"Fury is not in me" (chemah ein li)—is decisive. The Hebrew chemah (wrath, anger, heat) will not drive God's actions toward the vineyard or even toward those who oppose it. Instead, God's posture is clear-eyed, protective, and (paradoxically) merciful even in judgment.

The rhetorical question "who would set the briers and thorns against me in battle?" frames the would-be enemies of the vineyard as presumptuous. Any power that attempts to attack God's vineyard is, by definition, attacking God Himself. The conditional clause that follows—"I would go through them, I would burn them together"—states what God would do if such enemies appeared. The verbs are futures of resolve: 'I will march against them' (efsah bah) and 'I will burn them' (atzitennah). This is not hesitation or weakness but a clear statement of capability and will. God can annihilate these thorns instantly if they pose a threat. However, notice what verse 4 does not do: it does not command immediate burning. It presents a hypothetical: IF anyone tries to harm the vineyard, THEN God will respond with overwhelming force.

But verse 5 will offer a third option, complicating this picture further. Verse 4 establishes that God has the power and right to destroy all opposition; verse 5 reveals that God prefers reconciliation. The absence of fury from God does not mean tolerance of evil; it means that God's judgment is not driven by emotional heat but by justice and purpose. God will destroy what must be destroyed, but He will also extend peace to those willing to accept it.

word_study.meaning: Heat, wrath, anger, burning indignation. In theological contexts, chemah represents God's passionate response to covenant violation and evil.
word_study.significance: The statement 'chemah ein li' ('fury is not in me') is a declaration of divine intention and character. God is not driven by emotional rage toward the vineyard or its adversaries, but by purposeful justice. This distinguishes God's judgment from human vengeance.

word_study.meaning: Shamir: a prickly plant or sharp growth; shayit: a thorny plant. Together, they represent desolation and judgment, the opposite of cultivated vineyard fruit.
word_study.significance: These are the same briers and thorns from Isaiah 5:6 and 7:23–25. Their appearance signals judgment and abandonment. In Isaiah 27:4, they are no longer signs of the vineyard's fall but potential threats to its restoration—enemies to be dealt with, not conditions to be endured.

word_study.meaning: To kindle, to light a fire, to burn, to destroy by burning. In judgment contexts, it represents the complete destruction of what opposes God.
word_study.significance: The future tense 'atzitennah' ('I will burn them together') expresses both power and resolution. If burning becomes necessary, it will be total and simultaneous—no enemy will escape. But as verse 5 clarifies, burning is not God's first choice.

word_study.meaning: War, battle, combat. A conflict between opposing forces.
word_study.significance: The potential battle against briers and thorns is framed not as a genuine war (which would suggest real danger to God) but as hypothetical presumption. Those who would set briers against the LORD invite swift destruction, but God frames it as unlikely and unnecessary—if only they would accept peace.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah 5 announces that God will lay waste the vineyard and let briers and thorns grow; Isaiah 27:4 reverses this, promising to burn the thorns if they threaten the vineyard, establishing that judgment on the thorns is certain, only the vindication of the vineyard is delayed.
Isaiah 7 describes a land covered with briers and thorns, places of judgment; Isaiah 27:4 declares God's authority to burn these thorns and restore fruitfulness instead.

Nahum affirms that God's fury is expressed against His enemies, yet even Nahum acknowledges God's patience and compassion; Isaiah 27:4's claim that 'fury is not in me' reflects this tension between God's justice and His mercy.
A fire goes before the psalmist's God and consumes His enemies; Isaiah 27:4's promise of burning thorns echoes this image of divine fire conquering opposition.

The Book of Mormon quotes Isaiah 5:5–6, and by extension, Isaiah 27:4 clarifies that while God allows weeds to grow in judgment, He retains the power and intention to clear them away and restore blessing.

commentary.historical_context: Briers and thorns represented one of the major agricultural threats in the ancient Levant. The Mediterranean climate, with its dry summers, could cause cultivated plants to wither while hardy, invasive thorny plants thrived. A neglected vineyard would quickly be overrun. Burning was a common method of clearing land of these pests before replanting. The ancient reader would have understood God's promise to burn the thorns as both a literal agricultural reality (clearing the ground for new growth) and a metaphorical statement about removing obstacles to blessing. The idea that God could destroy these threats "together" (yachdav) emphasizes total, simultaneous eradication—not a piecemeal effort but a complete transformation of the landscape.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently emphasizes that God will not suffer His covenant people to be destroyed, but He will visit judgment on those who oppose His purposes. In Alma 26:15–16, Alma describes how God protects the righteous while destroying the wicked. Isaiah 27:4's promise echoes this pattern.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:13–14 states that the Lord 'will come to his temple' and 'will suddenly come to his house,' and 'the Lord whom ye seek shall suddenly come to his temple.' The burning of thorns in Isaiah 27:4 is part of the eschatological cleansing that prepares the Lord's house (temple, kingdom, Church) for His return.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the place where God's enemies are excluded and the righteous are protected. Isaiah 27:4's burning of thorns parallels the temple's function as a place of separation between the holy and the profane, between God's order and spiritual chaos.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's victory over evil is prefigured in Isaiah 27:4. The burning of thorns represents the final destruction of all opposition to God's kingdom. In Revelation 19:11–16, Christ returns as a warrior on a white horse, treading out the winepress of God's wrath. Isaiah 27:4's burning of enemies in defense of the vineyard finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ's role as judge and protector of His church.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 27:4 offers both reassurance and a warning. The reassurance is clear: God has more than sufficient power to defend His vineyard (the Church, Israel, the covenant community) against all threats. Briers and thorns—whether doctrinal error, persecution, or internal corruption—cannot ultimately harm God's vineyard. The warning is directed at those who would oppose God's purposes: presume not to set yourselves against the Lord; if you do, you will be consumed. However, the verse also opens a question: Why does God not immediately burn all opposition? Verse 5 answers: because He offers peace first. Verse 4 thus calls the righteous to trust God's protection and calls potential enemies to accept the peace He offers before judgment falls.

text_kjv: Or let him take hold of my strength, that he may make peace with me; and he shall make peace with me.

commentary.narrative:
This verse presents a stunning alternative to verse 4's promise of burning. The conjunction "or" (au, 'or, whether') introduces a choice: the thorns (and by extension, any enemy of God's vineyard) can choose a different path than annihilation. Instead of facing the fire, they can "take hold of My strength" (yachaziq beme'uzi) and "make peace" (ya'aseh shalom). This is not weakness on God's part but the ultimate expression of His covenant character: He prefers reconciliation to judgment. The repetition of "he shall make peace with me" (shalom ya'aseh li, shalom ya'aseh li) emphasizes both the earnestness of the offer and the certainty of the outcome if accepted. God does not begrudge this peace; He actively wishes for it.

The phrase "take hold of My strength" is arresting. What does it mean for thorns—for enemies—to grasp God's strength? In biblical anthropomorphic language, 'taking hold of' someone's hand or arm signifies trust, dependence, and alliance (e.g., Deuteronomy 33:3; Ruth 3:11). To take hold of God's strength would mean to abandon one's own resistance and to lean upon God's power instead. This is conversion, reconciliation, and submission in a single image. The Hebrew me'uzi ('My strength, My refuge, My stronghold') is from the root 'oz, which denotes power, security, and firm protection. To grasp it is to move from opposition to God into the security of God's protection.

Verse 5 reveals that God's ultimate intent is not vengeance but peace. The absence of "fury" in verse 4 now makes sense: without fury, there is room for grace. This verse represents perhaps the most merciful offer in all the Isaiah Apocalypse. Even those who have set themselves against God's vineyard can enter into peace if they will grasp His strength. This is the logic of the covenant: judgment is threatened, but redemption is offered. The same God who can burn the thorns can also save them if they turn. Isaiah 27:5 thus presents a theodicy: God's long-suffering patience is not indifference but the patient offering of peace to all who will accept it.

word_study.meaning: Strength, power, fortress, refuge. From the root 'oz (to be strong), me'uz denotes both the quality of strength and a place of secure refuge.
word_study.significance: To 'take hold of My strength' is to move from reliance on one's own power (which is powerless against God) to reliance on God's power, which is invincible. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes 'refuge' (ma'uzi as 'My refuge'), suggesting that God's strength is a safe place to which the enemy can flee.

word_study.meaning: Peace, completeness, wholeness, harmony, covenant well-being. Shalom denotes not merely the absence of war but the presence of right relationship, justice, and blessing.
word_study.significance: The promise of shalom is comprehensive: those who make peace with God receive not just absence of burning but restoration to covenant relationship, complete well-being, and place within God's purposes. The emphasis on making peace ('ya'aseh shalom') is active: peace is not passive but constructed through submission to God.

word_study.meaning: To seize, to grasp, to hold fast, to strengthen, to be strong. The hiphil form 'yachaziq' means 'to take hold of, to seize with intent to keep.'
word_study.significance: The choice of chazaq (to seize, grasp) suggests active, determined movement toward God's strength. It is not a passive reception but an active grasping, a deliberate choice to align oneself with God's power.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah 55 extends an invitation to 'come,' 'buy,' and 'eat' without cost; Isaiah 27:5 similarly offers peace to anyone willing to grasp God's strength, emphasizing God's desire to give rather than to withhold.

Paul writes that 'being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ'; Isaiah 27:5's offer of peace through grasping God's strength prefigures justification and reconciliation in Christ.
The psalmist affirms that when others fail, 'the LORD will take me up' (yishlahi); Isaiah 27:5 promises that those who grasp God's strength will find similar refuge and care.

Lehi teaches that men are 'free to choose liberty and eternal life...or captivity and death'; Isaiah 27:5 presents a similar choice: choose to grasp God's strength and make peace, or resist and be burned.

The Doctrine and Covenants teaches that in the latter days, those who 'continue in faith' and are 'valiant in the testimony of Jesus' will inherit celestial glory; Isaiah 27:5's offer of peace to those who grasp God's strength is part of the same eschatological promise.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern vassal treaties, the pattern of offering terms—surrender and submit, or face destruction—was standard. A conquering king would approach an enemy city and offer: submit peacefully and you will be spared and protected; resist and you will be destroyed. Isaiah 27:4–5 follows this pattern, but with God as the ultimate suzerain. The offer of peace is not weakness but the civilized alternative to total war. The hand-grasping imagery reflects ancient covenant-making practices: two parties would clasp hands to seal an agreement. To grasp God's strength is to enter a new covenant with Him, exchanging resistance for alliance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows enemies of God's people being given opportunities to repent and accept God's peace. In Alma 22:27–32, the Lamanite king Aaron instructs in the covenant, and the king's cry is 'O God, Aaron hath told me that there is a God; and there is a Christ that shall come.' The king grasps at God's strength through repentance. Isaiah 27:5 presents the same pattern on an eschatological scale.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:33–35 states: 'I say unto you, that ye must repent or the Church which I have consecrated shall be taken away from you' and yet also promises 'Blessed are they who have kept the covenant and observed the commandment.' Isaiah 27:5's choice between judgment and peace is reflected in D&C language throughout.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is where peace is made with God—where covenants are entered, atonement is acknowledged, and sealing is secured. Isaiah 27:5's invitation to grasp God's strength and make peace finds its practical expression in temple worship and covenant-making.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the mediator of the peace offered in Isaiah 27:5. Through His Atonement, enemies of God are reconciled (Romans 5:10). To take hold of Christ is to take hold of God's strength; to make peace with Christ is to make peace with God (Colossians 1:20). The offer of verse 5 is Christologically the offer of redemption itself—that through Christ, even those who have opposed God can be restored to covenant relationship.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 27:5 presents a theology of second chances and reconciliation that should transform how they view both personal repentance and their ministry to others. If you have found yourself in opposition to God—whether through doctrinal confusion, personal sin, or spiritual rebellion—this verse offers a way forward: grasp God's strength through repentance, and peace is yours. Conversely, if you have been called to help others come to God, this verse models God's patient, non-punitive approach: the offer of peace comes before judgment; reconciliation is preferred; the door to God's strength is always open to those who will grasp it. This invites both personal humility (no one is so far gone that God will not make peace with them if they reach out) and ministerial compassion (others deserve the same chance at reconciliation that you have received).

text_kjv: He shall cause them that come of Jacob to take root: Israel shall blossom and bud, and fill the face of the world with fruit.

commentary.narrative:
The final verse of this opening section of Isaiah 27 fulfills the promise of the entire prophecy. After the slaying of Leviathan (v. 1), the new vineyard song (vv. 2–3), the promise of protection (v. 3), the destruction of opposition (v. 4), and the offer of peace (v. 5), Isaiah now unveils the purpose of it all: the global abundance and blessing that comes when Jacob takes root and Israel fills the earth with fruit. This verse shifts from God's activity (keeping, watering, judging) to Israel's flourishing. The subject changes from the LORD to Jacob/Israel, but the causation remains clear: "He shall cause them...to take root" (yashrish). God is the one who enables the growth, but the growth itself becomes Israel's fruitfulness and witness to the nations.

The agricultural progression is precise and complete: "take root" (yashrish—establishing foundational stability), "blossom" (yatsits—producing the first flowers), "bud" (farach—developing into fruit), and finally "fill the face of the world with fruit" (umale'u fenei-tevel tenuvah—universal abundance). Each stage is essential and sequential. A plant cannot bud without first taking root; it cannot bear fruit without first blossoming. Isaiah is describing maturation, not instantaneous transformation. But the climax is explicit and almost overwhelming: Israel's fruit will fill not just its own land but "the face of the world" (fenei-tevel). The Hebrew tevel means 'earth, world, inhabited land'—the same word used in Genesis 1:1 for creation itself. Israel's blessing is cosmic in scope.

This verse reverses the curse that followed Adam's sin: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread" (Genesis 3:19). Here, there is no toil, no scarcity, no struggle—only abundant fruit that fills the world. It also answers the question posed by Isaiah 5: "For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel...and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry" (5:7–8). After chapters of judgment and purification, Israel will indeed produce the righteousness and fruit that God sought. The arc from judgment (ch. 5) through apocalyptic purging (chs. 24–26) to restoration and abundance (ch. 27) is now complete.

word_study.meaning: To cause to root, to establish firmly, to make stable. From the root sharesh (root), the hiphil yashrish means to establish as if by putting down roots.
word_study.significance: Rooting is foundational. Without roots, growth is temporary and vulnerable. God's promise to cause Israel to take root speaks to permanent establishment in the covenant and the land, not temporary visitation but eternal settlement.

word_study.meaning: To bud, to bloom, to burst forth with flowers. The verb conveys sudden, visible expression of growth.
word_study.significance: Blossoming is the moment when potential becomes visible, when hidden growth manifests as beauty and promise of fruit. Spiritually, this represents the public witness of Israel's restoration.

word_study.meaning: To bud, to shoot forth, to spread, to flourish. Similar to yatsits but emphasizing spread and multiplication.
word_study.significance: While yatsits emphasizes the moment of bursting forth, farach emphasizes continuation and spread. Together, they suggest both the moment of restoration and its continued expansion.

word_study.meaning: To fill, to make full, to satisfy, to complete. The perfect form suggests completion and fullness.
word_study.significance: This is not partial, but complete filling. Israel's fruit does not merely exist alongside other fruits; it fills the entire face of the earth. The abundance is total.

word_study.meaning: Fruit, produce, yield, harvest. From a root meaning 'to produce, to bring forth.' Tenuvah is the concrete product of growth.
word_study.significance: Fruit represents completed growth, usefulness, and blessing that can be shared. The promise is not that Israel will merely exist but that Israel will produce fruit—visible, tangible blessing—that nourishes the world.

word_study.meaning: Earth, world, inhabited land, the realm of creation. Appears in Genesis 1:1 and denotes the whole created order.
word_study.significance: By using tevel ('world'), Isaiah indicates that Israel's blessing is not local or national but cosmic in scope. The vineyard's fruit feeds all humanity, bringing God's blessing to every nation.

cross_references.connection: God commands humanity to 'be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth'; Isaiah 27:6 is the fulfillment of this creation blessing transferred to Israel in the eschatological age.

Isaiah 5 presents the disappointing vineyard that yielded wild grapes; Isaiah 27:6 describes the redeemed vineyard that fills the earth with fruit—the complete reversal and redemption of the judgment announced in chapter 5.
The psalmist describes how the righteous king's reign will cause the earth to be 'filled with the fruit of thy works'; Isaiah 27:6 applies this fruitfulness to restored Israel.

Paul writes that 'the casting away of them [Israel] be the reconciling of the world,' suggesting that Israel's restoration brings blessing to all nations, echoing Isaiah 27:6's universal fruitfulness.

The Lord promises that those who receive the covenant will 'bring forth much fruit' and will be 'a light unto this people'; Isaiah 27:6's vision of Israel filling the earth with fruit is applied to the Latter-day Church's mission.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern world, fertility and abundance were the ultimate goods. Drought meant death; flood meant ruin. A land that produced fruit in abundance was a sign of divine blessing and kingly success. The promise that Jacob would take root and fill the world with fruit would have resonated powerfully with an exiled or distressed Judean audience: despite current devastation, restoration is coming, and it will be so complete that Israel will not only survive but will bless all surrounding nations. This echoes the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 12:3: 'in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed'), now applied to Israel's future restoration.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, the promise that Jacob's seed will flourish and fill the earth is reiterated. 2 Nephi 6:10–11 (Jacob's prophecy) describes Israel's restoration in language very close to Isaiah 27:6. The Book of Mormon emphasizes that the gathering of Israel and the restoration of the Church in the latter days fulfill these ancient promises.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 10:67–68 promises that the Church will grow and expand to all nations. D&C 65:2 declares that 'the kingdom of God...shall cover the whole earth.' Isaiah 27:6's vision of Israel filling the world with fruit is the fulfillment of which these D&C passages speak.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the center from which blessing flows to the world. Isaiah 27:6's promise that Israel will fill the earth with fruit has its earthly manifestation in the temple work—the ordinances performed in temples bless not only the living but all of God's children, extending blessing across the entire human family.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate fruit-bearer. In John 15:5, He states 'I am the vine; ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.' Isaiah 27:6's vision of Israel filled with fruit-bearing branches is fulfilled in Christ, the vine, and in those who remain in Him. Christ's kingdom, filled with the faithful, fills the entire earth with the fruit of righteousness and redemption (Daniel 2:35).
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Isaiah 27:6 transforms the understanding of both personal spiritual growth and the Church's mission. On a personal level, the promise that God will cause believers to 'take root, blossom, and bud' with fruit is a promise that your spiritual development is not left to chance or your own weak effort alone. God actively establishes you, causes you to grow, and multiplies your influence. On a corporate level, this verse affirms that the gathering of Israel and the spread of the gospel to all nations is not merely a good idea but a literal fulfillment of ancient covenant. Every member who produces spiritual fruit—whether through teaching, serving, witnessing, or living righteously—participates in filling the earth with the fruit of God's kingdom. The application is thus both affirming (you are part of God's cosmic purpose) and demanding (your growth and fruit-bearing matter to the world's redemption).

text_kjv: Hath he smitten him, as he smote those that smote him? or is he slain according to the slaughter of them that are slain by him?

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah poses two rhetorical questions that demand a resounding 'No.' The verse contrasts God's discipline of Israel with His destruction of the nations that opposed her. The verb 'hath he smitten' (hikkahu) appears twice with different subjects—God strikes Israel, and God strikes Israel's enemies—but the nature and outcome of those strikes are radically different. This is not a verse about equivalence; it is about distinction. Israel's punishment, though severe, is measured and corrective; the destruction of the nations is final and complete. The question 'is he slain according to the slaughter of them that are slain by him?' points to the fundamental asymmetry: Israel will survive her discipline, while her enemies will not survive their judgment.

The theological weight here is enormous. After chapters of warning about judgment on Judah, Isaiah reassures his audience that God's purpose toward Israel is not annihilation. The exile will come—chapters 39-40 make this clear—but it will not be the end. This verse establishes the principle that governs the entire final section of Isaiah: God disciplines His covenant people, but He does not abandon them as He abandons the nations. The distinction between corrective punishment and destructive judgment becomes the foundation for the restoration promises that follow.

word_study.meaning: to strike, smite, hit; can mean to wound or inflict a blow. The root carries the sense of violent contact with the intent to harm or correct. In different contexts, it describes physical violence, divine judgment, or corrective discipline.
word_study.significance: The repetition of hikkah with different subjects is deliberate: 'Has He struck Israel as He struck those who struck her?' The Covenant Rendering captures this parallel structure. The verb emphasizes that while God does indeed 'strike' (discipline) Israel, the nature and purpose of that strike differs fundamentally from how He strikes her enemies. In covenant language, God's striking is remedial; His striking of the nations is retributive.

word_study.meaning: to kill, slay, put to death. Often used in contexts of military defeat or capital judgment. The noun form hragim means 'the slain' or 'those killed in battle.'
word_study.significance: The verb harag appears in the second rhetorical question: 'is he slain according to the slaughter of them that are slain by him?' The parallelism suggests that while Israel experiences divine discipline, she does not experience the finality of death that befalls her enemies. This preserves the distinction between exile (temporary separation) and extermination (permanent end).

cross_references.connection: The vineyard song in Chapter 5 pronounced judgment on Israel for bearing bad fruit; Chapter 27 reverses this judgment with a new vineyard that will produce fruit abundantly. Verse 7 establishes that God's striking of Israel is not the same as His destruction of enemies—enabling the restoration promised in 27:2-6.

Jeremiah likewise distinguishes between God's corrective discipline and His complete abandonment: 'I am with thee, saith the Lord, to save thee: though I make a full end of all nations whither I have scattered thee, yet I will not make a full end of thee.' The principle established in Isaiah 27:7 is echoed throughout Jeremiah.

Hosea describes God's discipline as a necessary wound that precedes restoration: 'Come, and let us return unto the Lord: for he hath torn, and he will heal us.' This illustrates the distinction between God's striking (tear) and His final purpose (heal).

The Lord teaches the early Saints: 'I give unto you a commandment, that ye shall let your houses be built up speedily...and I shall make myself known unto my people, and the trials of your faith shall make you strong in the Lord.' Discipline strengthens rather than destroys.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, military conquest typically meant the complete destruction or enslavement of a defeated people. When a great power 'struck' a nation, the result was usually permanent subjugation or extermination. The Assyrian empire, which conquered the northern kingdom of Israel around 722 BCE, was notorious for its policy of deporting entire populations to prevent rebellion. Isaiah's assertion that God's striking of Israel is not the same as His striking of the nations would have been radically counter-intuitive to his audience. It asserts that Israel's God operates by different principles than the empires that dominate the Near East. Exile is not extinction; discipline is not destruction.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly teaches this principle of Israel's preservation through discipline. In 1 Nephi 20:4-5 (quoting Isaiah 48:4-5), the Lord says of Israel: 'I know that thou art obstinate, and thy neck is an iron sinew, and thy brow brass; therefore have I told thee from the first that thou art refractory, that I gave my promise, lest thou shouldst say—Mine idol hath done them.' Israel will be refined but not consumed. Nephi's people are told they are branches of Israel, subject to the same principle: they will face exile and scattering, but as a covenant people they will be gathered again.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-9 teaches Joseph Smith while imprisoned: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high.' The Lord explicitly distinguishes between the temporary nature of affliction and the permanent nature of exaltation. This mirrors Isaiah's distinction between striking and slaying.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that covenants are preserved even through the most severe trials. The washing and anointing endowment portrays the passage through mortal experience as a refining process—we are 'struck' by mortality but not 'slain' by it. The covenant promises that we are sealed to redemption despite our weakness reflects the principle Isaiah announces here.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the one who endures the strokes meant for Israel and her enemies alike. In Isaiah 53:5, Christ bears the stripes that procure our healing: 'By his stripes we are healed.' Yet unlike Israel, who survives her discipline, Christ dies and rises again—He experiences both the striking and the slaying, then transcends both through resurrection. His experience encompasses and transforms the distinction Isaiah announces here.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members face trials and disciplines within their faith journey. This verse teaches that such trials are not signs of abandonment but rather evidence of God's covenant relationship. The Lord does not discipline those outside His covenant. If you experience correction, it is because you are His. The discipline you face is not the 'slaughter' of your enemies but the measured striking of a Father who intends your restoration. When facing hardship within the covenant community, recall that God's striking is corrective, not destructive—it produces fruit, not ruin.

text_kjv: In measure, when it shooteth forth, thou wilt debate with it: he stayeth his rough wind in the day of the east wind.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 8 deepens the contrast established in verse 7 by introducing the language of legal contention. God does not simply strike Israel arbitrarily; rather, He 'contends with her' (terivenah)—using language drawn from the covenant lawsuit tradition. The dispute with Israel is judicial, not capricious. The opening phrase 'In measure' (besah'asea'h) is debated by scholars, but The Covenant Rendering suggests it means 'by measure' or 'by exile'—indicating that even the method of discipline is calibrated and proportionate. The 'rough wind' (rucho haqqashah) that removes Israel into exile is not uncontrolled fury but the deliberate instrument of a measured judgment. The 'east wind' (qadim) is the sirocco from the desert that would have been familiar to Israelites as a force of desolation—yet even this destructive natural phenomenon is employed by God as a tool of discipline rather than destruction.

The restraint expressed in 'stayeth his rough wind' is crucial. The wind that drives Israel into exile is fierce, but it does not blow without limit. God 'stays' (removes, restrains) His wind—He sets bounds on the discipline. This verse assures Israel that even in exile, even under the harsh conditions of deportation and separation from the land, they are not abandoned to chaos. The hand that drives them also restrains the forces that drive them. Their exile is exile, not annihilation; the wind of judgment, though fierce, is stayed by the hand of a God who contends with them through established legal processes rather than arbitrary destruction.

word_study.meaning: The term is difficult and disputed. It may derive from 'seah' (a dry measure of grain), suggesting 'measure by measure' or 'by measured amount.'
