Yet Christ's encirclement by evil becomes the means of redemption. Where Isaiah announces inescapable judgment, Christ announces inescapable grace. The siege at Calvary is, from one perspective, the ultimate judgment upon covenant violation (Christ bearing the curse); from another perspective, it is the ultimate mercy (Christ's death opening the way to forgiveness). The 'forts against thee' become the instruments of Christ's humiliation and exaltation.

word_study.meaning: From the root hanah: to encamp, pitch tents, establish a siege position. The verb is military in connotation—it describes the setup of a military encampment.
word_study.significance: God uses military language to describe His judgment. The theological claim is that God is the ultimate military commander, orchestrating the geopolitical events that will bring judgment upon Jerusalem. This vocabulary appears throughout ancient Near Eastern conquest narratives and siege accounts.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'like a circle' or 'in a circle.' The noun dûr means encirclement, circle. The image is of complete enclosure—no escape route.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes inescapability. A siege 'round about' means the city is trapped. This reflects the ancient siege strategy: cut off all supply lines, all escape routes, all reinforcement. The theological implication is that there is no evading God's judgment through cleverness or military maneuvering.

word_study.meaning: A siege mound or rampart constructed by the besieging army. Archaeological evidence from Iron Age siege sites shows these earthen siege ramps built up against city walls to breach them or to provide vantage points for assault.
word_study.significance: This is military terminology grounded in archaeological reality. The Covenant Rendering's 'siege works' more accurately conveys the engineering aspect than the KJV's 'mount.' Isaiah is not speaking in vague abstractions; he is describing the actual military technology of his time.

word_study.meaning: From the root tzar: fortifications, fortified positions, siege towers. These are the military structures from which besiegers conduct assault operations.
word_study.significance: The comprehensive siege apparatus is laid out: encirclement, siege ramps, fortified assault positions. Isaiah leaves nothing to chance. The image is of overwhelming military technology arrayed against Jerusalem.

commentary.historical_context: The siege imagery in Isaiah 29:3 reflects the brutal military tactics of the Iron Age Levant. Assyrian kings, including Sennacherib (8th century BCE), were renowned for their siege warfare. Assyrian relief carvings from palace walls show siege operations in detail: battering rams, siege ramps, towers, and encirclement strategies. When Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem in 701 BCE, the Assyrian annals boast of 'shutting up' King Hezekiah 'like a bird in a cage.' The biblical accounts (2 Kings 18-19, Isaiah 36-37) corroborate this siege but add the theological claim that God miraculously delivered the city at the last moment. Isaiah 29, however, does not promise deliverance during the siege itself; it promises judgment. The destruction of Jerusalem actually occurred in 586 BCE under Babylon, more than a century after Isaiah prophesied. The long delay between prophecy and fulfillment is theologically significant—God's patience with covenant violation is extended, but inevitably judgment comes.

text_kjv: And thou shalt be brought down, and shalt speak out of the ground, and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be, as of one that hath a familiar spirit, out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 4 moves from military siege to a more haunting, almost supernatural image. Jerusalem, once proud and elevated, will be 'brought down'—reduced from her heights to the ground. But Isaiah is not speaking merely about physical destruction. The vivid language describes a city reduced to the state of a ghost or spirit of the dead—speaking from beneath the earth like the shade conjured at Endor in 1 Samuel 28. The Hebrew word 'ov (אוב) refers specifically to a familiar spirit, a necromancer's ghost.

This is a profoundly disturbing image: Jerusalem, the living capital of God's covenant people, will become like the dead, mute and invisible except for a faint whisper rising from dust. The repetition of 'from the ground,' 'from the dust,' and 'whisper' emphasizes the degradation—the city that once spoke with authority and power will be reduced to an inaudible murmur. Her words will be 'low out of the dust,' barely audible, powerless to effect anything.

The theological significance runs deep: Jerusalem's pride and confidence in her religious institutions will be replaced by shame and silence. She will not even be able to speak her defense or her plea; she will be reduced to ghostly, powerless murmuring. This is not mere military defeat; it is the stripping away of all authority, all voice, all agency. The image suggests a kind of spiritual death—the city is alive but acts like the dead, speaks but has no power. This is the ultimate humiliation for a city that boasted in her temple, her king, her religious status. All of that will be silenced.

Yet embedded in this judgment is a strange promise: the city will still speak. Even in her degradation, Jerusalem is not utterly annihilated. She will rise again, will find her voice again—but not until she has passed through this valley of death, this complete humiliation. The image is preparatory for the restoration that comes in verses 5-8, where God intervenes to restore the very city He has brought low.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that covenant violation brings not just external judgment but a kind of internal silencing—a loss of spiritual voice and authority. A person who has broken sacred covenants may continue to live and to function socially, but spiritually they become like a ghost, speaking without power or conviction. The passage thus serves as a warning: the worst consequence of apostasy is not destruction but voicelessness, the reduction of one's spiritual testimony to a faint whisper. Conversely, the verse also promises that even in the deepest humiliation, one is not utterly destroyed. Like Jerusalem, one can be restored. The path to restoration begins with accepting the humiliation, with being brought low, with acknowledging that one has lost one's voice. Only after that acknowledgment can the voice be restored. For modern members, this means recognizing that if they have compromised their covenants, the path back begins with humility and honest acknowledgment, not with attempts to maintain the appearance of power and authority.

cross_references.connection: The witch of Endor summons the shade of Samuel, which 'comes up out of the earth'—the exact image Isaiah uses. The connection is intentional: Jerusalem will be like a ghost, speaking faintly from the grave.

The psalmist describes his own humiliation using similar grave imagery: his strength is poured out, his heart melts, his tongue cleaves to the roof of his mouth. The condition of utter powerlessness mirrors Isaiah's description of Jerusalem.

The book of Lamentations, composed after Jerusalem's destruction in 586 BCE, uses similar language: the poet calls 'out of the dungeon,' his voice rises from the depths. The language of Isaiah 29:4 is prophetically fulfilled in Lamentations.

Nephi explicitly quotes Isaiah 29:4 as part of his interpretation that these prophecies apply to the Nephites as well. The Book of Mormon understands Isaiah's language of Jerusalem brought low as prophetic of the Nephites' condition before their restoration.

Alma describes his spiritual death and despair in similar language—brought low, unable to speak, in darkness. Alma's experience of spiritual humiliation and subsequent restoration parallels the arc of Isaiah's prophecy for Jerusalem.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 27:5-8 quotes Isaiah 29:4 and applies it to the Nephites. Nephi interprets the prophecy as describing not just Jerusalem but the condition of all covenant peoples who fall into apostasy and are brought low. The Nephites, like Jerusalem, will be reduced to a faint whisper—their records will be sealed, their voice will be suppressed. But restoration will come.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:21-23 describes how those who reject the covenant will be brought down and humiliated. The principle of judgment through humiliation and reduction of power is consistent with Isaiah's theology and Isaiah's language is echoed throughout the Doctrine and Covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where God's voice is heard most clearly. When Jerusalem is reduced to a ghostly whisper, it is partly because the temple's voice—God's direct communication through prophets and priesthood—is cut off. The restoration of the temple (after 586 BCE exile) is restoration of the people's ability to hear God's voice clearly again. In latter-day perspective, the restoration of temples in the latter days is part of restoring the voice of God to His people.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ on the cross is brought low, humiliated, reduced to apparent powerlessness. He speaks faintly from the dust of death itself—His blood is spilled, His body is buried. Yet His apparent defeat becomes the source of ultimate power and restoration. Like Jerusalem in Isaiah 29:4, Christ experiences spiritual death and humiliation. But unlike Jerusalem, which must experience siege and destruction before restoration, Christ's death itself is the instrument of resurrection and redemption. Christ's 'whisper from the dust' is the still, small voice of the Spirit calling all to repentance and salvation. The progression from humiliation to restoration, which Isaiah traces for Jerusalem, is perfectly realized in Christ's passion and resurrection.

word_study.meaning: From the root shaphal: to be low, humbled, brought down. The verb is passive—the city is brought down, not bringing herself down. God is the active agent.
word_study.significance: This is a word of humiliation and loss of status. In covenant theology, 'being brought low' is the consequence of breaking the covenant. But it is also the prerequisite for restoration—one must be humbled before one can be exalted (a principle central to both Hebrew Bible and Book of Mormon theology).

word_study.term_english: speak out of the ground / whisper out of the dust
word_study.term_original: מֵאֶרֶץ תְּדַבֵּרִי... מֵעָפָר תִּשַּׁח (me'eretz tedabberi... me'afar tisshach)
word_study.meaning: Literally 'from the earth you will speak... from the dust your words will come muffled/low.' The preposition 'from' (min) indicates the source and location of the speech—subterranean, beneath the surface.
word_study.significance: The imagery is of grave speech, the voice of one buried. In the Ancient Near East and Hebrew thought, the dust and the grave were associated with death, powerlessness, and silence. The psalmists often contrast the living God's power with the silence of the dead in Sheol. Isaiah inverts this: Jerusalem, the living city, will speak as if dead, powerless to assert herself.

word_study.meaning: A spirit of the dead, a ghost summoned by necromancy. The term appears in Leviticus 19:31 (prohibition against consulting mediums and familiar spirits) and in 1 Samuel 28:7-11 (the witch of Endor summoning the shade of Samuel). It refers to the faint, powerless voice of the dead.
word_study.significance: Isaiah's comparison is devastating: the proud city of Jerusalem will be reduced to the status of a ghost—spectral, voiceless, powerless. This is not merely death but the spiritual death of losing all authority and agency. The use of 'ov also echoes Levitical prohibitions, suggesting that Jerusalem's humiliation is so complete that she becomes the very thing the Torah forbids consulting—the powerless voice of the dead.

word_study.meaning: From the root tzaptzaf: to chirp, peep, whisper faintly. The word is onomatopoetic—it mimics a thin, barely audible sound.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures this: the speech will literally 'whisper.' Isaiah's language enacts the image—the words themselves become thin, faint, difficult to hear. This is a masterpiece of poetic technique: the words perform what they describe.

commentary.historical_context: The image of a city 'brought low,' speaking from the dust, reflects the archaeological reality of destruction. When Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE, the city's walls were breached, buildings were burned, and the population was deported. The city that had been the center of political, military, and religious power became a ruin—a place where prophets would later mourn over the rubble (as in Lamentations). The image of speaking 'from the dust' is not poetic fancy; it is a literal description of a devastated city where survivors would have lived amid rubble and ruins. The metaphor of 'ghostly whisper' captures the sense of a once-great city reduced to powerlessness, its former authority stripped away. Yet historically, Jerusalem was also restored—the city was rebuilt after the Babylonian exile, the temple was reconstructed, and the people returned. Isaiah 29:4 is thus both a prophecy of destruction and a harbinger of restoration.

text_kjv: Moreover the multitude of thy strangers shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the terrible ones shall be as chaff that passeth away: yea, it shall be at an instant suddenly.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 5 marks a stunning reversal. After announcing Jerusalem's humiliation—brought low, speaking as a ghost from the dust—Isaiah now announces the destruction of Jerusalem's enemies. The 'multitude of thy strangers' (the foreign armies encircling the city) will become 'like small dust.' The 'multitude of the terrible ones' (the brutal, ruthless soldiers of Assyria or Babylon) will be 'as chaff that passeth away'—dispersed, powerless, annihilated. The imagery is of complete reversal: just as Jerusalem is brought to dust, so her enemies will become dust and chaff.

The theological pivot is essential: God is not abandoning Jerusalem to her enemies. Rather, God will use the siege and humiliation as a means of purification, and then will turn upon the enemy itself. The besieging armies, instruments of God's judgment, become themselves subject to judgment. This is a consistent pattern in biblical theology: God uses one nation to judge another, then judges the instrument itself for its arrogance and cruelty (as in Isaiah 10:5-19, where God judges Assyria for its excessive brutality).

The phrase 'it shall be at an instant suddenly' (lepeta' pit'om in Hebrew) emphasizes the shocking rapidity of the reversal. The enemies will not gradually weaken or withdraw; they will be destroyed in a moment. This sudden reversal is beyond human military capability—it must be an act of God. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this text identically, confirming that this promise of sudden reversal was part of Isaiah's message in antiquity.

The structure of verses 1-6 is now clear: (1) Woe upon Jerusalem; (2) God will bring distress upon her; (3) Siege will encircle her completely; (4) She will be brought low, speaking as a ghost; (5) But suddenly her enemies will be destroyed; (6) And God Himself will intervene with thunder, earthquake, and fire. It is a pattern of judgment-humiliation-restoration that mirrors the entire arc of Israel's history.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 5 teaches a crucial theological principle: opposition to God's work is ultimately futile. Those who attack or oppose the Church, those who work to undermine it, those who persecute its members—all of this opposition will ultimately be 'like dust' and 'like chaff.' This is not a promise of protection from all opposition or difficulty, but a promise that the final outcome belongs to God. A member facing opposition from hostile forces—whether family members, employers, governments, or cultural pressures—can take courage from verse 5. The reversal may not come instantly in earthly time, but it is assured in God's eternal plan. More subtly, verse 5 also challenges members to distinguish between genuine enemies of the covenant (those who actively oppose God's work) and merely disagreeing persons or cultures. The verse teaches that God's judgment falls on true opposition, not on disagreement or cultural difference.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah explicitly teaches that Assyria is 'the rod of God's anger' used to judge Israel, but God will judge Assyria itself for its arrogance and brutality. The principle of verse 5 is elaborated here: God uses one nation to judge another, then judges the instrument for exceeding its mandate.

This passage recounts the miraculous deliverance of Jerusalem from the Assyrian siege under Sennacherib: 'And that night the angel of the LORD went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand.' The sudden destruction of the enemy army fulfills the pattern Isaiah describes.

The psalmist compares the wicked to grass and herbs that wither, using similar imagery of transience. The righteous endure; the wicked are like chaff, like dust. Isaiah applies this principle to the political and military sphere.

John the Baptist uses the same chaff/grain imagery: Christ will 'thoroughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.' The metaphor of chaff for what is destroyed and worthless is continuous from Isaiah through the New Testament.

The Lord tells the Saints that those who receive the word of God will be exalted, but those who reject it 'shall be cut asunder and their sins shall be upon their heads.' The principle of sudden reversal—preservation of the faithful and judgment upon the rebellious—is applied in the Restoration.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 28:31-32 cites Isaiah 29:5 and applies it to the Nephites. Just as Jerusalem's enemies will be suddenly destroyed, so the Lamanite enemies of the Nephites will be defeated—a reversal that comes through God's power, not through the Nephites' own military might. The principle is consistent: God protects His covenant people, even if they must first be humbled through judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:15-21 describes Christ's judgment upon the wicked in similar terms: they will be like chaff, scattered, destroyed. The principle of sudden judgment upon the enemies of God's people appears throughout the Doctrine and Covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the symbol of God's presence and protection. The sudden reversal described in verse 5—enemies destroyed, the city spared—is understood as the fruit of God's presence in the temple. In the Latter-day restoration, temples are built as a sign of faith in God's protection and power. The promise of verse 5 is that those who build and maintain the temple, who remain faithful to covenant, will ultimately be protected even in the midst of siege and opposition.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's enemies—those who persecute Him, crucify Him, attempt to destroy His cause—become 'like chaff' before the power of the resurrection. The cross is the moment of apparent victory for those who oppose Christ; the resurrection is the sudden reversal. Christ's enemies (including Satan and death itself) appear powerful until the moment of Christ's exaltation, when they are revealed as dust and chaff before God's power. The principle of verse 5—sudden reversal, enemies destroyed, the seemingly defeated vindicated—is perfectly fulfilled in Christ's resurrection and exaltation.

word_study.meaning: Hamon: multitude, crowd, throng. Zarayik: your strangers, your foreigners (from zar, foreign, strange). The phrase denotes the foreign armies, the multitude of invaders.
word_study.significance: The term 'strangers' (zarim) is significant: they are not part of the covenant community, they are outside the people of God. The implication is that while God will humble His own people through judgment, He will not allow external powers to destroy them permanently. There is a distinction between God's judgment of His own covenant people and God's judgment upon the nations.

word_study.meaning: Avak: dust (especially fine dust raised by wind). Dak: small, fine, thin. The phrase suggests dust so fine and light that it is easily blown away.
word_study.significance: The image echoes verse 4, where Jerusalem is brought to dust. Here, the enemies are reduced to the same dust. There is a justice in this symmetry: those who brought Jerusalem low are themselves brought to dust. This reversal is characteristic of biblical justice theology—those who oppress the innocent face equivalent judgment.

word_study.meaning: From the root artz: terrible, fierce, ruthless, tyrants. The term often refers to oppressive rulers or fierce warriors.
word_study.significance: The term 'arizim is used in Isaiah and the Psalms to describe brutal, oppressive powers that must be judged by God. The judgment upon the 'arizim is God's vindication of the oppressed—a core principle of biblical justice theology.

word_study.meaning: Motz: chaff, the husks of grain separated in threshing. Over: passing, transient. Chaff is the worthless part of grain, separated from the grain in winnowing and easily scattered by wind.
word_study.significance: Chaff imagery appears throughout Isaiah and the biblical prophets as a metaphor for the worthless, the destructive, the easily destroyed. Jesus uses the same image in Matthew 3:12 (John the Baptist's preaching). Chaff represents what has no lasting value and is easily disposed of.

word_study.term_english: at an instant suddenly / lepeta' pit'om
word_study.meaning: Two near-synonymous terms: petaʿ (suddenly, unexpectedly) and pit'om (at once, suddenly). The doubling emphasizes the immediacy and unexpectedness of the reversal.
word_study.significance: The doubling (like 'Ariel, Ariel' in verse 1) is emphatic, marking this as a moment of divine intervention beyond human expectation or military planning. The suddenness suggests that what is about to happen is not the result of military tactics but of God's direct action.

commentary.historical_context: The promise of sudden reversal in verse 5 is grounded in Isaiah's actual historical context. After Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem in 701 BCE, the biblical account (2 Kings 19:35-37) reports that the Assyrian army was suddenly struck—whether by plague, divine intervention, or other cause (scholars debate the mechanism). Sennacherib withdrew, and Jerusalem was spared. From Isaiah's perspective, this was the fulfillment of the pattern: judgment-humiliation-restoration. Later, when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE, the exile lasted 70 years, after which the Persian king Cyrus allowed the Jews to return and rebuild the temple. Both of these historical events are understood in Isaiah's theology as fulfillments of the pattern of judgment followed by divine restoration. The 'sudden' destruction of enemies may refer to plague, military mutiny, or natural catastrophe—all understood as expressions of God's will. The Ancient Near Eastern texts document the fragility of empires and the sudden reversals of fortune that characterized geopolitical history.

text_kjv: Thou shalt be visited of the LORD of hosts with thunder, and with earthquake, and great noise, with storm, and tempest, and the flame of devouring fire.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 is the climax of the oracle. God Himself will 'visit' Jerusalem—the Hebrew word 'paqad' can mean both to judge and to care for, so the visitation is ambiguous in tone but unmistakably direct divine action. God does not send intermediaries; God Himself comes. The manner of God's coming is described through a theophany—a manifestation of God characterized by the classical signs of divine presence: thunder, earthquake, great noise, whirlwind, tempest, and devouring fire.

This language echoes the greatest theophanic moments in Israel's history. When God appeared at Mount Sinai to give the Law (Exodus 19:16-18), there was thunder, earthquake, fire, and trumpet blast. When Elijah encountered God on Mount Horeb (1 Kings 19:11-12), God manifested in great wind, earthquake, fire, then finally in a 'still, small voice.' These classic theophanic elements signal that what is about to happen is not a matter of political or military power but of the direct intervention of God Almighty.

Yet the theophany in verse 6 is not for Jerusalem's edification but for the destruction of her enemies. God's thunder, earthquake, fire—these are not addressed to the city to bring comfort (as in other salvation oracles) but are directed against the foreign armies encircling Jerusalem. The 'flame of devouring fire' will consume the siege works, the soldiers, the engines of war arrayed against God's city. This is God's active warfare on behalf of Jerusalem.

The passage thus completes its arc: Jerusalem is brought low through siege (verses 3-4), the enemies seem triumphant, but then God Himself intervenes (verses 5-6) with overwhelming power. This pattern—judgment, humiliation, divine reversal—becomes the defining narrative of Israel's covenant experience. It is not a pattern that avoids hardship or suffering; it is a pattern that affirms that God's ultimate control over history is certain, even when the immediate situation appears desperate.

The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve verse 6 identically with the Masoretic Text, confirming the ancient textual tradition.
commentary.application: Verse 6 concludes the oracle with an affirmation of God's ultimate power and control. For modern covenant members, this verse teaches that opposition to God's work—whether from external enemies, cultural pressures, governmental restrictions, or internal apostasy—is ultimately futile before God's power. This is not a promise that persecution will not occur or that hardship will be avoided. It is a promise that God's ultimate triumph is certain. For those experiencing opposition or persecution for their faith, verse 6 offers assurance that they serve a God whose power cannot be ultimately defeated. However, the verse also carries a warning: God's theophanic visitation is directed against 'the terrible ones,' those who actively oppose God's work. The verse thus calls members to alignment with God's purposes and power—to be on the side that will ultimately be vindicated, not on the side that will be consumed. The ultimate application is that genuine faithfulness to covenant guarantees not escape from difficulty but final vindication and restoration.

cross_references.connection: God's descent on Mount Sinai to give the Law is accompanied by thunder, earthquake, fire, and trumpet blast. Isaiah's theophanic language echoes this foundational theophany, suggesting that God is now acting with the same power as at Sinai.

Elijah encounters God on Mount Horeb through great wind, earthquake, fire, and finally a still small voice. Isaiah's invocation of these theophanic signs signals that God Himself is about to act—not through human agency or political processes.

The psalmist describes God's judgment against enemies using identical theophanic language: the earth shakes, God's voice thunders, fire flashes forth, arrows fly. The pattern is consistent across biblical psalms and prophecy.

Nahum similarly describes God's judgment through whirlwind, tempest, fire, and earthquake. The prophet applies this theophanic pattern to God's judgment upon Nineveh, just as Isaiah applies it to the enemies of Jerusalem.

The Doctrine and Covenants describes Christ's coming in judgment using similar theophanic language: thunder, lightning, earthquakes, fire. The principle of God's direct intervention through theophanic signs is maintained in Latter-day revelation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 27:12-13 quotes Isaiah 29:6 and applies it to God's vindication of the Book of Mormon and the Restoration. The theophanic language is used to describe God's power in bringing forth the restored word and destroying opposition to it. The principle is that God's restoration of His work will be accompanied by manifestations of divine power.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:11-21 contains the most extended Latter-day treatment of theophanic judgment language. Christ will come in judgment 'with thunder, and with earthquake, and with great noise, with storm, and tempest, and the flame of devouring fire' (D&C 29:16)—language directly echoing Isaiah 29:6. The principle that God's ultimate triumph will involve direct divine manifestation is fundamental to Restoration eschatology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where God's presence is most directly experienced in the covenant community. Isaiah 29:6 describes God manifesting for the sake of Jerusalem (and by extension, the temple as its center). In Doctrine and Covenants 97:15-17, the Lord warns that while the temple is holy ground, those who approach it with unclean hands face swift judgment—an echo of verse 6's theophanic judgment. The principle is that God's presence (manifest at the temple) is both the source of greatest blessing and most severe judgment, depending on the state of the covenant people's hearts.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ in His resurrection and subsequent appearances manifests the power described in verse 6. When Christ appears to Paul on the Damascus road (Acts 9:3), the encounter is accompanied by overwhelming light and power. When Christ returns in judgment and exaltation (described in Doctrine and Covenants 29 and Revelation 19), He will come with power and great glory, with theophanic signs. More profoundly, Christ's passion is a kind of 'visitation' of God upon human sin and rebellion. The earthquake at the crucifixion (Matthew 27:51), the darkness at noon, the rending of the temple veil—these are cosmic signs accompanying God's judgment upon sin at the cross. Yet the resurrection is simultaneously a theophanic manifestation of God's power overcoming death and judgment. The pattern of judgment-humiliation-vindication (which Isaiah traces for Jerusalem) is perfectly realized in Christ's passion and resurrection.

word_study.meaning: From the root paqad: to visit, oversee, judge, care for. The root carries semantic range from judgment (Numbers 14:29, God will punish the Israelites) to care and restoration (Ruth 1:6, God 'visited' His people by restoring them to blessing). Context determines whether the visitation is judgment or grace.
word_study.significance: In verse 6, 'visited' clearly means judged/acted against, but the ambiguity of the word is theologically rich. God's judgment upon Jerusalem (in verses 1-4) was a form of 'visiting' to purify; God's judgment upon her enemies (verse 6) is another form of 'visiting,' but to destroy. God is the active agent in both cases. The term emphasizes God's direct, immediate relationship to events—nothing happens to God's people without God's direct attention.

word_study.meaning: The name emphasizes God's sovereignty over the heavenly armies and all cosmic forces. Tseva'ot ('hosts') may refer to the heavenly angels, the stars, or the armies of earth—all under God's command.
word_study.significance: The title 'Lord of hosts' appears frequently in Isaiah, especially in judgment oracles. It emphasizes that the God who is about to act is not merely a local deity but the sovereign ruler of all forces in heaven and earth. No power—military, political, cosmic—can resist the Lord of hosts.

word_study.term_english: thunder / earthquake / noise / storm / tempest / devouring fire
word_study.term_original: בְּרַעַם וּבְרַעַשׁ וְקוֹל גָּדוֹל סוּפָה וּסְעָרָה וְלַהַב אֵשׁ אוֹכֵלָה
word_study.transliteration: bera'am ubare'ash veqol gadol suphah useʿarah velahat esh okhelah
word_study.meaning: Ra'am: thunder. Ra'ash: earthquake. Qol gadol: great noise/sound. Suphah: whirlwind, tempest. Seʿarah: storm, tempest. Lahat esh: flame of fire. Okhelah: devouring, consuming. The six phenomena together constitute a comprehensive theophany.
word_study.significance: Each element carries theological weight. Thunder and earthquake are the fundamental signs of God's presence (Psalm 18:7-15). Whirlwind and tempest appear in theophanic contexts (Ezekiel 1:4, the throne-chariot surrounded by whirlwind and fire). Devouring fire is the instrument of purification and judgment. Together, these six elements constitute an overwhelming manifestation of God's power. The Covenant Rendering's precise language preserves these distinctions.

word_study.meaning: Fire that consumes, devours, destroys. The participle 'okhelah' emphasizes the active, aggressive quality of the fire.
word_study.significance: Fire, in biblical theology, is the instrument of God's judgment and purification. It purifies what is precious (as in testing of faith, 1 Peter 1:7) and consumes what is evil (as in the judgment of Sodom, Genesis 19:24). Here, it consumes the enemies of God's people—the foreign armies and their siege apparatus.

commentary.historical_context: The theophanic language in verse 6 is rooted in Israel's ancient experience of encountering God. Earthquakes, though terrifying, were not uncommon in the seismically active region of the Levant. Thunder and storms were dramatic natural phenomena that ancient peoples understood as signs of divine power. From an Ancient Near Eastern perspective, such phenomena (earthquake, storm, fire) would be interpreted as signs of divine intervention—whether understood as the action of a national god (the Assyrians might attribute these to their gods) or of Israel's God (as Isaiah interprets them). Isaiah's claim is that when Jerusalem faces its greatest danger, God will intervene with overwhelming natural power to destroy the enemies. Historically, the deliverance of Jerusalem from Sennacherib's siege in 701 BCE was accompanied (according to biblical accounts) by some form of catastrophe that affected the Assyrian army—whether plague, mutiny, or natural disaster is debated by scholars, but the biblical tradition interprets it as God's direct action. Verse 6 poetically expresses the expectation of such divine intervention.

text_kjv: And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, even all that fight against her and her munition, and that distress her, shall be as a dream of a night vision.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah pivots from Jerusalem's judgment to her unexpected deliverance. The vast military might arrayed against Ariel—the city Isaiah has just warned of siege (vv. 1-4)—will prove as insubstantial as a dream that evaporates upon waking. The word Ariel carries multiple layers: it means 'God's altar-hearth' (from ar, 'lion,' and el, 'God'), suggesting Jerusalem is God's sacred center, yet it also literally designates the city itself as a place of fiery judgment. The "multitude of all the nations" (hamon kol-hagoyim) emphasizes the sheer numerical superiority of the attacking forces—yet number proves meaningless against God's purposes.

This prophecy found historical fulfillment in the siege of Jerusalem by Sennacherib in 701 BCE, when an Assyrian army numbering perhaps 185,000 soldiers surrounded the city. Isaiah 37:36 records that "the angel of the LORD went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses." The enemy's conquest, though it seemed inevitable, proved as evanescent as the shadow in a night vision—the soldiers never entered the city.

The Covenant Rendering emphasizes the parallelism of the Hebrew: Jerusalem's attackers, her stronghold (mesudat), and those who distress (hamamtzikim) her all collapse together under a single metaphor. Isaiah uses the dream image not to suggest unreality, but to stress the radical discontinuity between human expectation and divine intervention. What appears certain to human calculation—an overwhelming military siege—becomes the very occasion for God to display His power.

word_study.meaning: tumultuous crowd, multitude, noise; from a root meaning 'to make a noise' or 'to be in commotion.' Carries connotations of chaos and overwhelming noise as much as number.
word_study.significance: The term stresses not just the quantity of the nations but their tumultuous, disorderly nature—yet even this chaos proves illusory before God's purpose.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'a dream, a vision of the night.' Chalom (dream) and chazon (vision) are nearly synonymous, creating emphasis through repetition. The nocturnal setting suggests not prophetic vision but the fleeting phantasm of sleep.
word_study.significance: Isaiah deliberately pairs two words for visionary experience—but empties them of substance. The dream-vision dissolves, leaving nothing behind. This reversal of prophetic language is striking: instead of visions revealing divine truth, these visions reveal the futility of human military might.

word_study.meaning: Possibly 'God's lion' or 'God's altar-hearth' (from ar, 'lion,' and el, 'God,' or from arah, 'to kindle'). The term appears primarily in Isaiah 29. It designates Jerusalem as God's sacred city, the place where His fiery judgment and protection meet.
word_study.significance: The name itself encodes the paradox of chapter 29: Jerusalem is simultaneously under divine judgment and protected by divine purpose. Ariel is not merely a city under siege but God's own altar-fire, where purification occurs.

cross_references.connection: Records the literal fulfillment of this prophecy: the angel of the LORD struck the Assyrian camp in a single night, destroying the multitude of the nations without Jerusalem firing a shot.

Uses similar dream imagery to express the unreality of restored blessing: 'When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream.' Both passages use dreams to express the discontinuity between despair and divine deliverance.
Nephi applies this passage to the final conflict over Zion, emphasizing that enemies of God's covenant people will ultimately be brought to nothing, as if their strength had been a dream.
The Lord promises to 'overcome all things, by patience,' suggesting that God's deliverance, like the dissolution of a dream, comes in His timing, not through visible strength.

commentary.historical_context: Sennacherib's invasion of Judah (701 BCE) provides the immediate historical backdrop. The Assyrian king documented his siege of 46 fortified cities and had extracted tribute from King Hezekiah. However, the siege of Jerusalem itself ended mysteriously—2 Kings 19:35 records a plague that decimated the Assyrian camp overnight. Ancient Near Eastern siege warfare typically involved months of encirclement and starvation; Sennacherib's failure to take Jerusalem stood out as anomalous even by ancient standards. The Annals of Sennacherib (now in the British Museum) confirms the siege occurred but records no explanation for its sudden termination. This silence in the Assyrian record—the absence of expected conquest—functions almost as dramatically as Isaiah's prophecy: what should have been a footnote in Assyrian imperial expansion became the very proof of God's power.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 19:13-14 presents Isaiah's prophecies as applying not only to Jerusalem's historical deliverance but to the ultimate protection of Zion in the last days. The Nephites understood this dream-vision language as describing how God's enemies, though they appear overwhelming and imminent, will be swept away like phantoms before the coming of Christ.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 97:25-26 reveals that the Lord will 'defend Zion and all the residue of my people'; the enemies of Zion 'shall be scattered and trampled under foot.' The imagery echoes Isaiah's dream-dissolution: human power arrayed against God's city proves substanceless.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Ariel, as 'God's altar-hearth,' connects to the temple as the center of covenant life. Just as the temple cannot be destroyed (though surrounded by enemies), the sealing powers and covenant ordinances available there form an unbreakable connection to God that no external enemy can sever.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 29 as a whole addresses Jerusalem's siege and deliverance, prefiguring Christ's ultimate vindication. Jesus, like Jerusalem surrounded by enemies, appeared defeated and crushed; yet His Resurrection proved that death itself was a dream from which He awakened. The nations that seemed to have triumphed—Rome and the religious establishment—found their victory hollow and evanescent. Christ's deliverance of His people mirrors Ariel's deliverance: what appeared certain proved illusory.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that the numerical or visible strength of opposition to God's covenant people is ultimately irrelevant. We live in an age when the Church faces skepticism, legal opposition, and cultural headwinds. Yet Isaiah invites us to see these challenges through the lens of faith: they are real, but they are also like dreams—substantial only to those who do not see God's hand. Modern members facing persecution or doubt can find strength in the promise that what appears overwhelming to earthly sight dissolves before divine purpose. The test is whether we perceive with the eye of faith or remain caught in the dream of worldly power.

text_kjv: It shall even be as when an hungry man dreameth, and, behold, he eateth; but he awaketh, and his soul is empty: or as when a thirsty man dreameth, and, behold, he drinketh; but he awaketh, and, behold, he is faint, and his soul hath appetite: so shall the multitude of all the nations be, that fight against mount Zion.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah deepens the dream metaphor through one of Scripture's most psychologically acute similes. The dreaming man is not passively observing a phantasm; he is *engaging* with it. His mouth chews, his throat swallows—the sensations are real within the dream. Yet the moment of waking shatters the entire experience: the belly remains hollow, the throat parched, the appetite still burning. This is not a vision that fades gently; it is the violent severance between dream-experience and waking reality.

The parallel structure—hungry man eating / thirsty man drinking—creates perfect balance in the Hebrew, as the Covenant Rendering notes. The attacking nations, like these dreamers, will experience what seems like triumph. They will taste conquest, feel the satisfaction of taking the city, sense victory within their grasp. But the awakening will be catastrophic: the city remains unconquered, their armies destroyed, their goals utterly unfulfilled. The dream-conquest will prove as nourishing as dream-food.

Isaiah shifts from the generic "all nations" of verse 7 to explicitly naming "mount Zion" here—the spiritual center, the place of God's presence. This particularity matters: it is not just Jerusalem that cannot be taken, but specifically the mount where the temple stood, where God's name was invoked and His glory manifested. Against that sacred geography, all military might becomes dream-weight.

word_study.meaning: Hungry, famished; the term carries both physical hunger and the anxious desperation that accompanies it. The word's sound seems to contain the urgency it describes.
word_study.significance: Isaiah chose this term to emphasize not mere appetite but desperate, burning need. The dream-eater is not casually dreaming of food but is consumed by hunger—and awakens to find that desperation confirmed by empty reality.

word_study.meaning: To awaken, to rouse from sleep; the root suggests both the sudden break in sleep and the return to consciousness and awareness.
word_study.significance: The word marks the decisive moment when illusion ends. In biblical thought, awakening often signals judgment or clarity—moving from blindness to sight, confusion to understanding. Here it marks the shattering of false confidence.

word_study.meaning: Soul, self, life-force, appetite, desire. In this context, it refers to the seat of hunger and desire—the deep need that remains unsatisfied.
word_study.significance: The repeated phrase 'his soul is empty' and 'his soul hath appetite' underscores that the dream leaves the essential self untouched and unsatisfied. No surface satisfaction can fill the deep need. The nations' 'souls' will hunger still after their dream of conquest dissolves.

word_study.meaning: The mountain-stronghold of Jerusalem, identified with God's sanctuary and the seat of His throne. In prophetic usage, Zion became synonymous with the covenant people and God's redemptive purposes.
word_study.significance: By naming Zion specifically, Isaiah stakes the claim that it is not merely a city but a threshold of the divine—a place where God's purposes cannot be defeated because they are rooted in eternity, not in temporal military strength.

cross_references.connection: Jesus applies Isaiah's language of spiritual blindness to those who 'seeing see not, and hearing hear not'; the dream-awaking here parallels the moment when spiritual eyes are opened or remain closed.

Paul writes, 'Now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.' The dream-awaking imagery parallels the transition from mortal dimness to celestial clarity.

The psalmist uses similar imagery: 'How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment! they are utterly consumed with terrors. As a dream when one awaketh; so, O Lord, when thou awakest, thou shalt despise their image.'

Alma compares faith to a seed that grows; he also acknowledges that false beliefs are ultimately like dreams that leave no lasting satisfaction—'ye have discovered that ye cannot do all things of yourselves.'

The Lord assures His people that 'all things shall be done by common consent in the company of the saints'; the enemies of the Church, though they may seem to prevail temporarily, will find their victory as unfulfilling as the dream-eater's feast.

commentary.historical_context: The psychology embedded in Isaiah's simile reflects acute observation of sleep and dream experience as understood in the ancient Near East. Dreams held profound significance in Mesopotamian and Egyptian religious practice, often seen as vehicles of divine communication. Yet Isaiah deliberately inverts this: the dream here is not revelatory but delusional, satisfying yet empty. The vivid sensory detail—the taste of food, the coolness of water, the swallowing and chewing—suggests Isaiah's own experience of how compellingly real a dream feels until waking. Ancient peoples, lacking modern sleep science, understood dreams as encounters with other realms; Isaiah's genius lies in using that very immediacy to expose the unreality of human ambition when set against God's purposes. The dream-metaphor would have struck his audience with particular force because dreams were culturally freighted with significance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 17:45 records Nephi's declaration that the Lord has 'made the way' and 'leadeth away the righteous into precious lands'; enemies may dream of conquest, but that dream will not satisfy. Lehi's vision in 1 Nephi 8 (though not directly about warfare) uses the imagery of seeking and hunger to describe spiritual need; those who satisfy themselves with worldly treasures find themselves empty.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:24-25 reveals God's perspective on the attempts of His enemies: 'Cursed are all those that shall lift up the heel against mine anointed, saith the Lord, and cry they have conspired against him.' The 'conspiring' is ultimately like a dream—real in intention but powerless in effect.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Mount Zion centers on the temple as the dwelling place of God's name and presence. Just as the nations' dream of conquest cannot touch Zion itself, no power outside the covenant can compromise the sealing authority and ordinances performed in God's house. The temple stands as the historical and eternal vindication of this prophecy.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus' Gethsemane prayer (Matthew 26:39-44) echoes this imagery of desire and disappointment: the cup He prayed might pass was not passed; yet in His awakening to the Father's will, true satisfaction came. The disciples' dream of a Messiah who would restore the kingdom politically dissolved upon the crucifixion—only to awaken to the reality of resurrection and the kingdom spiritual. The nations that dream of a world without God's covenant people will similarly awaken to find their conquest empty and their victory reversed.
commentary.application: Isaiah's twin images of the hungry and thirsty dreamer speak directly to anyone whose hopes rest on worldly achievement or opposition to God's people. Political movements, ideologies, and institutions arrayed against the Church may seem to be advancing, may taste of temporary victory, but Isaiah promises they are dreams. When the ultimate awakening comes—when all are brought before God's judgment—these apparent triumphs will prove as empty as a feast consumed in sleep. For members of the Church, this verse becomes a call to patient faith: do not be afraid of how many oppose you or how powerful they appear. Their apparent strength is dream-weight. Trust in Mount Zion, in the sanctuary that God Himself sustains. Your hunger for truth will be satisfied; theirs, set only on temporal power, will be eternal disappointment.

text_kjv: Stay yourselves, and wonder; cry ye out, and cry: they are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink.

commentary.narrative:
The tone shifts abruptly. Isaiah moves from prophecy about the nations' destruction to direct address of Jerusalem's own people—and the address is cutting. The imperatives here are bitterly ironic: "Stay yourselves and wonder!" (Hitmahmahu u-tmahu) and "Cry out and cry!" (Shi'u sha'u) are not invitations to repentance but rather sardonic commands to continue in their self-deception. The Covenant Rendering captures this edge: "Stupify yourselves and be stunned! Blind yourselves and be blind!" The rhetorical effect is that of a parent telling a stubborn child, in exasperation, to go ahead and do the foolish thing—knowing the child will pay the price.

The drunkenness Isaiah describes is not literal intoxication. The people stagger spiritually—reeling in confusion, blindness, and poor judgment—yet not from wine or strong drink (shekhar). This spiritual stupor is far more dangerous than any physical drunkenness because it masquerades as sobriety and reason. They *think* they are clear-headed while actually lost in a divinely-imposed fog. This echoes Isaiah 28:7-8, where the priests and prophets are described as erring through wine, but here the roles reverse: the people are drunken without wine, which means their condition is self-inflicted, a willful turning away that has become a judgment.

The passage implies that Jerusalem has reached a point where further words will not penetrate. The people have closed their ears and God has closed their eyes (as v. 10 will make explicit). All that remains is to let them continue in their chosen blindness until the reality of judgment crashes down. It is judgment as abandonment: God allows them to have what they want—continued self-deception.

word_study.meaning: To be stupefied, astonished, bewildered; the reflexive form suggests 'go ahead and stupefy yourselves.' The root conveys both the state of shock and the deliberate blinding of oneself.
word_study.significance: The reflexive form is key: it casts responsibility for the stupor back on the people themselves. They are not victims of circumstance but active agents in their own blindness. This semantic choice makes the judgment more severe—it is a judgment that lets them pursue their own folly.

word_study.meaning: To be astonished, amazed, bewildered; in context, to be so confused as to lose all clarity of judgment.
word_study.significance: Wonder here is not awe before the divine but confusion and disorientation. Isaiah wants to emphasize not that these people will see something amazing, but that they will be lost in confusion.

word_study.meaning: Intoxicated, reeling, stupefied; the state in which judgment and perception are utterly compromised.
word_study.significance: The metaphor of spiritual drunkenness appears throughout Isaiah and the Prophets to describe those in whom God's Word produces no change—they are so caught in their own ways that even divine speech leaves them unmoved.

word_study.meaning: Strong drink, fermented beverage (distinct from wine); any intoxicating drink beyond wine, including beer and mead.
word_study.significance: By explicitly negating both wine (yayin) and strong drink (shechar), Isaiah emphasizes the totality of the negation: their condition stems from no external substance. They have done this to themselves and God has sealed it as judgment.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah previously condemned the priests and prophets who 'are out of the way through wine, and through strong drink are gone astray.' Now the entire people have fallen into this same spiritual stupor, suggesting judgment spreads from failed leadership to the community itself.

Paul quotes Isaiah: 'God hath given them the spirit of slumber, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear'; Isaiah's language of divine-imposed stupor becomes the Apostle's explanation for Israel's rejection of the Gospel.

Paul warns that some 'may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will.' The spiritual drunkenness Isaiah describes is one such snare—the person caught in it is unaware of their captivity.

King Benjamin's people, by contrast, cry out 'with one voice' to bind themselves to God's covenant; Isaiah's people cry out in confusion and stupor. The choice to listen or remain blind determines whether one's crying is a prayer or a sign of lostness.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, intoxication was understood through a physiological model lacking modern neuroscience: the spirit of drunkenness was believed to literally possess or cloud a person. Drunkenness itself often carried moral and religious stigma—drunken persons were seen as especially vulnerable to demonic influence or divine judgment. Yet Isaiah's innovation is to describe a drunkenness *without wine*, suggesting a spiritual or psychological condition that mimics intoxication without any material cause. This would have puzzled and unsettled his audience: how can someone be drunk without drinking? The answer—that they have so thoroughly chosen blindness that God has ratified it as judgment—struck at the heart of Jerusalem's false confidence. They were not simply mistaken; they were in a state of judicial stupor that they themselves had chosen and God had sealed.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 5:43-45 describes those who have 'wilfully rejected the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ' as being in a kind of spiritual stupor; King Noah's priests in Mosiah 11-12 exemplify this willful blindness despite abundant evidence to the contrary. The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows how leaders and people who refuse to hear the prophets fall into a confusion that leads ultimately to destruction.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:57 warns that in the last days, 'many shall be called, but few shall be chosen.' The un-chosen are those who, like Isaiah's stupefied people, close their ears and harden their hearts despite clear word from heaven. D&C 10:37 declares, 'And this shall be my voice unto thy people,' emphasizing that God's word is always available—the drunkenness is those who refuse to hear it.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where clarity of purpose and heavenly vision are meant to be renewed and strengthened. Those who spurn the temple, who do not engage in the ordinances and covenants offered there, are choosing a kind of spiritual drunkenness—clarity withheld. Conversely, faithful temple worship guards against the stupor Isaiah warns of.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus in His earthly ministry encountered this exact condition: "Then answered the Jews and said unto him, Say we not well that thou art a Samaritan, and hast a devil? Jesus answered, I have not a devil; but I honour my Father, and ye have dishonoured me" (John 8:48-49). The spiritual drunkenness Jesus faced—where His words, however clear, could not penetrate hardened hearts—is the same condition Isaiah predicts. Yet Jesus' response was one of patient clarity, not ironic sarcasm. The ultimate irony is that Jesus Himself would be rejected by those in this stupor, and His death, like the destruction of the nations in verse 7, would be misunderstood as defeat—until the Resurrection revealed it as the supreme triumph.
commentary.application: Isaiah's bitter sarcasm should wake modern readers from complacency. If we close our ears to the Spirit, if we refuse the counsel of prophets and apostles, if we harden our hearts against clear truth, we are choosing a kind of spiritual intoxication—and God may, in His justice, allow us to persist in that chosen blindness. The remedy is the opposite: actively seek to hear, remain soft to the Spirit, cultivate wonder at divine things rather than stupefaction. Ask yourself: Are there truths I have closed my ears to? Are there prophetic words I have dismissed? Are there promptings of the Spirit I have ignored? The drunkenness Isaiah warns of is not always obvious to the one experiencing it. The very nature of the condition is that it feels like clear-headedness to those caught in it. This is why continuous, humble, prayerful openness to correction is essential.

text_kjv: For the LORD hath poured out upon you the spirit of deep sleep, and hath closed your eyes: the prophets and your rulers, the seers hath he covered.

commentary.narrative:
Here Isaiah reveals the source of the stupor he just described: it is God Himself who has poured it out. The language is judicial and solemn. The Hebrew word "nasakh" (poured out) typically describes the outpouring of libations in sacrifice or the pouring out of God's wrath in judgment. God does not simply allow the people to remain blind; He actively imposes blindness as a judgment. The "spirit of deep sleep" (ruach tardemah) is the same stupor that fell on Adam before the creation of Eve (Genesis 2:21) and on Abraham before the covenant revelation (Genesis 15:12)—but here it is not preparatory for divine blessing but punitive.

What makes this verse devastating is not the judgment on the people broadly but the specific targeting of the leadership: the prophets and rulers, the seers—those whose entire responsibility was to see clearly and speak truly. These are the very people whose role was to pierce the darkness and guide others toward light. Instead, God has "covered" them (kisah—to cover, conceal, bury). The prophets cannot prophesy, the seers cannot see. This is judgment not merely on Jerusalem as a whole but on the very structures meant to preserve her connection to God. It is as if the city's immune system has been shut down.

The Covenant Rendering's distinction—"He has shut your eyes—the prophets; He has covered your heads—the seers"—clarifies that the judgment falls with particular weight on leadership. The 'eyes' of prophets and 'heads' of seers are their very means of functioning. To shut their eyes and cover their heads is to render them spiritually incapacitated. This explains why external judgment (the Assyrian siege) seems somehow merciful compared to this internal shutdown: at least the siege can be witnessed and resisted. This blindness is invisible, comprehensive, and cuts off the very means of discernment.

word_study.meaning: To pour, to pour out; used of pouring libations, pouring out water, and pouring out divine judgment or wrath. The root carries the sense of a liquid being poured in volume.
word_study.significance: The term emphasizes abundance and totality—God has not withheld or measured out the stupor in small doses but poured it out generously. The abundance of God's judgment matches the abundance of His mercy, suggesting the severity of the people's refusal to hear.

word_study.meaning: Tardemah specifically denotes a deep, heavy sleep—the kind that comes as a divine act. The term appears in Genesis 2:21 (Adam's sleep before Eve's creation) and Genesis 15:12 (Abraham's sleep during the covenant vision). Here it is judicial rather than preparatory.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes the profound theological resonance: the same word used for the sleep preparatory to covenant blessing now describes a sleep that prevents the people from entering into covenant renewal. The word carries the weight of God's direct action—this is not mere human drowsiness but divine imposition.

word_study.meaning: To shut, seal, or fasten the eyes closed. The verb atzam suggests not just closing but sealing shut, as if the eyes are locked.
word_study.significance: The physical action corresponds to spiritual reality: the eyes that should see revelation are now sealed. This is more than temporary blindness; it is the locking-down of the very faculty needed for spiritual perception.

word_study.meaning: To cover, to conceal, to bury, to hide from sight. Often used for covering something so it is no longer visible or accessible.
word_study.significance: The word suggests that the prophets and seers are not merely confused but actively hidden from the people—their heads covered, their capacity to lead obscured. It is as if they are buried while still alive, incapable of performing the function they were called to fill.

cross_references.connection: The same term 'deep sleep' (tardemah) falls on Adam before his covenant blessing and Eve's creation; here it falls as judgment, creating a reversal—the sleep that once preceded blessing now prevents it.

The same word describes the sleep God cast on Saul's camp, allowing David to escape; God's ability to impose sleep is used here for protection, there for judgment, showing the term's flexibility based on context and divine purpose.
Paul describes how those who 'knew God' but 'glorified him not as God' were given over to a 'reprobate mind'; Isaiah's covering of the seers parallels Paul's doctrine of judicial hardening.

Paul teaches that God Himself 'shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie'; the theological pattern of God imposing spiritual blindness as judgment for refusing truth appears consistently throughout Scripture.

Ammon tells Limhi of interpreters who have the 'spirit of revelation,' contrasting with those whose spiritual gifts are covered; the capacity to 'see' spiritual truth is presented as God's gift, and its withdrawal is judgment.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite theology, the prophetic office was not merely one role among many but the vital connector between heaven and earth. A prophet's 'blindness'—inability to receive revelation—was understood as catastrophic for the entire nation, not merely for the prophet personally. When Isaiah describes God closing the eyes of the seers and covering the heads of the prophets, his audience would have grasped the eschatological weight: this is not just a political crisis but a spiritual apocalypse. The covenant line itself has been severed. Later Jewish tradition would interpret the period before John the Baptist (roughly 400 years of 'silence' after Malachi) in exactly these terms—not that God had left, but that the prophetic voice had been covered, making restoration itself dependent on God's direct intervention. Isaiah's language here becomes, paradoxically, a framework for understanding how God Himself can withdraw the very means of knowing Him—and why such withdrawal is the gravest judgment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:24-26 describes how the Lord withheld revelation from the Nephites through corrupt leadership: 'And because of their pride and their wickedness, many of them were destroyed.' The pattern repeats: when spiritual leaders are covered in blindness, the people fall. Conversely, 3 Nephi 28:36-37 shows how the Three Nephites, because they sought 'that which is good,' were given power to see and to translate, contrasting sharply with those whose eyes are shut.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:4 reveals that without Joseph Smith's prophetic vision, the truths of the celestial kingdom would have remained sealed—'the heavens were opened upon us.' The Restoration itself is understood as God uncovering the prophetic eye after centuries of cover. D&C 21:4-5 emphasizes the necessity of heeding 'him whom I have appointed to lead you'—recognizing that losing prophetic leadership is losing the means of seeing God's path.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The sealing authority and power given in temples are the opposite of this 'covering' judgment. Where the prophets' heads are covered and their vision sealed, those who hold the priesthood keys have the eyes of their understanding enlightened (cf. Ephesians 1:18). The temple becomes the place where this covering is lifted—where the veil thins and vision is restored.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus in the wilderness was tempted by the devil to command stones to become bread (Matthew 4:3-4). Yet Jesus, though truly tested, never had His prophetic eye closed. In fact, John 1:18 declares, 'No man hath seen God at any time, the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.' Jesus is the one prophetic figure whose vision could never be covered because He is the Word Himself—the full revelation. The covering of the prophets in Isaiah 29 anticipates the desperate need for the final Prophet, the Messiah, who alone cannot be blind to God's purposes. In a paradoxical way, Jesus' crucifixion—which appeared to blind the disciples to His messianic identity—was followed by resurrection and the opening of their eyes. The covering of the seers in Isaiah is temporary; Christ's coming permanently restores vision.
commentary.application: This verse, sobering as it is, contains a hidden grace: it assumes that blindness is temporary and can be lifted. If God has imposed it, God can remove it. For modern members, it poses a searching question: Are we attentive to the voice of prophets and apostles, or have we allowed our own spiritual eyes to close? Pharisees in Jesus' day had access to the scriptures, the priesthood, the temple—yet their eyes were covered to the Messiah standing before them. The covering in verse 10 can happen to individuals as well as nations. Those who choose to ignore prophetic counsel, who treat warnings lightly, who harden their hearts to truths that challenge their comfort, are choosing the path toward covered eyes. Conversely, those who actively seek to hear the prophets, who make the effort to understand their teachings, who remain humble and willing to be corrected, are choosing uncovered eyes. The question is not whether blindness can happen to you—Isaiah shows it can—but whether you will actively resist it through faithful listening.

text_kjv: And the vision of all is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed, which men deliver to one that is learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I cannot; for it is sealed:

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah introduces one of Scripture's most powerful metaphors for spiritual blindness: the sealed scroll. The "vision of all"—the totality of God's revelation, the entire spiritual heritage available to Jerusalem—has become inaccessible, not because it has been destroyed but because it is sealed. The scroll sits in the hands of a learned man (one who knows sefarim, books), yet the very literacy that should enable him to read has become useless. He has the capability but not the access.

The image is psychologically brilliant. The man does not refuse to read; he cannot. The seal blocks him. His learning is irrelevant to his fundamental problem. This explains why straightforward exhortations to repent no longer penetrate—the people have reached a state where rational argument, appeals to history, even plain moral reasoning cannot touch them. They have crossed a threshold from temporary confusion into structural inability. The seal is not something they can break; it requires God's hand to open.

This verse lays the groundwork for verses 11-12 to function as a pair: two different people, two different excuses, one outcome. Whether the obstacle is external (sealed) or internal (illiteracy), the result is the same—the word of God goes unread. The genius of pairing them is that it covers all possible reasons for unreadiness. No one can claim 'If only I had the ability' (v. 12 shows even illiterates are addressed) or 'If only I had access' (v. 11 shows access without understanding is useless). There is no escape clause. Every excuse is preempted.

word_study.meaning: Vision, sight, something seen or perceived. Unlike chazon (which emphasizes prophetic content), chazut emphasizes the act of seeing itself—perception, awareness.
word_study.significance: The term stresses not just the words but the capacity to perceive them. The vision of all—God's entire revelation to Israel—is rendered perceptually inaccessible. It is as if a blindfold has been placed not just on eyes but on the faculty of understanding.

word_study.transliteration: chatom (from chatam, to seal, to shut, to finish)
word_study.meaning: Sealed, closed with a seal; often used of documents sealed with wax or clay to prevent tampering. In figurative usage, it means to shut, to mark as closed or final.
word_study.significance: The seal is official and authoritative—not a temporary obstacle but a deliberate, finalized closure. In the ancient world, a sealed document was legally protected and could not be opened by just anyone. The seal here suggests God's deliberate, lawful judgment.

word_study.term_original: יוֹדֵעַ הַסֵּפֶר (yodea sefer, literally "one who knows the scroll")
word_study.meaning: Learned, literate, skilled in reading; one educated in texts and books. The phrase emphasizes competence and training.
word_study.significance: Isaiah's point is not that the learned man lacks skill but that skill is irrelevant when the fundamental barrier is structural. Education, intelligence, and ability cannot circumvent God's judgment once it has fallen. This was a radical and humbling claim: learning has its limits.

word_study.meaning: I am not able, I cannot; expressing inability, not refusal. The verb conveys powerlessness.
word_study.significance: The man does not say 'I refuse' but 'I cannot.' The seal has rendered him unable, despite his desire and his ability. This underscores that the barrier is not moral failure but structural judgment.

cross_references.connection: Daniel is told, 'Many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased. But thou, O Daniel, shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end.' The sealed scroll becomes an apocalyptic symbol of truth hidden until God's appointed time.

John weeps because 'no man in heaven, nor in earth, neither under the earth, was able to open the book'; Jesus alone is worthy to open it. This passage echoes Isaiah's sealed scroll—truth locked until the Lamb appears.

Jesus explains why He speaks in parables: 'Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand...For this people's heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing.' The sealing is complete—eyes shut, ears closed.

Amulek is told, 'It is given unto many to know the mysteries of God; nevertheless they are laid under a strict command that they shall not impart only according to the portion of his word which he doth grant unto the children of men.' Sacred knowledge is sealed to those unprepared to receive it.

The Lord tells Oliver Cowdery, 'Put your trust in that Spirit which leadeth to do good—yea, to do justly, to walk humbly, to judge righteously.' The seal is opened only through the Spirit, not through intellectual effort alone.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern practice, important documents—contracts, wills, prophecies, royal decrees—were sealed with clay seals or wax bearing the impression of a signet ring. Only the person with proper authority (the king, the high priest) could break the seal. A sealed document was legally binding and legally protected. For Isaiah's audience, the image would have been immediately understood: the vision of God is no longer 'open-access' revelation but restricted, legally sealed, inaccessible without the proper authority. This may also reflect ancient scribal practice: sacred texts were sometimes deliberately obscured through use of symbolic language or written seals to protect them from profane understanding. Isaiah turns this practice into a metaphor for judgment—God has sealed His word against those who refused to hear when it was clearly spoken.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 13:34-35 describes how the plain and precious parts of the Bible were removed, 'taken away from the gospel of the Lamb,' leaving the testimony sealed from many. The Restoration, through Joseph Smith, broke the seal by recovering lost truths. The Book of Mormon itself functions as an 'unsealing' of truths hidden since ancient times.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 124:33-34 speaks of the sealing authority: 'I give unto you a promise that you shall receive and have fulness of the priesthood of the Son of God...who shall seal you up unto eternal life.' The sealing in Isaiah is a judgment; the sealing in D&C is a blessing. Only God can work both the judgment and the redemption from that judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where sealed ordinances are performed—the endowment and other covenants open what has been sealed. Joseph Smith taught that 'whatever God requires is right, no matter what it is, although we may not see the reason thereof till long after the events transpire.' The sealed scroll in Isaiah becomes, through Restoration understanding, the pattern for temple knowledge—truth sealed to the unprepared but revealed to the worthy.

commentary.christological_typology: Revelation 5:1-9 presents the sealed scroll in the context of the Apocalypse: a scroll sealed with seven seals that only the Lamb can open. Jesus is the breaking of every seal that separates humanity from God. Isaiah's sealed vision can only be unsealed by Christ's coming. When the risen Jesus appeared to the disciples on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:32), He "opened to them the scriptures"—He unsealed what had been sealed. The sealed scroll awaits its ultimate unsealer.
commentary.application: Isaiah's image of the sealed scroll should humble modern readers. It reveals that there is a level of spiritual judgment where human effort, intelligence, and even sincere desire cannot penetrate. If God has sealed something against you—closed the door to understanding—your education and capability cannot force it open. This calls for profound humility. It suggests that if we find ourselves unable to understand spiritual truths that others seem to grasp, or unable to feel the Spirit's witness despite our efforts, the answer is not to push harder or reason more persuasively, but to examine whether we have hardened our hearts against something God has been trying to show us. Conversely, it suggests that access to sealed knowledge is a gift. When the Spirit opens your understanding, when a passage of scripture suddenly illuminates your mind, when you receive personal revelation—these are unsealing moments. Treat them as sacred. Do not take for granted the ability to hear and understand God's voice. Make sure you are not sealing yourself through willful disobedience or stubborn pride.

text_kjv: And the book is delivered to him that is not learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I am not learned.

commentary.narrative:
The final verse of Isaiah's sealed-book passage completes the entrapment. If verse 11 presented the problem of access (the scroll is sealed), verse 12 presents the problem of ability (the reader is illiterate). Together they form a comprehensive picture of inaccessibility: no matter what you have or what you lack, the word of God cannot get through.

The second person—the one who "is not learned" (the one who does not know sefarim)—stands in deliberate contrast to the first. One has knowledge but no access; the other has access but no knowledge. Each makes the same discovery: the word cannot be read. Isaiah's construction is devastatingly logical. He has not left a single escape route. There is no argument a Jerusalem audience could make—'If only I had the ability' or 'If only someone would bring it to me'—that would answer his charge. Both have been preempted.

The phrase "I am not learned" (lo yada'ti sefer, literally 'I have not known a scroll') is humble and honest. The man does not make excuses or claim false knowledge; he simply states his limitation. Yet his honesty does not change the outcome: the scroll remains unread. Isaiah's point is that the fundamental barrier to receiving God's word in Jerusalem is neither external (access) nor internal (ability) but spiritual (unwillingness combined with God's judgment). The people have chosen blindness, and God has sealed it. No amount of education or access will undo it unless there is first a turning of heart.

word_study.meaning: Does not know, has not learned, is illiterate; literally 'has not known a scroll/book.' The verb yada carries connotations of both knowing through experience and knowing through study.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes lack of formal education and literacy. In an ancient context where literacy was limited and valued, not knowing how to read was not merely a personal shortcoming but a barrier to full participation in religious and civic life.

word_study.transliteration: nittan (natan, to give, to deliver, to hand over)
word_study.meaning: Given, delivered, handed over; in this context, placed in someone's possession or responsibility.
word_study.significance: The passive voice—'is delivered to him'—emphasizes that the scroll comes as a gift. The man does not seek it; it is brought to him. Yet even receiving it offers no advantage because he cannot read it.

cross_references.connection: Jesus enters the synagogue and is given the scroll of Isaiah to read; He reads and understands with perfect clarity, standing in contrast to those in Jerusalem whose scroll remains sealed. The ability to read and understand Scripture becomes, in Jesus' hands, the power to reveal its fulfillment.

Paul writes that 'the veil is upon their hearts' when the scriptures are read, until 'Christ came' and the veil was taken away. The sealed, unreadable scroll of Isaiah becomes the pattern for all resistance to God's word until Christ opens it.

Paul explains that 'the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them'; the illiteracy Isaiah describes is not merely educational but spiritual—the unregenerate mind cannot read the things of God.
